By the KING.

A PROCLAMATION,

For diffblving this present Parliament, and declaring the Calling of another.

GEORGE II.

WHEREAS We have thought fit, by and with the Advice of Our Privy Council, to dissolvc this present Parliament, which now (lands prorogued to Tuesday the Seventeenth day of next: We do,

for that End, publish this Our Royal Proclamation; and do hereby dissolve the said Parliament accordingly; and the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and the Commissioners for Shires and Burghs, of the House of Commons, are discharged from their Meeting and Attendance on Tuesday the said Seventeenth day of August next. And We being desirous and resolved, as soon as may be, to meet Our People, and to have their Advice in Parliament, do hereby make known to all Our loving Subjects Our Royal Will and Pleasure to call a new Parliament: And do hereby further declare, That, with the Advice

of Our Privy Council, We have given Order that Our Chancellor of that Part of Our United Kingdom called Great Britain, and Our Chancellor of , do respectively, upon Notice thereof, forthwith issue out Writs, in due Form, and according to Law, for calling a new Parliament. And We do hereby also, by this Our Royal Proclamation under Our Great Seal of Our United Kingdom, require Writs forthwith to be issued accordingly by Our laid Chancellors respectively, for causing the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, who are to serve in Our said Parliament, to be duly returned to, and give their Attendance in. Our said Parliament; which Writs are to be returnable on Tuesday the Thirty-first day of August next.

Given at Our Court at , the Twenty-ninth

Day of June One thousand Eight hundred and Two, in the Forty-second Year of Our Reign.

GOD save the King.

TH E King’s Most Excellent Majesty having, by His Royal Proclamation (hereunto annexed) dated the 29th day of June 1802, dissolved the last Parliament, and by His Writ of Summons, issued under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearingTefte at on Wednesday

the 30th day of the lame Month, and also by His Writ of Summons under the Great Seal of ,bearing

Teste at Dublin on Friday the 2d day of July following, and returnable on this Day, called a new Parliament, several Members appeared: And His Majesty having been pleased, by and with the Advice of His Privy Council, by an Order of Council, dated the 16th day of this Instant August, to declare that the said Parliament should be this day prorogued by Writ, the said Members went directly, without going into the House of Commons, or expecting any Message from the Lords, up to the door of the House of Peers; and, after a short stay there, the Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod opening the Door, they, with the Clerk Assistant, went up to the Bar of the House: And they being there, the Lord Chancellor {landing up uncovered, declared that there was a Writ issued under the Great Seal for proroguing the Parliament.

Which Writ lying on the Table, his Lordship di-tetted the Clerk to read: And the fame was read accordingly, for proroguing the Parliament until Tuesday the 5th day of October next ensuing; as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

GEORGEthe Third, by the Grace of God, of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland King, Defender of the Faith. To Our well-beloved and faithful the Prelates, Nobles, and Peers of Our said United Kingdom of Great Britain and , and to

Our beloved and faithful the Knights, Citizens, and Burgesses, and Commissioners for Shires, and Burghs of Our said United Kingdom, called and chosen to Our Parliament, to be begun and held at Our City of minster, on the Thirty-first day of this Instant Month of August, and to every of you. Greeting. Whereas

We, for certain arduous and urgent Affairs, concerning Us, the State and Defence of Our said United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, and the Church; did ordain the said Parliament to be held at the Day and Place aforesaid; and did command you, by Our several Writs, to be present at the City and Day aforesaid, to treat, consent, and conclude about those Things which in Our said Parliament then and there should be proposed and treated of: Nevertheless for certain causes and Considerations, Us, at this time especially moving. We have thought fit that Our said Parliament be prorogued unto 'Tuesday the Fifth day of October next ensuing; so that neither you, nor any of you, should be held or obliged to appear on the said Thirty-first day of Auglijl, at the aforesaid City: We also will that you, and every of you, be wholly discharged, as to Us, therefrom; commanding, and, by the Tenor of these Presents, strictly requiring you, and every of you, and all others whom this may concern, That you, and every of you, do personally appear, and be present, on the said Fifth day of October, at Our said City of Westminster, to treat, do, att, and conclude, upon those Things, which, in Our said Parliament, by the Common Council of Our laid United Kingdom (by God’s Allift-ance) shall happen to be ordained. Witness Ourself, at Westminster, the Sixteenth day of , in the

Forty-second Year of Our Reign;

By the KING Himself.

Signed with His own Hand;

My Lords and Gentlemen,

Wc have it in command from His Majesty to let you know, That as soon as the Members of both Houses shall be sworn, the causes of His Majesty’s calling this Parliament will be declared to you; and it being necessary a Speaker of the House of Commons should be first chosen, it is His Majesty’s Pleasure, that you, Gentlemen of the House of Commons, repair to the place where you are to fit; and there proceed to the choice uf some proper Person to be your Speaker; and that you present such Person, whom you shall lo choose, here, Tommorrow at twelve o’clock, for I Jis Majesty’s Royal Approbation.

Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of the United Kingdom* do make their election by this day three weeks for which of the places they will serve, provided there be no question upon the Return for that place; and, if any thing shall come in question touching the Return or Election of any Member, he is to withdraw during the time the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns, do withdraw till their Returns are determined.

Resolved, That no Peer of this Realm, except such Peers of that part of the United Kingdom called Ireland as shall, for the time being, be actually elected, and shall not have declined to serve for any County, City, or Borough, of Great Britain, hath any right to give his vote in the election Of any Member to serve in Parliament.

Resolved, That it is a high infringement of the Liberties and Privileges of the Commons of the United Kingdom, for any Lord of Parliament, or other Peer or Prelate, not being a Peer of Ireland at the time elected, and not having declined to lerve for any County, City, or Borough of Great Britain, to concern himself in the election of Members to serve for the Commons in Parliament, except only any Peer of Ireland at such elections in Great Britain respectively, where such Peer shall appear as a candidate, or by himself or any others be proposed to be elected; or for any Lord-lieutenant, or Governor of any County, to avail himself of any authority derived from his commilhon, to influence the election of any Member to serve for the Commons in Parliament.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath procured himself to be elected or returned a Member of this House, or endeavoured so to be, by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such person.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath been tampering with any witness, in respect of his evidence to be given to this House, or any Committee thereof, or di-fectly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person from appearing, or giving evidence, the lame is declared to be a High Crime and Misdemeanor * and this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such offender.

Resolved, That, if it shall appear that any person hath given fall'e evidence, in any case, before this House, or any Committee thereof, this House will proceed with the utmost severity against such offender.

Resolved, That, in all cases of controverted elections for Counties in England and Wales, the petitioners do, by themselves or by their agents, within a convenient time, to be appointed by the House, deliver to the fitting Members, or their agents. Lists of the persons intended by the petitioners to be objected to, who voted for the fitting Members; giving, in the said Lifts, the several heads of objection, and distinguishing the fame against the names of the voters excepted to; and that the fitting Members do, by themselves, or by their agents, within the same time, deliver the like Lifts on their part to the petitioners or their agents.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, take into his custody any Stranger, or Strangers, that he shall see, or be informed of to be, in the House, or Gallery, while the House, or any Committee of the whole House* is fitting; and that no person, so taken into custody, be discharged out of custody without the special order of the House.

Ordered, That the back door of the Speaker’s Chamber be locked up every Morning at the fitting of the House, and the key delivered to the Clerk, to be locked up by him; and that he do not presume to deliver the same to any person whatsoever without order of the House; and that the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care to clear the Speaker’s Chamber every day before the door is locked up.

Ordered, That no Member of this House do presume to bring any Stranger, or Strangers, into the House, or Gallery thereof, while the House is fitting.

Ordered, That the Constables and other officers of Middlesex and Westminster, do take care, that, from eleven of

the clock in the Morning till one in the Afternoon, and from four till fix in the Afternoon, during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets between Temple Bar and Westminster Hall shall be kept free and open; and that no obstructions be made by cars, drays, carts* or otherwise, to hinder the pafl'age of the Members to and from this House; and that the Serjeant at Anns attending this House do give notice of this order to the officers aforesaid.

Ordered, That the Constables in waiting do take care that there be no gaming, or other disorders, in Westminster Hall, or the passages leading to the House, during the fitting of Parliament; and that there be no annoyance by Chairmen, footmen, or otherwise, therein or thereabouts.

Ordered, That the said Orders be lent to the High Bailiff of Westminster -, and that he do lee the fame put in

execution.

Ordered, That no Footman be permitted to be within the lobby of the House, or upon the flairs leading thereto.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take care that there be no gaming, or other tliforders, in the room appointed for the Footmen attending the Members of this House to wait in.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do take into his custody such Footmen as shall presume to d fobey the Orders of the House; and that no such Footmen be discharged out of custody but by the special Order of the House.

Ordered, That to prevent the intercepting or losing of Letters directed to Members of this House, the person appointed to bring Letters from the General Poll Office to this House, or fume other person, to be appointed by the Postmaster General, do, lor the future, every day during the Session of Parliament, Sundays excepted, constantly attend from ten of the clock in the Morning till one in the Afternoon, and for two hours at the lead immediately after the riling of the House; and also from five of the clock in the Afternoon till leven, at the place appointed for the delivery of the said Letters, and take care, during his stay there, to deliver the lame to the several Members to whom they shall be directed, or to their known servant or servants, or others bringing notes under the hands of the Members fending for the lame.

Ordered, That the said officer do, upon his going away, lock up such Letters as shall remain undelivered, and that no Letter be delivered but within the hours aforesaid.

Ordered, That the said Orders be lent to the Postmaster General.

Ordered, That when any Letter or Packet, directed to this House, shall come to Mr. Speaker, he do open the fame; and acquaint the Ilouie, at their next fitting, with the contents thereof, if proper to be communicated to this House.

Ordered, That the Serjeant at Arms attending this House do, from time to time, when the House is going to Prayers, give notice thereof to all Committees; and that ail proceedings of Committees in a Morning, alter such notice, be declared to be null and void.

Ordered, That the Votes of this House be printed, being first peruled by Mr. Speaker; and that he do appoint the printing thereof; and that no person, but lueli as he shall appoint, do presume to print the lame.

and the commissions, pretended to be given to the said persons severally, were also illegal, informal, and effejitially defective; and on these grounds the votes of the said commissioners or delegates were objected to at the said election, but the Returning Officer nevertheless thought proper to return the said John Spalding as duly elected; and that the meetings of the respective councils or magistrates of the Burghs of Wigton and Whithorn, at which, in terms of the adb of Parliament regulating the elections of commissioners or delegates in Scotland, days were pretended to be fixed for electing commissioners or delegates for the said respective Burghs, were not attended by legal quorums, so as to render their acts legal and valid; that sundry members attending such meetings were legally disqualified from attending the fame} and all acts done at such meetings, and afterwards in consequence thereof, were illegal and void; and that, when the commissioners or delegates for the said Btirghs of Wigton and Whithorn were elected, the magistrates and council and town clerks of these Burghs were not duly qualified according to law; and that the Petitioner had the vote of the delegate for Stranraer, which was the only legal vote, to represent the said district of Burghs, or at least that he was entitled to be returned as duly elected by the calling vote of the said delegate for Stranraer: The Petitioner therefore prays, That the House will take the premises into their consideration, and declare him to be duly elected, or grant him such relief therein as may seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into consideration upon Tuesday the'25th day of January next, at three of the clock in the Afternoon.

Ordered, That Mr. Speaker do issue his warrant, or warrants, for such persons, papers, and records, as shall be thought necessary by the several parties, on the hearing of the matter of the said Petition.

said election; whereby, 'as the Petitioner conceives, the Petitioner and the said Sir John Borlafe Warren were duly elected the members to serve in Parliament for the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham; and that it was the duty of John Allen, who was one of the Sheriffs of the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, and who presided at the said election, to have returned the said Sir John Borlafe Warren and the Petitioner as duly elected; but, in violation of such duty, and for the express purpose of giving time to procure a third candidate, so that the free and unbiaffed choice of a great majority of the electors of Nottingham might be disappointed by means of tumult,- riot, intimidation, and violence, the said John Allen did, of his own authority, and by his own act, unnecessarily, vexatiously, and illegally, open a poll, and frequently and repeatedly urged the electors to name another candidate; and that he repeatedly declared, that if they did not pro-pole some other candidate, he mud close the poll; and that, although no other candidate appeared, and although he was repeatedly called upon by the voters in the interest of Sir John Borlafe Warren and the Petitioner, to declare Sir John Borlafe Warren and the Petitioner to be duly elected, the said Sheriff, contrary to the duties of his office, neglected so to do; and that, after a considerable time had elapsed, during which the electors had polled for no other persons but the Petitioner and the said Sir John Borlafe Warren, some person or persons intimated, that Joseph Birch, Esquire (a merchant resident at Hazle Hall, in the County of Lancaster, and at that time, and for some days afterwards, attending as a candidate to represent Liverpool in Parliament, at the election then depending) would come forward as a candidate; and that three voters only having polled for the said Joseph Birch, and forty-four for the Petitioner and the said Sir John Borlafe Warren, the said Sheriff adjourned the poll to the subsequent day, without any agent or other person, authorized by the said Joseph Birch or any elector, having demanded a continuance of the poll; and that on the subsequent day, and during the remainder of the poll, a seene of riot, confusion, tumult, and violence, utterly incompatible with the freedom of election, was continued, on the part of the electors and others in the interest of the said Joseph Birch; and that the top of the booth was, during all the time of polling, regularly occupied by persons who pointed out to the surrounding mob those persons who polled for the Petitioner, and that several of such persons were assaulted and seized by the mob, their cloaths torn, their persons beat and bruised, and other acts of outrage and violence were committed on them; and that the houses of gentlemen who elpoufed the interest of the Petitioner were attacked, and that every act of tumult and disorder, which could intimidate those voters who were in the interest of the Petitioner from exercising their firanchife in his favour, was practised; and that theft acts were attended with the desired effect; that five or six hundred voters at least were thereby prevented from voting for the Petitioner, a number much more than sufficient, with those also actually polled for the Petitioner, to have given the Petitioner a large majority upon the poll; and that the Petitioner himself, who has represented the town of Nottingham in four successive Parliaments, was repeatedly and violently attacked by the mob, and his life thereby exposed to imminent danger; and, for fear of a continuance of the fame, or greater violence, the Petitioner was under the necessity of withdrawing himself from the place of the election on the evening of the third day of the poll; and that the Mayor, John Davison, Esquire, as well as John Allen the Sheriff, attended on the huttings daily, and that Thomas Oldknow and Joseph Oldknow, Aldermen of the said town of Nottingham, who by virtue of their offices were magis. trates of the fame, also frequently attended the hustings; that they were all repeatedly applied to, to preserve the peace of the place and the freedom of election, and in.particular to remove the persons from the top of the poll booth, who, by the means before-mentioned, exposed the persons and lives of the voters who polled for the Petitioned to danger, and deterred many of the electors in the interest of the Petitioner from giving their suffrages; but that the said Magistrates took no effectual steps to remove such persons, or to prevent any of the other violent or illegal acts which

and that John Allen the Sheriff, who had served that office in the year 1796, and had been one of the Returning Officers at the election in that year, was on the approach of the late dif-solution of Parliament again placed in the situation of Sheriff; and that his former conduct and public declarations pointed him out as a proper person to promote such measures as were planned and concerted for preventing a free election for the said Town, and as the Petitioner has Hated, and has such just reason to complain of; and that, in violation, of his duty, the said John Allen was instrumental in preventing many electors from coming to the poll who would have voted for the Petitioner; and that he promoted the outrages of the mob in various ways, by encouraging those who committed them, and inviting or permitting many of the mob who were rioting on the outside to enter and fit in the bell places in the booth; and that promises of reward by treating were publicly, at the time and place of polling, in the presence and hearing both of the Sheriff and the Mayor, made to such persons as would vote for the said Joseph Birch; and that many of the electors who did so vote were publicly rewarded in such manner in the presence also of the Sheriff and Mayor, at the time and place aforesaid, without any measures being taken to prevent the lame by them or either of them, whilst, on the other hand, they permitted the Petitioner and the electors in his interest to be grossly insulted, reviled, intimidated, and attacked, with impunity; and that many persons who had no right to vote were admitted to poll for the said Joseph Birch; and that the said Joseph Birch did, by himself, his agents, and friends, corrupt the electors by various modes of bribery, treating, and other corrupt practices, by which means (and by the measures of intimidation and terror already Hated) he obtained a majority of votes upon the poll: And therefore praying the House will take the Petitioner’s case into their consideration, and grant to the Petitioner such relief, and to take such other measures in the premises, as to the House shall seem meet.

Several Petitions, complaining of undue elections and returns, being offered to be presented to the House, the fame were delivered in at the Table.

And several of the said Petitions appearing to relate to the elections and returns of places, concerning which the House had received Petitions on a former day, the lame were read, as followeth; viz.

A Petition of certain electors of the Town and County Nottingham of the Town of Nottingham, who voted for Daniel Parker Coke, Esquire, at the late election for the said Town and Petition of* County of the Town of Nottingham, and whose names Ele&w*. are thereunto subscribed, was read; setting forth. That in pursuance of a Writ directed to the Sheriff' of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham for an election of two members to serve in this present Parliament for that place, the Proclamation for l'uch election was regularly made* that the day, hour, and place were thereby fixed for such election, which was appointed to commence at the Exchange Hall, on Tuesday, the 6th day of July 1S02, at nine o’clock in the morning; that the electors, pui-suant to-such notice, assembled, and the election accord^ ingly commenced at the place, and on the day and hour which had been so fixed, when Sir John Baronet, and Daniel Parker Coke, Esquire, were the only Candidates nominated in the presence of the electors then and there affetnbled; and that no poll was demanded, and that no other candidate was proposed until near an hour after the different forms observed at the said election had been gone through; and the said Sir John Borlafe and Daniel Parker Coke had been nominated, and therefore the Petitioners conceive that the said Sir John Borlafe Warren and Daniel Parker Coke were duly elected, and ought to have been returned by the Sheriff as members to serve in Parliament for the Town arid County of the Town of Nottingham; and that the Petitioners are strongly at-

tached to the interest of the said Daniel Parker Coke, by U'hom they had been represented in four successive Parliaments; that they had observed his conduct as their repre-fentative with the mod peculiar satisfaction and approbation; and that his attention to the local interests of their populous manufacturing town had been uniformly marked by a mod anxious desire to promote, support, and conduct in Parliament whatever was for the benefit of the place; that his zeal and integrity in carrying the measures proposed into effect, were not more conspicuous than his judgment and diferimination in fclefting what was mod for their advantage; and that his conduct, in all matters of national concern, was marked by a steady and contci-entious adherence to what he considered for the public good, neither deviating into faction on the oiie hand, nor on the other into a submissive support of every measure of Administration; and that his tried integrity and found judgment, contemplated by the Petitioners with the greatest satisfaction for a period of twenty-two years, had attached them to his interest so firmly, that nothing but the risk of absolute destruction, the loss of life, or the ruin of their property, could have withheld them from exercising their franchises in his favour; and that it was the duty of John Allen, the Sheriff, as Returning Officer, to have so declared, and to have returned the said Sir John Borlafe Warren and Daniel Parker Coke, Esquire, duly elected; but in violation of such duty, and for the express purpose of giving time to procure a third candidate, so that the free and unbiaffed choice of a great majority of the electors might be dilappointed and frutlrated by means of tumult, riot, intimidation, and violence, the said John Allen did, of his own authority, and by his own aft, unne-ceffarily, vexatioufiy, and illegally, open a poll, and frequently urged the electors to name another candidate, and repeatedly declared, that if they did not propose some other candidate, he should be obliged to close the poll j and that, although no other candidate appeared, or was proposed, and although the said Sheriff was repeatedly called upon by the Petitioners, and by other of the elec* tors in the interest of the said Sir John Borlafe Warren and the said Daniel Parker Coke, to declare the said Sir John Borlafe Warren and the said Daniel Parker Coke to be duly elected, the said Sheriff^ contrary to the duties of his office, neglected so to do; a'nd that, as the said Sheriff had taken upon himself, of his own authority, to open a poll, as is

A Petition of certain electors of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, vthofe names are thereunto subscribed, was likewise read;' setting forth, That the Petitioners, in consequence of notice given by the Returning ’ Officer, according to law, of the time and place of election, were present at the Exchange Hall, on Tuesday, the 6th day of July 1802,.. at the commencement of the last election of two members to serve in Parliament for the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, when Sir John Borlafe Warren, Baronet, and Darnel Parker Coke, Esquire, were respectively proposed to represent the said Town in Parliament; and that, at the time of their nomination,

to have been concluded, was followed by the most daring acts of disorder, outrage, tumult, and violence, totally de-structive of the freedom of election, if any election could still have been legally proceeded in after such conduct and practices of the Returning Officer presidingatit; and that, at the conclusion of a poll so commenced and continued for several days, through such a course of tumult and violence, the Sheriff declared the said 1'joseph Birch, together with Sir John Borlafe Warren, duly elected to serve in this present Parliament for the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, and hath accordingly returned the said Joseph Birch as one. of the members so duly elected; and that the Petitioners having given their suffrages at the nomination, and when no third candidate appeared, did not tender their votes at the poll, considering the whole proceeding to be illegal, and that the election was completely concluded without any poll, and before it began; and that the Petitioners were strongly attached to the interest of the said Daniel Parker Coke, by whom they had been represented in four successive Parliaments; that they had observed his conduct, as their representative, with the most peculiar satisfaction and approbation; and that his attention to the local interest of their populous manufacturing Town had been uniformly marked by a most anxious desire to promote, support, and conduct in Parliament, whatever was for the benefit of the place; and that his zeal and industry in carrying the measures proposed into effect were not more conspicuous than his judgment and diferimination in selecting what was most for their advantage; and that his conduct in all matters of national concern was marked by a steady and conscientious adherence to what he considered to be for the public good, neither deviating into faction on the one hand, nor on the other into a submissive support of every measure of Administration; and that his tried integrity and found judgment, contemplated by the Petitioners with the greatest satisfaction for a period of twenty-two years, had firmly attached them to his interest; and that, by the proceeding of the Sheriff, they have been deprived of their lawful representative, the said Daniel Parker Coke, and that the said Joseph Birch his been unlawfully returned in his place:

Baronet, to be returned as persons duly elected; and that the said Marquis did, in presence of good and sufficient witnesses, so express himself before the poll as to announce a pre-determined resolution existing in his mind to render his illegal interference effectual, by means of bribery and corruption; and that the said interference of the said Marquis, to the great injury of the Petitioners, did essen-tially and materially contribute to produce that temporary success, and that return of the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert Lawley, Baronet, against which the Petitioners now pray; and that, in consequence of the said illegal interference of the said Marquis, a Baron and a Peer of Parliament and of the Realm, of his own unlawful and corrupt practices, and co-operating therewith, the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert Lawley, Baronet, obtained a colourable majority of votes on the poll, and were returned to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, in prejudice to the Petitioners, who are not duly represented; and that public and sufficient notice of the bribery and treating committed and done, and of the ineligibility of the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert Lawley, Baronet, to receive votes at the said election, and that votes given to them the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert Lawley, Baronet, would be thrown away, was given to the Eledors of the said Borough, but that, notwithstanding such notice, sundry of the Eledors of the said Borough did afterwards deliberately, and with foreknowledge of the bribery and treating committed by the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert L, Baronet, and others, persist in tendering and in giving their votes to the said Edward Wilbraharn Bootle, Esquire, and Sir Robert,

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury in . Ireland, be authorized to advance any Sums, not exceeding in the whole the Sum of Forty thousand Pounds, for defraying the expence of filling up vacancies in the Militia t)f Ireland; and that such Sums be repaid out of such Monies as shall be raised by the several Counties, and Counties of Cities and Towns respectively, for that purpose.

The said Resolution being read a second time, was, upon ‘ the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Ordered, That it be an Inllruftion to the Gentlemen, who are appointed to prepare, and bring in a Bill, for the more speedy and effectual Enrolment of the Militia of Ireland, that they do make provision in the said Bill, pursuant to the said Resolution.

That the Petitioner and the Honourable petfdoii of* Lord Spencer Chichester were Candidates at the last Election Mr. Wiiion. of a Member to serve in Parliament for the County of the Town of Carrichfergus, which election was had on Saturday, the 24th day of July 1802; and that at the said election Thomas Kirk and Barry Martin, Esquires, Sheriffs of the County of the Town of Carrickfergus aforesaid, acted corruptly', partially', and unfairly in execution of their office as Returning Officers; and that, during the poll, many persons who were not Freeholders of the County of the Town of Carrickfergus, or Freemen thereof, or otherwise legally qualified to vote at said election, were permitted by the Sheriffs to poll for the said Lord Spencer and

Were severally presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That an Act having passed in the 4ad year of the reign of His present Majesty, wherein certain Duties are charged on the Tonnage of Ships and Vessels entering outwards or inwards (except in ballalt) in any Port of Great Britain to or from Foreign Parts, and also certain Duties on Oil and Skins, the produce of the British Fisheries, the Petitioners humbly beg leave to Hate to the House, that the said Duties are extremely oppreffive on them and all other persons who are engaged in British Shipping; and they represent, with the deepest regret, that British Shipping, from many causes independent of the before-mentioned Duties, Hill labour under great depression, lb that the most injurious consequences to the Kingdom may be feared, if the additional burthen of these Duties is continued to be imposed upon the Tonnage of its Shipping; and the Petitioners submit, that the principle on which the said Act is founded militates against the spirit of the various Statutes which for a course of centuries have, from time to time, been enacted by the Legislature of this Country for the increase and encouragement of its Shipping and Navigation, and which have uniformly produced the most beneficial effects: That these effects have lately been conspicuous to the whole world, in the strengthof our Navy, the number of our mercantile Shipping, and in the spirit and enterprize of the persons intefefted in them; and the Petitioners further submit to the House, that the strength of th c British Navy, the true source of the securityand

glory of the Country, mull ever depend upon the number, dexterity, courage, and loyalty of her Seamen, who can only be prelcrved for the services of War by their finding constant employment in the Merchants service and Fisheries during the time of Peace; and the Petitioners most feri-ously apprehend that the inevitable consequences of the operation of the before-mentioned Duties, will not only be the still further depression of what remains of the British Shipping employed in the commerce of the Country, but will likewise greatly tend to weaken the means of its Maritime defence, and accelerate the departure of multitudes of British Seamen from their native land, driven to gain subsistence, and perhaps imbibe foreign affections and habits, in foreign and rival States; and that the Petitioners trust these considerations will appear of still greater importance to the House, when it is recollected that all the other Maritime

Yot

rowers of Europe are at this time most sedulously employed in adopting measures for the increase of

*1

is*

'tit

their. Shipping, the encouragement of their Fisheries, and the augmentation of their Navies, and that at a time when, from the general state of Europe, the Shipping of Great Britain have fallen in their value from thirty pounds to forty pounds per centum, and when numbers of British Vessels continue to lie unemployed, and many of them engaged in voyages which must turn out unproductive, and when numbers of British Seamen have emigrated to France, under the assurances which were made to them of being employed in the Fisheries and Merchants service of that Country; and that the Petitioners therefore hope the Hopfe will counteract the injurious effects which will be produced by the further continuance of a Tax that will prove at once dangerous tb the Shipping and Naval interests of Great Britain, and oppressive and ruinous to those individuals who have embarked their property in British bottoms: And therefore praying, That so much of the said Act as imposes the several Duties therein mentioned on the Tonnage of Ships and Vessels entering outwards or inwards (except in ballast) in any Port of Great Britain to or from Foreign Parts, and also the Duties on the Importation of Oil and Skins, the produce of the British Fisheries, may be repealed; or that the House will grant to the Petitioners such. other relief in the premises as shall leem meet.

And the said Petitions were severally ordered to lie upon the Table.

A Member present informed your Committee, That the Petitioners have proceeded to carry the said Acts into execution; but that material inconveniences have aril'en from the most minute affairs of the said Company being* under the provisions of the said Acts, necessarily submitted to the Company at large, whereby the decision and promptitude indispensable in managing their various and complicated concerns, is wanting: That the Petitioners conceive a l’elect number of Directors, chosen annually by ballot out of the said Company, subject to regulations and restrictions, would be a much more effectual body for the management and controul of the affairs of the said Company: That the Petitioners, as well as the kingdom at large, will derive essential benefit from the defects in the management and regulations of the said Company being remedied, and in the altering and amending the said Acts, they being found in several respects defective.

Manchjler, and the other Northern parts of the kingdom, are connected with Bath, Bristol, and the Western parts thereof; and that, although by the said Act a preference was directed to be given to the said Road from to Worcester on account of its great general importance, yet the directions so given have not been complied with, but, on the contrary, the said Road has been suffered to decay, and its revenues, which have been much more than sufficient to keep it in complete repair, and to pay the whole interest of the money borrowed, have been applied in the repair and amendment of another Road, which, in companion, is of trifling public utility; and that the Petitioners understand it is proposed by the said Bill, to add to the Tolls of the said Road from Bromsgrove to , while

those very Roads which render an additional revenue necessary, are exempted from any increase, by which, if the said Bill pal's into a Law in its present form, as well the Petitioners as the Public in general will be partially and unjustly burthened and aggrieved; And therefore praying. THE hour appointed for taking into confederation the Petition of the Honourable Captain Alexander Cochrane, of the Royal Navy; and also, the Petition of Sir John Henderson, Baronet, complaining of an undue

election and double return for the Clals or District of Burghs, consisting of Dunfermline,

Culrofs, and Queens/erry, in Scotland, being come;

The House proceeded to the appointment of a Scled Committee, to try and determine the merits of the said Petitions.

The Serjeant at Arms was sent, with the Mace, to the places adjacent, to require the attendance of the Members on the business i>f the House.

And being returned;

Several Members were sworn.

And the House was counted by Mr. Speaker; and one hundred and four Members being present;

The counsel and agents were called in.

And the door being locked;

The Order of the day, for taking the said Petitions into consideration, was read.

And the names of the Members were drawn, and read, in the usual manner.

And the name of Thomas Graham, Esquire, being drawn, he was nominated to serve on the said Committee by the counsel for Mr. Cochrane.

And the whole number of forty-nine names being complete;

The counsel for Sir John Henderson nominated Charles Dundas, of Berhjldre, Esquire, to serve on the said Committee.

Note. That in the course of drawing the names, the names of several Members were drawn, who were excused, as being sixty years of age, or upwards; and the names of several others were set aside, the Members being'petitioned against, or having presented a Petition, complaining of an undue election or return.

And lifts of the forty-nine names being delivered to the chunfcl; the door was opened, and the counsel and agents withdrew.

The Order of the day being read, for taking into confi-defation the Petition of James Dashwood, Esquire, complaining of an undue election and return for the Borough of Shafton, otherwise Shaftesbury, in the County of Dorset;

The House was moved. That an Act, made in the 42d year of the reign of His present Majesty, intituled, "An Act for the further regulation of the trials of contro-" verted Elections, or returns of Members to serve in " Parliament; and for expediting the proceedings relating " thereto," might be read.

And the same being read accordingly;

Ordered, That the cpnsideration of the said Petition be adjourned till Tommorrow, at Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

A Petition of the several Persons, whose names as there- AiMon and unto subscribed. Owners of Estates in the several Parishes of AJlaElon and Moulton, in the County of Norfolk, was Petition.:

Tf0 the pud Petition was brought up, and read; let- presented to the House, and read; letting forth. That there

ting forth, That in the 2d year of His present Majesty, the said Trustees represented to Parliament, that the sum allowed them for the establishment and support of the said Museum was reduced to a capital of £.30,000 Reduced Bank Annuities, the Dividend of which, amounting to £.900, was, notwithstanding their utmost attention to the forming their establishment with frugality, greatly insufficient for that purpose; upon which representation they have at sundry times obtained from the House various sums to supply the deficiency of their income, which sums, together with the salary allotted to the King’s Librarian, yearly amounting to about £.250, have proved insufficient to defray the necessary expences of the said Museum, and what now remains in the hands of the Trustees is not sufficient for the purposes of the Trust without the aid of Parliament: And therefore praying the House to grant them such farther support, towards enabling them to carry on the execution of the Trust reposed in them by Parliament for the general benefit of learning and useful knowledge, as shall seem meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

The House being informed that the Sheriffs of the City of London attended at the door; they were called in; and, at the Bar, presented to the House,

A Petition of the Lord Mayor, Aldermen, and Commons, of the City of London, in Common Council assembled.

And then they withdrew.

And the said Petition was read; setting forth, That the Hospital for the reception of mad or insane persons, called Bethlem Hospital, situate in Moorfields, in the City of London, is a very ancient brick building, and is become so ruinous and decayed as not to be capable of being well and effectually repaired; and that the area or space of ground in the . front thereof, which is of very considerable extent, is, in its present state, of very little value; and that it would tend greatly to promote the charitable and beneficial purposes of the foundation of the said Hospital, if the lame were taken down, and a new building of proper extent erected in some more commodious situation; and that it would be a great improvement to the City of London, and of public ‘utility, if a new square or buildings in some other shape or form were laid out and erected on the site of the said Hospital, and the ground in front thereof called the Quarters, in Moorfields; and if new streets were made from the site of the said Hospital to ‘Throgmorton Street and The Royal Exchange, and another new street from Moor gate to Mansion House Street; and if the streets and pail'ages leading from and to the said respective streets and places were widened and improved; and if certain streets, lanes, ways, and passages, leading into or communicating therewith, were also improved, and rendered commodious: And

therefore praying, That leave may be given to. bring in a Bill for the purposes aforesaid.

Burgesses, and Commonalty, of the Borough of Bedford, in the County of Bedford, and of the several other Persons, whose names are thereunto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the fame Borough, was referred.

Mr. Wright accordingly reported from the said Com5-mittee, That the Committee had examined, and found that the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Paving Bills and Bills for building Bridges, had been complied with; and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the lame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. Theed Pearfe being examined, said. That the said Borough of Bedford is a populous place, and public markets have for time immemorial been held there on certain days in every week, and a public fair at divers times in the year: That the present Guildhall of the said Borough is in a ruinous (late, and the present market-places and butchers lhambles are inconveniently situated for the purposes of the market, and the passage along the public streets is greatly obstructed, and rendered inconvenient to Passengers and Travellers by the number of flails placed therein on market days; and great nuisances are frequently committed by slaughtering sheep and cattle in the said public streets or in places open thereto*, and that the several streets, lanes, and public passages within the said Borough arc in many parts incommodious to Passengers, very ill paved, and not sufficiently cleansed, lighted, watched, or watered, and are subject to various nuisances and obstructions: That the present Bridge over the River Ouze, in the said Borough of Bedford, is very ancient, narrow, inconvenient, and dangerous, and the piers of the said Bridge are so constructed as to impede the current of the said River in time of flood, to the great injury of the Inhabitants of the said Borough and the Public at lan e.— And the Witncls further laid, That it would contribute much to the benefit and convenience of the Inhabitants of the said Borough, and to all persons retorting thereto, as well as to the increase of the trade and prosperity thereof, if the present Guildhall, market-places, and butchers (liam-bles, were taken down, and a new Guildhall and new mar-ket-houses and butchers shambles, with proper (hops and other conveniencies, were erected, and the streets and avenues leading thereto widened and improved, and if the streets, squares, lanes, and other public passages and places within the said Borough, were properly paved, repaired, cleansed, lighted, watched, watered, improved, and regulated, and ail nuisances and obstructions removed, and prevented in future; and also, if the said Bridge over the said River Ouze was taken down and rebuilt, and proper avenues, ways, and passages, leading to the said intended Bridge, were opened, and made commodious.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for rebuilding the Guildhall, altering and improving the Market-places within the Town of Bedford, in the County of Bedford, and making proper avenues thereto; for paving, repairing, cleansing, lighting, watching, watering, and improving, the highways, streets, squares, and other public passages and places, within the said Town of Bedford, and for preventing nuisances, annoyances, and obstructions therein; and for rebuilding the Bridge over the River Ouze, in the said Town of Bedford: And that Mr. Wright, Mr. Tierney, Mr. Whitbread, and Mr. Lee Antonie, do prepare, and bring in, the fame.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a sum, not exceeding Three hundred and fifty-six thousand Five hundred and thirty-eight Pounds Nine Shillings and Three Pence Sterling, being Three hundred eighty-six thousand Two hundred and fifty Pounds currency, be granted to His Majesty, for paying off' and discharging Treasury Bills that will become due on the 25th day of March. 1003,

The said Resolution being read a Second time, wa«, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Mr. Alexander, according to Order, reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolution'which the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Same was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Duty of Six Shillings and Sixpence currency per Barrel on Malt made in Ireland, which, by an Act of the last Session of Parliament, was continued and made payable until the 25th day of March 1803, Shall be further continued and charged upon all Malt which Shall be made in Ireland from the 24th day of March 1803 to the 25 th day of March 1804.

The said Resolution being read a second time, was, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Speei-i)Report Mr* Hawkins Brozvne also acquainted the House, That *ai(^ ^elect Committee had come to several Resolutions, BWtion'*"1 which they had directed him to report to the House; and Cwnmittee, he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered U in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That John Allen, being the Returning Officer at the last election for the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, acted contrary to his duty in opening a poll, and proceeding to take the votes of Eledors for the period of about an hour, and until forty-four Eledors had polled, there being, dunng the whole of that time, no third Candidate.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That, after the first day of the said election, the freedom of the election wasgrofsiy violated, by disturbances and riots, accompanied with personal intimidation and violence, practised and continued during the fix subsequent days of polling.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Petitioner Daniel Parker Coke, Esquire, after sustaining several insults, and fufftring personal violence, was obliged, born the just apprehension of hazard to his life, to leave the place, and could not venture to return; and that a large number of Eledors in his interest were deterred from exercising their franchise of voting.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That John

Davison, the Mayor, and Joseph Oldknow and Thomas know, two of the Aldermen of the said Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, took no effectual means to preserve the freedom of election, or restore it when so violated, or to punish the Oflenders.

Vol. 58. V

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, by an entry in the Corporation Book of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, that at a Common Hall, held on Thursday the 8th day of January last past (after reciting the Petitions referred to this Committee) it was " Resolved,

" that this Corporation will defray all such legal expences " as have already been or shall hereafter be incurred by " them the said John Davison, Joseph Oldknow, Thomas " know, and John Allen, or either of them, or George Cold-" ham, under their direction, in preparing for or making " their defences; and that the Chamberlains for the time " being be hereby authorized and directed, from time to " time, to advance Mr. Coldham all and every such sum and " sums of money as may be necessary for this purpose."

It appearing that the Mayor and Aldermen have, by charter, an exclusive jurisdiction within the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, and the Committee thinking it highly expedient to provide feme better security than is likely to be provided by the Corporation of Nottingham, to preserve the peace within the said Town and County thereof, and to prevent the repetition of the fame disgraceful seenes;

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That. the House be moved for leave to bring in a Bill, to give the Magistrates of the County of Nottingham concurrent jurisdiction with the Magistrates of the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, unless such or some other measure to the like effect, be taken previously to the next election for the Town and County of the Town of Nottingham, there is no reasonable hope that a free election can be had.

Resolved, That the Evidence adduced before this Committee be laid before the House for its consideration.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That Alexander Foxcroft was employed to procure signatures to one of the Petitions referred to this Committee, namely, that signed by Five hundred and thirty-seven Petitioners, and containing the following Allegations: ’

" That at the said election they had determined to poll " for the said Daniel Parker Coke, but that such was the *c violence of the mob, systematically regulated and con-" ducted for the purpose, that they were completely inti—

" midated, and thereby prevented from polling for the said " Daniel Parker Coke.

" That the said John Davison, the Mayor, John Allen, the i

<c Sheriff, Thomas Oldknow and Joseph Oldknow, two of the " Aldermen of the said Town, and who, by virtue of their;

" offices, were Magistrates, frequently attended on the " Hustings, and were repeatedly applied to to preserve the j

" peace of the place, and the freedom of election, but the |i

" laid Magistrates took no effectual steps to prevent any " of the violent or illegal acts which took place at the said i

" election."

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the said Alexander Foxcroft Hated to those who signed that Petition, that it was a Petition for those who would have voted for Mr. Coke, but he admitted that the major part t

of them were not acquainted with the Allegations against the Magistrates and Sheriff, and that about sixteen of those who signed the Petition were, to his knowledge, not at Nottingham at the time of the election.

Frederick Shuttleworth was, according to Order, brought Frederick to the Bar; where he received a reprimand from Mr. reprimanded* Speaker; and was ordered to be discharged out of custody, and dif-me ’ paying his fees. «harged.

The reprimand was as followeth;

Frederick Shuttleworth,

A Scleft Committee of this House, appointed to try and determine the merits of the "Nottingham Election Petitions, have reported, that you gave contradictory evidence before them, and were guilty of wilful prevarication.

Offences like yours tend to destroy all reverence for the most sacred test of truth among men: they tend to defeat the ends of justice, and to break up the foundations of civil society.

But the quality of your offence is highly aggravated; for, at the time you were vainly endeavouring to suppress the disclosure of those disgraceful seenes at,

your education, situation, and habits of life, must have !.

made you know, that you were exhibiting a most pernicious example to others.

In the punishment of your offence, the lenity of this House has been most conspicuous; for, in committing you to the custody of its own Officer, it has spared you the disgrace and infamy of a common gaol: and it has done this in the persuasion, that to a mind, which has at any time been acquainted with sentiments of justice and honour, its own compunction for such an offence must be its severest punishment.

You

Militia Officers Bill, icferretl.

Bill to continue Irish Bank Reitritfion, committed.

You are now to go forth to your friends and to the world, branded with this stigma; which nothing can efface but a continued and manifest repentance, and the strictest regard, throughout the rest of your life, to the civil and political rights of your Fellow-subjects.

This House has ordered that you be now discharged; and you are discharged accordingly, paying your fees.

A Message by Mr. Quarme, Yeoman Ulher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords, authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission, for declaring His Royal Assent to several Acts agreed upon by both Houses, do desire the immediate attendance of this Honourable House in the House of Peers, to hear the Commission read.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to the House of Peers.

And being returned;

Mr. Speaker reported, That the House, at the desire of the Lords authorized by virtue of His Majesty’s Commission afore-mentioned, had been at the House of Peers, where a Commission under the Great Seal was read, giving, declaring, and notifying, the Royal Assent to the several Public and Private Bills therein mentioned; and also empowering His Royal Highness the Prince of , His Royal Highness the Duke of York, His Royal Highness the Duke of Clarence, His Royal Highness the Duke of Kent, His Royal, Highness the Duke of Cumberland, His Royal Highness the Duke of S His Royal Highness the Duke of Cambridge, His Royal Highness the Duke of Gloucester, the Lord Archbishop of , the Lord High Chancellor, and several other Lords, to declare and notify the Royal Assent to the said Bills; and that the Lord High Chancellor, the Lord and the Lord

A Petition of the several Persons, whose names are thereunto subscribed, on behalt of themselves and others, House -holders and Inhabitants of the Parish of Saint in

the County of Micld/efex, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for providing ground, and erecting a Workhouse, for the use of the Parish of Saint Patterns, in the County of Middlesex; for railing Money for that purpose; for the better ascertaining and collecting the Poor Rates; for the better relief, government, and employment of the Poor of the said Parish, and for other purposes; and letting forth. That the said Bill, if passed into a Law, will prove highly injurious to the property and interests of the Petitioners and other Householders and Inhabitants of the said Parish, in many respects, and particularly as it would entirely subvert the ancient and long approved mode of supporting, maintaining, and regulating, the Poor of the said Parish under the existing Laws, and transfer the exclusive care and management of the said Poor to a newly constituted and select body of the Parishioners, under the name of Guardians of the Poor of the said Parish: And therefore praying, That they may be heard by their counsel, agents, and witnesses, against the said Bill; and that the fame may not pass into a Law.

Sir James St.Clair Erskine reported from the Committee, KmrofsRmdi to whom the Petition of the Persons thereunto subscribing, Pe"tI!£I£ Owners of Land in the County of Kinross, was referred;

That the Committee had examined, and found that the said Petition is not within the Standing Orders of the House, relative to Turnpike Bills, the application being only for regulating the Statute Labour in the said County; and that the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, which they had directed to be reported to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, Mr. George Melville being examined, said. That the Laws now fubfilting for the making of Roads, and building and repairing Bridges, have been found ineffectual in the County of Kinross, and that other and further powers are necessary, in order to carry the purposes of the said Laws into execution; and it is attended with difficulty to render effectual, and properly to apply, the statrute labour of the said County.—

And the Witness added, That a reasonable competition in money, in lieu of actual labour, is in many places found to be more useful, effectual, and convenient, for the purpose of making and repairing the said Roads and Bridges; and it would therefore be for the advantage of the said County to convert the statute services into money, and to ascertain the rates thereof, and mode of levying the lame; and also to authorize an additional Assessment on the Heritors and other persons in the said County, for the making Highways and Bridges through the lame.

Ordered, That leave be given to bring in a Bill for regulating and converting the Statute Labour in the County of Kinross, and for more effectually making and repairing the Highways within the said County: And that Sir James St. Clair Erskine and General Ciephane do prepare, and bring in, the Gune.

Mr. Milford, from the Select Committee, appointed to try and determine the merits of the Petition of Adams, Esquire, complaining of an undue election and return for the Borough of Harwich, in the County of Essex, informed the House,

That the said Committee have determined.

That Thomas Myers, Esquire, is not duly elected a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough:

And also, that the said Committee have determined, That James Adam, Esquire, the Petitioner, ought to have been returned a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough;

And also, that the said Committee have determined. That the said James Adams, Esquire, is duly elected a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough:

And also, that the said Committee have determined. That the opposition of the said Thomas Myers, Esquire, to the said Petition, did not appear to the said Committee to be frivolous or vexatious:

And the faic! determinations were ordered to be entered in the Journals of this House.

Ordered, That the Deputy Clerk of the Crown do attend this House, immediately, with the last return for the Borough of Harwich, in the County of Essex, and amend the fame, by rafing out the name of Thomas Myers, Esquire, and inserting the name of James Adams, Esquire, instead thereof.

And the Deputy Clerk of the Crown attending, according to Order, amended the said return accordingly.

passed in the 39th and 40th year of His present Majesty’s reign, and also an Act, passed in the 41ft year of the said reign, for preventing the damaging of Raw Hides and Skins in the flaying thereof, were read; whereby it appeared, that the said Acts did not extend to the Cities of London and Westminster, the Borough of Southwark, or any of the Liberties thereof, or to any places within fifteen miles of the Royal Exchange of the said City of London:—And,

Mr. Thomas Cuff being examined, laid, That the said Acts have, as far as they extend, been found very beneficial, by having increased the quantity of good lerviceable Leather, but the exemption contained therein has rendered the benefits intended to have been produced, much less effective than they would have been if the provisions had extended throughout the kingdom, and more especially that of the prohibition of the use of Horle Hides, which, in the present mode of dressing, are become extremely useful in making boots and shoes.—And the Witness further said

Ptiidooo of the A Petition of the Foreman and Grand Jury of the

Xing's Stag's County attending the Spring Assizes at Philipjiown,

County. 1803, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth,

, That, by an Act, passed in the last Session of the Irish Parliament, the sum of £ 500,000 sterling was granted, for the purpose of extending Agriculture in that part of the United Kingdom, by encouraging the making of Canals, and opening River Navigations on reduced Tolls, and for purchasing of the exorbitant Imports levied by the Proprietors of such Canals as had been already made; and that, in pursuance of this principle, the Petitioners have been informed, by public advertisement, that the Directors General of Inland Navigation have caused the Tolls on the Royal Canal, and those on the navigation of the River Barrow, to be reduced to the moderate rate of One Penny per ton per mile on all corn, meal, malt, flour, and potatoes, going to Dublin; and that, by an Act, paflecl by the Irish Parliament in the 29th year of His Majesty’s reign, for the promotion and encouragement of Inland Navigation, the Petitioners find, that, in consideration of a Bounty of £. 57,100, granted by the said Parliament to the Company of Undertakers of the Grand Canal, all corn, meal, malt, and flour, brought to Dublin by the Grand Canal from any place ten miles below Athy and Banaghar respectively, after the navigation of the Rivers Barrow and Shannon shall be completed, shall pay no higher Toll than One Penny Halfpenny per ton per mile, although the general Toll previously allowed to be taken on the said Canal, and actually levied by the Proprietors thereof, on all Goods and Merchandize whatsoever, was Three Pence per ton per mile; whereby it appears, that the signal bounty and wisdom of the Legislature operates most injuriously to the interest and welfare of the! Inhabitants of the King's County as well as to that of the County of Kildare, part of the County 1 of Galway, the Queen's County, and to a considerable portion of the Northern part of the County of Tipperary; in-asmuch as the said Counties not lying ten miles below Athy and Banaghar respectively, the corn, meal, malt, and flour thereof, conveyed to Dublin by the Grand Canal, will be subject to the heavy Toll of Three Pence per ton per niile, while the fame articles brought by the Royal Canal from the Counties of Meath, Weshneath, Roscommon, ford, and Leitrim, will be carried to Dublin at a Toll not exceeding One Penny per ton per mile for the whole distance; and the fame commodities brought from the Counties of Carlow, Kilkenny, and Waterford, by the River Barrow, or from the Counties of Clare, Limerick, Kerry, and the Southern parts of the County of Tipperary, by the Bl'itr Shannon, will be transported on the said Rivers at the low loll of One Penny per ton per mile; and as the fame will be brought from a nearer distance than ten miles below Athy and Banaghar respectively,- they will be conveyed on Jhe Grand Canal to Dublin (parting by the doors of the Petitioners) at the reduced rate of One Penny Halfpenny per ton per mile, while the fame articles produced on the Lands of the Petitioners within the King’s County are tub*-jest to a Toll of double the amount; viz. Three Pence per ton per rpile; and that the Petitioners, deeming the Landholders, Merchants, Manufacturers, and other Inhabitants of this County, to be deeply injured by the foregoing fyf» tem of bounty on the one band, and exclusion on the other, do earnestly intreat the House to take their Situation into consideration, and to grant them relief, either by the ge-

A Petition of the Tanners of the City of Cork, was presented to the House, and read; letting forth, That the Tanning trade of Ireland is now in such an alarming Hate ofdeclension on account of the restrictions laid upon it by the exitling Excil'e Laws of Ireland, that the Petitioners mull, with many others similarly circuinftanced, be alto- Committee, to whom the Bill for consolidating and amend go ther ruined, if the House do not interpose some remedial ing the several Laws for providing relief for the Families of

arrangements; that the present Duty is raised, not upon the quantity of leather tanned, but upon the number of cubic feet contained in each Vat in which the process of tanning is carried on; and, so great is the disproportion between the old and the present method, that the annual amount of the Duty now paid on the cubic feet exceeds by very near two-thirds the Excil'e paid on the Hock taken up in that course of time by the late regulation: And therefore praying the House to make such a reduction in the present Duty, as may place the Petitioners upon fair and equal terms of trade with the Eng/ish Tanner, so far as the nature of the charge by the cubic foot will admit of.

Ordered, That the said Petition do lie upon the Table.

Mr. John Fane reported from the Committee, to whom Kent Gaol the Petition of the several Persons, whose names are there- mA unto subscribed, being Inhabitants of the County of Kent, petitimi, *te* was referred; That the Committee had examined the reported, matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at i

the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as;

followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition, an Act, i

passed in the 9th year of the reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, "An Act to enable the Jut- 1

" tices of the Peace acting for the Western Division of the " County of Kent, to purchase a convenient piece of " ground for building a Gaol for the said County, and for empowering the said Justices to apply part of the " County stock of the said Division towards the fame," was read :—And,

Mr. John Dudlow being examined, said. That the said Justices purchased a convenient piece of ground at MaiJjione, in the said County, and did thereon build a Gaol, the expences of which purchase and building were discharged out of the surplus of the County stock then in the hands of the Treasurer of the Western Division, and by Rates, as directed to be made by the said Act.—And being further examined, he laid. That ever since the building of the said Gaol, the expences of repairing the fame have been discharged by sums of money raised within the said Western Division, according to the directions of the said Act; and that, for a series of years past, functioned by no Law, but custom, the said County has been divided into an Eastern and Western Division; that the Eastern Division has contributed towards the maintenance of such prisoners only as were sent to the felons part of the said Gaol from such Division, and the Western Division has, at the charge of the Inhabitants of such Division, supported all the prisoners sent from the said Western Division to the said.

Gaol; that the said custom is partial, unjust, and opprefftve, inasmuch as, from the contiguity of the said Western Division to the Metropolis, the prisoners committed from that Division far exceed the number of prisoners from the Eastern Division, and the consequent expence therefore iniposed on the Inhabitants of the Western Division exceed, in an unreasonable proportion, the expence of the Eastern Division; and that, independent of the expence of the repairs of the said Gaol being borne exclusively by the Inhabitants of the said Western Division, they support also, at their foie charge, two Bridewells, situate in the

Western

' Western Division, viz. one at , and one at Dart-

ford; and that all Debtors in the custody of the Sheriff of the said County are confined in the said Gaol at,

and the expences charged to the County for their maintenance, whether they be sent from the Eastern or Western Division of the said County, is borne solely by the Inhabitants of the said Western Division; and that the said Gaol is the only prison of the said Sheriff.—And the Witness added. That as the Justices, as well of the Eastern as of the Western Division of the County, are appointed under one and the fame commission, and the Police of the County is general, the Petitioners submit, that the expence incident to the due administration of it ought to attach on the Inhabitants of the whole County at large; and that it is inequitable, that, from any circumstance of locality, one district of a County, in a matter which affects the interest

of the whole, should, for the furtherance of general justice, be partially burthened.—Then,

Mr. Thomas Fuller being examined, said, That, conceiving the general Rate of the County, in its present mode of assessment, to be unequal, it is highly expedient power should be given to the Justices of the Peace for the said County, in their General or Quarter Sessions assembled, to make a fair and equal County Rate, and for that purpose to assess and tax rateably, and in equal proportions, according to the annual rent or value of Estates, all and every the Parishes, Towns, Liberties, Precincts, Villages, Hamlets, and Places, within the said County, for and towards the lame, and to be applied for all the purposes and objects to which the County Rate is by Law liable.—Then the Witness delivered in the following Account:
