Mr. Wilberforce reported from the Committee, to whom

the Petition of the several Persons, whole names are thereunto subscribed, being Merchants and Manufacturers concerned in the Woollen Manufacture in the County of 7'ork-, and also, the Petition of the Merchants, Manufacturers, and others, concerned in the Woollen Trade in the Town and Parish of Halifax, in the County of were severally referred; That the Committee had examined the matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petitions, An Act, passed in the 5th year of the reign of Queen Elizabeth, intituled, "An Act containing divers Orders for Artificers,

" Labourers, Servants of Husbandry, and Apprentices," was read :—And,

John Lees, Esquire, of Halifax, in Yorkshire, Merchant and Woollen Manufacturer, being examined, said, That he has been engaged in the Woollen Trade and Manufacture for thirty years: that the Statute of the 5th of Elizabeth, chapter 4th, concerning apprenticeships in the Woollen Trade, has been considered to be o'ololete; he 1 himself served an apprenticeship only four years; not one ' in ten of the workmen employed in the Woollen Manufactory has served a regular apprenticeship, many have not been apprenticed at all, and the others have been apprenticed for three, four, or five years) according to their ages; apprenticeships for seven years are quite unnecessary; a youth from sixteen to eighteen years of age would learn the art of Weaving in twelve months: that he has some persons now in his employment that have been actually engaged for seven years* but does not by any means consider them as more competent workmen than others who have not been apprenticed for so long a time; the consequence of being obliged to employ none but legally apprenticed Weavers mult reduce the business to one-tenth of its present extent: that he knows of no legal Weavers now out of employment in consequence of others who have not been legally apprenticed heing employed; on the contrary, Weavers are wanted: that he apprehends nine-tenths of the present workmen would be thrown out of employ, if the Statute of the 5th of Elizabeth, chapter 4th, should be enforced: that for want of men, many women are employed as Weavers and Wool-sorters; in some forts of cloth, they work as well; that he considers it essentially necessary for the well-being of the Woollen trade, that the Manufacturer, as occasion requires, should have it in his power to employ such work people in every branch as may be requisite; if the trade were restricded to the employment of work people who had been legally apprenticed, it would not be possible to extend the trade on any occasion of extraordinary demand; that from his own experience, the employment of persons not having been regularly apprenticed to the bufineisof W<}aving, does by no means tend to destroy the good quality of the Manufacture; he knows of no difference between the work of apprenticed and of non-apprentired, that he knows no distinction between the situation of Manufactories in Towns and Manutactories in the Country’, as to the employing of apprenticed or non-apprenticed workmen; that in the present extended lcale upon which the Woollen Manufacture is carried on, the quality of the goods is moil certainly the best security for the welfare of the trade in general, as well as for that of the individuals engaged in it; as there is a l'carcity of workmen, he conceives, that the employing of non-ap-p enticed workmen has not increased, and is not likely to increase the Poor Rates, by throwing apprenticed workmen out of employ. When he takes a workman, or de-. livers out work, he never thinks it advisable to enquire, whether the workman has served a regular apprenticeship; that he does not by’ any means think that the repeal of the Statute requiring Weavers to lerve apprenticeships, would prove injurious to the legal Weavers or their families; that he recollects no prosecutions under the Act of Queen Elizabeth rctpecting Apprentices.

Mr. Nathaniel Murgatroyd, of Bradford, Wool-

len Stuff Manufacturer, being examined, said, That he has been engaged thirty years in that Manufactory; did not 1

serve any apprenticeship himself; began to work at the trade at twelve years of age; more than nine out of ten of t he workmen in the Woollen Stuff manufactory have not been legally apprenticed; cannot speak so positively to the Woollen Cloth Manufacture, but conceives, that there also, more than nine out of ten have.not been regularly apprenticed; very few of the Master Manufacturers in general have been legally apprenticed. To acquire a '

| competent proficiency in the Woollen Manufacture, re-1 quires, in weaving, five or six months; he himself learned I in three, and has supported himself from twelve years of I age: in combing, he learnt in less than three months, j but in general it requires five months to make a proficiency; five months is considered the established time: the other processes require very little time to be master of them.—Being asked, Whether the work of apprenticed workmen in general is better than of non-apprenticed ? he replied. That hejcould not lpcak to that, because he did not know of any who had served a regular apprenticeship; in the taking or employing of workmen, no questions are ever asked, or any difference of price or wages made between apprenticed and non-apprenticed workmen. Many women are employed in the Woollen Stuff Manufacture in Weaving, and other branches. The Spring Shuttle is now in use among the Weavers in Yorkshire-, thinks nine-i tenths use it; Weavers can weave quickest with a Spring Shuttle, and, by facilitating the operation of Weaving, it also mull diminish the demand for Weavers; the goods are as perfect, and bear as great a price in the Market worked with the Spring Shuttle as with a common Shuttle. The Spring Shuttle was the Weavers invention. The use of the Spring Shuttle has not lowered the price of Weaving; the Weavers have all the advantage of the facilitation it has introduced.—Being asked, Whether unapprenticed workmen are not equally orderly with those apprenticed? he replied. That he did not know of any apprenticed workman; does not think that the Poor Rates have been increased, but rather they have been lessened by employing unapprenticed workmen. In the Town of Bolton, he him-fe.f employed a Pauper that had never been accustomed to Weaving before, and who had been a burthen upon his Parish all his life until that time; after weaving the first warp, he said, he kept himself by weaving; he now continues to employ him, who is the best Weaver the witness has; he has worked with him only six months. Thinks the Act of t'ne ytli of Elizabeth, if enforced, would attach as much upon the Workmen as upon the Matters. If the Weft of England alone should obtain a repeal of the Statute of the 5th of Elizabeth, they would have the advantage of the ’Yorkshire People, becausethcy could get hands and wo could not.

Jeremiah Naylor, Esquire, of IVakefielel, Merchant, being examined, laid, that lie has been in the Cloth business twenty-eight years; that an apprenticeship, agreeably to the Statute of the 5th of Elizabeth, moll certainly is not necessary for a person’s attaining such a proficiency in the art or business of a Cloth-dresser, as to enable him to ex-iecute his work in a workmanlike manner; after he attains the age of seventeen or eighteen years, he may learn fit in twelve months, and before the age of sixteen years, he has not strength sufficient for that business; that he never law any cropping done by machinery, and therefore can form no opinion whether the cropper is a necessary man in the finishing of cloth, where machinery is uled te its fullest extent; knows not one man who has served a legal apprenticeship, and at present there is full employ for all good workmen where lie carries on his business; if the Statute of the 5th of Elizabeth was enforced, the consequence would be, that there would be very few workmen legally apprenticed to be found in the Town of his own trade would be totally flopped; it is most certainly his advantage, as well as to that of the whole trade, to employ none but competent workmen.

Thomas Atkinson, Esquire, Mold Green, near,

in Yorkshire, Merchant and Woollen Manufacturer, being examined, said, That within his particular Manufactory there may, perhaps, be one in five or six that have served a regular apprenticeship, because they make it a rule not to turn off any of their workmen so long as they are capable of being employed in arvy way; and they have perhaps

one-fifth or one-sixth workmen who are very old, excepting those; does not know that they have a Angle workman that has served a regular apprenticeship. With regard to the Manufactory in general, does not think one in twenty has served a regular apprenticeship. The work of apprenticed is not better than of non-apprenticed work-l men. There is no difference between the prices paid to

apprenticed and non-apprenticed workmen. The strict enforcement of the Act of the 5th of Elizabeth would, as he believes, be very injurious indeed to the Woollen Manufacture. The trade of the Woollen Manufacture has greatly increased of late years. It could not possibly have increased to that extent in the same time, under a strict enforcement of the Act of the 5th of —Then,

Edward Swaine, Esquire, Woollen Merchant in London, being examined, laid. That he has a Woollen Manufactory in the West Riding of that so far as regards

his Manufactory, not one in forty has been regularly apprenticed, nor does he believe there are more in the Manufactory in general; the work of apprenticed is not better than of non-apprenticed workmen; there is no difference in the prices paid to them respectively. In the Witness’s opinion, the consequence of a strict enforcement of the Act of Elizabeth would be, that nine-tenths of the people now employed would be deprived of their employment, and consequently the Parishes must provide for them. The Woollen trade in the County of York has increased of late years very considerably; it could not possibly have increased to that extent in the same time under a strict enforcement of the Act of Elizabeth.

S'ctf A Petition of the Tanners of the Town and vicinity S' of was presented to the House, and read; set-

ting forth, that the Tanning Trade of Ireland is now in such an alarming state of dcclension, on account of restrictions laid upon it by the existing Excise Laws of -land, that the Petitioners mult, with many others similarly circumstanced, be altogether ruined, if the House do not interpose some remedial arrangements; and that the present Duty is raised, not upon the quantity of Leather tanned, but upon the number of cubic feet contained in y. each vat, in which the process of tanning is carried on;

a,nd so great is the disproportion between the old and pre-lent method, that the annual amount of the Duty now; paid on the cubic feet exceeds, by very near two-thirds,.

the Excise paid on the Stock taken up in that course of time by the late regulation: And therefore praying the House to make such reduction of their burthens as may place therti upon fair and equal terms of trade with the English Tanner, so far as the nature of the charge by the cubic foot will admit of the lame.

A Petition of the Tanners of the Town and vicinity of Wexford, was presented to the House, and read; setting forth, That the Tanning Trade of Ireland is now in such an alarming state of decline, on account of restrictions laid upon it by the existing Excise Laws of Ireland, that the Petitioners must, with many others similarly circum-stanced, be altogether ruined, if the House do not inter-pose some remedial arrangements; and that the present

Kingdom, have, in various instances, suffered great distress and hardship on account of the crowded state of the vessels, the want of a sufficient (lock of provisions, water, and other necessaries for the voyage, and in various other respects.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient to regulate the vessels carrying Passengers from the United Kingdom to His Majesty’s Plantations and Settlements abroad, or to foreign parts, with respect to the number of Passengers which they shall be allowed to take on board, in proportion to the tonnage of such vessels, as well as with respect to the provision of proper necessaries for the voyage.

Ordered, That the said Report do lie upon the Table. Ordered, That the said Report, with the Appendix, be

Mr. Chancellor of the Exchequer acquainted the House, That he had a Message from His Majesty to this House, ligned by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks it proper to acquaint the House of Commons, that he has judged it necessary to adopt, without delay, all the means within His Power which may contribute to defeat the avowed designs of the Enemy, and to afford the most effectual protection and security to His faithful People.

In pursuance, therefore, of the Aifts of Parliament, enabling His Majesty to increase the number of His Militia Forces, His Majesty makes this communication to the House of Commons, to the end that His Majesty may cause the Supplementary Militia to be forthwith raised and enrolled, and thereafter to be drawn out, and embodied, and marched as occasion may require.

Post Meridiem.

MR. Speaker reported to the House, That the House attended His Majesty, this day, with their Address; to which His Majesty was pleased to give this most gracious Answer:

Gentlemen of the House of Commons,

I return j'ou My warmed Thanks for this loyal and dutiful Address.

It is highly gratifying to Me, to receive these assurances of your firm and cordial support, in the prosecution of the.

Contest in which I am lieceflarily engaged, for maintaining the Honour of My Crown, and for preferring the dearest Rights and Interests of My People*

Ordered, That Mr. Stnrges hare leave of absence for a fortnight, on urgent private business; he having served upon the Sclent Committee for trial of the Taunton Election.

A Petition of John Ogle, Esquire, was delivered in at BoftonElec the Table, and read; setting forth. That at the last elec- potion of tion of a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the Borough of Mr. Ogle. Boston, in the County of Lincoln, in the room of Thomas Irydell, Esquire (whose election had been declared void)

Thomas Fydellthe younger, Esquire, son of the said Thomas Fydcll the elder, and the Petitioner, were severally pro-poled as Candidates; and that at the time of such election the said Thomas Fydell the younger was not seised of, or entitled to, such an Estate in Lands, Tenements, or Hereditaments, either in Law or Equity, as did qualify him to be elected and returned to serve as a Member for the said Borough; and that the said Thomas Fydell the elder, whose election had been declared void for bribery, did, by the means of the undue and corrupt influence which he had acquired in the said Borough by such bribery, procure the election and return of the said Thomas the younger,

who was at the time of, and had been for a long time previous to, such election, out of this Kingdom in parts beyond the seas; and that public notice was given to the Electors at such last election, immediately previous to the Returning Officer proceeding to take the poll, that the said Thomas Fydell the younger was not capable of being elected and returned as a Alember to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, for the reasons above-mentioned; and that divers Persons, acting as the avowed agents and managers for conducting the election of the said Thomas Fydell the younger, were guilty of bribery, and of other undue, illegal, corrupt, and unwarrantable practices, in order to procure the election and return of the said Thomas Fydell the younger; and that many persons, not entitled to vote at the said last election, were admitted to poll for the said Thomas Fydell the younger, and many Persons entitled to vote, and who tendered their votes for the Petitioner, were rejected; and that by these, and other undue means, the said Thomas Fydcll the younger was returned as a Burgess to serve in Parliament for the said Borough, whereas the Petitioner was duly elected, and ought to have been returned: And therefore praying the House to take the premises into consideration, and to grant such relief as to the House shall feern meet. v

Ordered, That the said Petition b‘e taken into conficlcration upon Tuesday, the 23d day of August next, at Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

Mr. Alexander accordingly reported from the said Committee, the Amendments which the Committee had made to the said Clause, and which they had directed him to report to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered the Clause, with the Amendment, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Amendment was twice read; and, upon the Questionput thereupon, agreed to by the House.

And the said Clause was read the third time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

November, the hostile spirit of France had (in the judgment of His Majesty’s Ministers, as now avowed by them) already been manifested, for more than six months, by one continued series of aggression, violence, and insult, for which neither reparation nor redress had, down to that moment, been obtained: That the often five principle had already been distindfly advanced, of excluding His Majesty from all concern in the affairs of the Continent; that the Spavish and other priories had already been withdrawn from the Order of Malta; Piedmont; Parma, Placentia, and , had been annexed to France; Switzerland had been attacked and lubjugated, and the remonstrance of His Majesty’s Government upon that subject had been treated with indignity and contempt; the territory of the Batavian Republic was at that very moment {bill occupied by the armies of the Chief Consul of France, and its internal administration still controuled by his interference; and the French Government was then actually engaged in the pursuit of those plans and measures for the subversion of the Empire, to which

His Majesty’s Declaration refers, as a violation of the Treaty of Peace: That in directing, under such circumstances, the final surrender of The Cape, without having previously explained or arranged the numerous points of difference and complaint which then actually subsisted between the two Governments, His Majesty’s Ministers acted in contradiction to the sense which they had themselves manifested Vo t '

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, in order to provide Relief for the Families of non-commis-honed Officers, Drummers, and Privates, of the Militia of Scotland, when embodied and called out into actual Service, it will be expedient to raise the sum necessary for such purpose by an Assessment upon Lands and Houses in each County respectively, to be continued so long only as a provision for a similar relief shall exist in England.

iagerelfttivcto had a Message from His Majesty to this House, signed by His Majesty; and he presented the same to the House; and it was read by Mr. Speaker (all the Members of the House being uncovered); and is as followeth; viz.

GEORGE R.

His Majesty thinks it right to inform the House of Commons, that, from an anxious desire to prevent the calamities of War being extended to the Batavian Republic, He communicated to that Government 11 is disposition to respect their neutrality, provided that a similar disposition was manifested on the part of the French Government, and that the French forces were forthwith withdrawn from the territories of the Batavian Republic: This proportion not having been admitted by the Government oi France, and measures having been recently taken by them in direct violation of the independence of the Batavian Republic, His Majesty judged it expedient to direift IJ is Minister to leave the Hague; and He has since given orders that Letters of Marque and General Reprisals should be issued against the Batavian Republic cand its Subjects.

His Majesty has at all times manifested the deepest and most lively interest for the prosperity and independence of the United Provinces: He has recourse therefore to theie proceedings with the most ilncere regret, but the conduct of the French Government has left Him no alternative; and in adopting theie measures, He is actuated by a fenfc of

Sir John Stewart reported from the Committee, to whom Report on the several Petitions, which have been presented to this ct,t,ons rc~ House in thk Session of Parliament, relj>ecting the Tanning Trade in Ireland, were referred; and who were empowered 10 report their Observations thereupon to the House; That the Committee had examined the matters of the said Petitions, and had directed him to report the fame, as they appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered it in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the fame was read; and is as followeth; viz.

Your Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the matter of the said Petitions; and it appeared, by the Evidence laid before them, that the Tanners feel themselves aggrieved by an inconvenience which at present exists in not having it in their power to declare oft’ Ids than one-fourth of their works, upon which Your Committee beg leave to observe, That if power were given to the Tanners to declare oft' one-eighth of their works, it might, under the subsisting regulations, be done with safety to the Revenue and the fair Trader, who pays the full Duties.

A Petition of the Fishermen of Greenwich, in the County of Kent, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for incorporating certain Persons, and their Successors, by the name of " The Fifiling Company," for more effectually supplying the Metropolis with Fish, and for enabling them to conduct and support their Establishment; and setting forth, That the Petitioners are Proprietors of Vessels solely employed in supplying the Metropolis with Fifii, and, should the said Bill pass into a Law, they will be most materially injured: And therefore praying the House to protect them from the ruin they would inevitably experience, unless it should be enacted that the proposed Fishing Company should not interfere with the old Establishment.

Mr. Alexander, according to Order* reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred, to consider further of Ways and Means for raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, the Resolutions wifich the Committee had directed him to report to the House; which he read in his place; and afterwards delivered in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the lame were read; and are as followeth; viz.

Resolveed, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of Excise of Four Pounds Ten Shillings, Irish currency, be charged on every Tun of all Madeira Wine, which shall on the 19th day of this instant June be in His Majesty’s (lores, or in the (lores or warehouses of any Dealer in or Retailer of Wine in Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That* towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of Excise of Four Pounds Ten Shillings, Irish currency, be charged on every Tun of all Portugal, Sptinish, and Canary Wine, and all Wines of the Dominions of Spain, and the Wines of Naples and Sicily, which shall on the 19th day of this instant June be in His Majesty’s (lores, or in the (lores or warehouses of any Dealer in or Retailer of Wine in Ireland.

Refolded, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of Excise of Three Pounds Ten Shillings, Irish currency, be charged on every Tun of Rhenish, German, and Hungary Wine, which shall on the 19th day of this instant June be in His Majesty’s (lores, or in the (lores or warehouses of any Dealer in or Retailer ot Wine in Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted to His Majesty, an additional Duty of Excise of Three Pounds Five Shillings, Irijli currency, be charged on every Tun of all other Wines, which shall on the 19th day of this instant June be in His Majesty’s (lores, or in the (lores or warehouses of any Dealer in or Retailer of Wine In Ireland.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, Thaty towards raising the Supply granted to His Majesty, an act-* ditional countervailing Duty of Ten Pence and One-twelfth part of a Penny, Irish currency, be charged on every Gallon of Spirits distilled and made in Great Britain, and which shall be imported into Ireland.

ReJ'o/ved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That, towards railing the Supply granted, to His Majesty, an additional countervailing Duty ot Nine Pence Three Farthings* Irish currency, be charged on every Barrel, containing thirty-two Gallons, of Beer and Ale made in Great Britain, and which shall be imported into Ireland\

The laid Resolutions being severally read a second time, were, upon the Question Ieverally put thereupon, agreed to by the House.

Bridge, and for making and repairing the Road therein mentioned; without any Amendment: And also.

Mr. Annejley reported from the Committee, to whom the Petition of Isaac Du Bois, Esquire, late a Captain in His Majesty’s reduced regiment of Northumberland Fen-cible-men, was referred; That the Committee had examined the matter of the said Petition, and had directed him to report the fame, as it appeared to them, to the House; and he read the Report in his place; and afterwards delivered the fame, with an Appendix thereunto, in at the Clerk’s Table: Where the Report was read; and is as followeth; viz.

To prove the Allegations of the said Petition,

M:Gwire of Wimpole-street, Cav Esquire, for-

merly Advocate General, Attorney General, and Member of Council for the Province of North Carolina, being examined, said, That he has known the Petitioner more than 30 years, and knew his Father, John Du Bois, several years before his death, who lived in the Town of Wilmington, in North Carolina, was an active Magistrate of the Province, and reputed to be one of the richest merchants there; that in the year 1776, alter the death of the Petitioner’s father, Mrs. Du Bois, his widow, with, the Petitioner and two other of her children, were banished from Wilmington into the Back Country, and in their way thither Hopped at the Witness’s house; that tire property of Mr. John Du Bois, in his lifetime, and of his family after his death, was very considerable, and confided of a bakehouse, which was the only one in that part of the country, a mill, a number of valuable houses in the Town of Wilmington, a great number of valuable boat Negroes, and Tradesmen, and lighters, the whole of which property was confiscated and destroyed, as the Witness understands and believes, whilst the family were in banishment, by the then American Government, for their loyalty to the nation.

Alexander Fothmngham, Esquire, late a Captain in His Majesty’s Fencible Regiment of Hants Cavalry, now of Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, and formerly of North Carolina, being examined, said. That he has known the Petitioner more than 30 years; that he knew the Petitioner, his Mother and Sifters, when they lived at Wilmington, before the commencement of the American war, from whence they were all banished into the interior in the year 1776, by the then American Government, as the Witness understands, for their known loyalty and attachment to the British Government, and were not permitted to return until the year 1779; that the Witness saw the Petitioner and his family frequently during the 3 years of their banishment, in which time they were supported wholly by the bounty of their friends; that, before their banishment, the family possessed a very considerable freehold property, consisting of dwelling-houses, warehouses, and wharfs, and a baking-house for l'upplying shipping and the West India market with biscuits, which was in itself a very valuable property, from its being the only one in that part of the country; and that they had also a large personal property, consisting of Negroes belonging to lighters, Negro Tradel-men, and lighters and merchandize; that when the family returned to Wilmington in 1779, all their property had been either destroyed or confiscated by the then American Government, whilst they were in banishment; that the computation then made of the Losses of the family exceeded £.30,000 sterling; that before the property was destroyed and confiscated, the income arising from it amounted to more than £• 4,coo sterling per annum.—And the Witness further said. That he has carefully looked over the paper annexed, entitled, " Schedule and computed value of the Real and " Personal Estate, held in trust by Jane Du Bois, for her " son Isaac Du Bois, and three other children, at the time " of their banishment from Wilmington into the interior " of North Carolina, in the year 1776 ;" the total whereof amounts to the sum of £.29,756. 15 and thinks that it is correct both in specification and value; that the Witness has also carefully looked over the other Paper annexed, entitled, " Schedule and computed Value of " the Real and Personal Estate of Isaac Du Bois, F.squire * (the Petitioner) which was confiscated, destroyed, or " made away with, during the American Resolution, and " for which he claims compensation from the British Government;" the total whereof amounts to £. 11,944. 15J. which he thinks is correct, and the estimation of the value of the property therein specified is rather under than over what it ought to be.

Mr. M‘Gwire also Hated to the Committee, That, from the general reputation of the family’s property, he thinks himself justified in supposing that those Schedules and Estimations are correct.-—Then,

Lieutenant General Sir James Craig, K. B. being examined, said, That his first knowledge of the Petitioner was in January 1781, when he was introduced to him by Lieutenant General (then Lieutenant Colonel) ,

regions he was on the point of failing with a detachment of His M;.jeily’s Troops for the Fear River, for the purpose i f furming a poll there, with the view to open a communication with the army of Lord Cornwallis Lieutenant General Balfour introduced the Petitioner as a young Gentleman of undoubted loyalty, and who, from the urcurmtance of his family residing in the part of the country to which lie was going, and from his own knowledge of it, might be of great ule to him; that the Petitioner accordingly accompanied the detachment under the command of the Witness, and during the whole of his remaining at and about Wilmington^ which was until the month of November following, he received every active assistcince from the Petitioner that could be expected, or that he could require from him, in the course of which be always found him actuated by the wannest principles of loyiiry and affection for His Majesty’s service; that the Witness found the Petitioner’s mother and family resident at Wilmnitton, where they were particularly obnoxious to the prevading party, on account of the known loyalty of their sentiments; and he always understood that they had suffered much in their property on that account; that the Witness having, from the confidence repoled in the Petitioner’s zeal and activity, appointed him to act as Com miliary of Captures, in which employment it was his duty to take charge of, and deliver over for His Majesty’s ule, all cattle and other property, which, belonging to the enemy, were at anytime captured or lcized on, and the Petitioner having returned to Wiimhipon some time after the war, about the year 17S5, the people there made a pretenee of this circumstance to molest and injure him; in consequence of which he wrote to the Witness, then in England, and the Witness remembers receiving his letter, requdn g a certificate from him that he had been cm-ployed by him, and that what he had done had been by his order and directions, which certificate he accordingly lent to him: That the Witness cannot, of his own knowledge, fcy any thing of the particulars of the Petitioner’s loli'es, but he always understood that the family was amongst the most respectable in the Province, and that they were in P'hi’euion of confulerablo property.—And the Witness further laid, That the Petitioner never received any pay or remuneration hum him for his services while acting with the detachmeni under his command.—And,

Lieutenant General Balfour informed the Committee, That he first knew the Petitioner in December 1780, in South Carolina, when he recommended him to Sir James Craig. who was then going on an Expedition to Wilmington, m North Carolina, in which he considered that the Petitioner, being a native of the place, would be able to render his services very useful to the Commander; that the Petitioner came to the Witness as a refugee, being driven from his house; that the Petitioner embarked with Sir James Craig on that expedition, and, as far as the Witness recolicfls, Sir James reported, that he had received considerable afiillance from the Petitioner's information; that the Witness, in conficquence of thinking the Petitioner a deserving Loyalist, recommended him to the Commander in Chief for, and who gave him a Lieutenant’s commission in, the New Turk Volunteers, which the Witness considered as a regiment moll likely to be put

on the Establishment, but which was hot, and the fame was disbanded; that during the whole of the war, the Petitioner acted as a zealous Loyalist:; that he received no pay for his services under Sir James Craig, and that the Witness always considered the Petitioner the son of a respectable family at Wilmington.

That it appeared to the Committee, from a Report made by John Wilmot, Esquire, the surviving Commissioner for American Claims, to the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, dated the 19th of January 1802, That the Petitioner was heard by the Commissioners for American Claims, respecting his Claim, on the 5th of November 1784, being then about 21 years of age; that it appeared he had been an active Loyalist from his earliest youth, and that his Father having died in 1763, he was entitled to property in North Carolina, but it not having been confiscated (probably on account of his minority) the Commissioners considered it as protedled by the Treaty of Peace between Great Britain and,

and therefore thought themi'elves obliged to disallow the Claim for real property, but allowed the Petitioner the sum of £. 50 for the loss of some small articles of personal estate, and which sum he received; that the Petitioner returned to North Carolina in 1785; but that instead of recovering any part of his property, he was ill treated, and thrown into prison.

Niel M-'Niel, of Char lejl own, South Carolina, Owner and Commander of the ftiip 'Two Friends, belonging to Charles-town, being examined, said, That he has known the Petitioner since the year 1785; that the Witness arrived at Wilmington in December 1785, and found the Petitioner was then confined by the American Government, and had been so confined from the month of March preceding, at which time the Petitioner had arrived at Wilmington from England to look after his property, and had been then immediately arrested; that about three or four weeks after the Witness first saw the Petitioner, he attended the Petitioner’s trial before the Judges of the State at Wilmington, and a Special Jury, for his having been a Traitor to his Country, and taking an active part for Great Britain during the war, when the Jury found him guilty of those charges, and the Judges sentenced him to perpetual Banishment from the State of North Carolina, and ordered him to leave it in 48 hours, and to be kept in close confinement until the order was complied with; but a Petition being presented to the Governor of the State by the Petitioner, the time for his leaving it was extended to six weeks; the sentence is still in force; that in the course of the trial the Petitioner, by his counsel, claimed the indulgence allowed by the British Treaty, of 12 months to settle his affairs, but the Court refused to allow the Claim, infilling the Petitioner had forfeited all right to it by his conduct and activity in the British cause.

Mr. MrGwire being again examined, said. That he remembers the Petitioner making repeated applications to the British Government for a compensation for his Losses.

And it also appeared to the Committee, from the Report of Mr. Wilmot, already referred to, That a Memorial was presented by the Petitioner to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury in the latter end of the year 1801, praying compensation for his losses in America.

It is agreed, by all the persons examined, that it is practicable to erect a Lighthouse on this Rock, upon principles similar to those of the Lighthouse; but

that the expenCe will be considerable. That this Rock is not, however, so much exposed as the Eddyjione is, the swell of the Eastern Sea not being equal to that of the Western Ocean. That it appears that a sufficient foundation might be prepared on the North end of the Rock; where the surface is highest, and of greatest dimensions. That artificers could work five hours at the times of each low water in the day-time of the summet months; and that if the building should be of masonry, the stones to form it might be prepared on fltore, marked and numbered, and carried off to the Rock, and properly placed.

Your Committee next proceeded to examine the several Act, which have passed for erecting Lighthouies in the Northern parts of the Kingdom, and find, that an Act passed in the 26th year of 11 is present Majesty, " for erect-ing certain Lighthouses in the Northern parts of Great Britain" and that the Commissioners therein named were authorized to erect four Lighthouses, one at naiitl's Herd, in the County of Aberdeen; one on the Island of North Ronddjha, in the Orkneys-, one on the Point of Sctdpa, in the Island of Herries; and a fourth on the Mull of Kintyrc. By this Act the Commissionersare authorized

tocolledl and take a Duty of One Penny sterling per ton on British ships passing any of the Lighthouses, and Two Pence for every Foreign ship. But that vessels, though passing the whole of them, should only pay once; and refills employed in the Greenland Fishery, or going to Archangel, or returning from thence, provided they return before the 15th September in each year, are exempted front Duties. The Commissioners are authorized to borrow £• 1,000 upon the security and credit of the Duties. But it is provided, that if liny surplus shall remain after the ne-ceilary expenditure, the same shall once in every year be veiled in one or other of the Public Funds of the Kingdom, and shall be allowed, together with its interest, to accumulate, until the'yearly interest of the same shall amount to a turn equal to defray the whole annual expence attending the Lighthouses, and that then and in that case the sums that shall have been heretofore payable by the several ships and vessels passing the said Lighthouses, shall W0 fNlo cease, detertmine, and be no longer payable; and the Commissioners are by this Act likewise directed to transmit. once in every year. Accounts of their Receipts and Dilbiirfements to the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treal'ury, and to the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Customs at Edinburgh, to be presented to both Houses of

Parliament*

« APPENDIX.

Extract of a Letter addressed to the Earl of Northejh, by Charles Roberts, dated 17th September 1802; containing the result of a Survey which he made of the Cape or Bell Rockon the Eastern Coast of Scotland, near the entrance of the Firth of Forth, which was transmitted by his Lordship to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty.

To the Right honourable the Earl of Northejk.

My Lord,

In consequence of the number of vessels which have been wrecked on the Cape or Bell Rock within these last four years during my residence in this neighbourhood, I was induced to examine its situation, extent, and * with respect to the different Points and Headlands in its vicinity; and, in order to accomplish the fame, I made an actual Survey of part of the adjacent Coast, and went out in a boat to the Rock, and placed my Theodolite on the N. E. part of it, which is the highest and out of tvater, and took the following bearings, and afterwards calculated the distances, viz. Montrose Nefs, N. 90 24' VV. fourteen miles and three quarters; the Redhead, N. 16' 24' W. nine miles and a half; the Pierhead of Arbroath, N. 420 W. eight miles and a half; the Bluff Point of the Sands of Barry to the North of the entrance of Fay, N. 79" W. ten miles j the Eastermost Steeple of St. Andrew's, S. 67° 26' W. twelve miles and three quarters; Balcome House, S. 38° 4* W* ten miles; Fife Nefs, S. 340 44' W. nine miles and three quarters j and the Lighthouse on the Isle of May,

S. 200 26' W. thirteen miles and three quarters.

This dangerous Rock trenches in a line towards Fife Nefs, S. 240 VV; It is bold and steep too, except on the S. W. end, where it runs off in a flat. On the inside of it, close to the Rock, there are twelve fathom water; and on the outside, from sixteen to twenty-two. The breadth of the lloek is a hundred and ten yards j its length near

half

sn

1° Jul

A. 1803.

half a mile; dry at low water. On the N. E. ehd the fur-face is Very uneven; but in general the Rocks are from four to eight feet above the low-water mark for nearly a quarter of a mile, and at high-water spring tides there may be from ten to twelve feet over the highest part of them, as the tide rises at the lprings about twenty feet; and then, if the wind is in any direction off the land, it becomes particularly dangerous, as from the smoothness of the water in consequence thereof, there is then no break, and its landmarks are so distant, that if there is any haze on the shore they cannot be seen; and at all times in the night, which is particularly long on this Coast in winter, land-marks can be of rto service in avoiding this dangerous Rock, which has proved the destruction of many vessels, loss of much property, and sacrifice of numbers of lives.

This dangerous Rock lies in the fair way of vessels navigating along the Coast from North to South and from South to North, as also those to and from the East Country, particularly bound to the Ports within the Firth of Forth, Dundee, Arbroath, Montroje, and Aberdeen; it is also particularly dangerous for His Majesty’s ships which may be cruizing or failing along this part of the Coast of , Scotland.

For some time past it has been in agitation among the Ship Owners, Matters, and Seamen of this part of the Coast t)f Scotland, to take the dangerous situation of this Rock, with respect to the navigation of the Coast, under their particular consideration, and endeavour to fall on the readied means to induce Government to give its aid and assistance to remove this bane of sailors, by erecting a Light-hdufe thereon for the guiding of ships along the Coast, and facilitating the navigation thereof; and in consequence of representations made by them to the Commissioner for Arbroath, at the meeting of the Royal Burghs of Scotland at Edinburgh, to bring forward the fame, he did so; and they ordered tome of their Members to correspond with the Commissioners for the Northern Lights respecting the matter; and some estimations have been made of the expence of and erection for a Light on the said Rock, and also the Duty necessary to be laid on the Tonnage of Vessels navigating the East Coast of requisite to defray

the expence of the fame.

Which Duty appeared to be but trifling; but it was

assemble and meet again upon this day, at Eleven of the clock in the Morning, the Committee met accordingly, when the Minutes of the Proceedings of the Commissioners appointed to take evidence in Ireland, respecting certain fafts, allegations, matters, and things, referred to them, and specially assigned and limited in and by an order of the Committee, having been laid before them, the Committee proceeded to take the fame into consideration; and it appearing that the said Evidence and Proceedings wrere exceedingly voluminous, and contained a great variety of matter,' and that it would require several weeks to make the necessary copies thereof, the counsel on both fides, with the consent of the parties, made it their earned and particular request to the Committee, that they might be allowed some considerable time after such copies should be made and delivered to them, to prepare themselves to state their observations upon the effect of the said Evidence; and that the Committee, having duly considered the said request, and also the advanced period of the Session, and being satisfied that, in the present stage of the cause, the ends of justice would be materially promoted by granting the said request, and that very heavy expences might be saved to both parties in consequence of an adjournment of the Committee for the purposes aforesaid, desire leave of the House to adjourn, from the rising of the Committee this day, until the 25th day of August next, if the House shall think fit.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That a sum, not exceeding Five Thousand Pounds, be appi.ed out of any Monies unapplied to the use of the Navy, in the hands of the Treasurer of the Navy, towards encouraging and rewarding such Person or Persons who shall make any discoveries for finding the Longitude at Sea, which, though they do not entitle the Discoverers to the greater rewards specified in an Act, made in the fourteenth year of the reign of His present Majesty, yet may be adjudged by the Commissioners for the Discovery of the Longitude at Sea to be of considerable ule to the Public; and all such other Person or Persons as shall make any other useful discoveries and improvements in Navigation, and towards the better making of Experiments relating thereto; and for discharging certain Debts incurred by the said Commissioners in carrying the Acts relative thereto into execution.

A Petition of the Planters, Merchants, and others, interested in the British West India Colonies, was presented tivetothe to the House, and read; setting forth, That, with deep regret, the Petitioners feel themselves compelled, by an accumulation of distress, which they have of late years experienced, to lay before the House the chief causes of that distress, and to pray for such relief as, upon principles of public justice and public policy, the House, in its wisdom, shall think fit to apply; and that the Petitioners have, by the employment of a vast capital in the improvement of the Plantations in the Indies (to which they have been encouraged by many express Acts of the Legislature) not only been able, for a long time palt, plentifully to supply the markets of the Mother Country with their great staple article of Sugar, but also to provide a considerable surplus thereof, which, by its re-export to other parts of Europe, has greatly contributed to iwell the balance of British trade, and to preserve and nourish

A Message from the Lords, by Mr. Wihnot and Mr. Popham:

Mr. Speaker,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to permit Portugal Wine to be landed and warehoused in the United Kingdom without payment of Duties, under certain Restrictions, for a limited time; without any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to explain and amend an Act, made in the kill Session of Parliament, intituled, "An Act to amend an Act, made in the twenty-second year of the reign of His present Majesty, for the better Relict and Employment of the " Poor, lo far as relates to the Payment of the Debts in-" curred for building any Poor-housewithout any Amendment: And also.

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act to amend the Acts now in force for securing the Collection of the Revenue upon Malt, and for regulating the trade of a Distiller in Ireland \ without any Amendment: And also,

The Lords have agreed to the Bill, intituled, An Act for the Improvement of the Town of Bedford, in the County of Bedford, and for rebuilding the Bridge over the River Ouze, in the said Town; without any Amendment': And also,

The Lords have passed a Bill, intituled, An Act for effectuating an Exchange of Lands belonging to the Trustees of the Charity of Sir Henry Marten, Knight, and Henry Marten, Esquire, for Lands belonging to Edward Love den Loveden, Esquire; to which the Lords desire the concurrence of this House.

And then the Messengers withdrew.

A Petition of several Merchants, and Owners of British Ships trading to the Baltic, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, and Germany, was presented to the House, and read; taking notice of the Bill for erecting a Lighthouse on the Bell or Cape Rock, on the Eastern Coast of Scotland, and for amending the several Acts for erecting Lighthouses in the Northern parts of Great Britain, so far as relates to the Exemption granted to Ships employed in the Northern Whale Fishery, or trading to Archangel; and setting forth, That the said Lighthouse will not be in the trad of any Ship or Vessel coming from, or failing to, the Baltic, Denmark, Sweden, Norway, or Germany, or any of those Countries, unless they are respectively bound to the Eastern Ports of Scotland\ and consequently that the said Lighthouse will not be of any advantage whatever to Ships trading from England to those Countries respectively, but such advantage will be confined to Ships and Vessels employed in the Coasting Trade, or actually bound to the Ports on the Eastern fide of Scotland: And therefore praying, That they may be heard, by counsel, against so much of the said Bill as affects them, and that the said Bill may not pass into a Law as it now {lands.

Ordered, That the said Petition be referred to the consideration of the Committee of the whole House, to whom the said Bill is committed; and that the Petitioners be heard, by counsel, before the said Committee, upon their Petition, if they think fit.

By the Lord Lieutenant and Council of Ireland.

A PROCLAMATION.

Hardzcicke.

Whereas divers persons engaged in a treasonable and daring Insurrection against His Majesty*s Government, did in the evening of yesterday, the 23d day of July instant, suddenly assemble in the Liberties of Dublin with fire-arms and pikes, and did there commit several outrages, and particularly in T/nmas-Jireet, in the Parish of Saint Catherine, within the said L iberties, did atTault the carriage of the Right honourable Arthur Lord Viscount Kilwarden, Chief Justice of His Majesty’s Court of King’s Bench, and one of His Majesty’s Most honourable Privy Council, and did drag the said Arthur Viscount Kilwarden, together with his nephew the Reverend Richard Wolfe, Clerk, from the said carriage, and did there basely and inhumanly murder the said Arthur Lord Viscount Kilwarden, and Richard Wolfe, Clerk, by {tabbing them respectively with pikes in various parts of their bodies, of which wounds they both soon after died: Now we the Lord Lieutenant in Council, in order to bring such enormous Offenders tocond-gn punishment, do by this our Proclamation publish and declare, That if any person or persons shall within six calendar months from the date hereof, discover any of thencston or persons who committed the said inhuman murders on the said Lord Viscount Kilwarden and the said Reverend Rickard Wolfe, or either of them, or who aided and assisted therein, or who advised, encouraged, instigated, moved, llimulated, or incited the persons concerned therein to commit the fame, such person or persons so discovering, shall receive as a reward tl.c sum of One Thousand Pounds sterling, for each and every of the first three persons who shall be apprehended and convicted thereof: And we do likewise publish and declare. That if any of the persons concerned in the murders aforesaid, save and except the persons who actually {tabbed the said Lord Viscount Kilwarden and the Reverend Richard Wolfe, or either of them, as aforesaid, shall discover any other of the persons concerned in said murders, or either of them, so that such person or persons lb discovered shall be con-v, victecl thereof, such person or persons so discovering, shall, over and above the said rewaref, receive His Majesty’s most His Majesty feels the deepest regret in acquainting the gracious Pardon for said offences.

The value and importance of* the Reports contained in the foviT printed volumes, as well as of those specified in the above arrangement, is very generally known and admitted but the benefit to be derived from them will be greatly enhanced, if direct ions shall be given for preparing and printing with them a well-digested Index of the whole.

Your Committee have further, in pursuance of the In-structions of the House, directed an Estimate of the Expence of completing the existing copies of the four first volumes of the General Indexes to the Journals to the number of 1,200; and they have also directed an Estimate of the probable Expence of printing 1,750 sets of eleven new volumes of Reports, that being the number to which they think it probable they will amount; and also of the fame number of copies of one volume of a General Index to the whole fifteen volumes; which several Estimates are included in the Appendix hereunto annexed. (Appendix N® 2)

It appears to Your Committee, that in general the more recent volumes of the Journals contain matters of more frequent and general reference than those of an earlier date; they therefore beg leave to recommend, that in reprinting of the first 34 volumes, the Printer should be directed to begin with the 34th volume, and to continue retrogressively with the others; and that the fame be printed with the Date at the top of each page, and marginal Notes, as has been done in the volumes lately printed.

As in the progress of time, the number now recommended to be printed must gradually be exhausted or reduced, it might be a matter of confidetable convenience if some general rule could be adopted for a successive, and, in some degree, periodical renewal of the sets of each volume; Your Committee therefore would suggest, that it may be proper that the Clerk of the Journals should report to the Speaker, towards the end of each Session, the number of copies of each volume of Journals, Reports, and Indexes, then in his custody; and, that when the copies of any volume shall be reduced to nearly a number to be specified (suppose 2co) the Speaker should state the same to the House, and that an Order should thereupon be made for completing the copies of such volume to 1,200.

Your Committee afterwards proceeded to consider of providing some place, near the House of Commons, sufficiently large and commodious for keeping the several Volumes when printed, and to prepare an Estimate of the Expence attending the fame; and directed an Order to the Surveyor General of His Majesty’s Works to attend them, that they might receive his opinion thereupon; but having been informed by Mr. Lewis , Nephew

to the said Surveyor General, that he is now on business at such a distance from Town that it is extremely improbable that he can receive and obey the said Order within a convenient time; and the said Mr. Wyatt hav-

ing stated, that he is an Architect, and employed by his Uncle as an Afllstant, Your Committee have thought proper to examine him upon this subject; but in the first place, they directed a Computation to be made, and Appendix, laid before them, by Mr. of the extent

(n°4-) of space that would be requisite for containing such part of the copies of the volumes comprehended in his Statement (Appendix, N® 2.) as in his opinion, it is likely will be in the custody of the Clerk of the Journals at any one time, and which he thinks can never exceed one half the whole number.

And there having been laid before Your Committee, by theirdirection, a Statement of various places near thefcloufe of Commons, where it was conceived sufficient accommodation might be found, the (cite opposite St. adjoining the stone building betwixt New and Old Palace-yards, appeared clearly to Your Committee, from the local fifuation, to be the most eligible for this purpose. But the said Surveyor General not having attended Your Committee, they are unable to proceed to prepare any Estimate of the Expo nee of providing such building as may be nc-ceifary for depositing, in a proper manner, the said several volumes of Journals, Reports and Indexes.

Upon the whole. Your Committee have come to the following Resolutions viz.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That 1,200 copies of the first 34 volumes of the Journals, together with the Sessional Indexes thereto, and of the four volumes of Reports heretofore printed, should be

gradually reprinted in the proportion of about fix volumes in a year, by the appointment and under the direction of John Ley, Esquire, Deputy Clerk of this House.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expence which will attend the reprinting of the said Journals and Reports, may be estimated to amount to the funi of £.41,000, or about £.6,oco. per annum, according to the proportion mentioned in the preceding Resolution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion bf.this Committee, Thai it may be proper to print eleven volumes of Reports in addition to the four which have been already printed; together with a General Index to the whole fifteen volumes, of which the series will then consist; and that the impression of such eleven volumes, and of a volume containing such General Index thereto, should consist of 1,750 copies, and be printed in the proportion of one, volume in a year, by the appointment and under the di-re«5tion of the said Deputy Clerk of this House.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expence which will attend the printing of the said Reports and Index thereto, may be estimated to amount to the sum of £. 18,000. or about £. 1,500. per , according to the proportion mentioned in the preceding Resolution.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That such a number of copies of each of the volumes of the Journals, together with the Sessional Indexes thereto, from the 35th volume to the fiftieth volume, both inclusive, and of the four first volumes of the General Indexes, as will complete the number of copies of each volume to 1,200, should be gradually reprinted, in the proportion of one volume in a year, by the appointment and under the direction of the said Deputy Clerk of this House.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the Expences which will attend the reprinting of the said sixteen volumes of Journals, and four volumes of the General Indexes, may be estimated to amount to the sum of £.21,000. or about £. 1,000. per , according to the proportion mentioned in the preceding Resolution.

Resolved, That it appears to this Committee, That the ground on the East fide of Saint adjoin-

ing to the King’s Bench Record Office, and extending from thence towards New Palace-yard, might also rda space sufficiently large and commodious for ereifting a building thereon to keep the said volumes when printed.

Appendix, N° 4.

Warehouses, or Space, required for storing up, and accessible for delivery of, the Journals, Indexes, Reports, and Sessional Papers of the House of Commons. '

s p a c e.

One thousand copies of a volume of Journals generally take up a lpace of 6 feet determined by 5 feet, and in height about 12 feet.—The gross total lpace therefore for 1,000 copies of 50 volumes is about - - - 300 feet long by 250 broad.

DISTRIBUTION of the space.

A Building 150 feet long by 60 feet broad, of 4 stories, each 14 feet high, besides Garrets and Cellars, would contain 1,000 copies of perhaps 60 volumes, or upwards (besides recelles for odd volumes and smaller articles) piled up in flacks of 5 volumes bale, with Passages of 2\ feet wide between the flacks.

If the light comes in on one side of the Building only, the length should be greater and the width less; and such a form would be the most convenient for access.

It w ould also be most convenient, if the height of the Building were Ids, on account of the lifting and carrying up such weights into the upper stories; but in that case, the length of the Building nmft be Itill greater in proportion to the reduction of the height, and would evidently be unadvifable, except so far as it might make part of a huge Building principally intended for other purposes. I

SITUATION.

The Situation of the Building should be contiguous to, or not very distant from the House of Commons. The vacant or likely places which have occurred to me, are,

1. The Cotton Garden.

2. The spaee in St. Margaret's Street, between the King's

Bench Record Office and the Exchequer Offices, parallel to Westminster Hall.

3. The spaee 011 the North fide of St. Margaret's Church.

4. The old Houses, some of which are uninhabited and fall*

ing down, opposite New Palace Yard.—\ have heard that this fcite or island of Houses, or some part of it, wfas intended for a new Guildhall.

5. Weft cm Wharf, at the end of Abingdon freely In some

Outhouses on this Wharf were formerly kept several volumes of the Journals.

6. Thefcite of the ruined Buildings in Dean's Yard.

7. The vacant Ground in De/ahay-street.—This seems a

most extensive piece of Ground; the Freehold may be purchased; and is capable of being converted into other useful public purposes, of a firailar nature to printed Papers and Journal Warehouses.

But as I do not conceive it possible that more than one half of the whole impreilions of the aforesaid volumes will be on hand at one and the same time, a Building of half the above dimensions would be sufficient, were it not to be taken into consideration to provide room also to deposit copies of the various Bills, Reports, Accounts, and other Papers, printed in the course of every Session of Parliament.

Luke Hanfardy Printer to the 'Honourable the House of Commons.

A Petition of Colonel John Henry Loft, John Bates, Samel Alford, and Thomas JVardall, Burgesses of the Borough of Great Grimsby, in the County of was delivered

in at the Table, and read; letting forth. That on the 18th day of this inllant July, an Election was holden for chusing a Burgess to serve in this present Parliament for the Borough of Great Grimsby, in the County of Lincoln, in the Vox.. 58.

place of Ayfcoghe Boucherett, Esquire, who had vacated his

(cat by accepting a Stewardship of one of the Chiitern Hundreds; and that the original writ to the Sheriff, to deliver his precept to hold such election, was diipatched from London several hours before it bore date, by which means the precept was issued from the Sheriff, and proclaimed in the said Borough, at leaf! one day earlier than it ought to have been; and that Richard Nell, Esquire, the younger, the Mayor and Returning Officer of the said Borough, did ad partially and corruptly in proclaiming the election to be holden sooner than by Law it ought to have been, whereby the Petitioner, John Henry Loft (who was on his road to the said Borough) was deprived the opportunity of offering himself a Candidate for the Lid Borough, at which place he would have arrived in sufficient time if the said Returning Officer had given the proper notice, and not taken the Burgesses by iurprize, and proceeded to such election earlier than he ought to have done, to the great prejudice of the said John Henry Loft, mho would have had a very large majority of legal Voters; and the Petitioners John Henry Loft, John Bates, Samuel Alford, and Thomas War dull, for themselves and others, date, that they have, in conl’equence of such illegal conduct, been deprived of their legal franchises; and that on the said 18th day of July, the said Returning Officer, without being sworn, or even opening a poll, did proceed to, and did illegally, corruptly, and partially, and contrary to the usage of the said Borough, return the Honourable Charles An~ derson Pelham duly elected a Burgess, to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough of Great Grimsby, and that the said Charles Anderson Pelham, by himself, and his agents, managers, and others on his behalf, before and. during the said day of election, after the proclamation of the precept, and before his return, was guilty of bribery and corruption of the Eledors of the said Borough, to give their votes for the said Charles Anderson Pelham; and of attempting to bribe and corrupt the Burgesses of the said Borough, to give their votes for the said Charles Anderson Pelham, in order that he, the said Charles Anderson Pelham, might be elected, and returned a Member to terve in this present Parliament for the said Borough: And the said Charles Anderson Pelham also, by himselft his agents, and managers, and by other persons on his behalf, both before, and at, and during the said election, did, by gifts and rewards, and by promises, agreements, and securities for gifts and rewards, and by treating, and promises of treating, and by gifts, meat, drink, and money, and by promises of gifts, , meat, drink, and money, corrupt and procure, and attempt and endeavour to corrupt and procure, divers persons, being Eledors of the said Borough, to give their votes at the said election for the said Charles Anderson Pelham, in order that he, the said Charles Anderson Pelham, might be elected, and returned a Member to serve in this present Parliament for the said Borough: And that, by the aforesaid means, and by divers other illegal and corrupt practices, and by the partial conduct of the said Returning Officer, the said Charles Anderson Pelham was illegally returned a Member to serve in the present Parliament for the said Borough, in manifest violation of the rights and privileges of the legal Eledors of the said Borough, and in open defiance of the Law's and freedom of election; particularly of the Ad regulating the notice to be given of an election; the Ad to prevent Bribery and Corruption; and the Ad commonly called the Treating Ad: And therefore praying the House to take the premises into consideration, in order that they may obtain such relief in the premises, as to the House may feera meet.

Ordered, That the said Petition be taken into confederation upon Monday, the 26th day of September next, at Three of the clock in the Afternoon.

And the said Clause was thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the

Bill, by way of Rydg-, to prevent Surveyors making vexatious Surcharges.

And the said Clause was brought up; and twice read, with a blank.

And it being proposed to fill the said blank with a pecuniary Penalty;

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed.

Resolved, That the said Clause be committed to a Committee of the whole House.

Resolved, That this House will, immediately, resolve itself into a Committee of the whole House, upon the said Clause.

The House accordingly resolved itself into the said Committee.

Mr. Speaker resumed the Chair.

Ordered, That the Report be now received.

And the said Cla«cfe was read the third time; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

Another ingrossed Clause was offered to be added to the Bill, by way of Ryder, for providing. That in cases where Referees are appointed, if the Commissioners do not receive a certificate from the Cashier of the Bank, they shall proceed as in cases in which Referees have not been appointed.

And the said Clause was thrice read; and, upon the Question put thereupon, agreed to by the House, to be made part of the Bill, by way of Ryder.

A MESSAGE from His Majesty, by Sir

Molyneux, Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod:

Mr. Speaker,

The King commands this Honourable House to attend His Majesty, immediately, in the House of Peers.

Accordingly Mr. Speaker, with the House, went up to attend His Majesty; where His Majesty was pleated to give the Royal Assent to the several Public Bills following; viz.

An Act for granting to His Majesty certain Sums of Money out of the respective Consolidated Funds of Great Britain and Ireland; for applying certain Monies therein mentioned for the service of the year one thousand eight hundred and three, and for further appropriating the Supplies granted in this Session of Parliament:

An Act for repealing the several Duties under the management of the Commissioners for the A flairs of Taxes, and granting new Duties in lieu thereof; for granting new Duties in certain calls therein mentioned; for repealing the Duties of Excite on Licences, and 0:1 Carriages constructed by Coach makers, ant! granting new Duties thereon, under the management of the said Commissioners for the Affairs of Taxes, and also new Duties on Persons selling Carriages by Auction, or on Commission:

An Act for granting to His Majesty the sum of Fifty Tlioufand Pounds, for building Glebe-houses in Ireland:

An Act for settling and securing a certain Annuity on William Lord Amherst , and the Representatives of the late Jeffery Lord Amherst, in consideration of the eminent fer-

vices performed by him during his command in America:

arriving in tins Kingdom, or resident therein; and for establishing, until three months after the ratification of a Definitive Treaty of Peace, Regulations respecting Aliens arriving in this Kingdom, or lefiding therein, in certain cases:

An Act for repealing so much of an Act, passed in the fourth year of the reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the lighting the streets and places within the Borough and Soke of Doncaster, in the County of York; and for more effectually lighting, watching, and otherwise improvir.tr, the said Borough, and for preventing nuisances therein.

After which. His Majesty was pleased to make a most gracious Speech from the Throne, to both Houses of Parliament; as followeth; viz.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am at length enabled, by the state of public business, to release you from your long and laborious attendance in Parliament.

In closing the Session, I have the utmost satisfaction in expressing the strong lense which I entertain of that zealous and unwearied regard for the welfare and honour of your Country which has distinguished all your proceedings.

During the continuance of Peace, your conduct manifested the just view which you had taken of our actual situation, and of the dangers against which you were peculiarly called upon to provide; and since the recurrence of Hostilities, you have displayed an energy and promptitude which have never been iurpalied, in the means which you have supplied for the Defence of the Country, and for the vigorous prosecution of the War.

Your proceedings, in consequence of the late treasonable and atrocious occurrences in Ireland, will, I taift, have the eftlft of preventing any further interruption of its internal tranquillity; and of convincing My loyal Subjects in that part of the United Kingdom, that they may confidently rely on that protection to which they are so justly entitled.

In the midst of the deliberations, which were oqcafioned by the immediate exigency of the times, you have not been unmindful of other objects, to which I had directed your attention; and I have great satisfaction in observing that you have completed a system for consolidating the Duties, and regulating the collection and management of the several branches of the Revenue; and that you have

upon my faithful People: But I cannot sufficiently applaud that wisdom and fortitude which have led you to overlook considerations of temporary convenience, for the purpose of preventing a large accumulation of Debt during the continuance of the War. You may be allured that there shall be as drift an attention to economy on My part as may be confident with those preparations and exertions which will be bed calculated to frudrate the designs, and to weaken the power, of the Enemy; by whose arrogant pretentions, and redless ambition alone, these lacrifices have been rendered unavoidable.

My Lords, and Gentlemen,

I am fully persuaded that, during the ceflfation of your Parliamentary duties, you will continue to be actuated' by the fame spirit which has been uniformly dilplayed in your Councils. It will be your duty to afiid in carrying into eiil ft those important measures which your wisdom has matured for the defence and security of the Realm; and particularly to give the mod beneficial direction to that ardour and entiiufiasm in the cause of their Country which animate all dalles of My People.

Justly sensible of the date of pre-eminence in which it has pleated the Almighty to support us for so many ages arnongd the Nations of Europe, I rely with confidence that, under the continuance of His Divine Protection, the exertions of My brave and loyal Subjects will prove to the Enemy, and to the World, that an attempt to subvert the Independence, or impair the Power, of this United Kingdom, will terminate in thedifgraceand ruin of those by whom it maybe made; and that My People will find an ample reward for all their lacrifices, in an undidurbed enjoyment of that Freedom and Security, which, by their Patriot ism and Valour, they will have preserved and inlurcd to themselves and their Poderity.

And afterwards the Lord Chancellor, by His Majesty’s Command, said,

My Lords and Gentlemen,

It is His Majesty’s Royal will and pleasure, that this Parliament be prorogued to Thursday, the 6th day of October next, to be then here holden; and this Parliament is accordingly prorogued to Thurlclay the 6th day of October next.

By that Ad an opportunity wras afforded of disposing of those parts Kinds of Proof the property of the Crow n which were found to be lead productive, in proportion to their worth, and likely to be of much more value to the Purchasers of them, than they ever could be to the Crown, if retained.

With that view, and preparatory to the commencement of the Tales of property of this description, I presented a Memorial to the Treasury, Appendix, in which were distinguished, under nine different heads, the kinds of N° 10. (A.) property, which, according to my apprehension, fell under that description: These were as follows;

1. —Such Manors or Lordships belonging to the Crown as conlift of Manerial Rights only, or Manerial Rights and Quit Rents, without any Lands, or with very small quantities of Land belonging to them, and where the greater part of the Lands, over which the Manerial Rights extend, is the property of Individuals.

2. —Manors or Lands of which llis Majesty is not the foie Proprietor, but is entitled only to an undivided lharc, jointly with Individuals.

3. —Lands dispersed in small quantities, and intermixed with the property of Individuals, and lying remote from other property belonging to the Crown.

4. —Tythes belonging to the Crown, issuing out of Lands which are the property of Individuals.

5. —Mills.

6. —Fisheries.

7. —Ferries.

8. —Mooring Chains.

9. —Wastes belonging to the Crown, the possesslon of which has been usurped, or encroached upon.

(B.) perty comprised under those heads. From this Abstract it appears that the actual Increase of the Land Revenue, arising from that part of the property of the Crown which has been let or dispoTed of, under the new System of Management, is, in Rents and Dividends of Stock, £. 24,438. 2. 9. per annum, and £. 12,637. 3. 5. in Fines; besides what may be derived from Leases of Mines, and other property of uncertain produce, of which a proportion is referred to the Crown,

The most important of the Improvements stated in the Schedules annexed to this Report, has arilen from the Embankment on au Estate belonging to the Crown, called The Sunk Island, in the River Ilumber.

for 99 years, at the fame Rent of £.5. At his death the Eli ate de-volved to his Grandson, William Gylby, Esquire, by whufe exertions 1,560 acres had been embanked and divided into Farms, prior to the | year 1744.—In 1755, a third Lease was granted to Mrs. Margaret
