On the application made by the LelVees for the Renewal of the Lease, since the Act for the better Management of the Land Revenue was passed, I directed the Surveyor employed by me to survey and value the Estate, to report particularly, not only what was the actual Rate and value of those parts of the Island which had been embanked, but also what Improvement could be made upon it by farther Embankment, or otherwise, and at what expence. From his Survey and Report, made in 1797* R appears that the quantity of inclnfed Land in the Island was 1,561 a. or. 14P. no addition to the Embankment having been made since 1744; that the Outmar/hes contained 3,208 a. ou. 2 ip. which, together with the embanked Lands, were let to several persons for Rents amounting to £. 1,820. per annum; besides which there were Lands overflowed at the time of neap-tides, and of no value, containing 4,663a. ok. 23p. making the Total Contents of the Island, at low-water-inark, 9,432 a. u. i8i\ or nearly 15 square miles.

Ol the Outmarlhes, containing 3,208 acres, the Surveyor reported that 2,714a. 2R. 27 r. might be embanked, and that the proposed Embankment, with proper Drains and Sluices, would not only serve to drain those Lands, and prepare them for cultivation, but to impVove the state of the Land before inclosed. The expence of the new Embankments, and of the Buildings, Subdivision Fences, and other Works, necessary for completing this Improvement, was estimated to amount to £. 8,940. 18. and when these should be executed, it was computed that the Island would be of the yearly value of £. 3,441. 14. 8.

A proposal having been made to the Lessees of this Estate (the Re-

prelVntatives of the Family of Gylby) to grant a new Lease to them,

on the condition of their executing the Improvements suggested by the

Surveyor, they very readily engaged in the Work, and undertook to

expend not less than £. 10,000. thereon within three years, and to pay

a Rent of^.704. 2. 8. for the first year; £.2,090. for the second

year; and£.3,190. per annum for the relidiie of a Lease for thirty-

one years; and I have the satisfaction to add, that the scheme has

been executed with a spirit of enterprize and liberality highly creditable

to the Lessees, and beneficial to the Estate; that 2,835a. 2r. 371\

of the Outmarlhes have been embanked and brought into cultivation;

and fix new Farm Houses erected, besides several other Houses and

Cottages for Artificers and Labourers, and a Chapel for Divine Service;

in all which works, and in the making arid repairing of Roads within the Island, and communicating with the continent of Yorkshire, the

LelVees have expended not less than £. 20,000.; and there is every

reason to expect that the undertaking will prove very benclicial to

them, and that the Estate will revert to the Crown at the end of the

Lease, in a very high state of Improvement.

The Plans adopted, with the approbation, and under the authority Corenams for of that Board, for the Management of those parts of the Crown's Le ifes of Lane Estates which con/iit of Houses, were pretty fully explained in my tcs* former Report; but as few of the Leases of Land Estates had then come within the period of renewal, and as there are not many lubjects on which a greater diverlity of opinion prevails, or on which it is more difficult to determine, than on the nature and extent of the restrictions which it is for the advantage of the Owner of a Landed Estate, and of the Public, to put on the Occupier, I deemed it advisable to take as much time for the confuleration of a matter of lb much importance, as the circumstances would allow, before I ventured to submit to the Treasury the particular Covenants which ought to be inter ted henceforward in the Leases of the I.and Estates of the Crown.

The Memorial which I presented on that subject to the Treasury, is Appendix, given in the Appendix to tins Report; and, as I have therein pretty *6.)

fully shewn the grounds of the advice I have presumed to offer, I think it better to refer to that Memorial, than to lwell this Report by a repetition of its contents. I shall here only mention, generally, that the principles on which that advice is founded are, that the Leases granted by the Crown being commonly lor so long a term as thirty-one years, the Lessee may be considered as having a common interest with the Proprietor and the Public during the tirft twenty-one years, but that, during the last ten years of the term, the Occupier’s interest becomes different from that of the two-other parties: he may gain by exhausting the Soil, and therefore it becomes necessary for the lake of the Public, as well as the Proprietor, to restrain him, during the latter period, by Covenants that will secure and preserve the Improvements before made, for the permanent benefit of the piopr-rty.

In consequence of the authority given to the Surveyor General by plans for Im-the Lords of the Treasury, as mentioned in my First Report, to employ Architects to furnish Plans of such Alterations in the different Estate ia Lon-parts of London, in which the Crown’s Estate is situated, as might Jon. tend to the Improvement of the Property, the ornament of the Capital, and the accommodation of the Public, various alterations have been projected; but great difficulties have occurred in the attempts to carry them into effect, arising chiefly from the length of the remaining terms in some of the existing Leases. In all the instances in which Improvements of this naturejhave been proposed, the Ground Rents expected from letting the Areas for building, according to the Plans formed, far exceed the present Rents paid to the Crown for the Houses, and in some of them even those which the LelVees receive from Subtenants; but the remaining terms in the existing Leases, and other circumstances, are such as to prevent the Improvements from being carried into immediate effect; and the interejis of all concerned fuller by the delay.

These circumstances I represented in a Memorial to the Treasury*, Appendix* Submitting whether it might not be advisable that the Surveyor Ge- r.erul should be authorized to make proposals to the present LelVees of those parts of the Crown's Estate which are susceptible of such Improvements, to allow to those LelVees the whole or any part of the advantage to be derived from them, during the remaining terms in their respective Leases, provided they shall permit the proposed Improvements to be carried into cflect, with the approbation of the Treasury, mid under the direction of this Office.

Such an arrangement, it was obvious, must be for the advantage of all the parties interested. The Lessee would derive a profit from the Improvement, which he could not by any other means obtain, during the term of his Lease, and the difficulties arising from the termination of Leases at different periods, by which Improvements, so much for the benefit of the Crown, and the accommodation of the Public, are obstructed, would be removed, without depriving the LelVees of the fame preference for new Leases of any parts of the Estates, to which they might be thought to have a reasonable claim, as they would have had if no such alteration had taken place, and under new Rents to Commence from the end of their former terms.

The authority desired by that Memorial was given by the Treasury; and there is reason to hope that, by means of it, Improvements may be accomplished, which might w ithout it have been impracticable.

Fines were uniformly paid into the Exchequer. From that time, in consequence of more extensive works being carried on in that Department, Fines for Crown Leases began also to be paid to the fame Surveyors General; and, on an average, sums exceeding £.2,000. per annum, have been paid to them out of the Fines, in addition to the

| payments from the Rents. Finding, however, that the increase of the

! Rents, and other Improvements of the Land Revenue, since the commencement of the new Syftein of Management, afforded ample means of supplying as large an Amount of Payments to the Surveyors General of the Woods as had been drawn by them both from Rents and Fines,

| Appendix, I thought it my duty to propose that the Fines for Leases /hould in N" 19* (A*) future be paid into the Bank of England, and invested in the purchase I of Three-per-Centum Consolidated Annuities, and the Dividends be

applicable to the fame purposes as the Annual Rents of the Land Revenue, in the like manner as the Dividends of the'Stock purchased with the produce of the Sales of Fee Farm Rents, and of other parts of the Land Revenue, now are.

I had reason to know that the Commissioners of the Land Revenue would have recommended that the whole Consideration for Leases of Houses, for which alone Fines can be now taken, as well as that for Leases of Lands, should be reserved in Rent, if it had not seemed to them to be necessary to strengthen the security for Rents of Iloules, by taking a part of the value in Fine; and the necessity for paving those Fines to the Surveyor General of the Woods no longer existing, it appeared to me to be advisable that they should be applied in the manner most conducive to the object of increasing the permanent Income to be derived from the Land Revenue.

The Lords of the Treasury have approved of that suggestion; and

Though the stateinents annexed to this Report shew that a very which the Trea- great increase of the Land Revenue has been obtained, in consequence n certain cases. °* ^e change which has been made in the Syftein of Management, it is proper to remark that, in every case, in which it has been shewn that Houses have been built, or large sums expended on Improvements, by Lessees, at a time when no adequate term remained of the exiffing Leases for their reimbursement; the Board of Treasury has acted on the most liberal principles, by grauting such additional term, at Ground Rents only, as the circuinstances seemed to entitle the LeflTee to expect; and in no instance, that has come to my knowledge, has any

party suffered, in consequence of expences incurred in the confidence of obtaining a new Lease.

The further progress made in the Improvement of the Crown’s Estates, since the making of my First Report, tends to confirm the expectation held out to the Public by the Commissioners of the Land Revenue, of an important increase in the Income to be derived from this source. Objections to this Syfiem have, however, been strongly urged in a Ohjedions mad Memorial to the Treasury, subscribed by many persons of the highell ^rfTeeTof* ‘HoScsi respectlability, all of them Lessees of Houses in London, belonging to the Crown; in which Memorial they state the grounds on which they think themselves, and other Lefices of the Crown, entitled " to have M renewals of their Leases upon the payment of a moderate Fine, or " a liriall and reasonable Rent, in the like manner as Renewals of " Leases had from time immemorial been granted."

The Lords of the Treasury having referred that Memorial to the Proceedings on Surveyor General, and directed him to state, whether he law any ground tl

to recommend an alteration of any of the provisions of that Ad, I think it better, in a matter of so much consequence as the queliion, whether the new Syftein should be continued, or the ancient System restored, to insert the Memorial itself, with the Report upon it, in the Appendix, than to give any abridged account of what is Hated in those Papers, on either lide.

Appendix, No. 10. (A.)—To the Right honourable the Lords Com-

millioners of His Majesty s Treasury.

My Lords,

lx order to cariy into efieft the Provisions of the Act of the last Session of Parliament, cap. 60, relative to the Redemption of the Land Tax, charged on the Estates belonging to the Crown, it becomes necessary for me to submit to your Lordships consideratiun what parts of those Eilatcs may be most eligible and proper to be sold for raising a Fund for this purpose; and likewise to folieit your Lordships Instructions with respect to the mode to be adopted for ascertaining the value thereof, and acquiring, according to the directions of the Ac% the belt price which can he obtained for the fame.

In the arrangements to be made for this purpose, it is undoubtedly proper that the general Advantage and Improvement of the Landed Estate of the Crown should be kept in view; and it is desirable that such parts of the property should be selected for sale as are leaf! productive in proportion to their value, and such as are likely to be of more value to the Individuals who may be the Purchasers, than they can be to the Crown, if retained.

The articles of this description may, I apprehend, be comprised generally under the following heads:

1. Such Manors or Lordships belonging to the Crown as consist of

Manerial Rights only, or Manorial Rights and Quit-Rents, without any Lands, or with very hnall quantities of Lands belonging to them; and where the greater part of the Lands over which the Manerial Rights extend is the property of Individuals.

2. Manors or Lands of which His Majesty is not the foie Pro-

prietor, but is entitled only to an undivided share, jointly with Individuals.

3. Lands dispersed in small quantities, and intermixed with the

property of Individuals, and lying remote from other property belonging to the Crown.

4. Tythes belonging to the Crown issuing out of Lands which are

the property of Individuals.

5. Mills.

6. Fisheries.

7. Ferries.

8. Mooring Chains.

There is a ninth kind of Property from which, perhaps, a considerable sum might be drawn, and which it is extremely delirable to be able to dispose of without special Acts of Parliament; namely,

9 H those

thnfc parts of the W&ftos ludonging to the Crown, in Wales, the polTHlion of which has been usurped, or encroached upon, and the foil improved by Individuals; who, though they would oppnle any attempt of the Crown to recover the Lands, would probably confont to pay a good price for a confirmation of their Titles.

from the falc of articles of the above description, it is probable that a Fund may he raised iiillicient for the Redemption of a con-fojerable portion of the Land 'Fax charged on the other parts of the Land Revenue, without any material diminution of the preterit Annual Income anting therefrom.

In ascertaining the value of the Property to be disposed of, I apprehend that the nde prescribed by the Act for the better management oi the Land Revenue, relative to Eltutes to be granted by Lc-afe, must be adhered to in all cases where it will be found to apply; namely, that an actual Survey should be made by practical and competent Surveyors upon oath, where the value of the Premises is capable of b'bng afeertaihed by Survey. This, though not expressly directed by the Act for the Sale of the Land Tax, fecins clearly to be intended determined by that Claute of the Ad which empowers your Lordships to order any Exponrcs that may be necessarily incurred " for making Sur-" Tci/s oj the ilftates, or otherwise, in relation to the Sale thereof," to be defrayed out of the Purchase-monies arising from the Sale.

When the value is thus ascertained by competent Surveyors upon oath, where the nature of the property will admit of it, 1 humbly conceive that the Parties holding the Premises as Tenants of the Crown may be considered to have a reasonable claim* to the preference of purchase, at a rate to be fixed with the approbation of your Lordships, and which may be varied from time to time, as the fluctuation in the price of the Funds may render it necessary or expedient.

But in the case of Manors, and more dpecially of such as conlift principally of Manorial Rights extending over the private property of Individuals, and which have little or no Land belonging to them, and the value of which to the actual PolVelVor depends more on the degree of personal convenience arising from the privileges annexed to the Manor, than the pecuniary profit which it yields, it seems to me, that the best price is most likely to be obtained by means of the competition which would probably be occasioned by advertising the Sale of such Manors, and desiring that Persons inclined to treat for the purchase thereof would deliver Proposals in writing to the Surveyor General, dating the highest price they are willing to give for the fame; and therefore I submit to your lordships, whether that mode should not be adopted in the fule of articles of this description, unless

Sir,

THE Lords Commissioners of His Maj city's Treasury having had under their ronfub*ratinn your Representation, dated 14th of October lull, relative to the Sale of certain parts of His Majesty's Land Revenue, to raile a Fund for the Redemption of the Land Tax on the Residue, I am commanded by their Lordships to acquaint you, that they agree with you in opinion, that it will be desirable that such parts of the Property lhoukl be li lecied as are leaf! productive in proportion to their value, and Inch as are likely to be of more value to the Individuals who may become Pure halers, than they can be to the Crown, if retained; my Lords are therefore pleated to authorize you to dispose of Articles failing under the following general heads; viz.

I. Such Manors or Lordships belonging to the Crown as consist of

Manerial Rights only, or Manorial Rights and Quit Rents without any Lands, or with small quantities of Lands belonging to them, and where the greater part of the Lands over which the Manerial Rights extend is the property of Individuals.

J. Manors or Lands of which His Majesty is not the foie Proprietor,

but is entitled only to an undivided share, jointly with individuals.

Lands dispersed in small quantities, and intermixed with the Property of Individuals, and lying remote from other Property belonging to the Crown.

4. Tythes belonging to the Crown inking out of Lands which are the

Property of Individuals.

5. Mills.

6. Fisheries.

Crown should have a preference of Purchase, at a rate to be fixed with the approbation of this Board.

My Lords approve of your suggestion of advertising the Sale of Manors, and Manerial Rights, and think it will be proper that Persons inclined to treat for the purchase thereof should deliver Proposals in writing to you, dating the highell Price they are willing to give for the fame, unless in any particular instance my Lords Ihoidd think a Sale by private Contract should be deemed more likely to be for the advantage of the Public; and as it will be necessary in these cases that Rentals should be previously obtained of the Quit Rents of such Manors, and Returns of Courts held, and Fines, Heriots, and other caliial Profits, with Accounts of Commons and Wades belonging thereto, and such other particulars as may be necessary for forming a judgment of their value, their Lordships direct you to require Accounts of those particulars from the respective Stewards, to be verified on oath if required.

With respect to the Price to be paid for Articles of the 9th Ckfs, mv Lords approve of your employing an intelligent Agent to investi-gate the circumstances of the Encroachments, and to treat with the Parties under your direction, subject to the approbation of this Board.

My Lords depend on you to report to them, previous to a Sale, the particulars of every Treaty, and of the Property which is the subject of it;—the means employed for ascertaining the value;—the Expends necessarily incurred in relation to the Sale; and the net Sum to be paid into the Bank, to be inveded in the purchase of Three-percent. Annuities, in order that their Lordships may grant their Warrant to authorize you to complete the several Contracts, os directed by the Ad before alluded to.

Appendix, No. 15.—A SCHEDULE of ACTS of PARLIAMENT,

passed from the time of making the Surveyor General’s First Report to the Legislature, to the time of making his Second Report, for the Division, Inclosure, Drainage, Embankment, Improvement, and Sale of Lands, and other purposes, in which the Interests of His Majesty are concerned; and which were referred by the Right Honourable the Lords Commissioners of his Majesty’s Treasury to the Surveyor General of His Majesty’s Land Revenue, for his Opinion and Reports thereon, previously to His Majesty’s consent being given thereto.

My Lords,

BY the Civil List Art of Queen Anne, which was intended not only to rellrain the Crown from alienating its Lands in perpetuity, but to ettublish a better course of leafing the Estates of the Crown than was before in practico, the granting of Leases of the Land Estates for a longer term than 31 years was prohibited; nor could a lower Rent be reserved for any Estate than had before been paid for it, nor less than one-third of llic value in cases where no Rent had before been reserved: The rest of the value might be taken in Fine, but no , Regulations‘were prescribed relative either to the rate of Dilcoupt to V.0 L. 58.

be allowed in computing the Fines, or to the periods of renewing the Leases; nor was any provision made that the value should be alccr-tained by the Oath of a Surveyor. The practice of renewing Leases, whenever applications were made by the Lessees, was continued alter that Art was patted; and no covenants were inserted in the JU*aic3 reiperting the management of the Land.

Under a mode of proceeding lb loose and unguarded, few improve* ments could be expected; nor, if improvements were made, could the preservation of them be secured; and the income arising from the Rents and Fines was very inadequate to the value of the F.ttates granted.

To prevent the continuance of those evils, the Art of 1794 was patted, for the better Management and Improvement of the Land Revenue of the Crown. By that Art a very different system h$s been established; and though it is ttill allowed to grant Leases of Lands for 31 years, no Renewal of such Leases is permitted till within five year* of the end of the preceding term; the value of the Estates mutt be ascertained by Surveyors acting upon oath; and by an order of the Treasury, not more than 5 per-cent, is dedurted from the yearly value so. ascertained, in fixing the Rent to be paid by the Lettee for the term of the ne# Lease.

The new system of management established under this Art of Parliament has already produced a very confulerable increufe of the Land Revenue of the Crown; and is likely, if llcadily peififred in, to be attended with all the advantages and improvements which were ex* perted from it. It is obvious, however, that, as the Rents are now brought so much nearer than formerly to the artual value of the Land, as to lei Veil the expectation of advantage from a Renewal, some Covenants are nccettary to be inserted in the new Leases, to protect the property from wattes, and to render those improvements lasting.

Shortly after the patting of the Art referred to, a Memorial was laid before the Lords of the Treasury by me, propoling that some general principles should be established for regulating the pror ceedings in this department; but, as few of the Leases of Land Estates were at that time so near expiring as to be veiy soon renewable, I thought it right to postpone, for further consideration, the fug* getting of such Covenants or Restrictions on the management of the Lettecs as it might be advisable to insert: But many Leases of Estates of confulerable value having lately come within the period of Renewal, and some new Leases having been agreed for, it becomes now my duty to suggest what occurs to me 011 this important subject, and to call for your Lordttiips attention to it, that such Rules may be laid down for the direction of those who may hold this Office, respecting the Covenants which should be inserted in the Leases of Lands, as may be best suited to the circumstances.

In the Instructions given to the Surveyors employed by this Office to survey Land Estates, they are directed to set forth what Covenants they would recommend to be inserted in the new Leases, and to put such Rents on the Estates as they think them worth under those Covenants. From the value lb estimated, a dedurtion of 5 per-eent. is directed by the Treasury to be allowed to the Lettee in pofiettion, in ascertaining the Rent to be paid on a Renewal; and a term of 31 years has been generally granted. No doubt, therefore, can exist, as to the understanding between the parties,; and the Lettecs can have no right to complain of the inlertion of reasonable Covenants, or of their being obliged to fulfil them; but it is desirable to give as much liberty as can with safety be given to the Lessees; and the object of consideration is rather how little restraint it is necessary to require, than how much may with juliiee be infifred on.

That system of Hufkandry is in all respects the best by which, with-out'exhauliing the foil, and with the greatest profit to the Occupier, the most food or nourishment can be produced; or, in other words, the greatest number of people can be maintained. These considerations undoubtedly demand attention in this Country, in which, in the actual state of its population and agriculture, a sufficient quantity of food is not raised, from all the Land now in cultivation, for the fufte* nance of the Inhabitants; and perhaps, where lb great a public object is added to the inducement arising from private interest, this subject calls more particularly for the attention of those who are en* trulled with the management of the Estates of the Crown, than that of any other persons.

But though it may not be very difficult to point out what plan of management hitherto known or prnrtiied is, with this view, to be preferred, ttill it is to be considered that Agriculture, as a lbience, is yet in a manner in its infancy, and that much greater attention has, within these few years, been given to it by men likely to make ufclul and important discoveries in the methods of improving the different kinds, of foil, than at any former period: Care should therefore be taken not to insert in Leases, for so long a torm as 31 years, any Covenants which may prevent the Lettee from adopting such improved system.

Where Leases are granted only for ttmrt terms, the Owner and the Occupier have obvioutty opposite interests. As it is for the advantage of the one to take all that lie can trom the Land; without regard to the state to which it may be reduced by exbautting or impoverishing crops, it mutt be the care and endeavour of the other to prevent any crops from being taken which may tend to diminish the value of the

By the means now propos'd, I humbly apprehend that sufficient liberty will be allowed to the LeiVces to enable them to cultivate their Lands to the Left advantage, profiting by any discoveries which may Le made in the management of Land; and that the hftates will revert to the Crown, at the end of the Leases granted on those condition*, in an improved state, from which a further increase of the Land he venue may be expected.

But the term of 31 years granted by the Crown avoids that danger: It leaves to the Occupier sufficient time to repay himself for any advance of money on the improvement of the Land in the early part of his Lease; and, for much the greater part of it, he has a common interest with the Crown, it being for the advantage of both that the management should be such as to make the Land as produriive as possible.

During that early part of the term, therefore, few reltririions, I apprehend, can be necessary; and I would humbly recommend to your Loruships, tinder all the circumstances which have been dated, that, beffdes the usual Covenants for payment of the Rent and Taxes, and repairing the Buildings and Fences, Covenants to the following effect be infer ted generally in Leases of Lands belonging to the Crown:

I am aware that there are parts of the landed property of the Crown, which it will not be an easy matter to bring under such regulations as are here proposed.

Lessees, by whose Families Estates have been long held without any rellriclion, who have let those Estates on what conditions they pleased, and been accustomed to no controul, will not like to Inbuilt to Covenants, however necessary, for the improvement of the Land, or to penalties for the prevention of cxliaulting crops; but as there can be no security, except by means of such Covenants, that improvements will be made, it is certain that no prudent Individual would grant his Land for so long a term as 31 years without them; and they arc Hill more necessary in the management of the Estates of the Crown, which cannot have the advantage of being under the immediate insperiixm-of the Proprietor.

Taking the matter in a very general point of view, it is undoubtedly of importance to the whole Kingdom, that every part of it should be brought to the higheli state of cultivation of which it is capable; and no obllacle to its improvement should remain which it is in the power of Government to remove. Upon the whole, therefore, if there do exist circumstances which prevent the Crown from taking those means that arc necessary to make the improvement of any of its landed property as certain as it may be made in the hands of Individuals, the public interest would seem to require that Estates of that description should be fold, and the price invelled in the purchase of Three-per-cent. Consolidated Annuities, like the Fee-Farm Rents, and other unimproveable subjects.

If the general principle here recommended of felling all such Estates as would more probably be brought into the highest state of cultivation if they belonged to private Proprietors, than it they should remain the property of the Crown, shall be adopted by your Lordships, it will be necessary to have powers for that purpose from Parliament, which perhaps may be most easily obtained by having a Clause inserted in the proposed amended Ari for the Sale of Land Tax, to enable the Lords of the Treasury to fell such Estates as it might appear to them that it would be most advantageous to the Crown to dispose of, though the amount of the sums arising from such sales, in addition to those already authorized to be made, should exceed the price of the Land Tax to be purchased. It will also be necessary to determine what mode of sale is to be taken, whether by. public auriion or by making knowu the intention to fell, and receiving sealed offers, in the manner that has, in several inftunces, been pur-sued, or by private contract.

Little doubt can, I think, be entertained that the first is the most likely to excite competition; but, if, from attention to the Lcftees, the lust /hould le thought to be a more proper mode of proceeding, your Lordships will be pleased to fix the loweit price that the Surveyor General may accept of; and I submit to your Lordships consideration, whether it may not be advifablo that this should be regulated by a reference to the price of-Sttrck at the time of sale.

the improvement of the Property, the ornament of the Capital, and the accommodation of the Public; but that the Leases ut different portions of that Eft at:*, expiring at different periods, created obljacles to those desirable alterations; and I recommended to tluur Lordships that in all such cases the Renewal of Leases should be pc It polled, till Plans, to the satisfuciion of their Lordships, should be obtained from the moll eminent Architects, for the projected Improvements, so th.*t no future Lease might be granted incunliltent with the Plan that might be adopted: And, in answer to what I so tinted, a Minute of the Treasury was transmitted to me, dated 4th November 1794, in the following terms: " My Lords coincide perfectly m opinion with the " Surveyor General, that eminent Architects should be deli red to offer u Plans for the general Improvement of the Buildings on the Crown’* u Ellate; and that, no Lease should be renewed whichjs inconliih%ti M with the general Improvement.'

Appendix, No. 19.—(A.)

My Lords,

BEFORE the change in the management of the Land Revenue took place, under the Act of 1794, Fines were couliuntly taken on grunting Leufes from the Crown, both of Lands and houses. The' reloned Rents were, in general, not more than an eighth part of the estimated yearly Value of the Estates; and the proportion taken in Fine was, conleqiiently, about 7-Sths of the eltminted yearly Value: Yet it appears, from the Reports of the late Commissioners of the Land Revenue, that the net produce arising from the 1-8th in Rent, exceeded that which, according to the strunge fyfterri then pursued, ar»*le from the y-Stli parts for which Fines were taken.

From the Rents (as appears by the fame Reports) from the Ac-ceilion of IJis present Majesty to the year 1786’, when the Enquiries of those Commissioners began, various sums were paid to the Surveyor General of the Woods and Forests, amounting, one year with another, to £. 3,896 per annum.

The Fines were uniformly paid into the Exchequer from the earliest periods until the year 1772, when a larger supply of money being wanted for defraying the Expence of works in the Department of the Woods and Forests, than could be drawn from the Rents arising from the Land Revenue, the Fines were, for the rirft time, diverted from the Exchequer, and a part of them paid to the Surveyor General of the Woods. The average amount of the Fines so paid was £. 2,657. 16 s. per annum.

The Commissioners of the Land Revenue, on whose suggestions and advice the new course of Management was founded, recommended an entire change of system with regard to Fines for Leases. The purpose they had in view was, to render the Land Revenue productive of a tespectuLle and permanent Income, proportionate to the real value of the Property: instead therefore of hiking Fines both for Lands and houses equal to 7 *8th parts of the yearly Value, they recommended that no Fine whatever should be taken for any Leal'c of Lands, but that the whole Consideration for such Leases should be reserved in Rent; and that only one-third part of the Consideration for Leases of Hottfts should be paid in Fine, and the remaining two-thirds taken in Rent. Those Commissioners considered that Ertates in Land, improved as they probably would be, under proper Covenants in Leases for terms of 31 years certain, would afford ample security for the Rents which might be reserved for them; but that houses being of a periflmble nature, and not affording equal security for the permanent payment of R.en ts approaching to their full value, it was advilable, in order to flrerigthen the security for Rents of houses, that a part of the Consideration for Estates of that dele rip lion should he paid in Fine. Had the Rents of such Etlates however been considered by the Commissioners as l'ccure as those of Lands, it is within my own knowledge that the Commissioners would have advised that the Consideration for Leases of Houses should, likewise, have been taken wholly in Rent.

From the commencement of the Enquiry under those Commissioners, until the passing of the Act of 1794, in consequence of their Reports, the granting or renewing of Crown Leases was suspended, and as, during that time, no money could be received from Fines by the Office of the Surveyor of the Woods, there arose, as might be expected, a more than ordinary occasion for those Supplies which that Office had been accustomed to receive.

Though the new system of leafing the Estates of the Crown was well calculated to improve the annual produce of those Estates, the increal’e in the beginning was necesliuily How and gradual, depending, as it did, on the falling in of Leases, few of which were then expired, or very near expiring; and it would have been attended with inconvenience to have withdrawn at once the whole of the Fines from that channel, however desirable it might have been to employ them in any other way. Upon the revival therefore of the Proceedings for granting Leases of the Estates of the Crown, after the passing of the Act of 1794, Orders were issued from the Treasury for paying the Fines for Leases of House6 to the Surveyor General of the Woods, and these Orders have been continued to the present time. The amount of the Fines for such Leases granted, and directed to be granted, within that period, is £, 18,498.; the whole of which, excepting a ium of £. 2,015. applied towards building an Office for the Surveyor General of the Crown Lands, has been directed to be paid to the Surveyor General of the Woods.

But however necessary it might have been to continue the payment of Fines to the Surveyor General of the Woods, for some time after the commencement of the new course of Management, and before any jconliderable progress had been made in the increase of the annual Income of the Land Revenue, the case is now very different. It has been shewn that the average amount of Fines received by the Surveyors General of the Woods, in the 15 years next preceding the discontinuance of the old fyffem, was only £, 2,657. 16 s. per annum, and the yearly average since 1794 has been under that sum; but the amount of the Increase of the Rents reserved on new Leases granted, and ordered to be granted, and by Dividends of Stock arising from the Sale of Fee-Farm Rents,

And other parts of the Land Revenue fold (the Dividends of which Stock are applicable to the fume purposes as the Rents of the Land

Vol« $9*

Revenue) is, bcfldcs the Fines, £. 14,752. 15 e. per annum, being more than live times the average amount of the sums paid to the Surveyor General of the Woods from Fines.

This incroule in the annual produce of the Land Revenue affording | , a more than ample substitute for the supply hitherto derived from the Fines of Leases, and the necessity for paying them to the Surveyor General of the Woods no longer exiffing, it teems proper that they should be employed in the manner most confident with the principle of the present course of management of this branch of Revenue, and most conducive to the ubjett of increasing the permanent Incomt of it.

On this ground, I think it my duty to suggest to your Lordships the expediency of paying the Fines of Leases henceforward* into the Bank of England, for the purpose of inveffing them in the purchase of Three-per-cent. Consolidated Annuities, not to be transferable without the authority of Parliament, and the Dividends thereof to be applicable to the fame purposes as the annual Proceeds of the Land Revenue, in like manner as the Dividends of the Stock purchased with the produce of the Sales of Fee-Farm Rents, and of other Artieles formerly part of the Land Revenue, now are.

I have the honour to be, my Lords,

Your Lordships most obedient

and most humble Servant,

My Lords,

I ever to recommend to your Lordships to alter any of the provisions of

* the Ad alluded to; I have considered, with very great attention, the

i Memorial transmitted to me, which has been signed by many Persons

£ of the highest respectability; and I report as follows:

The Memorialids, who describe themselves as being Tenants of certain Estates held under the Crown whereon Messuages or other 'Buildings have been erected, represent, that their Leases were taken or purchased, by themselves or their aneeftors, under an expectation and

a confidence that the fame would be renewed upon payment of a [. moderate Fine, or a small and reasonable increase of Rent, in the

like manner as Renewals of leases from the Crown had, from time immemorial, been granted: That the Tenants of the Crown {iad been ' induced, by the expectation and confidence which such immemorial

usage had excited, to expend large sums of money in the substantial improvement of their respective Premises, with a view to permanent \ advantage to themselves and families, and a concurrent benefit to the

t Crown; that those improvements could not have been expected, if the

prospect of Renewal had not been relied upon by the parties making them, the term of Fifty years, to which the Crown was restrided in v granting Leases of Houses, being much too short to have induced the

Tenants of the Crown to expend the large sums which have been laid out by them in building; and that they were not apprised of the intention and object of the Legislature in passing the said Act, otherwise they would have represented against it, as being dcllnidive of the

' confidential compact which had fubfilled for ages between the Crown

and its Tenants, and by which the property of the Crown had attained its present unexampled prosperity:—The Memorialifls also (late their conception of the advantages which the Crown itself would derive from Renewals of their Leases at moderate Fines, and the usual Rents; and after putting several possible cases of extreme hardship and cala-mity, which may result to the Tenants of the Crown and their Families from a perseverance in the fyllem now in practice; and referring to the present (late of Renewals, few of which they suppose to have taken place, and those few obtained principally by persons of fortune; and declaring their conviction that the adopting a more liberal mode of Renewal for the Crown Tenants Svould, from the numerous applications which would be immediately made for Leases, produce a vast influx of money into the Treasury; they most humbly pray, that your Lordships will be pleated* to takethe provisions of the said Act into consideration, and to adopt such measures as may seem expedient for the purpose of relieving them from the hardships of the fame; or, in case your Lordships powers should be found not to be discretionary, 7

(as to the Rents or Fines to be imposed) that your Lordships would sanction with your approbation an application to Parliament, for modifying the terms of Renewal of that description of Ciown Lealea referred to in the Memorial.

But, though the prayer of the Memorial is expressed in those general terms, the kind of relief fought for is explained in the preceding parts of it; in which the long continuance of the ancient iyltein is hated to have formed a confidential compact between the Crown and its Tenants, under which they claim, " That Leases may be renewed " upon the payment of a moderate f ine, or a small and reasonable " increase of Rent, in the like manner as Renewals of \cafcs under the " Crown had from time immemorial been granted"

In order to bring before your Lordships, in the cleared manner, the etfed which would be produced by complying with this request, of returning again to that fyllem of management which had so long prevailed, it may be proper briefly to Hate to your Lordships some of the measures resorted to by the Legislature 011 this subject, which has been so often under consideration.

At the beginning of the lad century, an attempt was made, after long difeuflion in Parliament, to prevent, by the Civil Lilt Ad of Queen Anne, the wade and abuses in the management of the Crown s Estates, which had been in almost every age complained of. The avowed object of that Ad was u to increase the Land Revenues of " the Crown, and consequently to ease and lessen the burthen upon " the Estates of the Subjects of this Realm in all future provisions to " be made for the expences of the Civil Government " but it was found by the experience of nearly a century, that the provisions of that Ad were inadequate to the purpose for which they were intended; means had artfully been contrived for evading them, and defeating the proposed elTed; and little Revenue was derived to the Crown from a property of great value. An examination into the causes of this evql was called for; and, for that purpose, Commissioners were appointed by Parliament " to enquire into the date of the Woods, Foreds, and " Land Revenues of the Crown, and to fugged such plans for the " future management and improvement of those Estates, as they " should think bed calculated to render them mod productive and " advantageous to His Majesty and the Public." The performance of that duty occupied the sedulous attention of those Commissioners for nearly seven years; in the course of which they made feyenteen Reports to Parliament, the accuracy or fairness of which has not been called in question.

In those Reports, the errors and defects of that system of management, which had been the subject complained of, were fully displayed: Surveys had not always been made before new Leases were granted; and, when made, had not been verified by the oatiis of the Surveyors; Renewals had been granted whenever applied for:—Covenants were not observed One-eighth part only of the estimated value of Houses was taken in rent 3 and for the remaining seven-eigiilh parts a Fine was professed to be taken: but, as the Fines for new Leases were generally paid at a time when a great part of the terms of former Leases remained unexpired, and aDifcount w?as allowed thereon, computed at the rate of 8, 9, or 10 per Cent. Compound Interest, those l ines were very unproductive, indeed little better than nominal. It appears from the same Reports, that of the Total Value arising from Houses and LandEJlates, the seven-eighth parts taken in Fine amounted annually, on an average, to little more than the one-eighth part taken in rent, even after making allowance of Interests, on the sum actually paid as Fine, for the whole time of the anticipation; or, in other words, for the whole term remaining of the former Lease at the time of its payment; but if the Computation had been made on llouics and Land Estates separately, the Leases of Houses being for. Fifty years, and the Leases of Lands only for 31 years, and a much higher Rate of Interest allowed on the first than on the lad, the seven-eighth parts of Rent on Leases of Houses professed to be taken in Fine, would have been found not to have yielded near half as much as the one-eighth part taken in Rent.

In fa&, Renewals seem to have been obtained as soon as the Fine, computed in the usual manner, would produce enough to pay the Fees on passing the Leases, however small the pittance might be that was payable to the Crown in the name of a Fine; and it is dated by those Commissioners, in their 17th Report, that a Property belonging to the Crown, which, according to their estimation, might, under a proper system of management, be brought to yield an Income of £.400,000. a year, had, under the strange system which had been pursued, and after deducing what had been expended on the Foreds, Parks, and Chaces, yielded a clear Revenue of no more than £.<5,133* 4* 4^ one year with another, from the commencement of the present reign, to the year 1793, when that Report was made.

It appears, therefore, that if that property under the former system of management attained unexampled prosperity, as dated in the Memorial, a very small share of concurrent benefit had been enjoyed by the Crown.

The Commissioners found in the Proceedings for Renewals, under this loose and unguarded system, some forms which gave the appearance of the real value of the property granted being paid to the Crown; but those forms were ineffectual, and the appearance delusive.

The Commissioners did not conceive that the long endurance of a loose fyltem of Management, which admitted of such transactions, could be considered as having created a confidential compact between the Crown and its Tenants, or that it could establish any prescriptive right in those who profited by them to have them continued for ever. What they recommended therefore to the Legislature was, that every thing which feerued to be objectionable should, in the proceedings for all future Leases, be prevented; that Surveys should in every case be made, and certified by the oath of the Surveyor;—that Leases should not be renewed when more than twenty years of the emitting term remained. In conformity with the spirit of the Rules so elteblished, the Management of the Crown's Eft ate has ever since been conducted; and though it may be true, that, in some inltanres, the Surveyor of the Led be has thought the value put on property by the Surveyors of the Crown, acting on oath, too high, no example can be given where, on complaint thereof being made, and circumstanc.es tinted which were unknown to the Office Surveyors, but which were of a nature that ought to be considered in estimating the true and fair annual value of the premises, the Crown’s Surveyors have not been called upon to re-consider the valuation they had before made; nor can it be laid that I have, on any occasion, refilled to lubinit to the consideration of your Lordships any just Claim for more than the general Abatement, or that the Treasury has failed to give to such Claim a due attention, and to make in every such cul> a fair and adequate allowance.

It may not be improper to add, that the Memorialitis are completely miliriformed, in suppoting that few Leases have been applied for since the new system took place, or granted except to peopie gf fortune. The applications are numerous; many Leases have been granted;—in the lew instances in which the Lei lees have declined to renew on the terms proposed, other persons have, on the fame terms, readily accepted Leases. There are, indeed, instances of more having been olfered by others for Leases which the I.etlees had declined to renew, than had been required from them; and several emes have occurred of new Leases being brought to public Sale, and, on evny one of them that has come within iny knowledge, a considerable profit has been obtained determined by the Seller.

Perhaps the account I have given of the Proceedings of the Let if-lature, and of the Officers employed in the management of the Crown’s Kitate, may be too minutely detailed; but I thought that, in a in Jitter of so much importance, the llating the cale fully and di diner iy would be of far more utility than any opinion of my own, in enabling your Lordships to judge whether any alterations ffiotilii be made iii the provisions of the Act complained of by the Memorialitis.

All which is humbly fubinitted to your Lortifhipsi

The REPORT of Aaron Graiiam, Esq. Inspector of Convicts in the River Thames and at Portsmouth.

IN compliance with the directions of the Statute 42 Geo. III. cap. 28. requiring a Report to be made to both Houses of Parliament at the beginning of every Session, I have the honour to report to this Honourable House respecting the Convicts under my inspection, as follows:

That the said A cl was passed on the 22d of March; and His Majesty was graciously pleased to appoint me Inspector under it.

That, by direction of the Right honourable Lord Pelham, I went immediately to Portsmouth, and luperintended the fitting of the Captivity, an old sixty-fmir-gun ship, and the Portland, an old fifty-gun ship, as llulks, for the reception of Convids; and moored the former (where she now is) in Portsmouth Harbour, for the purpose of employing her Convicts in the Dock-yard; and removed the latter to Langston Harbour, that hcr's might be (as they now are) employed at Cumberland Port.

That a chaugc with regard to the Establishment of those Hulks took place on the lit of April, when Government, having provided the Ships before-mentioned, appointed Officers and Guards therein, leaving to the Contractor to supply, under my inspetiion, the Provisions, Cloathing, and Necessaries only, agreeably to a Contract entered into by him with the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury. When the Ships were ready, the Convicts were shifted from the old Hulks (then nearly in a sinking (bite) into them; and I made a Report thereof, and of all other my proceedings, to his Lordship.

At the end of the Midsummer quarter I went again to Portsmouth, and, having settled and paid the Accounts of that quarter, I made another very full Report to Lord Pelham.

In October I repeated my visit to those Hulks, and again made up, and paid, the Accounts of them to the end of September, which finished the second quarter on the new Establishment.

And I should, at the dole of the year, have made my next visit of enquiry, as directed by the Act of Parliament, but was prevented by indisposition, which, for several months palt, has (with the exception of some fiiort intervals) confined me to my room. I am, however, in a convalescent llate, and hope soon to be diffidently recovered to attend again to this very material part of iny duly. In the mean time, having settled and paid the Accounts of the lad quarter, 1 am enabled, in addition to what I have already-dated, to report, in conformity with the Act, to this Honourable l louse, as follows:

ill. That the said llulks are well and comfortably fitted. In addition to the common convenioncies of a Ship, they have each a capacious Hospital for sick Convicts, and a Chapel, wherein Divine Service is performed every Sunday with the fame regularity and decency as in any place of public worship on (bore. It contains conveniently the 7

whole number of Convicts; and has besides a Gallery for the Officers, Ship's Company, and Strangers.

'idly. That the behaviour of the Captain and Officers of the Captivity has, in every respect, met with iny approbation. Their treatment and care of the Convicts have been humane and attentive; and the Provisions and Cloathing are carefully and properly inspected by them, before they are approved as fit for the use of the Convicts.

But with respect to the Portland, 1 am lorry to observe it has been represented to me, that there lull cxifit irregularities on board her, which ought not to be in fie led; and if upon enquiry, when I go down,

I find it necessary, I shall report ihe Captain to Lord Pelham as unlit to be continued in the command of her, and will recommend a person better qualified for the situation to be his luccelTor.

At present I have the afhlhmce of the Surgeon of the Hulk, a very excellent man, who is well disposed to fee are the Convicts from ill treatment, by seeing them properly cloalhed, and other wise taken cara of with regard to their general health, in which he has been very iuc-cefslul; lb indeed has the Surgeon of the Captivity, who is also an able man, and particularly attentive to his duty. Their la.ll Reports date, that there are hut few sick Convicts in the Hospital of either Ship. This, cnnlidering the dreadful sickness which prevailed in the old llulks at Langston, immediately preceding the commencement of the new plan, and was no doubt, in a great degree, carried with the Convids into the Portland, is a gratifying circumltnnce, and reflects great credit on Mr. Moss, the Surgeon of that Hulk.

3dly. That the Convicts have been quiet and orderly; and I have the satisfaction to observe, that reasonable hopes may be entertained of an improvement in their moral conduct. Mr. Donne, the Chaplain, wdio is a devout man, most eminently qualified for his situation, dates in his Report, that they have during the last quarter conducted thern-selves, when attending Divine Service, with great decorum, and many of them with (trong marks of devotion; adding, in his Letter to me, that he is really happy to inform me he had an application iome time finer, addressed in very appropriate terms, and conveying lcntnnent* full of piety, and signed by fix Convicts on hoard the Portland, mid another from some very good men on board the Captivity, requeuing Inm to administer the Sacrament to them, which he meant to coinjoy with; and will repeat that part of lus duty on hoard both Hulks at proper intervals.

4thly. That the expence of the Portsmouth Pdlabl.foment, from if® lft of April (when the new plan commenced) to the 3ill ot December (including £.450 in lieu of interest for the nine months, at 7 * ppr" cent, per annum, upon £.8,000, which the two old Ships pc:h q>s might have been fold for, and JT. 2*21. 5*. three quarters of mV

And the Earnings of the Convicts at that place, for the fame period, according to an Estimate of the value of the daily labour of Artificers and Labourers, as settled at the Dock-yard and the Warren at Woolwich, and delivered to his Grace the IP.ike of Portland in July 1798, amounted to £. 6,679. 3. 3. which reduces the expence of providing for each Convict to £.0. o. 11 £,17. per day.

With regard to the Hulks on the River Thames, I beg leave to report as follows:

That they are in a very healthy state.

That Mr. Erskine the Overseer, and his Deputies, appear to conduct themselves with great humanity towards the Convicts, who, on their part are quiet and orderly.

That the Convicts are employed on ffiorc in the Dock-yard and the Warren at Woolwich every working day.

And, to afford them a better opportunity than hitherto they have had of attending Divine Service on the Sabbath, a large ship is fitting in the River with a commodious Chapel, upon the plan of those oh board the Captivity and Portland Hulks at Portsmouth.

That the expence of maintaining these Convids, from the lft of

April to the 31st of December, amounted to £. 10,586. 16. of. or £. o. 1. 4^,75. per day for each Convitf.

And their earnings for the fame period, according to the before-mentioned Estimate, to £*4,617. 15. 7.; which reduces the expence of providing for each Convict to £-0. o. 9 £,63. per day.

From which it would appear, that the expence of maintaining each Convict at Portlinouth (without deducting the earnings) exceeds the expence at Woolwich by £.0. o. 1 £,35. per day. This arises from the three items of—Interest, my Salary, and the incidental Expences alluded to-being charged in the Portlinouth Account, and with which the Woolwich Account is not burthened; but if these be deduced from the Portsmouth Account, the charge will be the fame at both places.

The value of labour too in the Woolwich Account exceeds in proportion the value of the labour done at Portsmouth. This is owing to the great fiekness on board the Ceres and Fortunee, which, for more than two months, retarded the (hitting of the Convids from those Hulks into the Portland, and for some time after they were shifted, prevented many of them from being sent on (bore to work.

/ All which is most humbly submitted to this

Honourable House, by

A. Graham,

William Irving,

Inspector General of the Imports and Exports of Great Britain.

Note.—In the Year 1607 certain Rates of Value were affixed to the several Articles Imported into, and Exported from this Kingdom; and, conionani to those Ehiinates, the Ledgers of the Inspector General’s Office are Dili kept, and the Public Accounts Hated accordingly.

By the Act of the 42 c! of His Majesty, cap 43. the Merchants Exporters are required to declare the Real Value of British Manufactures Exported, in order that the Amount of the Duty chargeable thereon may be ascertained; but, the Exports to Ireland, certain Articles tiled in the Fisheries, and Cotton Manufactures of all Descriptions, being exempt from Payment of this Duty, and consequently from the Declaration of the Exporters, as to the Value, the Inspector General therefore cannot make an Official Return to that part of the Order of the House, which requires the Difference between the Official Value and the Declared Value.

Affiuning, however, that Articles Exported to Ireland, or used in Fisheries, may be estimated at the fame Rate of V alue with Articles of a similar nature exported to other Countries, and that the Inspector General is correct in an Estimate which has with great pains been formed of the true Value of Cotton Manufactures exported; he thinks himself justified in Rating to Parliament, that the value of Britiffi Produce and Manufactures Exported from Great Britain to all Parts, amounted in the Year 1802, to £.48,500,683.

No Account can yet be prepared of the Value of the Imports from India and China, for the Year ending the 5th January last.

Note.—The Decrease'in the Total Value of Imports from all Parts, except the East Indies and China, in the Year 1S02, arofc from the Importation of Corn having been greatly dimimffied in that Year.

COPY of a CONVENTION between His Majesty and The United States of America;

signed at London the 8th of January 1802.

DIF FIC U LTIE S bavin*; arisen in the execution of the Sixth Article of the Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, concluded at London on the fourth day of November one thousand seven hundred and ninety-four, between His Britannic Majesty and the United States of America, and in consequence thereof the Proceedings of the Commissioners under the Seventh Article of the fame Treaty having been luipended, the Parties to the said Treaty being equally desirous, as far as may be, to obviate l’uch difficulties, have respectively named Plenipotentiaries to treat and agree respecting. the fame; that is to say, His Britannic Majesty has named for His Plenipotentiary the Right Honourable Robert Banks Jenkinson commonly called Lord Hawkesbury, one of His Majesty's most Honourable Privy Council, and His Principal Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs; and the President of the United States, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate thereof, has named for their Plenipotentiary Rufus King, Esq. Minister Plenipotentiary of the said United States to IIis Britannic Majesty, who have agreed to, and concluded, the following Articles:

Article I. In satisfaction and discharge of the money which the United States might have been liable to pay in pursuance of the provisions of the said Sixth Article, which is hereby declared to be cancelled and annulled, except so far as the fame may relate to the execution of the said Seventh Article; the United States of America hereby engage to pay, and His Britannic Majesty contents to accept, for the use of the persons described in the said Sixth Article, the funi of Six hundred thousand Pounds sterling, payable at the times and place, and in the manner following; that is to say, the said funi of Six hundred thousand Pounds lterling shall be paid at the city of Walhington, in three annual instalintiits of Two hundred thousand Pounds sterling each, and to such person or persons as shall be authorized by His Britannic Majesty to receive the same; the tirft of the said instalments to be paid at the expiration of one year, the second instalment at the expiration of two years, and the third and last instal-ment at the expiration of three years next following the exchange of the ratifications of this Convention. And to prevent any disagree-ment concerning the rate of exchanges, the said payments shall be made in the money of the said United States, reckoning four dollars and forty-four cents to be equal to one Pound sterling.

Article II. Whereas it is agreed by the Fourth Article of the Definitive Treaty of Peace, concluded at Paris on the third day of

September one thousand seven hundred and eighty-three, between His Britannic Majesty and the United States, that Creditors on either fide should meet with no lawful impediment to the recovery of the full value in (tolling money of all bona fide debts theretofore contracted, it is hereby declared, that the said Fourth Article, l'o far as respects its future operation, is hereby recognized, confirmed, and declared to be binding and obligatory on Ills Britannic Majesty and the said United States, and the same shall be accordingly observed with punctuality and good faith, and so as that the said Creditors shall hereafter meet with no lawful impediment to the recovery of the full value in sterling money of their bona fide debts.

Article III. It is furthermore agreed and concluded, that the Commissioners appointed in pursuance of the Seventh Article of the said Treaty of Amity, Commerce, and Navigation, and whose Proceedings have been suspended as aforesaid, shall, immediately after the signature of this Convention, re-assemble and proceed in the execution of their duties, according to the provisions of the said Seventh Article, except only that instead of the sums awarded by the said Commissioners being made payable at the time or times by them appointed, all sums of money by them awarded to be paid to American or British Claimants, according to the provisions of the said Seventh Article, shall he made payable in three equal instalments, the first whereof to be paid at the expiration of one year, the second at the expiration of two years, and the third and last at the expiration of three years next after the exchange of the ratifications of this Convention.

Article IV. This Convention, when the same shall have been ratified by His Majesty, and by the President of the United States, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate thereof, and the respective ratifications duly exchanged, shall be binding and obligatory upon His Majesty and the said United States.

In faith whereof, We, the undersigned Plenipotentiaries of His Britannic Majesty and of the United States of America, by virtue of our respective full powers, have signed the present Convention, and have caused the seals of our arms to be affixed thereto.

Done at London the eighth day of January one thousand eight hundred and two.

Hazvke/bury. (l.s.) Rufus King. (L.s.)

RESOLUTION reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider of several Acts, made in the last Session oi the Parliament ot Ireland, and in the 411! and 4‘id years of the Reign of His present Majesty, relating to the Revenue of Ireland.

RESOLV ED, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several and respective Duties of Customs payable upon the Importation of Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, into Ireland, and upon the Exportation of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, from Ireland, and the several and resperiive Drawbacks, Allowances, and Bounties, paid or allowed upon the Importation or Exportation of any Goods, Wares, or Merchandize, into or from Ireland (except the Drawbacks and Bounties, allowed by an Act of this Session of Parliament, on Sugar exported from Ireland) do cease and determine; and that the several and respective Duties, Drawbacks, Allowances, and Bounties, following, be paid and allowed in lieu thereof; viz.

A SCHEDULE of the Net Duties payable on Importation into Ireland of the Goods, Wares, and Merchandize, therein enumerated or described (not being the Growth, Produce, or Manufacture, of Great Britain) and of the Drawbacks to be allowed on the due Exportation thereof from Ireland.

REPORT from the Committee, to whom the Petition of the several Persons, whose Names are thereunto subsci ibed, being concerned in the WOOLLEN TRADE and MANUFACTORIES within the Counties of Someri'et, Wilts, and Gluucelier, was referred.

YOUR Committee have, pursuant to the Order of the House, examined the matter of the said Petition: To prove the Allegations whereof,

Statute 5 Eliz. c. 4. was read: And,

Mr. Edward Sheppard, Clothier, atUley, inGloucesterfture, upwards of 15 years, being examined, said, That if the said Statute was carried into effect, a very great part of the trade of the County of Gloucester must be loll, as a very great proportion of the Weavers at present employed have not been apprenticed—That in his own Manufactory, at one establishment he employs about seventy-five Weavers, out of which five only have been apprenticed according to the above Statute; that at the other he employs about eighty-three, out of which sixteen have been apprenticed; the greatest proportion are men, some are women. With respect to the Clothworkers he has not one amongst the whole who has been apprenticed seven years; he infers, that if none but legal Weavers were employed, he should lose the major part of his trade—That, notwithstanding the lnlrodtrctten of Spring Looms (which of late years have very much increased the number of Looms) there is not at this time any surplus of competent and good Weavers existing —So necessary is it that the number of Weavers Uiould not bedecreased, the coarse Woollen trade has already been, in a great degree, loft to the County of Gloucester, principally for want of Weavers to carry on that branch of Manufacture, lie conceives that a very short period of time (within a year) is necessary to acquire a proficiency in the art of weaving—That, by the change in the nature of the Woollen Manufactory, in consequence of Machinery, it has been and is necessary to form manufacturing eltaulishments in Villages, where the Advantages of Water and Fall are materially considered; therefore, in such situa-tions, apprenticed Weavers are not to be met with—That, in consequence of the great increase in the demand for Woollen Cloths of late years, a great number of people, of ever)’ description, have embarked in the trade as Clothiers, who have not been apprenticed, and therefore would, by the enforcement of the said Statute, be thrown out of bufi-neis; that he himself has never been so apprenticed, neither does he know any one who has; and he conceives it necessary for the wellbeing of the Woollen Trade, that the Manufacturer should, as occasion required, either from the opening of new Markets, or increased demand in old ones, have it in his power to employ such work people in c '-"v branch as may be requisite—That if Clothiers are refui&ed from tLt employment of workpeople who have not been apprenticed, an extcL'ion of their trade would be inpoftible on any occasion of extraordinary demand—That he believes it to be contrary to the fad, that the number of regular Weavers, able and willing to work at the arawent and usual prices, who are out of employ, is immense, or that their numbers are daily increasing; he speaks only of the County of Gloucester—That, from his own experience, the employment of persons, not regularly apprenticed to the bufmels of Weaving, does not tend to deiiroy the good quality of the Manufacture; that he has never known, or heard till lately, of any prosecutions for enforcing the above Statute—That the number of Apprentices has greatly diminished of late years, which he conceives to be the consequence of the present increase of the Woollen Trade—That, out of the number of Persons employed in both his establishments, he cannot exactly say what proportion are men to the women (as they work at their own houses) but a much greater proportion are men. That by the introduction of the Spring Shuttle, more Cloth has been made, which could not otherwise have taken place from the want of Weavers, as the operation of Weaving is now performed by one person, instead of two, to the great laving of the labour; it being a inealureof the Weavers own adoption, they are paid the fame per piece as before the introduction of the Spring Shuttles—That he gives no preference to apprenticed Weavers, but the very reverse, as they in general are old men—That, as the trade is now carried on, a great many persons are employed as work people, for their own benefit, at an earlier age than they could have been under the operation of the existing Statute, and that more women are now employed in weaving than formerly, in common with the increase of men—That it has not been the practice in Gloucester-shire for persons to be bound Apprentices in Villages (to which it is necessary to resort on account of Water and Fall) nor does he think legal Weavers could have been found to be transferred from one part - of the County to the other, sufficient to take the Apprentices; that he does not think any Apprentices would be bound on the conditions to the Woollen Trade generally, so as to be equally transferred irom one branch of the trade to the other, with those who are now employed as Workmen—That the repeal of the Statute requiring W eavers to serve A pprentice/hips, would certainly not prove miaous to the legal Weavers or their families—'That many Weavers receive work from different Matters, and have many Warps by them at the same time belonging to those different Matters, by which means the return of the work i6 very much delayed, and therefore the number of Weavers is

not in proportion to the quantity of Cloth required to be made.-----

5

Being asked. Whether any Prosecutions had been commenced, or threatened, under the aforesaid Statute? he stated, That there was a Prole-cution at the last Summer Affixes for Gloucesterffiire, but under what Statute he did not know, but he laulerstood that it was compromised by withdrawing a Juror—iie does not know that the Defendant did undertake that in future he would employ none but legal Weavers, or upon what terms, but he knows that a great many Notices have beeit given of Prosecutions against Matter Weavers since, and that Friendly Societies, or Clubs, have been formed with a view to commence Prosecutions against those who life or exercise the'Trade of a Woollen Cloth Weaver illegally: in confirmation of which, the Wit refs produced a Book, intituled, " llulcs and Articles of a Friendly Society, or Club, " called The Woollen Cloth Weavers Society, begun the 24th day of " September 1802; and also, Copy of an Advertisement infer ted in the " Gloucester Journal, September 6th 1802, " calling a Meeting of " One Weaver out of the Pavifh he represents, in order to determine " 011 prosecuting those who unlawfully exercise or follow the Trade of " a Weaver. Signed, Hhli.Jtjjup, Solicitor/'

Mr. Daniel Lloyd, Clothier, at Uley in Gloucestershire, 20 years, being examined, said, That the Woollen Trade would be injured if none but Apprentices were employed, and that they are not belter Workmen than the ordinary Weavers now employed, and that no preference is given to apprenticed Weavers—That he never recollects the Statute relative to Apprentices being enforced—That it is oftentimes necessary for the Manufacturer to have the power of transferring his Workmen to the different places where his huliness is conducted—Thathf does rot know of any Broad Weavers who are competent Workmen, out of employ; such Workmen could earn from 10s. to 12s. per week, on the old system, when two Workmen were en.ployed to eaah Loom; the fame Workman can earn from 185. to 21 a*, per weekp using the improved fyitem of the Spring Shuttle, oy which one Weaver only is employed in a Loom; the Spring Shuttle is not at present uni-vorfally ul>d, but at present he has full employment for all his con* petehL Workmen, with a prolpett of a greater demand for them—-That in his Manufactory the non-ap premised Weavers are eight partp out of nine, and of Cloth Drelfers hr has only one in thirty who bus been apprenticed according to the Statute of Elizabeth—That thf Poor Rates in his neighbourhood have not increased in consequence of employing illegal Workmen, but they certainly would be increased if the present Statute was enforced, by unapprenticed Weavers being thrown out of employ; that he has never been apprenticed to $ Clothier, nor dots he know any person in his line of business who liaSy according to the Statute; he docs not recoiled any other hardships in his Trade relating to Apprentices. And being asked, Whether he was aware of any combinations for commencing prosecutions against tin-apprenticed persons? he laid, that he and his Workmen have received menacing letters threatening to prosecute.

Mr. John Jones, Clothier, at Bradford in Wiltftiire, upwards of 20 years, being examined, said, That the Woollen Trade would most in* questionably be injured, if none but Apprentices were to be employed; that the Art of Weaving is by no means difficult to attain, it being customary for young children to he set in the Loom with their parents, and he conceives the Apprentices are not better workmen than the ordinary Weavers now employed—That he never heard of the Statute relating to Apprentices being enforced until lately, inGIoucestershire; that no preference is given to apprenticed Weavers; that he wa* never apprenticed, neither can he ipeak to any in his line of bulineu who has, according to the Statute of Elizabeth—That it is useful to the Manufacturer to transfer his Workmen to the different places where his business is conducted—That he believes people are now employed at an carlbu* age than they could have been under the existing Law; by the employment of Apprentices, many unappreutred Weavers would be thrown out of employment, particularly female Weavers, who may have been Parish Apprentices, and by the tenor of their indentures being limited for seven years, or until marriage, lcl-dom serve the term prescribed determined by the Statute of Elizabeth; he conceives there are about two parts Female Weavers out of five—That he cannot say exactly the proportion in his Manufactory of apprenticed to unapprenticed Workmen, but imagines the Weavers and Dyers to be about one-third part uuapprenticed ;, most of tine Workmen in the other branches are unapprenticed: that the uuapprenticed Weavers are equally as orderly as the apprenticed Weavers—That Spring Looms have been introduced in Wiltshire, but not in his neighbourhood—That the Poor Rates have not encreased in jiis neighbourhood in consequence of employing unapprenticed Workmen, but they would be very considerably increased, il the Statute in question was enforced, by throwing out of employ the unapprenticed Workmen—That his Workmen come from different Parishee to work, and return to iliofe Purishes to sleep; that in his neighbourhood he believes there is full employment for all Workmen, whether apprenticed or not, and particulurly for Broad Weavers, who, to hi» knowledge, have much

And being asked, Whether he was aware of any Combinations for commencing Prosecutions? he said, He knew oi several threats for that purpose in the Neighbourhood of Bradford; that he has seen a public Notice in the Newspapers, ligned by a Mr. Frampton, as Solicitor, that all Weavers unapprenticed in Bradford, Trowbridge, and that Neighbourhood, shall be prosecuted if they do not desist from working within a month from the date of such notice; and has also seen a Copy of their Articles, similar to those in Gloucestershire, with the addition of an Undertaking, on the part of Mr. Frampton, to be their Solicitor and President of their Meetings; and has likewise seen a Book of Rules and Orders of the Cloth Workers or Shearmen, printed in the year 180*2, which declares, that after the Date of their Rules, all Apprentices shall be deemed illegal who have not been apprenticed seven years.

Mr. Abraham Lloyd Edridge, Clothier, at Chippenham in Wilt-shire, 25 years, being examined, laid, That the Woollen Trade would certainly be injured, if none but Apprentices were employed; and that the manufacture of l'uperfine Broad Cloth, in the Town wherein he reftdes, has increased within his memory two-fold; consequently the Weavers in that place have not been futlicient to weave the work, and that he has drawn l’upplies of hands from nine and ten miles distance —That in his Manufactory lie thinks the proportion of apprenticed to unapprenticed Workmen, to be two-thirds of the Weavers, but cannot speak with accuracy;
