Mr. Thomas Joyce, Clothier, at Freshford in Somersetshire, 23 years, being examined, said, That the Woollen Trade would certainly be injured it none but Apprentices were employed—That his Workmen are about one-sixth part apprenticed, the rest are unapprenticed; thab the Apprentices are not better Workmen than the ordinary Workmen now employed—That he never knew till within these few * months any Prosecutions under-the Statute relative to Apprentices; that no preference is given to apprenticed Workmen—That it is elsentially useful to the Manufacturer to have the power of transferring his workmen to the different places where his business is conduced; that all the Work People in his Neighbourhood, from the age of seven years to seventy, both male and female, are employed, and he Employs as many women as men; that children are now employed at an earlier age than they could have been under the existing Law, in consequence of Machinery, and that the art of Weaving is not at all difficult to attain—That he has never been apprenticed, and only knows ot one in his line of business who has for seven years, and three others for five years—That he does not know what is the difference between the proportion of apprenticed and unapprenticed \\ cavers employed when he commenced business, and at the present time—That the Poor Rates in his Neighbourhood have not increased in consequence of the employment of unapprenticed Workmen, on the contrary, they are much ietfened; but would very considerably be increased if the present Statute was enforced, by unapprenticed V\ orkmen being thrown out of employment, and there is now full employment for all descriptions of Weavers in his Neighbourhood— That he does not use the Spring Shuttle, hut it was introduced about two years ago by a Person who had been in the North of England to work; he worked with it only a fow weeks, on account of the riotous VoL. 5#.

Mr. Daniel Llovd, being again examined, said, That he makes use '-----

of the Gig Mill, but cannot lay whether the Gig Mill, now in use in Gloucestershire, is the lame as that described in the above Statute; that since their introduction the Cloths are generally better made.

He manufactures no Fancy Cloths—that die trade has increased in those places where Gig Mills are used to a great degree; the Gig Mill is used in the drolling of Cloth; the ancient mode was, as is now understood, to have been by hand.

Mr. John Wallington, Clothier, at Stinchcombe in Gloucestershire, upwards of 30 years, being examined, said, That he knows only of one Gig Mill now in use, and is not applied for the purpose which is described in the Preamble of the Stat. 5 & 6 Edw. VI. namely, for perching and burling of Cloth. The Gig Mill in Gloucestershire is applied only for the purpose of rowing and moling of Cloth; if it was to be used for burling of Cloth, it would be highly injurious to the fabric, but it is found to be highly beneficial in the rowing and dressing of Cloth; at present the Gig Mills are equal to every good purpose in the rowing and dr effing of Cloth; although the Gig MiH is not used for perching and burling, yet it is capable of being so used. But perching and burling mean different things in different Counties: In Gloucestershire it is an operation performed before the cloth is fulled or milled; in Wilts, the term is used in dressing Cloth after being milled: Cloth, before it is milled, is open and loose, re-fembling flannel; after being milled, it is firm, and of the nature of Felt, and capable of resisting any impression necessary for the dressing of Cloth, it is certainly not for the interest of any Manufacturer to perch and burl Cloth by the Gig Mill, on the contrary, what he would wish to avoid; the Workmen in Gloucestershire would be very unwilling to have them difuled. The Gig Mill does not necessarily ltrain the Cloth more than dressing it by hand; it has a power within \ itself, capable of regulating the force so as to dress Cloths of the moll delicate fabric—That during his experience Spanish Wool has risen 100 per-cent. He uses no English Wools—That the increase of wages has been 100 per-cent, in the Clothworking Branch; and that the increase in the Price of Cloth has been an advance of about 30 per-cent.—That the use of Machinery, principally, is the re&fon in his opinion, that the Prices of Cloth have not increased in the fam* ratio with the Prices of Labour, and the raw material used in the Manufacture—That the introduction of Machinery, in its commencement, did not occasion Persons to be turned out of work in Gloucestershire, other Employment having been tound for those Persons in the Branches where Machinery has been uled; the Woollen Trade of Gloucestershire, during the period of the latt War, certainly could not have been carried on without Machinery—That it the Gig Mill was abolished, the Poor Rates would be much increased—The Cloth made by the Gig Mill now in use is by no means "deceitfully made;" if it was applied to the burling of Cloth, it might, but that is the abuse, not the use of it.—And being asked, Whether he did not conceive himself liable to Prosecutions for uling the Gig Mill under the Stat. Edw. VI. ? he said, He thought he might be liable, and that is the general opinion of the Trade of Gloucestershire.

Mr. John Wanfev, Factor in London, Seller of Cloths near 30 years, being examined, said, That as far as his experience goes, the Cloth drolled in the Gig Mill is the most acceptable in the Home Markets; the reason is, it is foster and mellower, likewise more accurate, and that he can execute his orders with more uniformity than if the Cloth was drelled by hand. Th? Gig Mill likewise renders it more acceptable in Foreign Markets; for instance, some years ago he sent specimens of both kinds of dressing to a Correspondent in Russia, desiring him to select those he approved of most, and to give him (the Witness) the numbers; accordingly he selected about ten, desiring him in future to adhere to that quality; and they were all dressed by the Gig Mill—That he has frequently sent down Cloths to be redrested by the Gig Mill, after he found them unfaleable when, dressed by hand.

Mr. Henry Dyer, Clothier, at Wootton-under-Edge in Gloucestershire, being examined, said, He has been a Manufacturer of Medley Cloths 20 years—That he has used the Gig Mill about ten years, prior to which he dressed by hand; that the Cloths have been very much improved by the Gig Mill, and he believes they have a preference over the Cloths of Wiltshire; Uiat when he dressed by hand he had always a flock of Cloths by him, which at present is quite the reverie, and that his trade has considerably increased in consequence of the new mode of dressing, and which would be most materially injured by abolishing the Gig Mill; that he can now supply his orders more quickly by the use of it; and that there is now full employment for all the Clothworkers in his Neighbourhood—That since the introduction of Machinery, there is much more work for the women and children in the villages than formerly; that upon the first

introduction of the Gig Mill, he was not under the necessity of turning away any of his Workmen, neither did any turn themselves away; that if the Gig Mill is properly used, there will he no greater ft refs or draining of the Cloth to as to injure it.—And being asked, Whether there were any Combinations of difeohtented Persons relative to the Gig Mill in his Neighbourhood? he laid, lie was not aware of any in the County.

Mr. Abraham Lloyd Edridge, being again examined, said, That he has used the Gig Mill three years, and that it is not necessary to strain the Cloth more by being drested by it than by hand, but that in every procels it is necessary to strain the Cloth, in a certain degree, to keep the Cloth true and even on its lurfnee; that in the dressing of 1,000 Cloths by the Gig Mill, each Cloth is (trained no more than one yard in twenty—That since the introduction of the Gig Mill, his trade has much increased, and he has not had it in his power to supply the demand for his Cloth in the London Market.

Mr. Edward Sheppard, being again examined, said, That he uses the Gig Mill, but not for perching and burling the Cloth, as it would be injurious if so used; he uses it only for the rowing and mofing of Cloth—That the greater stress or (training of the Cloth, under the operation of the Gig Mill, does not injure the Cloth; that Cloth may be strained without injury about one-twentieth part; that he never had any Cloth rowed wholly by hand, but conceives about three-fourths of labour will be saved by the use of the Gig Mill; the difference in the expence between mofing and rowing any given quantity of Cloth by hand and the Gig Mill, is about one-half less by the Gig Mill—That the Gig Mill has been used in Gloucestershire as long as he can remember, and he does not know of any people wanting work; that if it was not used he could not carry on his business; that the Cloth Trade has increased in those Districts where the Gig Mill is used to a very great extent indeed, and that the trade of Gloucesterftiire has increal'ed, to the prejudice of Wilts and Somerset—That in the rowing of Cloth by the Gig Mill, the Cloth is not " impaired," or w deceitfully madebut that an injudicious mode of managing any part of the manufacture of Cloth may be injurious.—And being asked, Whether he conceived himself liable to Prosecutions under the Statute respecting the Gig Mill? he said, He did.

The original Sub-(cription was for the Prosecution of the Rioters of the Weft of England, and afterwards, by desire of the Committee of Manufacturers, was agreed to be applied towards the Expences of the Petition, by all, I think, except the Houses of Stretfield and W ell, and Charles Brurif-don—'1 hat he has no doubt, that a Trade is more easily removed if carried on by Machinery, as it requires but a few skilful people to con-dud it; whereas the Woollen Manufactory carried on l'olely by hand, requires a whole did net to be long and regularly trained to the business —That he isv clearly of opinion, that if Machinery was laid aiide, that there would not have been found Hands enough to manufacture any thing like the quantity of Cloth that has been wanted for Home and Foreign Consumption.

Charles Brooke, Esquire (a Member), Basinghall-street, Merchant, being examined, laid, That the nature of his business is chiefly in the Sale of Spanish Wool and.Superfine Cloth.—And being asked, Whether he had any information to give respecting the Petition of the Clothiers for the; repeal or alteration of divers Statutes? he said, That he conceived it would be materially detrimental that any Laws should be repealed which tend to protect the Labourers in the different branches of the Manufactory—That it appeared to him that extreme caution will be necessary in repealing certain reltriCtive acts, of which the Manufacturers justly complain; that others which tend to protect the Labourers, be not blended in that repeal—That at one period of the War, he believes between 1797 and 1799, from the scarcity of Spanish Wool, the Labourers could not be employed in the Manufacture of Superfine Cloth; and at that period a great number of the Manufacturers enrolled themselves in the Militia, and entered in the Army. Subsequent to that period, the large importation of Spanish Wool, and confulemble orders for Cloth, called for the increased introduction of Machinery; and that he conceives, at the present period, those Men who have retnnied to the Clothing Towns, and are capable of reluming their

employment, should have that given them before any further addi-j tions are made to Machinery; that those Men should, he conceives, in every degree, be protected at this period, when offers are made to induce Manufacturers to quit the Country, in order to establish the Manufacture in Spain with all the advantages to be derived from Machinery. That it is a fact within his own knowledge, that a Manufacturer who is competent to introduce and establish the Manufactory, on the footing in which it is conducted in this Country, may have 1,000 guineas per Annum secured to him for a certain number of years, or a portion of the advantages to be derived from the Manufactory, at his option. That as a case in point with the Court of Spain, and to shew the good faith they have preserved, under fnnilar circumstances, with other Manufacturers, some years fmee, about the year 1780, a Tanner was induced to go to Spain, and was offered by that Government every facility to ei'tablish his business on a large scale; he Itated, that a large capital would be necessary; which was furnished him, the Witness believes, to the amount of ^.60,000; that a proper situation would be necessary to establish the business, and he was desired to travel the country, and to fix on any situation most likely to answer the purpose; that he was in conl'equence put in poll'elTion of a convent, at a short dilhmce from Seville; the Friars of the Order of St. Jago were removed to a different situation, to make room for the Labourers he thought necessary to bring from England; that nearly 40 English families did in consequence settle there, protected in their religious principles, and allowed every requisite for their comfort and convenience; and that this establishment has so far succeeded, that the Export of Tanned Leather, which at that time was very considerable, is now reduced to a very inconlidcrable quantity.—To shew how much interested Spain is in the cliablishment of the Manufacture of Woollen Cloth on the principle in which it is conducted by Machinery, it mud be observed, that the Raw Material, namely, Spanish Wool, can be procured at One-third less than here; and that Oil and Soap, two other material articles in the Manufacture, may be obtained at very little more than half the cod in this Country; and consequently, if our Labourers, from want of employment, are driven to seek that in another Country which they are deprived of here, we mud naturally lose our Foreign Trade for this article of Superfine Cloth, which can be rendered so much cheaper in Spain—That without the introduction of Machinery into Spain, he conceives it impraClicable for them to rival this Country in the manufacture of Cloth—That if Machinery was established in any other Country, this Country could not support a competition in the Foreign Market—That he has heard from the Report of Manufacturers themselves, that Persons are out of employment in consequence of the use of Machinery, hut does not know it as a fact—That he has never publickly pledged himself to use his endeavours to prevent the further introduction of Machinery. He never had any communication with the Labourers in any branch of the Manufacture—That he cannot date particularly as to those Restrictions of wdiich the Manufacturers judly complain, but they are those which preclude the Exportation of unfliom Cloth, and as to the meufuring and folding of Cloth, and others.

Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, in the Autumn of 1803;

By Tiiomas Telford, Civil Engineer, Edin. F. R. S.

My Lords;

tN reporting upon the Survey I made in Scotland, in obedience to thfc InstruXions I had the honour of receiving from your Lordships, dated the first of July 1802, 1 find the business may be most conveniently arranged under the following Heads:

L What regards rertdering the intercourse of the Country more perfect, by means of Bridges and Hoads.

Ascertaining various circumstances relative to the Caledonian Canal, especially with regard to the Supplies of Water on the Summit Level, and the best Communications from this Canal to the Fishing Locks at the back of the lile of Skye. The Means of promoting the Fisheries on the East and West C calls.

The causes of Emigration and the Means of preventing iri Improving the means of Intercourse between Great Britain and the Northern Parts of Ireland, particularly as to the Bridges and Roads between Carliflt* and Port Patrick, and also the Harbour of Port Patrick.

Under each of those Ilnids are comprehended subjects highly de-serving the attention of Government; the more they are invelligated, the more important they will appear, and the Public will become mote fully convinced that the general lnlmTts of the British Empire are extensively conneXed with the several Improvements which are mentioned in your Lordships InstruXions.

Of BRIDGES and ROADS.

THE obstacles which at present obstrud the Communications in the North of Scotland are numerous and well known, not only to the Inhabitants, but to every Person who has travelled through, or even enquired into the State of the Country.

Previous to the year 1742, the Roads were merely the tracks of Black Cattle and Horl'cs, interceded by numerous rapid Streams, which being frequently swoln into torrents by heavy rains, rendered them dangerous or impatlable. The Military Roads, which w'ere formed febout this time, having been laid out with other views than promoting Commerce and industry, are generally in such directions, and so inconveniently ftcep, as to be nearly unfit for the purposes of civil life; told in those parts where they are tolerably accessible, or where Roads have fmee been formed by the Inhabitants, the use of them is very touch circumscribed from the want of Bridges over some of the principal Rivers.

The general connexions of the Country may he dated as leading frertn Edinburgh to the North and North-welt Counties, by means of one Road through the Highlands, and by another along the East Coast and South Shore of the Murray Firth to the Town of Invemefs, and from

thence through Beanley and Dingwall, to Tain in Rofsshire. From Glasgow and Greenock, the communications by land are through Argyleshire, to the Western parts of Inverness and Rofsshire, and to the Shores oppoflte the whole of the Hebrides. There is an important communication from Inverness Westward, across the Country to Fort Augustus and Fort William, and from Fort Augustus there are just the vestiges remaining of what was once a Military Road to Bcrnera, oppoflte the back of the Isle of Skye.

In considering these lines of Roads, it appears most regular to begin on the borders of the improved Country, and near to the feats of Commerce and industry. In proceeding from Edinburgh Northwards, by the East Coast and Murray Firth to Inverness, or through the central Highlands to the same place, and from thence to Tain on the Dornoch Firth in Rofsshire, we find the communications intercepted, and learn that accidents frequently happen from the want of a Bridge over the River Tay at Dunkeld in Perthshire, another over the River Spey at Fochabers in Bamlfshire, a third over the River Beanley in Invernefsshire, and a fourth over the River Conon, near Dingwall, in Rofsshire. These Rivers are large, and at present are all crofted by means of Ferry-boats.

At Dunkeld the River Tay is deep and broad, and there is reason to expex the Foundations will be expensive, the bed of the River at and for a great distance above and below the Town being composed of alluvial earth and gravel. The best situation for a Bridge is a little way above the lower Ferry; at this place there is a strait reach of the River, and in Winter the ice is broke by passing over a Ford nearly oppoflte the mouth of the River Bran. This situation will also conned with the improved lines of Road which are proposed to be made on each side of the River. It is probable that a flat Rubble-ftofne will be got near the Slate Quarries, which are within a short distance of the place. Freeftone of a durable quality is to be had near Dundee; it -may be brought by water-carriage to Perth, and from thence by land to Dunkeld.

Under all these circumstances the Expence would be considerable, and taking into account the uncertainty of the Foundations, the Amount cannot be stated at less than £. 15*000.

The two Ferries which are now at Dunkeld belong to his Grace the Duke of Athol; he has authorized me to state, that if Government will defray One-half the Expence of a Bridge, that he will advance the other Half; that he will give up his Interest in the Ferries, if in lieu thereof a reasonable Tbll be put upon the Bridge, in order to liquidate the capital advanced by the Duke; after this has been accomplished, with a small surplus to answer the Repairs, the Bridge; ever after to remain free of Toll.

This seems a very reasonable and just mode of defraying the Expence; the safety and accommodation would be so great, that no Pertbn travelling that Road could object paying the lame Toll for a

safe and convenient Bridge, which at preH-nt is paid for a dangerous

and inconvenient-l’erry-boat, especiulLy when there will be a certain prospect ot having a Bridge free of Toll in a few years.

This Bridge is of the first importance to the central Highlands; it would accommodate a great District of that Country, and at the same time facilitate the communication with the North Highlands,

Hirer Spey. The River Spey is also rapid and deep, being the drain of a great extent of ihountainous Country, where there is much rain. It is of course a very dangerous Ferry. This Feiry is on the great Coatt Road Eastward from Inverness and Fort George, through the Towns and culthated Country in Murray and Bamtlshires, from whence it palies through Frazerbtirgh and Peterhead to Aberdeen.

Another branch of Road also bribes off Fochabers on the Spey, and palles determined by Huntley and Inverary to Aberdeen.

The nereftity of having a Bridge over the Spey at this place became so urgent, that his Grace the Duke of Gordon began a Subscription in the adjacent Country, in order to raise a part of the Money necessary to defray the Expence of a Bridge; his Grace let a liberal example, and it has been followed by mod of the Gentlemen in that part of the Country, in consequence of this exertion, a Contract has been entered into, and feme flops have been taken towards carrying this useful Work into execution; but unless Government will grant an Aid-equal to One-half the Expence, the Works mult shall be left unftnithed, and unlit for the pur poles intended.

The fitualion fixed upon for this Bridge is adjacent to the Ferry and Town of Fochabers. At this place a Rock patios quite through the River, at about from eight to ten feet below the surface of ordinary low water; and, as far as I could learn, it is the only place, unless at a great dilrunce up the Country, where the Rock pastes quite through the River. On these accounts it was judicious to prefer it for the situatioiT of the Bridge, and it was fortunate this happened preeilely in the line of the prefrnt Road.

As One-half of the Expence will be rnifed by Subscription in the Neighbourhood, if Government will defray the other Half, I under and it is proposed, that the Bridge shall be free of Toll. The Expence. cannot be Hated at less than £. 12,000.

I have made Rians and Sections for both those Bridges. On account of their being so nearly connected with the feats of the two before-mentioned Noblemen, I have introduced more decorations than what are ubfolutely necessary for common Road Bridges. This extra Expence will not amount to much; but, whatever it is, I propose it shall be defrayed by those Noblemen.

I, last year, produced Plans and Estimates for the Bridges over the Rivers Beanley and Conon; I have again examined the proposed fixations, and perceive that, on account of the uncertainty of the Foundations, and the alteration which must be made in some parts of the beds of . the Rivers, it will be necefiliry to take the Expcitccs of each Bridge at Five instead of Four Thou fund Pounds.

These two Bridges are greatly wanted in order to facilitate the Communications with Rulsshire, Sutherland, and Caithness; they are equally so for the North-wed Coast of the main Land and the Northern parts of the Hebrides; they are the roots from which a great number of branches of Roads are to proceed, which are necessary for the Improvement of the Country, and the Extension of the Fisheries.

Before entering upon the consideration of the Roads to the North of the Line of the Caledonian Canal, it is necessary to speak of the Communications from Glasgow and Greenock, through Argyleshire to Fort William. From Glasgow there is already a Road, which pafies through Dumbarton up the Weft lide of Loch Lomond, by the upper ends of Loch Long and Loch Fyne to Inverary. From Greenock, by crofting the Firth of the Clyde, there is a Road which pastes up the Fall lide of Gare Loch and Loch Long, and joins the Road to Inverary at the top of Loch Long. From Inverary there is one lload which pastes the upper end of Loch Awe, and another which Croft'es that Loch by a Ferry at Port Sonachan, and these Roads unite at Bunawe on the banks of Loch Etive. From Bunawe the Road is already made to Oban, and a branch erodes Loch Etive, and*pastes along the South lide of the Linnhe Loch and Loch Eil to Fort William. Between Bunawe and Fort William there are three Berries, over arms of the Sea, which running many miles into the Land, cannot well be avoided; in other respects the Communication trnm Glasgow and Greenock, thus far, is tolerably good. The Highland Society, in the excellent Report to which I shall frequently have orealion to refer, and which may be found in the Appendix, have pointed out a new Line of Road from the North tide of the Frith of Clyde, nearly opposite to Greenock, to be carried to the Bay of Strachan upon Loch Fyne; this would be a very direct Line from virecnock to Inverury, but it would be subjetft to two Ferries, and it seems doubttul whether this inconvenience would not overbalance the additional (Jiftao.ce round the upper end of the Lochs; at lealt, as there is already a very good communication by this Road, it feerns

most prudent to attend to the other more necessary portions of Road before this is undertaken. . ' ' ■_

From Fort William it will be very advifabie to improve and extend the Road which paTes along the North fide of the portion of Loch Eil, which turns from Fort William to the Weft, and to carry it from thence across the upper end of Loch Shicl, through Arrafaig to Merer, as described in the Report of the Highland Society. This would open a very direct communication from the-Clyde to the Fish-ing Locks at the back of Skye, to Skye itself, and to the Illunds of Egg, Rum, Muck, Barra, and South Lift. This would prove of ureat importance to the Fisheries on account of facilitating intelligence^ which is one of the most necessary steps to promote the success of this business.

In the year 1796, Mr. Brown, of Elgin, made a Survey and Estimate of this Road from Fort William to Morer, and stab-d the Expence at £. 6,456; fmee that time, I understand that about ^.1,500 has been laid out upon it, so that £. 4,000, and perLaps somewhat more, is ltill required to render it perfect. -

With regard to the Improvement of the Roads which lead from Fort William, East, to Inverness, there is one principle, which hi future ought never to be loft light of, which is, to shake the new Roads as near to the banks of the Rivers and Lociis as is practicable at a reasonable Expence. If the Caledonian Canal is executed, it is more than probable that many Improvements will be pointed out in the course of carrying on that great Work, and it would be imprudent to decide ralhly in a matter which is 1b much connected with this National ObjedL \

We now come to consider the Communications of the Countries which lie to the North and Welt of the track of the Caledonian Canal. From this Valle)*, which ruas from Fort William to lnver-ness, it is of great importance that there should be Lines of Communication with the Isle of Skye, and the Fishing Lochs which lie at the back of it; these Lines of Road are not only necessary for promoting the Fisheries, but are urgently called for by the litualioA.dJ the interior parts of the Country, where there are many fertile Vullies which hitherto haye remained nearly inaccetlible; it is incalculable the loss which the Public has sustained, and are about to lb tier, from the want of Roads in this Country. , '

From the Bridges of Beanley and Conon, Lines of Road, from the same important causes, are wanted in several directions to the West Coast, and through the whole of the Cotmties of Rossshire, Sutherland, and Caithness. The outlines of those Roads are well described in the Report of the Highland Society; and although there is a diversity of opinion as to the comparative importance ot fume of them, as well as of those to Skye, yet it is evident that they are all necessary for the welfare of the Country.

The Empire at large being deeply interested in those Improvements, as it regards promoting the Fisheries, and encreasing the Revenue and Population of the Kingdom, justifies Government in granting Aid towards making Roads and Bridges in a Country which must otherwise remain, perhaps for ages to come, thus imperfedily connected*

Yet as the Land-owners in those extensive Districts through which the Roads would pass, and indeed the whole of the adjoining Diliritls of Country, would enjoy improved Cultivation and Pasturage, encrealed Incomes, and all the blellings which are to be derived iroin a facility of Intercourse, it is certainly just that they should contribute a share with Government in the Expence of acquiring those advantages. They might be enabled to do this, without inconvenience to the present Possessorjs, by being empowered by an Act of Parliament to fell Land, or borrow Money upon the Land, to the amount of their proportion of the Expence to be incurred by the Roads and Bridges. This is reasonable, because the Money so raised would be applied to improve the Remainder of the entailed Estate, which would be enhanced in value, though somewhat diininished in extent

The Expence" of the Line? of Road which were surveyed and estimated by Mr. Brown, comprehending the whole of the before-mentioned Counties, and nearly 1,000 miles in length, did not amount to £• 150,000. If therefore we admit an equal quantity of Lines of Road to be undertaken and completed in the course of three \ears, would require an Annual Supply of £. 50,000, and supposing this to be raised in equal Moieties by Government and the Land-owners, it would be £. 25,000 each; but as it is not likely the whole could be brought so immediately into operation, it may with more probability be expected that six Years would be taken up in executing all the Lines, which would reduce the Annual Supply to £.25,000, or £. 12,500 from each Party. But this is exclusive of the four great Bridges, the total Expence of which is reckoned at £• 37>000’ they were undertaken by proper Persons they might be executed in three Years, which would require an Annual Supply of Sc/.; and if Government was to grant One-halt,

Speaking therefore generally, if Government was disposed to encourage these plans of Improvement, and would agree to advance £. 20,000 in each of the first three years, and £. 12,000 in each of the last three years, it would then remain with the Land-owners of the Distritfs of Country through which the Lines, were to be carried, to come forward with their Surveys and Estimates, and Subscriptions to One-half the amount of the Expence, proving at the same time to the satisfaction of Government, that the proposed Lines would be of public as well as of private Utility. It would be necessary also to provide that the Works should be substantially executed, mid that the Laud-owners or others interested, should always lay out a certain Sum before Government advanced an equal Moiety.

Means should be provided for the maintenance of the Roads and Bridges after they have been completed, and for this purpose there should either be a Fund reierved, or a final 1 Toll laid on, to go in aid of the Statute Labour of the Country. A very important consideration allb, is, the erecting and maintaining proper Inns upon the Roads.

Several of the Houses which were built by Government upon the Military Roads, are striking inlhinces of the necessity there is of giving the People who are to keep the Inns, l'oniething else to depend upon besides what ariles from fu|>plying Travellers; there should be some Land attached to the House, at a Rent to be settled by reference.

I am not prepared to say what the quantity should be, or of what particular ddcription; it is at present sufficient to point out the principle.'

Upon the whole, as far as regards the Bridges and Roads, I can have no helitation in stating, that they are of the greateti moment for promoting the improvement of the Country, and for pci ledting the connexions with the Pithing Lochs and the Hebrides; and I shall hereafter endeavour to explain my reasons for thinking, that some ihare of the Emigrations is to be attributed to the want of proper communications.

and experience would point out wlmt future Improvements were ne-cefiury upon this Coalt.

From Aberdeen, Peterhead, and Frazcrburgh, a communication might be kept ujl) with Cromarty, by means of Signals or a Telegraph, or by Land express to Nairn, where the Firth is only* three leagues over; or a fall-failing Vessel would fuori run with an Ealierly wind from Frazerburgh to Cromarty.

If Cromarty Bay was made a Roadfread, there would be wanted a Storehouse arid some other conveniences, which may be on a small scale, until the merits of tie place have been fully proved; allow an Expence here of £. 5,000.

NAVAL STATIONS.

BEFORE entering upon the subjetffof the Caledonian Canal, it will be proper to observe, that I again examined the Bay of Cromarty, and have procured some more Information respetffing it and the Murray Firth.

Mr. Henderson, the resident Custom-House Officer, a man of re-speciability, has, at my ddire, ascertained the depth of Water in the Wells, and also what quantity flows from a Spring about half a mile from the Town. From his Letter it appears, that at the depth of 20 feet from the surface of the plain upon which the 'Town hands, there are four feet of Water in their Wells; when at Cromarty I learnt that, at high Springs, this Water is brackilh, but it is generally used for walking and other domestic purposes. At the dillance of about half a mile from the Town there is a fine Spring, which was discovered by the late Mr. Ross during his ineffectual attempt to find Coal; from this circumstance it is called the Coal Well. This Spring produces on an Average upwards of 20 hogsheads of Water in an hour; this Water might be collected into a Reservoir at a finall expence; from this Reservoir it might be brought to the Shore, which is a short distance, in Pipes, and by means of hose run into Calks in a Ship's Boat; to protect the Boats, u small Pier might be formed at this place.

been so obliging as to reiblvc some Queries which I took the liberty of transmitting to him through his Brother-in-law, Colonel Dirotn. Captain Duff confirms the general Report of the Excel!‘nee of the Bay of Cromarty, and the entrance to it; his opinion respecting the Navigation of the Murray Firth is quite as favourable as I had been led to advance in my last; Report; from wlmt he Antes, it appears, that even with a contrary wind, a Ship of War could clear the Head-Lands in 48 hours from the time of leaving the Bay of Cromarty; from this Account, persons conversant in Naval Affairs will be able to judge how far this Bay would be suitable for a Squadron destined to watch the mouth of the Baltic, and protect the CoaA. THE CALEDONIAN CANAL.

I passed along the whole line of this Canal# that is, from Inverness on the Ead, to Fort William on the Well Coast. I took much pains to examine into the nature of the Navigation of the Lochs, their soundings and anchoring places. For this purpose I applied chiefly to Mr. Gwynn, who has commanded the Lochness Galley in Government Service 36 years; from him I obtained a very full and satis-fadory Account of Lochness; he also took the soundings of Loch Oich and a part of Loch Lochy for me.

From him I learnt that Lochriefs is 2d miles in length, and front one to two and a half miles in breadth, that its extreme depth is 135 fathoms, and generally 15 to 20 very near the Shores; that there are fix anchoring places on the North, and four on the South fide, and that at each end of the Loch there is good anchorage in from 3 to 5,

8 and 10 fathom water.

' That a Vessel passing from the Wed to the Ead end before a Wederly wind, or in a contrary direction before an Ealierly wind, has nothing to do but run before the wind the whole way, which /he would do in from three to five hours, and with contrary winds in moderate weather flie would work it in from 24 to 36 hours.

That the Eaderly winds generally prevail from March till the end of September, when the WeAerly winds set in and continue for the red of the year.

The Soundings he took in Loch Lochy are from seven to sixty-eight fathoms, with bold Shores and good Anchorage.

In Loch Quoich, which isathort Loch on the Summit Level, there are some shallow parts, but they may be made sufficiently deep.

I next proceeded to examine the supplies of Water which are on the Summit Level, and for this purpose I passed up the Valley of Glen-garey to Loch Hourn at the back of Skye. In this Valley I found Loch Garry, which appears to be upwards of five miles in length, and from half a mile to one mile in breadth; towards the head of the Valley is Loch Quoich, which appears to be upwards of eight miles in length, and from one to two miles in breadth; these natural Reservoirs, placed in an extensive Valley and a rainy Country, form an abundant proviAon for every purpose to which w'ater can be applied in the Course of the Canal.

Having ascertained these points, I passed by a very rocky and pre-cipilous track, down to the Head of Loch llourn; from Loch Mourn I travelled by a track scarcely less rugged, to the top of Glen Elg, and over the sleep Mountain of Raatachan to the top of Loch Duich; from thence I travelled along the vefriges of a Military Road, up Glen Shiel, down a part rif Glen Morrifori, and over a rugged Mountain to Fort Augustus. Iri Gleri Morrison and Glen Garry it is possible to make Roads, if judiciously laid out, upon an easy afeent; but the idea of Water-conveyance through them between the Caledonian Canal and the Fiffiing Lochs, i$ altogether unadvifable.

My next object was to examine the Country which lies between the top of Loch Eil and Loch Shiel, in order to find whether a Water Conveyance could be made at a moderate Expence from Loch Eil through Loch Sheil, and so into the Fiffiing Grounds to the South of Skye, without passing down the Linnhe Loch, up the Sound of Mull, and round the point of Ardnamurchan. I carried a Level across the Neck of Land which separates Loch Eil from Loch Shiel, the distance is about three miles. I found the summit of the Land 43 feet above high water in Loch Eil, and 35 feet 5 inches above the level of the fresh water in Loch Shiel. Io order to form a Canal, as there is no water to be got on this summit, the ground must be cut down to 12 feet below the level of the water in Loch Shiel, which would make 47 feet 5 inches of cutting, and this depth of cutting would be continued for nearly a mile; I also susped that in this distance Rock would be met with. I am therefore sorry to say, I cannot adviie the Work being undertaken before the nature of the ground has been fully proved, and the whole of, Loch Shiel has been examined with great care; and asjhis passage cannot be useful unless the Caledonian Canal be made and navigated from the East; if that event should take place, there will be plenty of time to re-examine this point with care; at present it ought, ifc my opinion, to be postponed.

Having investigated all the points which fell under my observation as a Civil Engineer, I became extremely defiroos of having the opinion of experienced and well-informed mercantile and seafaring people, with regard to the present Navigation by thi Pentland Firth and the Orkneys, and the proposed Inland Navigation by the Cale-

THE FISHERIES.

IN what regards the Eifhcries, I beg leave to quote a passage from my last vearV Report:—" I believe it is generally admitted, that in the Improvement of a Country, the interference of Government " should extend only to the removing obstacles, and affording convc-" niences, winch are of a nature not ealilv to he i'urmouiited by In-41 dividuals, or any body of Men who can he brought to ad together;

* and where il is evident that by removing those obstacles, and u affording these conveniences, the exertions of Individuals will be " greatly facilitated, so as to promote the general good of the " Empire."

The objects connected with the Fisheries, which seem to come Under the foregoing description, are, 1ft. The want of a ready communication by Water between the East and West Coasts; 2nd. The want of Communications by Land from the Low Countries and the East Coast, with the Shores and Filling Lochs of the West Coast; 3dly. The Inconveniences arising from the operation of the Salt Law’s; and, 4tldy. The want of a Harbour in Caithness.

The first and fecontl of those objrds have already been fully dif-cuffed under the heads of the Caledonian Canal, and the proposed Bridges and Roads. The third has been so often and thoroughly investigated, that I shall only in this place take the liberty <<r mentioning, that all the information I have received, tends to confirm the justice of the complaints against the Laws now in force which regard Salt. v

As to the fourth object, The Harbour of Wick in Caithness, which I examined, estimated, and reported upon last year, wiil remove the just complaints of want of PioteGion on the N. E. Coast.

THE EMIGRATIONS.

THAT Emigrations have already taken place from various parts of the Highlands, is a fad upon which there does not remain room to doubt; from the best information I have been able to procure, about three thousand Persons went away in the courl’e of last year, and, if I am rightly informed, three times that number are preparing to leave the Country in the present year.

I shall not encroach upon your Lordships time by investigating all the remote or unimportant collateral causes of Emigration, but shall proceed to that which I consider to be the most powerful in its present operation; and that is, converting large Dill rids of the Country into extensive Sheepwalks. This not only requires much fewer people to manage the fame track of Country, but in general an entirely new People, who have been accultnmed to this mode of life, are brought from the Southern parts of Scotland,

The difference of Rents to the Landlords between Sheep and Black Cattle is, I under and, at lead three to one, and yet on account of the extraordinary rife in the prices of Sheep and Wool, the Sheep Farmers have of late years been acquiring Wealth. As the introducing Sheep Farms over Countries heretofore flocked with Black Cattle, creates an extensive demand for the young Sheep from the established Farms, it is possible that the high prices may continue until a con-fidurable portion of the Country is fully (locked; after this takes place, the quantities of Sheep produced will bear a very great proportion to the demand, and then it is polTible the prices may fall below the average Value; in this case it is probable the Farms will be fubdi-virfed, and a proportion of Black Cattle and cultivation be Introduced in the lower eroimds in the Vallies, while the upper parts of the Hills continue to be pafhirrd with Sheep. This I consider its the most improved hate of Highland Farming, and is confident with a very con-lulerabh* population; a beaut iful iriftauce of tins is to be leen along the North tide of l.orh Tav. But improved communications, by means of Roads and Bridges, are necessary for tills date of Society, and for this reiifon 1 have ibid, that if these conveniences had been fuoner

introduced into the Highlands, it is possible this Emigration might not have taken place, at lead to the present extent.

The very high price of Black Cal tie has also facilitated the means of Emigration, as it has fumished the old Fanners with a portion of Capital which enables them to transport their Families beyond the Atlantic.

In some few cases a greater population than the Land can support in any (liapc, has been the cause of Emigrations; such was th* Island of Tiree.

Some have* no doubt* been deluded by Accounts sent back from others gone before them; and many deceived by artful persons, who hesitate not to sacrifice these poor ignorant People to feltish ends.

A very principal reason mult also be, that the people when turned out bf their Black Cattle Farms to make way for the Sheep Farmers, fee no mode of employment whereby they can earn a subsistence in their own Cotintry, and sooner than leek it in the Low Lands of Scotland, or in England, they will believe what is told them mav bt done in the Farming Line in America.

What I have here mentioned appear to me to be the immediate causes of the present Emigrations from the North-western parts of Scotland. To point out the means of preventing Emigrations id future, is a part of my duty upon which I enter with no small degree of hesitation. As the evil at present seems to arise chiefly from (he conduct of Land-owners, in changing the Geconoinv of their Estates, it may be questioned whether Government can with jutiice interfere, or whether any essential benefits are likely to arise from this Interference.

In one point of view it may be dated, that, taking the mountainous parts of Scotland as a Dillrid of the British Empire, it is the Interest of the Empire that this District be made to produce as much human Food as it is capable of doing at the least possible expence; that tills may be done by docking it chiefly with Sheep; that it is the Interest of the Empire the Food so produced should not be eon-fumed by persons residing among ft the Mountains totally unemployed, but rather in some other parts of the Country where their labour can be made productive either in the business of Agriculture, Fisheries, or Manufactures; and that by differing every person to pursue what appears to them to be their own Interest, that although lbme tempo-rary Inconveniences may arise, yet, upon the whole, that matters will in the end adjust themselves into the forms moil suitable for thi Place.

In another point of view it may be dated, that it is a great bard-ftiip, if not a great injustice, that the Inhabitants of an extensive District should all at once be driven from their native Country to make way for Sheep Farming, which is likely to be carried to an imprudent extent; that, in a few years, this excess will be evident; that before it is discovered, the Country will be depopulated, and that race of People which has of late years maintained lb honourable a share in the operations of our Annies and Navies will then be no more; that in a case where such a numerous body of the People are deeply interested, it is the duty of Government to consider it as an extraordinary case, and one of those occasions which justifies them in departing a little from the maxims of general policy; that for this purpose, Regulations should be made to prevent Land-owners from lessening the Population upon their Estates below a given proportion, and that some Regulation of this fort would in the end be in favour of the Land-ow’ners, as it would preserve the Population belt suited to the most improved mode of Highland Fanning, such as is pnuftiled at Breadalbane, and to the establishment of 1'idling Villuges, on the Principle laid down and practised so liiccefsfully by Mr Hugh Stevenson of Oban, at Arnililalc on Loch Mourn.

In whatever light the foregoing Statements may be viewed, there it another on which there cun, I think, be no difference of opinion. This is, that if there any Public Works to be executed, which, when completed, will prove generally beneficial to the Country, it i6 advilable these Works should be undertaken at the present time. This would furnish employment for the industrious and valuable part of the People in their own Country; they would by this means be accustomed to Labour, they would acquire fojiie Capital, and the foundations would belaid for future Employments. If, as I have been credibly informed, the Inhabitants are llrongly attached to their native Country, they would greedily embrace this* opportunity of being enabled to remain in it, with the prospect of bettering their condition, because, before the Works were completed, it must be evident to every oue that the whole face of the Country would be changed.

The Caledonian Canal, and" the Bridges and Roads before-mentioned, are of the description here alluded to; they will not only furnish present employment, but^romife to accomplish all the leading Objects which can reasonably be looked forward to for the Improvement and future Welfare of the Country, whether we regard its ’Agriculture, Fisheries, or Manufactures.

In answer to the first, they are persuaded that even the Lines of Communication by means of Military Roads in some parts of the Highlands, have been productive of benefit to the Country, though the motives which gave rife to their formation, having no relation to objects of Commerce and Industry, the advantages derived from them are very' imperfect. The Committee accordingly have no hesitation in declaring it to be their fixed opinion, that the want of farther Roads and Communications in the Highlands, has hitherto proved the greatest obstacle to the introduction of useful industry there, and that every attempt for that purpose must fail until regular and eafv Communication is afforded from one part of the Country to another, and more especially from the remote points where there is the best field for useful exertion to the present feats of Capital and Industry. With regard to what Lines would tend most effectually to open the Country, and promote the Public Good, the Committee humbly report their opinion as follows:

The Highlands, as to this question, may he divided into Three Districts :—The First, comprehending the Weft Coasts of Argyle and Inverncfsshire, as connected with each other;—the Second, including the County of Ross, and a part of the County of Inveraefs;—and the Third, or Northern District, compriiing the Shires of Sutherland and Caithness.

In the first of these Districts, the utmost benefit would arise from drawing a direct line of communication from* the Weft fide of the Firth of Clyde nearly opposite to Greenock, to the Bay of Strachur upon Loch Fyne, from whence there is already an excellent and well-conducted Road to Fort William. From this point the Road may be easily continued by Loch LII fide to Loch-na-Gaul, through Arifaig into Morer. Such a communication would tend very greatly to the fucceis of the Fisheries in the lilands of Ei and South Uift, all of which polfefs

Banks in and around them. The greatest advantages would arise from approximating these various Fiilieries andextenlive Coasts to the Firth of Clyde, where the Fishing Capital is at present almost exclusively resident. It is evident, that nothing can more discourage the employment of that Capital in those parts, than that difficulty of approach, amountingalrnoft to inacceftibility, which renders the communication of intelligence always flow, and even often precarious.

In the Northern District the Lines of Communication would, from the nature of the thing, be drawn to a different point. A central point at the South of that District is found at o/ near Inverihin, to which place the Firth of Dornoch is navigable, and where a Bridge can easily be thrown over, and from whence a direct and short communication could be made to Dingwall and Inverness. From this ppint several advantageous Lines of Road might be made, one stretching by the Banks of Loch Shin through part of Afiint to Kylofcow, another by the Kirk of Lairg to the head of Loch Loxford, and a third from the Kirk of Lairg by the Weft of Lochnaver to Tongue. Another Road again would conned together the Western-and Eastern extremities of this the Northern Coast of Scotland, proceeding from Loch Eriboll (at which place there is one of the finest Harbours in the Kingdom) by Tongue, Farr, and Thurso, to Honna on the East. From this point, where there is a Ferry to Orkney, the Road would return to Wick, and from thence along the East Coasts of Sutherland and Caithness, crofting the River Fleet by a Bridge, to avoid the little Ferry, till it terminated at Inverfliin. Such Lines as the above would open the whole of these Countries to all the trading Capital of inverness and the East Coast of Scotland, as well as by the way of Fort William to that of the Clyde; and it is well known, that all the way from the vicinity of Kylefcow round to Wick, the I ishing Grounds are abundant and excellent.

As to the Middle Division, the Committee would humbly*suggest the utility of certain lines of interfedion from East to West. One of these ought to be from the great Militajy Road between Fort William and Inverness in a Western direction, such as may best afford an easy intercourse between both these places and the Islands of Skye, Harries, and North Uift, as well as Loch Ilnura, Loch Duich, and the other valuable Fishing Lochs in that vicinity. A second will lead from Contin (which has already a good Road to Dingwall) by the South fide of Loch Garve, and the head of Loch Lie kart to Achnafhine, and from thence in one branch to Loch Carron, and in another to Pollew. I rom one or other of these branches, a Road of important benefit might be drawn to Loch Toni don; a third Road will extend trom the Port of Ullapool in Loch Broom, to Inverihin, at the head of the Firth of Dornock.

When the Lines of Road now mentioned are completed, the course of Poll will become rapid and regular., From the neighbourhood of Skye to Greenock, the Mail would be conveyed in three days, while from lnverfhin to Edinburgh by Aberdeen, or to Greenock by Inverness and Fort William, it w ould be conveyed at farthest in four, and thus the most remote points of the Highlands would be brought within five days course of Poll, at the utmost, of Edinburgh and the Firth of Clyde. It may fufiice for contrafting such a situation of the Highlands with that in which they are now placed, in relped to communication of intelligence, to relate what happened this very year.

When, after the return of the Clyde Vessels from a vain search for Herrings in the Northern Lochs, some considerable ftioals having appeared, intelligence was dispatched to Greenock; but, owing to the indirect coui le of the Poll, and the difficulties of some parts of the circuitous journey, several weeks elapled before any advantage could be taken of the information

The Lines that have been suggested, or nearly such Lines, are in the opinion of the Committee, the radical Lines of Road, as they may be termed, from which in process of time various ramifications will be formed, when the benefits of these begin to be perceptibly difiuied.

From consideration of the connection of the fifth Question with what precedes, the Committee in so far depart from Mr. Telfords arrangement, as to put next in order the Answer to it. They are fully persuaded of the reality of those views, both of public and individual benefit, which the fiatement of the question includes; and they think it highly reasonable, that the Land-owners should, according to their respective abilities, unite with Government in executing these plans, by contributing a certain proportional part of the expence, varying with the different circumstances of their several situations. But the Committee humbly report their opinion, that it would be advisable for the Lords of the Tre ifury, alter weighing such suggestions as have been made, and consulting their Surveyor, to feled the lines of Road which more immediately, and in a National view, invite the Public Aid; and then, aftey the lelection is made known, it will be the duty as well as the filtered of Land-owners, to come forward with their proposals, fiating, with regard to each separately, those local considerations which seem to fix the proportion of Public Aid that may fairly be solicited.

in answer to Query second, the Committee have no doubt that the Caledonian Canal, formed on the Icaie luggeftetl (sufficient for the paf-sage of large trading Ships and Frigates) will be attended with the greatest national advantage* I*1 respect to these objects, indeed, the benefit nnift lie so incalculably great, that this truly ulel'ul undertaking assuredly merits the attention and exertions of Government. The Committee have equally little doubt in concurring with the opinion inferred in the third Question, that by opening a free communication from the Eastern to the Western Sea, it would be highly beneficial to the Fisheries, particularly determined by transferring the skill in the Cod and Ling Fishery, possessed by the People on the Eastern Coast, by *whom it is certainly better understood than by the Natives of the Western, from the former to the latter of these Shores, where the field for its action is inexhaustible.

With regard to Query fourth, the Committee are well convinced, that the undertaking these Public Works mult produce the united good consequences of checking the spirit of Emigration, by affording useful employment to a great number of People, of improving the habits of the Country by teaching lessons of systematic industry, and of atlbrding at once the excitement to undertake, and the intelligence as well as (to a certain moderate extent) the means required for instituting those Ffshing and manufacturing Establfihinents, on which the future prosperity of the Highland:; must be founded.

On the lixtli Question the Committee have to observe, that they are fully aware of the Commercial as well as other National advantages derivable from the Caledonian Canal; but with regard to the Question, to what extent Commercial Men would be ready to contribute individually towards carrying the fame into effect, the Highland Society can have no means of forming an opinion, other than by reference to that general spirit of liberal enterprize which distinguishes the Commercial body.

Adverting to a supplementary suggestion from Mr. Telford, the Committee apprehend that it would be highly expedient to introduce a c.laufc into any Act of Parliament on the subject, authorizing and empowering Proprietors of entailed Estates, either to tell Lands for defraying the expence of contributing, along with Government, to the making of Roads and Bridges in the Highlands, or in their option to make the fame a Debt, affecting the subsequent Heirs of entail.

It has been Hated to the Committee, that Tutors and Curators of minor Proprietors, and Trustees holding post el lion of Estates concerned in these improvements, might feel some hesitation in venturing on the necessary outlays, as entertaining a doubt of such acts of Administratiou falling within their powers. The Committee are humbly ot opinion, that it would be proper to add to the clause already luggefted, an Enadment, that Tutors and Curators of a minor Ileir ot entail, or Trustees in possession of an Estate already entailed, or which is directed to be entailed, should have the lame power of felling Lands or charging the Estate, that is by the Ad conferred upon Heirs of entail themselves.

As also, that Tutors and Curators of Minors possessed of unentailed Estates, and Trustees holding possession of such, should be entitled by their Acts in the premises to bind the Minor or Trustee, and all Sue* cessors to the Estate.

MINUTE of the Committee of the Directors of the Highland Society of Scotland, which formerly drew up Answers, in the fliapc of a Report, to the Queries of Mr. Telfdrd, Engineer, respecting the opening of Communications by Roads and Bridges in the Highlands, and by a Canal from Invemefs to Fort William, upon considering a Letter from Telford, of date 14th December 1802, to llenry Mackenzie, Esquire, one of the Society’s Directors, owning receipt of laid Report, which he states to be able, full, and satisfactory, and that the " only in- stance in which it is rather less explicit than lie could wish, u is with respect to the Road in the Middle Division, which 4< should conned the Inverness and Fort William Road with u Skye, &c. &c." as to which Mr. Telford willies the Committee could say something more specific, and recommends their taking any information which can be furniihcd by Mr. Donald-t son, Surveyor of Military Roads, upon that point—The Right honourable Lord Macdonald, one of the Vice Presidents in office, in the Chair.

THE Committee, in their former Report, have pointed out the greaft objects to which Roads through the District inqueltion should in

their opinion apply; but there being a difference of opinion as to the precile Lines of Road by which those objects would belt be attained, the Committee do* not feel tbcmselves at liberty to specify those precise Lines. They would take the liberty of fuggetting the expediency of Government employing some able Surveyor or Engineer of relpedable character and abilities to report on the subject; and if, -relative to the present point of enquiry, they are to say any thing more particular, they may mention that the objects of this Line of Interfedion seem chiefly twofold; viz. to afford a Communication to the Head of Loch Houm, a very valuable Fishing Loch, and also to Berncra, the nearest point to Skye; both which they apprehend may be attained by two ramifications of a Road from the Military Road leading from Fort William to Inverness.

The Committee, adverting to Mr. Telford’s suggestion of an examination of Mr. Donaldson, called him before them; but found that he had never travelled any part of the Country from Fort Augustus, Weft ward, to Bemera or the Lochs, and that his information was solely, as to that part of the Country, derived from others.

THE Commissioners of Imprest Accounts have heretofore investi-gated the several Accounts of the Directors and Commissioners for Paving, Cleansing, and Lighting the Streets of Dublin, principally as to the Regularity of the Statements, the Expences being warranted by Law, and supported by Efficient Vouchers; in which points they have been generally thought correal.

But the Revenues and Debts of the Corporation appearing con-fidorably to in create, and doubtshaving arisen wdiether the Works are sufficiently well executed to justify so great an Expenditure of Public Money, the Conniiiffioiiers of Imprelt Accounts think themselves called upon by Law to examine minutely, not only into the Account before them, but also into the expediency of those Laws under which so large an Expenditure is warranted; and whether this greaURevenue appears to be expended to the bell advantage for the Public Service. -

In the Charge part of this Account, the whole sums of money ruifed upon the Public for Paving, Cleansing, and Lighting t^e Streets «vf Dublin, do not appear. The per-Centage allowed te the Collectors r.»

of Taxes upon above £. 20,000 per annum, being from 5 d. to 1 s. 5 d. in the Pound, is not mentioned; nor is there sufficient notice taken of Fines levied, or of Sums paid by private Individuals and Public Bodies for Paving, and for lighting private Lamps, the amount of which, though great, the Commissioners have not been able to ascertain.

In the Discharge part aHb similar inaccuracies occur. The above sums paid for collecting the ’Faxes, the application of Fines, or of sums paid by private Individuals, in part payment of the Salaries of Officers, do noLappear; nor is the whole amount of the Corporation Establishment, as we understand it, or the Salaries and Perquisites of its Officers, plainly fiated to the Public; so that* upon the whole, a very imperfect idea can be formed from this Account of the actual sums raised ^expended on this service: and though the Expenditure on the face of this Account (exclusive of the above not-mentioned sums) appears to be £. 32,118. 4. 6$. yet the real Expenditure of this period, viz. from the ill of Janeaiy j8oi to the 5th of January

Uv the pj'eicnt Laws, the whole dominion over, and management of the Revenues, js vested in the Iloards of Directors and Commissioners, but principally in the Directors, who have and cxeccile ex-clufi\ely the power of creating and nominating to Offices, and of regulating the amount of Salaries, Gratuities, and Allowances; and, upon a wile arrangement of those. Of;ices, a proper choice of Persons to fill them, and a most careful attention that they perform their duty, depends the efficiency of this EliabJiihnient. Formerly, if the Corporation enacted any live-laws, it was nerellary that they should be approved of by the Lord Chancellor, or Chief Judges; but this necclfity has been done away by a late Act of Parliament; so that the whole rel'possibility of the Institution imiis to remain with the Board ot Directors alone. To this uneontrouied power, the Commissioners of Accounts attribute the expence of this extensive Kfiabiifiiment, by which is meant the Salaries, Gratuities, and Allowances of all Officers, and the expence of the Corporation i Joule,-which has, in our opinion, exceeded the sums allowed by Law, amounting in the whole, as near as can be ascertained from the present Account, to about £.7,000, exclusive of all Contractors, Artificers, Labourers, Workmen, and Work-horles whalloever. The lull number of Odicers and Persons employed, or the total Expence attending thenf, do not however appear on this Account.

The Commissioners of Accounts have examined the Books of the Corporation, the Contends for Paving, Lighting, and Cleaning; and have also examined upon Oath a Director, a Commissioner, the Accountant, the Collectors, and many of the Insepctors, Supervises, and other inferior Officers of the Board, as well as many of the different Conlrudors; from the whole of which they have collected the following information: —

The Paving and Scavenging Contracts are all drawn in the fame terms respect. ely; but we could trace no infiance of their ever having been fully complied with. The Contractors themselves admit they never comply with them entirely; for instance, in every Paving Contract the Contractor obliges himi'elf to pave with Stones of from 3 to 6 inches diameter in a bed of new Gravel of 4 inches depth, and to cart away all the old bed. This they do not perform, though it is certain the Pavement would be much belter if they did.

In the Scavenging Contracts, though die Contractors are bound to cleanse all the Streets twice in every week, the) do not do so; and in the Lighting of the City, though this Contract appears better executed than either of the former, yet even in this the terms of the Contrail,

' viz. " That the Lamps should be kept lighted from Sunset to Sunrife," are not complied with.

The Inspectors and Supervisors acknowledge themselves totally ignorant of the Conditions of the several Contracts; they never had read them, and never report to the Board that the Works are done according to Contrail, but frequently that the Works, are, in general, in tolerable good order; though the Contrails uniformly specify, " That " they should be in good and sufficient order;" and upon this species of Report, untupported by affidavit, the full Amount of the Contrail is -paid.

T hough in every Contrail many heavy Penalties may be inflilled by the Board, or its Officers, for default, yet in the period of this Account, during which the Officers admit the Streets to have been in worse order than even they are at present, the Sum of 25 Shillings was all

that was levied upon the whole of the Contrallors fol* default Of Scavenging; about £. 8. on the w’hole of the Contractors for Paving, and the Sum of f. 77. o. 10. I on the folc Cornialfor for Lighting the whole City. Esther the Contrails are originally made too lev ere, and then, in fume mealiue, seem to authorize neglect; if not too severe, the Officers of the Board are culpable in not leeirg them executed; cr (as it has appeared) the Penalties are not infiilfi-d on the Contractors, though the Works may not be sufficiently well executed, because the Corporation is conllderably indebted to thele Contractors.

Under the Dead of Officers, some Persons appear to have been appointed without sufficient attention to their being adequate to the duty of different, and, in our opinion, incompatible Departments; for in-Ilance, Mi*. Daniel Farrell is Chief Inspellor of Globes throughout the City, winch requires that he should be out on this Inspeliion almost every Night, to lee that the Con traitors for Lighting, as well as the Officers of the Board, perform their respective Duties; he is also foie Collector of Taxes for the North fide of the City, being above one third part of the whole, wdiicli he declared occupied him almost everyday in the year; it appears nearly impossible therefore, that he should he able to execute the duty of both thele Offices eft'eltually. T he Collectors, Valuators, and Rental Books do not seem sufficiently controuled, being merely checked by the Collectors own Returns, and Books of the preceding Years; nor are the Collectors often changed in their Walks, whereby they might become Checks on each other, Mr. Farrell having been continued nine years in his present Walk: arid from a companion with the mode of Collection adopted by other Corporations receiving House Tax, it appears that a much more accurate Collection has been made by them, than by the Collectors of the Paving and Lighting Baxes, inaimuch as Hordes, which have been returned in Arrear or insolvent by the Collectors of the Paving Board, have been found to have discharged the Amount of thpir Taxes to the other Collectors; so that we are of opinion, a large proportion of the Paving and Lighting Tax remains either improperly uncollelted, or is fraudulently retained in the hands of the Collectors.

T he Corporation is so much in Debt, (now owing a Floating, or Unfunded Debt of £. 14,521. 3. 5 b) lliat tlley anticipate the greatest part of their Revenues, and frequently pay their Creditors by Bills drawn on their Treasurer, at 4, 5, and 6 months date; by which the Public mult loie atlealt the whole of the Discount on these- Bills, be-lides their allowance to their Treasurer for accepting and negotiating them, and exclusive of the high price Conti actors may probably be induced to con trull at, from a knowledge of the mode of Payment being so dilatory; and under these diladvantages the Public mult continue to labour, until this Debt flia.il have been paid, and the Revenues no longer anticipated.

From all the above-mentioned circumstances we are of opinion, ill. TJiat the Expences of the Establishmenl require some legal limitation.

2dly. That all Contrails should be better formed, or more accurately attended to.

3dly. That the appointment of Officers, and of efficient Checks over them, should be better arranged; and,

4thly. That the Revenues of the Corporation should be more effectually administered.

That this Account w not dated as fully as it might have been: That in the Charge-Part no credit is given for the sums deduded Ihefe Officers do not from the Conlradors for default; and in the Discharge no notice is ipeui on the Account. ^a^cn application of the Fines and Deductions, though it appears they are appropriated to pay the Salaries of Officers:

That, though the Streets are now worse paved and cleaned, and worse lighted than heretofore, notwithstanding the sums applied to those purposes are increased, and the Works all done by Contract, no sufficient reasons were assigned for it:

That the speeific Articles for which Bills are drawn, and Money paid (as in Law Cafes) are not sufficiently Hated:

That Officers appear to receive various sums of Money under many different Heads, so as not to make it clear what they actually get: That a large Floating Debt is not taken notice of:

And it also appearing, that the Paving, Lighting, and Cleansing the City of Dublin, is not executed in a manner to justify so great an expence ;—

The Board resolved to make a more minute i arc (ligation into the bufness, and ordered the present Account and Vouchers to be returned to the Directors and Commissioners of Paving, with the following Letter:

Mr. HENRY PETERS, Contrador for Paving the Streets of jy/r. peter, Dublin, attended ;—Sworn.—Deposed as follows:

Have you and your Securities entered into a Bond for £.500 for t performance of Conditions in Contract, and where is it?—-Delivered it to the Paving Board.

Are all the Conditions of your Contract duly fulfilled?—The Conditions of my Contract have been fulfilled* so far as to satisfy the Board.

Have you ever been fined the Treble Penalty, and when* and by

what Officer?—Never.

Do you give notice to an Officer of the Board when you are repairing or paving, and does one always attend?—I do not give notice/ nor does the Officer always attend.

If an Officer did not attend while the Works were going on, could he know if they were done according to Contract?—He could not; but there are scarcely two days in an hundred in which an Officer does not fee the Works in progress.

Have the Board ever executed any Works in your Contract, and charged you for them for default?—I do not recoiled that there was.

In what manner are you paid the Amount of your Contract?—Was paid sometimes in Bills at 4, 5, and 6 months, and sometimes in Calb or Bank Notes; once in Debentures.

Were you aware, before you contracted, that this would be the mode of Payment, and did you make your Ultimate accordingly; and would you have contracted for a lower Sum if you were lure of receiving your amount in Money di redly upon the day agreed on in the Contract?—If I was sure of being paid Cash, I would not have made this Estimate lower for that particular Contract.

DANIEL FARRELL, Principal Inspector of Lamps, and Collector of Paving and Lighting Tax for the North fide of Dublin, attended; Sworn.—Deposed as follows:—Has a Commission; is sworn every Wednesday as to his Report, and every Quarter as to his Collcdion; views Oil before Contrador buys it, it is of good quality; goes out when he thinks proper, but not at stated times; does no Jobbing Works for the Board; has no Perquisites but Salary and Gratuity, and per-Centage on Collection of Taxes; no alteration, for two years, in the construction of the Lamps, either as to Burners or Caps, from the Pattern in the Paving Office; and declares, that all the Lamps now in use are as near that Pattern as possible.

He believes he never saw any Lamp that had the appearance of being purposely (lopped at top to save Oil, or that had the Cap altered for that purpose; there are about six thousand public Lamps now in use; irequently finds the heads choaked with (team and dirt of Oil, but constantly orders them to be cleaned.

He thinks Lamps burn as bright, and thinks they continue longer in than formerly; he does not count the Lamps, Mr. Austin does; but knows whether the number is right by the view.

Thinks Lamps remain in longer, and there is more Oil used than formerly.

Salary £.100 a year for inspecting Lamps; no Perquisites; does no Jobbing Work.

Never was offered any Fee, Gift, or Gratuity, by any Contractor.

Reports every Wednesday, and seldom so as not to admit of Fines being ordered by the Board, if they choose? during this Account £' 77* °* 10f wns levied. Colletts the Fines, and pays them into the Treasury.

He attends the Paviors sometimes when doing, sometimes when the Works are done.

He never read any Contract, but reports according to his Instructions; which are, in general terms, to see that the Streets are paved in a proper manner, and with proper materials.

Is never sworn, except in the case of nuisances; nor ever gave security when he entered into Office. There has not been, to his knowledge, any Officer lent after him to cheek him. His Salary and Gratuity is £. 70 in all; ltoppages sometimes made for neglect.—He reports Jobbing-works necessary from view; and makes the Estimate, which he refers to the Board.—Is paid his salary in Cash.—Has fined Contractors for Paving for default.—Never reports that Works are performed agreeable to ContraCL—Contractors are not fined in Calli; the way they are fined is by running on them, and charging double; but does not know whether of Contract Price or Expence.

During a period last winter, the Streets and Pavements were in much worse order than ever he remembered, owing to frost and damp.

When Inhabitants break up Streets for their own purposes, as to lay Pipes about areas, &c. he receives a deposit from them, and pays the Contractor; and he endeavours to take care that the Works are well done, but is not always able to succeed.

Payments are made to Sweepers once a week, to I Jorfe-owners one# a quarter; he is solely employed on Scavenging (chiefly on the South tide); also, he fees that the Contractors for Scavenging do their duty* and if not, runs upon them with the Corporation Carts, and charges them a Crown a load; he has done so every year, but more particu- i

Lilly this year; and it frequently happens that they run more upon a Man than his Contract amounts to. There are also Persons who get weekly payment for Handing over the Carts of the Board.

He thinks the City was dirtier a year or two ago than now.

He thinks the Streets would be better cleansed by Contractors than by the Board.

Some Weeks he has run as far as Ten Pounds, some Three Pounds, and lower; lie has a discretionary power to run, which is charged on |,

whole; lie is obliged to make a Return daily how many turns each Cart runs in a day; there are twenty-nine lots; a Cart runs on an average fix turns a day, and holds a ton, which dries into about half a ton.

Soil is now offered for Sale from 18 </. to 14 d. per ton. Overseers of

delivery of Soil are employed merely when the Soil is fold, to fee it

properly delivered; he takes care to fee it deposited from the Carts in

Tuesday, 15th March 1803.

Present:—Mr. Herbert, Mr. Magenis,
