Thursday, 17th March 1803.

Present:—Mr. Herbert, Mr. Magenis,

Mr. Cane, Mr. Barry, Mr. King.

This Day Mr. LEAHY, a Dircdor, and Mr. MITCHELL, a Commissioner of the Paving Board, attended; Sworn,—And they deposed as follows:

Is all the money levied on the Public included in the Charge-part of this Account?—All, except Fines in general, the Balances of which, after certain payments only, are brought in Charge, and the Poundage to Collectors allowed in their Quarterly Accounts, which they retain in their hands.

Is all money paid, allowed, or expended by the Board, set forth in the Discharge ?—-All, except Payments as above.

has the Amount of Taxes increased of late?—They increase Annually.

What is the Amount of the Floating Debt?—About £. 14,521.3. 5 J.

What is the Annual Loss on uncolle&ed Taxes for the last year 1801, and the average of the last three years?—We will fend in the Account; it is to be found in the Rentals, whence they must be taken.

Is there any, and what check on the Collectors Returns?—Yes, by Check Books, Rental Books, and Quarterly Affidavits.

Are Collectors or Officers changed so as to check each other; how long has Mr. Panel been Collector at North Side ?—Whenever they fee occasion they change; Mr. Farrell has been about nine years.

What check have you on your Rental books?—Not any but change of Officers, and Original book, and reports of Collectors.

Are the Officers sworn to their Reports?—Collectors are sworn; hat inferior Officersrare not sworn as to their Certificates.

Do you take Securities?—We take Securities from Collectors and Treasurer only.

Are there any Officers appointed to employments difficult to execute together?—Not unless the Board thinks they can be done properly together.

Do all Officers bearing commissions, and Persons doing duty, appear under the toad of Establishment?—No; the persons who do duty are not on the Estabhshment, nor are the Collectors of Taxes, who pay them 1 elves,.or the Chief Inspector of Globes, who are paid partly by 1toes in the peiiod of this Account.

Contracts are all given to the bed bidder; the Contrails are all drawn so finer, that the Board does not conceive they can be generally fulfilled, but are drawn so for the purpose of having the Contractor* more under controul.

Wc think the Contractors do the Works tolerably well; but we have been more lenient as to fining them, on account of the flow mode of payment, the Board being in their debt considerably.

As the City increases, the Funds do not increase in the proportion of their Expences.

* These Sums include the Expence of a thorough Repair of the Governor's House, and building a large strong Room for their Deeds and Papers, for fate Custody, and to fuve the Expence of Duplicates.

TH E whole clear Revenue of the Governors is Annually appropriated for the Augmentation of small Livings.

The nominal Capital Sums, (landing in the Name of the Governors in the Books at the Bank and South Sea House, constitute the Fund to answer the appropriated Money unlaid out in the purchase of Land, which is the ultimate object of the Institution. As more Purchases are found the Sum in Stock becomes proportionably less.

The Governors, in their Annual Appropriations, consider not only their Revenue, but the Price of the Public Funds. If the Price is so high that their Capital will allow an Appropriation in addition to the one they make from their Hated Revenue, an extra Appropriation is made accordingly, the Surplus Interest (i.e. the Interest uriung from the appropriated Money beyond the Interest allowed the Clergy) contlituting part of the Fund for that purpose; but if from any Fall in the Price there is an actual or probable Deficiency to answer the appropriated Money unlaid out, no extra Appropriation is made, and then the Surplus Interest is allowed to fink into the Capital, and so becomes auxiliary till the Capital Sum, through that Aid, or a Rife in the Stocks, becomes equal to the Money appropriated and not laid out in Land. Since 1786, 782 Augmentations have been given by the Governors to fuiall Livings in addition to those made from their Annual Revenue.

And the Values of many other small Livings that were omitted, have fmee been certified.

The Governors at first augmented Livings not exceeding £. 10. per annum, and then all which did not exceed £•‘20. per annum. In 1792 they began to augment Livings not then exceeding £.30. per annum, of which there were 2,382, and ot thele about 900 have been augmented.

The Number of Benefices augmented is computed at about 3,200. The number muff necessarily be less than the number of Appropriations, because the smaller Benefices have received two, three, or four Appropriations to bring them nearer an Equality with those of greater Value.

Besides the Money received from Benefactors, many Benefactions have been given in Lands, Tythes, and Rent Charges; and in some cases, particularly of late years, Houses for the residence of Ministers, and a great number of Stipends to the Clergy have been made permanent which before were uncertain.

The Interest allowed to the Clergy was reduced at Michaelmas 1720, from 5 to 4 per-Cent.

Sir, Treasury Chambers, i ft April 1803.

I am commanded, by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to desire that you will take such measures as are least calculated to excite public notice, to prevent the Exportation to France, Spain, or the Batavian Republic, of any Saltpetre, Gunpowder, or Naval Stores, until you shall receive positive directions from His Majesty s Government upon the subject.

I am, Sir, &c.

Chairman of the Board of 7 ' N. Vansittart.

Customs in Waiting. 3

Sir, Custom-House, a8th April 1803.

In consequence of your Letter of the lit instant to the Chairman of this Board in Waiting, desiring that such measures as were least likely to excite public notice might be taken to prevent the Exportation to France, Spain, or the Batavian Republic, of any Saltpetre, Gunpowder, or Naval Stores;—a Representation by the proper Officer has been privately made to the Board, that an Entry has been made for 33 tons of Lignum Vita?, in the Venus, Daniel Nicliolfon, for Amsterdam; and dating, " that it was a prohibited article during " the late War, and the quantity unusually large:"—I am directed to communicate this circumstance to)Tou, and to represent, that Lignum Vita' is a Naval Store, and is used, as the Board are informed, in the making of Ships Blocks. In case their Lordships should fee fit to prevent the Exportation, on receiving directions for that purpose, proper steps will be taken for carrying their Lordships orders into effect.

I have the honour to be, Sir, &c.

N. Vansittart, Esq. Ac. J. Ilunie.

(Private.)

Sir, Treasury Chambers, 29th April 1803.

I am commanded, by the Chancellor of the Exchequer, to desire that the necessary measures may be taken to prevent the Exportation of the 33 tons of Lignum Vita?, alluded to in your Letter of yester-dav, as entered for Amsterdam in the Ship Venus, Daniel Nicholson Mailer.

I am, Sir, &c.

James Ilume, Esq. &c. Ar. Vansittart.

In consequence of your private Letter to me of yesterday, deliring that the Commissioners would prevent the Exportation of 33 tons ot Lignum Vita?, mentioned in my Letter to you of the preceding day, immediate orders were issued to the proper Officers accordingly; and the said Officers having represented that about three tons of the article had been put on board the Ship, the Board have directed the same to be relanded.

- I have the honour to be, Sir, See.

N. Vansittart, Esq. See. J. Hume.

I have the honour to be, Sir, &c.

ORDERS in COUNCIL, respecting Gunpowder, Saltpetre, Arms, Ammunition, and Naval Stores.

Appendix (No. 51.;

At the Court at the Queen’s Palace, the 6th of April 1803;

Present,

(l. s.) The KIN G*s Most Excellent Majesty in Council.

WHEREAS ati Act of Parliament Was passed in the 29th year of the reign of his late Majesty King George the Second, intituled, " An u Ad to impower his Majesty to prohibit the Exportation of Saltpetre, " and to enforce the Law for empowering his Majesty to prohibit the ■H Exportation of Gunpowder, or act, fort of Arms and Ammunition, M and also to impower his Majesty to restrain the carrying Coastwise " of Saltpetre, Gunpowder, or any sort of Arms or Ammunition And His Majesty judging it necessary to prohibit the Exportation of Gunpowder or Saltpetre, or any sort of Arms or Ammunition, out of this Kingdom, Or carrying the fame Coastwise, for some time, Doth therefore, with the advice of his Privy Council, hereby order, require, prohibit, and command. That no Person or Persons whatsoever (except the Master General of the Ordnance for llis Majesty's Service) do at any time, during the (pace of two months from the date of this Order in Council, presume to transport into any parts out of this Kingdom, or carry Coastwise, any Gunpowder or Saltpetre, or any sort of Arms or Ammunition, or ftiip or lade any Gunpowder or Saltpetre, or any sort of Arms or Ammunition, on board any Ship or Vessel, in order to transporting the fame into any parts beyond the Seas, or carrying the fame Coastwise, without leave or permission in that behalf first obtained from His Majesty or His Privy Council; upon pain of incurring and fc.<v*nng the respective Forfeitures and Penalties inflicted by the aforementioned Ad.—And the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty's Treasury, the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, the Lord Warden of the Cinque Ports, the Mailer General of the Ordnance, and His Majesty’s Secretary at War, are to give the necessary directions herein, as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed) Stcph. Cottrell.

At the Court at the Queen’s Palace, the 11th of May 1803;

Present,

(l. s.) The KIN G’s Most Excellent Majesty in Council.

Whereas by an Act, passed in the 33d year of His Majesty’s reign, intituled, u An Act to enable His Majesty to restrain the Exportation " of Naval Stores, and more effectially to prevent the Exportation 44 of Saltpetre, Arms, and Ammunition, when prohibited by Procla-14 mation or Order in Council," It is Enacted, amongst other things, That His Majesty may, by Proclamation or Order in Council, when He shall fee cause, and for such time as shall be therein expressed, prohibit the exporting, or. the attempting to export, Pig Iron, Bar Iron, llemp. Pitch, Tar, Roftn, Turpentine, Anchors, Cables, Cordage, Malls, Yards, Bowsprits, Oars, Oakum, Oker, Sheet Copper, and other Naval Stores: And His Majesty judging it necessary to prohibit the Exportation of the said several articles, for a limited time, Doth therefore, with* the advice of His Privy Council, hereby order, require, prohibit, and command, That no Person or Persons whatsoever do, at any time during the space of two months from the date of this Order in Council, presume to transport into any parts out of this Kingdom any Pig Iron, Bar Iron, Hemp, Pitch, Tar, Rosin, Turpentine, Anchors, Cables, Cordage, Malls, Yards, Bowsprits, Oars, Oakum, Oker, Sheet Copper, or other Naval Stores, or do ship or lade any Pig Iron, Bar Iron, Hemp, Pitch, Tar, Roftn, Turpentine, Anchors, Cables, Cordage, Malls, Yards, Bowsprits, Oars, Oakum, Oker, Sheet Copper, or other Naval Stores, on board any Ship or Vessel, in order to transporting the fame into any parts beyond the Seas, without leave or permission first being had and obtained from His Majesty or His Privy Council, upon pain of incurring the Forfeitures infilled by the afore-mentioned Act: But it is nevertheless His Majesty's pleasure, that nothing herein contained shall extend, or be coniirued to extend, to any of His Majesty's Ships of War, or any other Ships or Vessels or Boats in the service of His Majesty, or employed or freighted by His Majesty’s Board of Ordnance, or by the Commissioners of His Majesty’s Navy; nor to prevent any Ship or Vessel from taking or having on board such quantities of Naval Stores as may be necessary for the use of fuelvShip or Vessel during the course of her intended voyage; or by licence from the Lol d High Admiral of Great Britain, or the Commissioners of the Admiralty for the time being; nor to the Exportation of the said several articles to Ireland, or to His Majesty’s Yards or Garrifdns, or to His Majesty’s Colonies or Plantations in America or the West Indies, or to Newfoundland, or to His Majesty’s Forts and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, or to the Island of St. Helena, or the Britishi Settlements or Fadlorics in the East Indies: Provided, that upon the Exportation of any of the said articles for the purposes of trade to Ireland, or to His Majesty's Yards and Garrisons, or to His Majesty’s Colonies and Plantations in America or the West Indies, or to the Island of Newfoundland, or to His Majesty's Forts' and Settlements on the Coast of Africa, or to the Island of St. Helena, or the Britishi Settlements or, Factories in the East Indies, the Exporters of such articles do first make oath of the true destinalion of the same to the places for which they shall be entered outwards, before, the entry of the fame shall be made, and do give full and sufficient security, by Bond, to the satisfaction of the Commissioners of His Majesty's Customs, to carry the said articles to the places for whichr they are so entered outwards, and for the purposes specified, and none other; and such Bond shall not be cancelled or delivered up until proof be made, to the satisfaction of the said Commissioners, by the production, within a time to be fixed by the said Commissioners, and specified in the Bond, of a Certificate or Certificates, in such form and manner as shall be directed by the said Commissioners, /hewing that the said articles have been duly landed at the places for which they were entered outwards.—And the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of Great Britain, and the Lord’ Warden of the Cinque Ports, are to give the neceflhiy directions herein, as to them may respectively appertain.

(Signed), W. Fwksncti

FIRST REPORT.

Hie COMMITTEE, to whom the * 44 Survey and Report of

44 the Coasts ami Central Highlands of Scotland, made by the 44 Command of the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners 4< of llis Majesty's Treasury, in the Autumn of 1802," is referred; and who were empowered to report their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House

H A VIN G proceeded to the invefeigation of the various matters contained in the Survey and Report referred to them, have thought it their duty, with as little delay as possible, to fubinit to the considera-tio« of the I Joule such brio.‘.nation as they have received on the fub-jeri of the Emigrations which have already taken place, and which are still going forward, to a consideruble extent, in the Highlands or Wands oi Scotland; as that part of the subject referred to their consideration seems to them most immediately to require the attention of Parliament, not only on account of its interesting nature, but on account of the flbufes and fulferings by which it appears to be attended. Tk:*' ivfnrmotion is contained in several Reports from the Highland Society cl Scotland, ?ud is confirmed by various other documents, and by such parol* Evidence as Your Committee have been able to procure, and of which they have annexed, in the Appendix to this Report, such extracts as appear to them most material.

Your Committee will immediately proceed to the investigation of those measures which, by giving employment at home to the industry of a hardy race of People, may preclude them from the necessity of forking fubiistence in distant countries, and which will at the lame time promote the general improvement and prnfperity of the Empire; but, in the meantime, they think it nccclVary to call the most serious attention of the House to the futferings and hardships which those who ha ve already emigrated, appear to have endured, for want of proper treatment on their paftkge, which, in the opinion of Your Committee, demand the immediate interpolilion oi Parliament, to prevent die recurrence of similar calamities.

Resolveod, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That Persons emigrating from different parts of the United Kingdom, have, in various instances, fullered great dill refs and hardlliip, on account of the crowded hate of the \'cfiVIs, the want of a sufficient stock of provisions, water, and other necefiavies for the voyage, and in various other Yelped.

Resolved, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That it is expedient to regulate the Vessels carrying Patiengers from the United Kingdom to His Majesty’s Plantations and Settlements abroad, or to Foreign Part«, with n speet to the number of Passengers which they shall be allowed to take on board, ih proportion to the tonnage of such Yfifids, as well as with rdpecl to the provision of proper ueceffarics for the voyage.

AT a General Meeting of the Highland Society of Scotland, continued by Royal Charter, held this day, attended by about one hundred of its Members, a Report was brought up from the Committee of Directors, and laid before the Society; whereof the tenor follows;

44 That the evil of Emigration is likely to be progressive, if not interrupted, may be inferred trom the fa<!:t, that so great a number of 44 persons propose to quit their native Country during the enfutng 44 summer. The industry of those who make profit by the conveyance 44 of these deluded People acrufs the Atlantic, cannot be expected to 44 suffer any abatement; and their profits are encreufed by means 44 which excite in the Committee the strongest regret, and which expose the Emigrants to circumstances of fullering ami distress, during 44 the passage, which are shocking to humanity. The Committee had 44 accels to leam some particulars of a voyage of this fort, from direct 44 communication with a person who was a Passenger on board an u Emigrant Ship that faded for North Carolina in 1773. It tfas a 44 Vessel of 300 tons burthen. T he number of persons on board were 44 about 450, of whom 25 had, at coming on board, no birth nor bed 44 of any fort, nor could any be adorded them during the paftago ex* " cept as fumished by vacancies owing to death. T he water be- came scarce during the voyage, which lalied twelve weeks and 44 three days, The tlnrtt of the poor people was of course ftimul&ted 44 by feeding entirely on lait meat. For the last fortnight the allowance to each Passenger was only au English pint of watef for 44 44 hours; and many of the calks having been made of staves used in 44 the tobacco and indigo trade, the waiter was often so impregnated 4t with these nauseous ingredients, that the people lickened and threw 4C it up. The consequence was, that they were kazed with a dylentery, " and 23 of them died before reaching Carolina, and the rest were u landed in the most exh&ufted and debilitated ft ate.

" The Committee have alto had occasion to fee a printed Petition to u the Court of Setlion, taking notice of fume facts 1 elating to an Eiui-*• grant Ship that took on board Passengers at Skye, for Carolina, in 44 1791. In that case it appeared the Veiled was of about 270 tons 44 burthen: the number of Passengers about 400, including women and 44 children; lo that their fituutiou was most uncomtortable and dan-u gerous, there being hardly room for them to ft retch themselves. a T here were three tiers of beds fore and aft, and two mid/hip. The u births for a full Passenger* were 18 indies broad. Those lore u and aft were only about two feet high, including the space occupied 44 by bedding, so that it was fcarely possible to creep into them. The " others were a little higher, so that the Passenger could turn himself 44 on his fide, and rest on his elbow.—To add to their calami lies, they 44 neither had sufficLency of viduals, nor proper cooking ntcnlils, there u being only two pots, of 24 pints each; which were quite inadequate u to the preparation, in any reasonable time, of a meal for 400 per-" ions. 44 The Committee of the Highland Society, to whom it was remitted 44 to consider and report upon the subject of Emigration, have already, 44 at two periods, laid before the Society what information they had 44 acquired, with the observations which seemed to arise out of it. It 44 is now, a third time, the Opinion of the Committee, that they are 44 called upon to furnish some further detail* on the subject. It assumes 44 more and more a serious and alarming afped. The Highland Emi-u gration can no longer, by any Person be contemplated as an imma- terial circumstance; far less (as some have thought it) benelicial in 44 the way of draining a surplus population.—It is sass approaching to u the point of complete depopulation of a large district of the* Kingdom, 44 a fad-which the Society cannot, without betraying its duty, fail to * submit to the wisdom of Government.

44 The Committee have received* by thte aid of a very intelligent

Correspondent, a Statement of Vessels actually ascertained to have carried Emigrants, in the year 1802, from the Highland* Northward of Fort William, to the Provinces of Nova Scotia, Canada, and North Carolina, a Statement which must be far ftiort of the actual Emigration, both in as much as a very extensive trad of Coail is not included, from whence many VeHels failed, and also because even on the Coaff, which is included in the Account, many Vessels are believed to have failed from unfrequented Bays and Creeks, which accordingly have entirely eluded inquiry.

44 Defective however as the account must be, it specifies eleven Vessels bearing about 3,300 Persons from their native Country.

44 As to the present year, it is of course impossible to say what nnm-‘ ber will follow the example of those who emigrated during the last; but the fads that have come to the knowledge of the Committee, persuade them that it will be immense. They have specific information of a number, far exceeding that of last year, who are already under engagement to that effect; and the opinion which they are led on the whole to form, is, that this summer will witness about twenty thousand Highlanders conveyed acrose the Atlantic

44 On this point (the extent of Emigration) I do not pretend to any great degree of accuracy; I speak from the bed verbal and written informations I have been able to procure, respecting the number of Ships already freighted and departed, or Hill expected for the purpose of conveying Emigrants to America; together with the circumstances and dii of the people on those estates from whence emigration is apprehended. SECOND REPORT.

The COMMITTEE, to whom the " Survey and Report of the 44 Coasts and Central Highlands of Scotland, made by the *l Command of the Right honourable the Lords Commission-u ers of His Majesty’s Treasury, in the Autumn of 1802,* is referred; and who were empowered to report their Observations thereupon, from time to time, to the House;—

HAVING considered, in their former Report, the nature and extent of the Emigrations from the Western and Northern Highlands Off Scotland, and being strongly impressed with the necessity of affording immediate employment to the Inhabitants of those Islands, proceeded, in the next place, to the consideration of that part of Mr. Telford’s Survey, which relates to forming an Inland Navigation between Inverness and Fort William, with the view of improving the Fisheries, and advancing the general interests of the Kingdom, in War as well as in Peace. But, as Your Committee, in order to obtain a more accurate knowledge of this iuljecl, have thought it material to order several Persons before them from Scotland, and as some time mud elapse before those Persons can arrive, Your Committee proceeded, without further delay, to consider with attention the part of the Survey relating to Roads and Bridges, which they are of opinion are of the higbed importance, for the fame laliitary purposes which the Inland Navigation is designed to promote; especially such of them as will open Communications with the Eishing Lochs and Stations on the different Coasts, through a dittrict of Country at present nearly inaccessible, and which forms a Barrier against all probable Improvement.

VOL. 53.

Your Committee are fenttble, that Bridges cannot be built* ot Lines of Road formed through this mountainous and difficult Country* without the aid of Public Liberality and Encouragement: Thefirft and original expence of such Works, it is in vain to expect that the means of the Proprietors of Land can altogether defray; but it feemsjuR that the Land Owners should assist the Public to the exent of their ability; and for that purpose it may be expedient to afford every facility for enabling them to raise such Sums of Money as may be necessary, as they will share the general benefit which mutt result from difiilfing habits of industry among the People, and opening a free and ready aa-cess to the more cultivated part of the Countiy.

It therefore appears to Your Committee to be advisable, that pro* viflon should be made, for the present year, by Parliament, for defraying one-half of the estimated expence of the Roods and Bridges, which may appear most immediately necessary:

And, That the remainder of the expence of making such Roads and Bridges should be defrayed by the Proprietors of Land, or other Persons who may be benefited thereby; and that provision should be made for keeping such Roads and Bridge* in proper repair:

And, That, in order to provide for the proper Expenditure of the Public Money, and in order that the said Roads and Bridges may be carried on with prudence and ceconomy, it will be proper that Coin-missioners should be appointed to superintend and direct the execution

of the fame:

The COMMITTEE, trf whom the " Survey and Report of the " Coasts and Central Highlands of Scotland, made by the " Command of the llight honourable the Lords Commission-" ers of His Majesty’s Treasury, in the Autumn of 1802," is referred; and who were empowered to report their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House;—

HAVING considered, in their two former Reports, the nature and extent of the Emigrations from the Western and Northern Highland* of Scotland, and the necessity of making Roads and Bridges to open communications with the Fishing Lochs and Stations, and with dil-trids of Country which are at present nearly inaccessible, have proceeded to the consideration of that part of Mr. Telford’s Survey which relates to forming an Inland Navigation from the Eastern to the Webern Sea, by Inverness and Fort William: and have now received all the Evidence they think necestary, to enable them to form an Opinion on this subject.

Your Committee, being aware of the importance of this great National object, have, with much care, examined sundry experienced and re-spedable Shipmasters, with regard to the present Navigation by The Pentland Firth, Cape Wrath, and the Minch, to the Irish Channel: From the testiinony of several Persons long experienced in this Navigation, it appears to Your Committee, that this Navigation, so far as regards the commercial intercourse between the Western and Eastern Coasts of Great Britain, or between a considerable part of Ireland and the Eastern Coasts of Great Britain, or between a considerable part of Ireland and the Northern parts of Europe; or between the Western Coast of Great Britain and the fame Countries, by the Pentland Firth, is not only very circuitous: but, during the Autumn and Winter, especially in long nights, on acount of the thickness of the weather, the violence of the waves, the rapidity and diversity of the tides, is peculiarly difficult and dangerous. It appears, however, to Your Committee, that some difference of opinion prevails, as to the extent of that danger; for Captains Huddart and Frafer, whose authority mult in all cases have great weight, seem not to think it very considerable. But the contrary opinion is entertained by all those who have had personal experience of that Navigation, and is supported by the acknowledged fafts of frequent and distrclling losses of Property to a large amount, and of many valuable Lives.

Your Committee having also examined, with much attention, sundry experienced Mariners and Civil Engineers, as well as Captain Gwyn, the Commander of the Government Galley on Loch Nefs, a man of thirty-seven years experience in that service, as to the practicability of forming the Canal, and navigating both that and all the Lochs between Inverness and Fort William with Ships of burthen; and likewise as to the difference of time and safety in passing through this Navigation, when compared with that by The Pentland Firth, Cape Wrath, and the Minch; Your Committee find, that the Navigation of the Murray Firth from Buchaness to Fort George is very lafe, has favourable tides, a spacious and commodious Harbour in the Bay of Cromarty on the North-west side of the Murray Firth, and a tolerable good one at Brough Head on the South fide thereof'That, between Fort George and Inverness there is a Loch of lafe Navigation and good Anchorage; from Inverness to the N. E. end of Loch Nefs, adiltance of about seven miles, that the ground is favourable for a Canal; and that Loch Nefs, which is about twenty-two miles in length, and from one to two and a half in breadth, is of great depth of water, and quite free in its Channel from rocks or impediments to the Navigation; that there are/ix anchoring places on the North, and three on the South fide thereof, besides excellent anchoring ground at each end; that it never freezes; and, though subject to occasional gusts of wind, yet they are not sufficiently violent to be dangerous, except from the end of November to the beginning of February: From Ixich Nefs to Loch Oich, a distance of about five miles, the ground is yery favourable for making a Canal. Loch Oich, which is on the summit level between the East and West Seas, is only about one hundred feet above the level of high-water-mark; it i3 about four miles in length, and receives the waters from Loch Garry, Loch Quoieh, and all the Valley of Glen Garry, and Glen Quoieh affording a ftfpply of water beyond every possible demand. Loch Oich is narrow, being only from one quarter to three quarters of a mile in breadth, and is calculated to be navigated by means, of tracking, in the manner of a Canal.— J-roin I^oich Oich there is only a distance of one mile and a half of ground to the N. E. end of Loch Locby: and this ground is also fa-

vourable for makirfg a Canal.—The N. E. end of Loch Lochy is pe* culiarly well formed as an entrance Bason, being separated from the body of the Loch by a narrow Channel, there is a sufficient depth of water, and good anchorage.—-Loch Lochy is about ten miles and a half long, and from one and a half to two rtiiles in breadth; it is quite clear of rocks, and has good anchorage at each end, and also good

anchorage near to the middle of the South fidt at Letter Findlay_Th6

From tlieS.W. end of Loch Lochy to the Shore of Loch Iail, which is an arm of the Weltern Sea, the distance is about seven miles; a Road might readily be formed along the South lirte of IakIi Lochy, and Y'dlels might )>• tracked in calms, or against light breezes. Betweeft Loch Locby and Loch Eil, the ground iB more rugged than in the oth^r Difftricls; but, conlifting of small rifuigs, the tops of which may be thrown into the Vallies, is not unfavourable for a Canal; and there is 110 appear-* ance of rock any where upon the surface, in the fine of the pro* posed Navigation. The entrance into the Sea at Loch Eil, is at it place where there is good ihclter and anchorage for any number of Vessels of burthen. From Fort Williairr down the Linnlie Loch, until it becomes part of the main Sea, between Oban and the South end of the Isle of Mull, the Navigation is clear, and the tides are favourable; in the collide of this Loch there is (belter and anchorage, and within a little of the extremity of the Linnhe Loch are the excellent Harbours of Oban and Tobermory.—From Oban the Navigation lies within the Islands, pastes near the mouth of Loch Criftan to the Irish Channel, or through the Crinal Canal to the Firth of Clyde; so that from the entrance of the Murray Firth on the East, to the Mull of Cantyre on the Weft, there is no risk from Storms or an Enemy.

Fnftn the evidence of three respectable Shipmasters, who have been many years employed in navigating those seas, it appears, That from Buchaness, oft the Eastern extremity of the Murray Firth to the entrance of the Irish Channel, the average passage at prefeift is above a fortnight; it has frequently been from two so three months; it has been performed in five days; but for so short a passage, not only very fair winds are necclVary, but they must change three times.

From Buchaness to the entrance of the Irish Channel, by the Inland Navigation, with a moderate and fair wind, the passage might be readily and regularly made in five days; with a moderate, but contrary wind, in nine days: and with any contrary wind, when fail could be carried, in twelve days; the great superiority therefore of the proposed Canal to the present Navigation is evident, in expedition as well as safety.

There have been submitted to the consideration of Your Committee, several communications from well-informed Persons of the Ports of Dublin, Liverpool, Greenock, Leith, Aberdeen, and Peterhead; which all agree with respect to the dangers attending the present Navigation by the Pentland Firth and Cape Wrath; and with respect to the advantages before stated, which must arise, from the proposed Navigation, to Commerce and the Fisheries.

Your Committee are therefore deeply imprefied with the immediate necessity of employing the People of the Country in the execution of this great National Work; which will excite a spirit, and introduce habits of industry; and will moil probably check the present rage for Emigration, and prevent its future progress.

Your Committee are equally convinced of the practicability, as of the importance of tills work. The ft rata under ground along the line of the Canal have not yet been proved, by sinking Pits or boring; but from the general appearance of the foil near the surface, there is no reason to suppose that there is any rock near the surface of the ground in the line of the Canal; and from Estimates, which have been made under this supposition, it appears to the Committee, as far as they can depend upon Mr. Ttdford’s knowledge of local circuin-stunces, stated in his Report, that, exclusively of the value of Land, which, except near Inverness, isr in general of inferior quality, the execution of the works in a very plain though substantial manner, with the materials to be tound in the Country, and with the advantage to he derived trom the luperabundant supplies of water on the summit level, which will enable the Engineer to introduce a new and very (Economical mode of forming the Lochs, that the whole expence of a Canal, to contain twenty feet depth, would not exceed Three hundred and Iilty thousand Pounds, it appears, however, to the Committee, from Mr. Jellbp's mode of calculation, that his Efrimate would amount to lour hundred and Seventy-eight thousand Five hundred Pound 5, but

BETWEEN the Bay of Ohan and the South end of the Sound of Mull, an arm of the Sea, called Thfe Linnhe I.och, runs in a N. E. It is through this Valley that the Inland Navigation is proposed to be made. Between Oban and the Coast of Morven, this arm of the Sea is about 12 miles in width; it is contracted to about three quarters of a mile at a place called Ardgower; after which it becomes and continues a mile in width to Fort William; it there takes a Westerly direction, and approaches within the diiiailcc of four miles of the Head of Loch Sheal.

The portion of the Loch, which lies to the Weft of the Strait of Ardgower, is called the Linuhel.och; that to the North-east is called Loch Ell. In the Linnhe Loch there are the Islands of Lismore, Shema, and the Sheep Island. They are composed of Lirneftone; the most considerable is Lismore, about seven miles in length, upon which there are several Limekilns, and some fertile Fields: Shema is a fine grazing Island.—The heft Channel for Navigation is on the North fide of Lismore, and the other Islands; it is clear of lunken rocks, and of sufficient depth of water for the largest Vessels; at Ardgower, on account of the hidden narrowing of the Channel, there i3 a strong current, but as the passage is clear, it is only necessary to take the Flood-tide lb going up, and the Ebb-tide in returning: I am informed that Vessels can readily bear down against Westerly winds, if they can carry fail during Ebb-tides, and that there are anchoring grounds, where Vessels may stop with safety until the tides are suitable. The Hills along the North Ihore are lofty, rugged, and rocky. The Hills do not approach so near to the Weft end of the South Shore.

CALEDONIAN CANAL.

Having given some account of the Linnhe Loch, and Loch Eit, the next object is the Survey, which commences at Fort William, and is carried through the Country to the Coast of Inverness.

It is evident that the modes of conveyance ought to vary according to the nature of the Country in which they are formed, and the business which is ex petted to be transutted by their means; it therefore became fteceiTary, before I entered upon the Survey, to weigh all the circumstances, in order to determine the direction and plan of Navigation which is bell suited to that particular place, and bdl calculated to promote the general good.

I considered, if I Humid find that the Country abounded with w*ater upon the linn mi t level, that the height of this fmnniit above the level of the sea was inconsideruble; that there w as no serious obltacles in the way; that a great part of the dillance was already navigable for Vessels of the largest dimenliems, and that at each extremity they might be immediately passed into deep water, in saie Bays; then, that the general good required that the Navigation should be made to admit Ships of large dimensions, both for Commerce and War; and that, un-Jess a Navigation could be made for Ships of very considerable burthen, it would answer no good purpose.

Upon enquiry, I found that the leading circumstances relative to the nature of the plan, afforded all the advantages that were required, and justified the making a Navigation on a large seale. This determined my condutt, and led me to examine the track in question, with the view of making a Navigation which should admit of Vessels of Urge dimensions-

The advantages to be derived from forming an Inland Navigation through this Valley have not escaped the attention of some persons who were acquainted with it, and were disposed to promote public improvements.

In the year 1773, the Trustees for the forfeited Estates employed Mr, Watt to make a survey of this track, which he did, and furnished them with a Report and Estimate of the Expence of making a Canal of ten feet water. This Report is so able and just, that, had I considered that iize of Canal as most advisable, I should have adopted the calculations of the expence to the present day, and mentioned foine-alterations which have taken place in the country fiiice his survey was made, and should have recommended the Survey to your Lordship’s attention. But Mr. Watt's views were merely to alceitain how far Navigation of any fort was practicable, and therefore he fixed upon ten feet of water as aii alVumed standard to enable him to make his Estimates.

I lose therefore the benefit of his particular calculations; and I am Under the necessity of departing, in some initances, from his line of Canal; especially at the entrances into the Lochs and Tideways, in order to obtaih a greater depth of water; but I have followed him wherever the circumstances would pciniit; and I cannot refill the introducing his general description of the Country through which the Navigation is proposed to be made; because, after having examined the whole with care, I find it to be so correct, that I could only repeat the fame deleriptions, and dwell upon the fame points.

Mr. Watt, instead of proceeding from the Weft to the East, came from the Fall to the Weft; and gives the following Report:

Loch Oich, lying on the summit level, may be called the Canal of Partition; I did not measure the length of it, but it is said to be 4J miles long, and on an average £ mile wide, which is about the width of the River Thames at Westminster Bridge. It is narrowed where the River Garry falls in, but sufficiently broad for the purpose of an Inland Navigation; there are three small Blands in this Lake. The hills on each side are rough and rocky down to the (bores nearly: the /bores are fiat and gravelly; on the South fide are flat and cultivated ground, and the fides of the hills grow a great deal of bru/h-u'ood. There are some plantations of firs on the N. fide. About half way down the Lake on the N. fide, and near to the mouth of the River Garry, Hands the old Cattle of Glengarry; the house of the present Proprietor Hands very near the Cattle, and there is a very lofty peaked hill immediately behind it. These circumstances, with the opening of a deep Valley towards Loch Garry, combine to render this a very romantic landscape.

Loch Garry is said to be fix miles in length, and Loch Quoich eight miles; the water of this latt Loch falls into Loch Garry, and runs thence into Loch Oich on the summit level of the proposed Navigation.

The Feeders to these Lochs branch into a very considerable tra£ of country; one fiream, called the Joine Water, penetrates almott to the /bores opposite the S. end of the Bland of Sky. The rains in that part of the country are heavy and frequent, so that the waters which the Rivers carry offwoidd probably be more than sufficient to supply all the lockage. In case there was at any time apprehensions of this proving insufficient, the two Lochs above-mentioned, taken together, make a reservoir 14 miles in length, and with Loch Oich, upwards of ]8 miles. This removes completely every doubt respecting the supply of water, which is the moll important of all questions relative to Canal making. The fupcrabundance of water would add greatly to the value of this proposed National Improvement, and is applicable to many very valuable purposes, some of which I shall take an opportunity of mentioning in the course of this Report.

The point of land upon which the Fort and Town of Fort Augustus (lands appears to be composed chiefly of gravel. There is another River falls into the Loch, to the South of the Fort it is called The Tars.

The shores of the upper or Weftem end of Loch Nefs, towards each side, are flat, owing to the gravel which is brought down by the River; in the middle, near to the Pier, the (bore shelves down very suddenly. The general direction of the Loch is N. E. and S. W. very nearly. The prevailing winds are from the S. W. and they almost always blow up or down the Valley. The hills on each side are lofty and rugged, and deep, down to the very edge of the water. They are mostly covered with brulh-wood.

The Military Road leaves the Loch, pafles over the tops of the hills on the South fide, and returns towards the Loch at the Fall of Fyers; pafles the General's Hut, and then falls down to the Loch fide; near which it continues to the lower end of the Loch, at the village of Dores: On the North fide of the Loch, a road pafles Eadweard along the edge of the Loch to Glen-Morrison; it there leaves the Loch and erodes the river by a bridge, about a mile from its mouth, it then returns to and continues down the edge of the Loch for about a mile; it afterwards ascends the hill, and pafles along the brow of it to Urqu-hart, which is on the margin of the Loch. From Urquhart it pafles down the margin of the Loch to the lower end opposite to the Ferry.

I did not measure the length t)f the Loch, but it is laid to be about 22 tnilcs, and it seems to be above a mile in breadth; it is. in general deep to the very shores. From Fort Augustus, I pafieddown the Loch in a boat to the mouth of the River Fye^s, and examined the shores as I went along; from thence I rode along the South fide to Dores, taking notes as I went. I have represented the form and nature of the shores as accurately as I could upon the Chart. 1 am of opinion it is practicable to make a road close to the shore, either on the South or North fide, whichever should answer the best purpose for towing or tracking Vessels. It would require a more accurate examination and compa-rifon, to decide upon which shore it is the moll advisable; in either case, the road would require to be carried over the mouths of the Rivers which fall into the Loch; and it appears to me, it would be best to do this by means of wooden Bridges. I shall speak as to the manner of navigating this Loch, as well a3 the others, as soon as I have carried the survey to Inverness.

From the lower end of the Loch at Dores, the hills which form the South fide of the Valley begin to turn away to the i.aft; those on the North fide continue in almost a direct line nearly to Inverness, where they end abruptly at Loch Beauly; although the general valley becomes wider, there are considerable irregularities between the lower end of the Loch and Inverness, which divide this District into two lesser Vallies; that to the South is called the Strath of Dores, and is well cultivated. The River Nefs runs along the North Valley; the fides of the hills near the end of the Loch, and down to Inverness, are clothed with extensive plantations of fir; along the vallies and banks of the river, the arable land and plantations are intermixed; the River, which is a very considerable stream, pafles along with several windings to the Town of Inverness, and falls into Loch Beauly, about a mile below the Town. Loch Beauly is here contracted into less than one mile in width; it opens both below and above to about three miles in width, and is terminated at the Village of Beauly, seven miles Westward; and at Fort George, about fix miles Eaihvard; it is contracted to a narrow entrance between Loch Beauly and the lower end of Loch Nefs; there are several very good houses, on well-chosen filiations, along the fide of the hills; and, altogether, this District is beautiful and interesting.

Near to where the River, Nefs comes out of Loch Nefs, there must be made a regulating W ear across the River, and an eligible filiation chosen for connecting the Canal and Loch; and erecting piers for protecting its entrance. The Canal should pass down the North fide of the River, and at no great distance from it, along arable land and meadow grounds, until it reaches a steep bank at Moulin Duar: The River mult here be turned out of its present course, and the Canal be made along the present bed of the River; this may be done with facility, as there is already a division of the stream which runs another way; and if the Mill Wear was taken away, the whole of the River would run in the channel to the Southward, where it is proposed to turn it. There would be a Mill destroyed here, but that will be amply provided for in the subsequent part of this Report. From the Mill, the line of Canal pafles along a gently Doping bank, partly cultivated, and partly heathy, past the Bleachfield, to the upper corner of the steep bank called Tourvaine; along this last distance,. the Canal mute defeend by lockage: The river here flows close to the bottom of the steep bank, and mud be turned into a new channel, cut for it on the South fide of the present stream; and the Canal mud be formed in the present bed.

From the N. E. point of the steep bank at Tourvaine, the Canal must pass through the fields on the South fide of the public road, to the skirts of the suburbs of Inverness, called the Muir 1 own; it there crosses the road, and pafles through some fields to the road which goes from Inverness to Beauly; it erodes this road also and pafles through the Marfti, and on a line through the fields to Loch Beauly, into which it falls a little way to tlje East of Kefiock Ferry. From a little above

the Muir Town, the Locks must be placed at proper distances, so as to suit the ground and entrance into the Loch; near to the Loch there should be an artificial Bason made capable of containing a few Vessels to be in readiness to fall down at the proper time of tide. Where it is proposed to make the Canal enter, the shore (helves down very suddenly into deep water, and good anchoring ground; and I was informed by some experienced Seamen that this l’pot is always (heltered and safe. The Longman and Dollan Points defend it against the North and East winds, and there are no heavy seas with the Westerly winds. Owing to the hidden contraction here* there is a strong current, both with the flowing and ebbing tides; but this current runs chiefly along or near to the North shore, and is of service to carry Vessels out and in, if the wind is not very fair.

The whole of the Loch to Fort George is good anchorage. At present* the Vessels generally bring to on the South fide of the Loch, about four miles below the Town of Inverness, in five fathom water, in the Carse Road. Up towards Beauly, the Loch (hallows. The ordinary spring tides life here eleven feet. Neaps about seven feet. Extra Springs fifteen feet. The highest tides are with Westerly winds, but the roughest sea with the wind at N. E. and East. The tides are highest on the third day after full and change.

From the lower end of Loch Nefs, to the place where it is proposed that the Canal shall fall into the Loch Beauly, the distance is seven miles and 67 yards. The fall from the surface of water in Loch Nefsr to the line of high-water mark at Loch Beauly, is 36 feet.

Mr. Watt makes the fall 45 feet; but, from the depth he mentions, Loch Nefs must at that time have been fuller by about 4 feet; and he took his level from the time of high-watermark neap tides, which makes a difference of other 4 feet; and, allowing for theie two circumstances, the levels agree within 1 foot.

With regard to the materials for the Piers, Locks, and other works, necessary for such a Navigation:—Near to Inverness, stone, lime, and sand, are to be had in futiicient quantities; the Hone and (and are got in the neighbourhood; the lime is brought by sea. There is freestone near Red Castle, and in Manloehie in Loefli Beauly, and likewise at Brughhead on the Murray Firth. At Dores a good building stone can be had, situate about a mile up the hill on the South, upon the estate of Frazer Tytler, Esq. The lime is got from Inverness and Fyers. Sand from the shores of the Loch and Rivers. Timber may be had from Glen-Morrison or Inverness. Near to Fort Augustus there is an excellent building stone; lime is got from Fyers or Aber-halda above Loch Oich.

I had no opportunity of examining the Stone Quarries on the Dimmit level; but, as the hills on both iides of the Valley are composed of rocks, there can be little doubt that proper stone may be found. 1 observed good stone near to the bottom of Loch Lochy, on ik« South fide; and likewise by the lides of the River Spean. Lime can be had on the summit level, near to Fort William, and from the Island of Lismore. Freeftone may be had from the Coast of Morven, or the South end of the Island of Mull; sand can be had almost any where; and the Country Timber in Loch Eil, Loch Arkeg, and Glengarry, might be made to answer most purposes.

In forming this Navigation, I think that a very considerable saving might be made by departing from the common mode of constructing the Locks. Locks are in general composed entirely of Masonry, and are very expensive. They are formed after this manner, in order that they may be made nearly of the fame size as the Vessels, so that as little water may be loft as possible, and that as short time may be taken in fitting them. In the present case, as there is a superabundant quantity of water, the liufbanding the use of it is not an object to (b much attended to; I therefore propose to make two pair of gates* with the necessary bulwarks, for each Lock; and make the space between the gates of earthen banks, (loped in the usual way of China! Banks; the Lock would in this way require a longer time in filling and emptying; but the Paddles might be construCled so as to remedy this in a great measure; and belidcs this, two or more Vessels might pass through the Lock at one time.

The Vessels would of course be tracked by horses along the Canal, and also Loch Oich, because this Loch is narrow. On Loch Nefs and Loch Lochy they might easily run before a fair wind in the course of a few hours; with a contrary wind they might beat up when they could carry fail, and they might be tracked by horses in calms or against light breezes.

The lands in the course of the Valley, from Fort William to Inverness, belong to the following Proprietors. The improvement of the Central Highlands, and indeed of all the Highlands, may be expected*to follow from forming the Inland Navigation, and building the Bridge^. Besides facilitating the intercourse w hen completed, habits of industry would be introduced during the execution of the works. The industrious part of the Inhabitants would thereby obtain some capital, which Would enable them to embark in other employments, at present totally out of their power; and many such employments would occur to the People who would be engaged in the different operations attending the making the Inland Navigation. —To persons who are acquainted with the nature of Manufactures, it will appear a matter of no flight importance to have the command of Falls of Water inexhaustible as to quantity, and which never freezes; and these conveniently situated for procuring raw Materials from the Northern parts of Europe and America, and connected with a water* conveyance for Vessels of any magnitude.

1 am of opinion, that the spinning and weaving of Sail Cloth and-Sacking of all descriptions might be done there by means of Machinery worked by Water; also the twitting of Rope6, sawing of Timber, and many other purposes, which are simple, and want only the constant operation of a great and unexpenfive power. With such Reservoirs as these Fresh-water Lakes afford, it becomes a great National object to enable them to be applied to beneficial purposes.

The Rubble Work in the Bridges is estimated at the rate for which it is performed in Bridges in the Northern parts of Scotland, and, which is about Two Shillings per cubic yard higher than wha$ is paid for House Building.

The Rubble Work in the Locks is estimated at the rate of 2.s. per cubic yard higher than in the Bridges, and 4s. higher than in house Building, on account of more Water Lime being uled.

The Freeftone is estimated at the rate of 6 d. per cubic foot higher than it can be delivered at Dunkeld, from near to Dundee; and which I think an average for the works upon the Canal.

All the Timber (a few pieces excepted) for Bridges, Locks, Piling, Sheeting, Defenders, &c. is proposed to be of the Country Timber, which may be got from Glen-Morrison, Glengarry, and Loch Ark eg, at from 12 d. to 18 d. per foot.

l.v—Copy of a Letter from Francis Trench, Esquire, respecting the Use of the Caledonian Canal, as it regards the City of Dublin.

Dated Navigation Office, Dublin, 23d January 1803.

Dear Sir,

I have been prevented from replying to your esteemed favour by the Gentleman whom I consulted on thesubjett (a leading Member of the Insurance Office) being called suddenly out of Town, and taking your Letter with him.

Since his return, he has laid it before mod of the Gentlemen who frequent his Office; and be informs me, that the general opinion among them is, that a Canal made through the Lakes of Scotland for Vessels of so large burthen, would be resorted to by almost all Vessels coining from the Baltic, and neighbouring Countries, to the North, North-east, and North-weft of Ireland, iti time of War; and that, even in time of Peace, if the Tonnage was moderate, it would be frequented during great part of the year. In my opinion, the Vessels bound for Liverpool, and that fide of England, with valuable Cargoes, such as Tallow, Hemp, &c. would prefer this ftiort route to faye Interest of Money, while the large Timber Ships, whose Cargoes are not much more value than double the value of the freight, would prefer the longer sea, at least during a Peace.

It surprized me to find that you cross Scotland with so small au afeent at one hundred feet; the two Canals, which cross this from East to West, have three hundred feet rife before they reach their head level.

(Signed) Francis Trench,.

3.—Extract of a Letter from Hugh Crawford, Esq. of Greenock.

Dated Greenock, 13th November 1802.

Before I ventured to make up my own mind cm the subject of a Canal from Loch Linnhe to the Murray Firth, I was inclined to consult impartial and intelligent Merchants and Navigators, and the result tends to strengthen the opinions which my own deliberations liad 'led me to form in a matter confessedly of high National importance.

I therefore hasten to befiow that unequivocal approbation which the undertaking projected is so jufily entitled. The advantages which the whole of Ireland and Welt of England would derive from it are iiriking and prominent; since a tedious and dangerous failing would be avoided, by a communication formed to admit the reception of Vessels of the largest burthen. In truth, trade to a greater extent than there is at present would be created; for where obstacles are so encountered, mercantile enterprize grows languid, and is prone to resort to sources calculated to repay, with ease and readiness, its exertions. The Weft of Scotland would derive equal advantage did the Crinan Canal admit Vessels requiring as great a depth of water, as is proposed that the Caledonian Canal shall possess. Still, however, the larger Vessels, which are the most proper for transporting the bulky commodities of the North, are also the most fit to fail round the Mull of Cantire without danger; to preclude which, and prevent delay so common in voyages of the Smaller and chiefly Fishing Vessels, the Crinan Canal was at lirft deligned. The Caledonian Canal would certainly induce the Merchants of the Eastern Parts of Scotland more to attempt the West Indian and American commerce than their local situation has hitherto rendered eligible; but which, freed from the circuitous and dangerous Navigation by the Pentlund Firth, or the Orkneys, would no longer be uninviting. The Fillieries might be also eminently forwarded by the easy tranlition which this Canal would afford from the one to the other verge of the United Kingdoms.

If what I have presumed to state be reasonable, and its objects deserving of consideration in a period of Peace and general security, how many strong arguments may be jufily advanced for the execution of the Canal, if War lhouldbc again forced upon this Country; which however deeply to be deplored, would, in my humble apprehension, by such an improved Navigation, protected by a proper Northern Naval Station, with reference to the commercial relations of which I have ventured to obtrude my opinion, be disarmed of no small portion of its destructive power.

(Signed) Hugh Cranford.

5.*~Letter from William Sibbald, Esquire.

Leith, 2olh December 1802.

I am favoured with your Letter of 14th instant, acquainting me that it is in the contemplation of Government to open a Canal from Invemefs to Fort William, on a scale to admit the largest West India and Baltic Ships; and desiring my opinion, how far such Canal would be of advantage to the Commerce of the United Kingdoms.

It appears obvious to me, that the proposed Canal will be of very great advantage to the Commerce of the United Kingdoms, in particular to the East and 'Weft Coafis of Scotland, North of the Forth and Clyde, and to Ireland. To the East Coast it will open the trade to Ireland, from which it is presently nearly precluded; it will open to them a ready participation of the Weft Highland Herring Fishery, and will open a ftiort passage to their Ships in the West India and American trade. To the West Coast of Scotland and to Ireland, it will open a ftiort and safe communication to the North Sea, by which their trade to the Baltic, and the Continent will be greatly improved, and the Slate and Keep of the Weft Highlands will be brought to Market on the East Coast of Scotland and England much quicker, and with less expence and danger than at present. In short, it appears to me, and to every intelligent Person with whom I have conversed since I received your Letter, that the proposed Canal will be a work of very great public utility, and deserving the attention of His Majesty’s Ministers.

I have the honour to be,

Sir,

Your most obedient Servant,

Wm Sibbald.

4.—A Letter from Thomas Williamson, Esq. of Leith.

Although I have considered the subjet of the intended Canal, mentioned in your Letter, with great attention, I feel much diffidence in hazarding any opinion on a matter of so much importance.

It has always appeared to me, that the principal advantage the Country derives from Canals from Sea to Sea, depend on the depth of water in such Canals. If the one in question is to be of the capacity reported, there is no calculating the possible advantages that the Kingdom may derive from it, especially in time of War. Such a Canal would in fact cut the I (land across, and aff ord a more effectual way of escaping the Enemy’s Cruizers than any hitherto devised, as Ships from the West Indies and America would make the land to the Northward, and passing through the Canal, arrive at London with little or no risque of capture, thereby avoiding the great danger of running the gauntlet in the British Channel. The Ships from London to Greenland and Hudson’s Bay would likewise, by the Canal, avoid the delay they often experience in getting to the Westward, as would also the Greenland Ships from Hull, Whitby, Lynn, Sunderland, and Newcastle.

The Canal would also afford great facility to the Ships^of Liverpool, &c. going to and from the Baltic, Hamburg, &c. and save them the dangerous Navigation of the Pentland Firth, or of going round the Orkney Islands. Ships of burthen reaping these great advantages could afford to pay for them, but the Coasting Vessels could bear only a small charge. In short it appears te me, that unless the advantages to be derived from such a Canal could be deemed entirely National, so as the Dues to be collected would not exceed the expence of uphold-

7.—A Letter from James Arbuthnot, junior.

Peterhead, 5 October 180*2.

Dear Sir,

I have your esteemed favour of the :y.h nit. and loft no time in looking about for the information you defir^a mpeding the adjutages that wfiil most certainly accrue to the Trade o.nci Navigation of this Country, from the grand and very uieiul Canal in contemplation to be shade from the Murray Firth to the Weft of Scot, and. Every incel-ligent person^here concerned in Trade and Shipping are foil of its incalculable value, to the safe and speedy Navigation of the Nation at large, as well as particularly so to this quarter of the Kingdom, and gladly contributes his mite of communication upon the miereiting subject. As they contain the fuhftance of the general opinion, I shall quote the sentiments of two of our bell informed Men of Trade upon the advantages of the Canal in question; which those Gentlemen were ib obliging as to set down in writing.

The one writes thus:

ift. The Navigation from the East to West Coasts of Scotland, England, and to Ireland, and back from thence, is both tedious and often dangerous; if the winds prevail anyway from S. to N. in a Vefterly direction, no Vessel can get further than Orkney, and from S. to N. in an Easterly direction, they cannot get from the Westward. It is also dangerous by there being no Harbour or place of safety for Vessels betwixt Orkney and Cape Wrath, except Scrabfton ltoad and Loch Erribol; and many Ships are wrecked, and the Crews loft on the North Coast of Caithness and Sutherland in Winter. Could a Canal be made to admit Vessels of 3 to 500 tons from the head of the Moray Firth to the West Coast, it would completely obviate these delays and dangers.

2d. The direction for such a Canal as is proposed could not probably be in any other than Lochness, and from thence to Loch Eil; and from the succession of Lochs that are already navigable in that direction, less expence must be occasioned than having it anywhere file.

3d. A Navigation in this direction must be of prodigious benefit, not to tke Fisheries only, but to the Trade of the Kingdom in general; and in a more particular manner, it must he of the bighell conference to the internal improvement of all that part of the Highlands; and its influence in every respect must extend far and wide over that Country; it will probably occasion the erection of Towns*and Villages, both for the extension of the Fisheries and Commerce in general; and improvements in Agriculture will loon become rapid and great; and Emigration to America, if such a Canal as is proposed takes place, would loon entirely cease and be forgot.

Vox# 58,

4th. It is not very easy for loaded Vessels to beat up the Moray Firth against unfavourable winds; on the South fide there are little tides below Burghead and Tarhit Nefs; above that the tides become regular; and all along the North fide the tides are regular; and vessels, by managing these with judgment, can beat up, if the wind is not very violent, in the course of three or four days from this place. In Autumn, winds in this country prevail much from the Western quarter; and this makes it difficult to get up the Moray Firth, or farther than Orkney. It is very easy (unless it blows so as Ships cannot carry fail) to beat down the Moray Firth, as after passing Burghead, any tide there is generally sets down on the South fide; a Vessel will beat down the Firth in two days, or two days and a half.

The other Gentleman writes thus:

The advantages arising from the Caledonian Canal, to Ships bound to the Westward, would be many; with the winds from S. W. being off Kinnaird's Head, a Ship would fail Tarbit Nefs, which is within 15 miles of Cromarty; as the tides are regular on the Caithness fide. Ships would in one tide get to Cromarty; as also with lire winds from N. W. to N. N. E. Ships off the Muijay Firth, or in Orkney, would suit the East end of the Canal, and with these winds they could not get to the Westward from Orkney; at which place it often happens in the fall of the year, when the westerly winds blow', that Ships lay five and six weeks; often Ships are put to Cromarty with gales of wind from the East, and, if the wind continues to blow from that quarter, they could not ealily get down; hut if there was a Canal, they could easily make their voyage. Also, in failing to the Eastward by the Canal, there would be many advantages; Ships from most places on the Coast of Ireland, with the wand from N.W, would suit the Weft end of the Canal; and as the distance from the Sound of Mull to Cape Wrath is above 60 leagues. Ships from the Weft of England and Ireland for the Eafhvard would save a great deal of time if the winds were blowing from the North; as it is very difficult with that wind to make a passage to Cape Wrath.

I shall be happy if these observations afford you any additional light on this subject; and it will always give me very sincere pleasure to yield you every service that may anyway lay in my power.

Being very truly, with much regard,

Dear Sir,

Appendix, No. 3.

The Examination of Mr. John Rennie, Civil Engineer.

Have you been much employed in different works of Inland Navigation?—Yes.

Name a few.—The Lancaster Canal; the Kennet and Avon; the Rochdale; Ulverfton in the Bay of Lancaster; the Crinan; and another at Grimsby in Lincolnshire, for large Vessels of seven hundred tons burthen, loaded; and the London Docks. I knew a Ship of a thousand tons burthen enter Grimlhy Haven; *lhe was a Foreign Ship; but I don't know whether flie was laden or not.

Of what length is the Grim/hy Canal?—About one mile and a half; the Ulverfton about the fame length; the Crinan about nine miles.

Are you of opinion that the Navigation of a Canal can be mader safe and convenient for Ships of considerable burthen?—I am.

Do you apprehend any material accidents are often likely to happen, either in passing through Locks, or in tracking a Ship along a Canal against a moderate hut contrary wind?—If the Canal is of a sufficient capacity, and the Locks properly confiruded, I am of opinion, that a Vessel tracking against a moderate but contrary wind, would he little liable to accidents, so much so, that I scarcely think the chance of accident worth consideration.

Do you apprehend any danger could arise from the velocity a Ship mkht acquire in case the wind was favourable, either supposing he# under fail, or to be tracked by horses?—I apprehend Ships will never use their fails unless in very moderate winds indeed, and in such case, they would always take in their fails before they come up to the Lock; and it would be the business of those who manage them, to check the velocity by throwing out ropes to proper Mooring-posts fixed to the fides of the Canal by the entrance to the Lock.

You mean to lay, that by proper caution no accident will happen?

__With proper caution no accident need to happen; but I have some-

times known accidents happen on Vessels going into a Lock. I recoiled two instances, one on the Forth and Clyde Canal, when a Vessel was coming from the Westward; her velocity had not been checked in time, flie carried away the Gales of the Lock, and went down into the second Level; a fiinilarone happened in the Crinan Canal,

Do you take those accidents to have been unavoidable, or to have-arisen from the inattention or mismanagernent of persons employed? —1 believe from inattention and miftnanagement of the perfoss employed, j

Do you mean to apply these observations to large Ships of 500 tons burthen or upwards, as well as to small Vessels?—I should think the danger or accidents of that fort would be greater with large Vessels than small.

Do you think that the danger, although greater, might be avoided with proper care?—I believe it might.

Are you acquainted with that part of the Highlands of Scotland which extends from Fort William to Inverness ?—I passed through that Valley about ten years ago, but I did not enter into such an Examination as a person ought to do who is to lay down a line of Navigation in it.

Did you, in passing through that Country, observe any particular tircumitunce, either favourable for the formation of a navigable Canal, or particularly adverse ?—It seemed to me that the ground in the Valley lies in such a manner that navigable Cuts might be made between the different Lakes into the Sea at each end.

Car you, from your general knowledge of the 1‘uhjed, and your observatiom on that part of the Country, form any judgment of the expence at which such a Canal would be made, supposing it to be made navigable for Ships and Vessels drawing twenty feet water?—If the depLh of water in the Canal is suppoied to be twenty feet, and the width sufficient for two large Vessels to pass, taking the rile and fall of the Canal at 200 feet, and 25 Locks of eight feet rife, I am of opinion such a Cana?, with the necessary works, such as Harbours, Basons, Jetties, &c. with the communication at the entrance of each of the Canals into the Locks, would cod from 6 to £.700,000 at lead. I calculate the Locks at £.14,000 each: At this rate 25 Locks will amount to £.350,000. My reason for that opinion is, that a Lock of large dimensions at Grimsby in Lincolnshire, where the materials were remarkably cheap, exclusive of the extra expence of its foundation, cod £. 14,000, over and above the expence of piling a bad foundation *.

Do you apprehend it would be necessary to line the Locks with brick or done in such 1 Canal as we are speaking of?—I apprehend it is necessary, and doo* being cheaper in that country than brick, should be preferred.

At how much per mill do you edimate the other expences of the Canal, besides the Locks?—Without making a particular survey, I Cannot give an accurate answer; but taking in the other Works re-quisite, besides the Locks for the Canal, I think it would cod the sum 1 have before mentioned.

What is the depth of water in the Canal of Great G rimfby ?— Twenty feet. The width of the Lock was 36 feet at the surface of the water; the length, I think, was 146, and the height of the wall about 26 or 27 feet; but where Vessels are to go from a lower to a higher level, it would, m a Lock of that dimension, require 10 or 12 feet more in length.

Supposing the depth of water required to be 13 feet, can you form ■any guess of what would be the expence of the Navigation between Fort William and Inverness ?—I cannot pretend to form an accurate judgment, but I apprehend about £.300,000.
