In taking a view of the trading Ports in the Northern parts of Europe, I conclude that Norway may be excluded, as very little could be saved in dillance, to the Wetlern Coasts of Great Britain or Ireland;

Ships from the Cadegate would have more; but the greatest advantage, in point of dillance would be from the Elbe, the United Provinces, and the Eastern Coast of England and Scotland; bound to the Clyde, or the Northern Ports in St. George's Channel, or the contrary by the Inland Navigation.

The trade to America from the German Ocean, whether from the Continent or East Coast of Britain, may often prefer the British Channel; but a Ship intending to go North about, being without or to the Eastward of the heads of the Firth of Murray, would find it more eligible to go round, than by the Inland Navigation, as (lie would looner get clear of the Land, an object always very deferable to the Navigator; and the Lighthouses on Pentland Skerries afford great accommodation to the Mariner, in safely passing the Firth with a commanding breeze by night; her distance would not be increased by fleering to the N.W. for Pentland Firth; for, though Hie would go a few leagues to the Northward, she would afterwards in fleering to the Westward, cross the Meridians quicker, the degree of longitude being less, which would be a compensation. And Ships from America, for the same reason, would shorten their distance, by keeping in the higher latitude of Pentland Firth, than in making the Coast of Ireland, or failing to the Southward of Barrow Head, for this Inland Navigation.

The trade from London to St. George's Channel prefer failing round the Land's End; therefore in those inllances, it is my opinion, that no benefit can be expected to arise from the Inland Navigation.

1 shall now contrail the two passages, by supposing a Ship off Peter Head, or Kinnaird's Head, bound to the Clyde, or St. George's Channel, and mull pals the Mull of Cantire. The distance from Kinnaird’s Head (where the Piiot must determine, and direct a course accordingly) to Inverness, or to Pentland Skerries, are nearly the fame, about *24 leagues, therefore allowed to be equal, in point of time end risque, from the danger of the Seas.

The oliip being arrived at Inverness, some time ought to be allowed for dei-. ntion in procuring a Pilot, hoifcs for tracking, finders, Hoppers, or short pieces of Cables, of a large size, to secure the Ship in the Locks (as they ought not to cut or injure their proper Cables); an addition to the rudder, for Ships will not fleer well when near the ground with their common rudders; hence Vessels frequenting the grand Canal (from Clyde to Forth) have generally an additional part fitted, and ready to apply to the back of the rudder to increase its breadth, or deals may be nailed to each side of the rudder, pointing diagonally into the water; and at best, Ships are often too long in yuilwering their helm, especially when near the fide of the Canal, in passing each other (occasioned by the various motion given to the £uid) and often subject to run foul, and do considerable damage to each other, which by the increased size of the Ships, will be augmented in the ratio of the weight of the Vessels, multiplied into the sum of their velocities with which they meet, and therefore £n extraordinary width should be given to those Canals intended for large Ships.

I shall now suppose that the Ship has entered the bason of the Canal, with the moll favourable weather, viz. calm, or light breezes of fair winds, and that in the course of one day, (he arrives at the entrance of Loch Nefs, where the next morning, with the fame favourable breeze, (lie sets her fails in the Loch, and proceeds to the South-weft ward, and in five or six hours arrives near the other end, where ihe must bring up with an anchor, furl her fails, and again prepare for the Canal, which may probably take a great part of the remainder of the fecund day; but, if calm, would take this day to trad the length of Loch Nefs. The Ship has now two more Canals, and two more Lochs to pass, which, in my opinion, cannot well be performed in two days more; and if the whole is performed in five days from anchoring at Inverness to her failing from Fort William, will be as short a period as can well be expected, as the passage from Loch6 to Canals must render, it more tedious than a continued Line of Canal.

The distance from Fort William to the Mull of Cantire (where the two different passages coincide) by the inner Sounds, or Sound of Ifia, is about 33 leagues, but to the Westward of Ida, about 40 leagues; for which we mull allow one day more, or six days from her arrival at Inverness to the Mull of CaMire.

The passage from Pentland Skerries, round* Cape Wrath to the Mull of Cantire, a distance of about 10a leagues, may be effected in about four days, in the fame light winds and weather; but supposing •it the calmed weather that we experience in those Seas, an average . distance of 20 leagues in 24 hours, for five days together, may be reasonably expected from Land and Sea-breezes, and variable flaws of wind, therefore a saving by this passage in point of time, compared with the Inland Navigation.

* If the winds are (uppefed contrary, or from the S. W, the detention by the Lochs seem to be fully equal to the detention by \he outward passage, and the fame inferences may be allowed to lahe place, if

bound to the Eastward, from Cantire to Peter Head, with light winds and calms; but if the winds are favourable, with a fresh breeze at W.S.W. or S.W. which are prevailing winds, a Ship failing at the rate of 5k. 2f. would, in three days, fail from the Mull of Cantire to Kinnaird’s Head, ;a dillance of about 126 leagues, or in half the time Hie would be in failing by the Inland Navigation; and the fame difference may be expected in failing to the Westward, with opposite winds.

The distance by the Lochs from Kinnaird's Head to the Mull of Cantire, I estimate at 77 leagues, and the difference, or saving in distance, is about 49 leagues.

Ilefpeding the damage or Losses that Ships may be liable to, it is 4 very uncertain conclusion that can be drawn between the risques on those different passages; it may be a total loss to Ship and Cargo, and fatal to the Crew, by the outer passage; but I can scarcely think it probable, though possible, that Ships may bulge themselveS against the Rocks, and go down in deep water. However, it is my opinion that they will be much more liable to partial damages to both hull and materials, by working in narrow Lochs, with rocky (bores, anchoring upon rocky ground, and injuring the Cables, the preservation of which is of the greatest consequence to the safety of the lives and property on board, and in the aggregate, may be equal to the less frequent, but heavier Losses, in failing round Cape Wrath.

I am therefore of opinion, that if any Master should take his VessiJ* of 400 tons, through those Lochs and Canals, supposing them com* pleted, that he would not be desirous of repeating it; and that this Navigation, for the above reasons, would not be much used by such Ships, if free of any Tax or Duty, therefore would not be attended with great advantage, in time of peace, to the trade of the country.

With regard to your query, respecting the practicability and utility of the proposed Inland Navigation, I have not a doubt of either; being well allured that the carrying it into effect, as soon as it possibly can be done, will be the means of promoting Industry, Commerce, and Population, and enriching the Country in particular through which it pafles, and the United Kingdoms of Great Britain and Ireland in general; and on the contrary, that, if it does not, it will prove the ruin of the Highlands of Scotland, especially at this time, when the spirit of Emigration leans to have pervaded all ranks, and more especially the poorer class, who, though naturally strongly attached to their native Country, must leave it for want of the means of subsistence, unless Government furnishes it, which the employment in making the Central Roads and Bridges, Inland Navigation, &c. would effectually do.

When I left Fort Augustus on the 30th May, a Ship was to have failed from a Bay near Fort William with 250 Emigrants, chiefly from Urquhart and Strathglass, for Picton in Nova Scotia; I saw* them pal’s through the place, as also Mr. Mac Lean, the Supercargo; who informed me, that on the 10th of this month another Ship was to fail for the same place, both chartered by Major Frafer, of Pi&on; and that in the course of two or three weeks, three or four more were expected to fail for Quebec, with Emigrants for Upper Canada. Many of those poor People had been induced to suspend their determinations of going, in expectation of the Canal, Roads, and Bridges going on; and, knowing that I had been in correspondence with Mr. Teltord on the subject of founding the Lochs, &c. came in great numbers to me for information, which I always gave with encouragement to wait a little longer, as the business was of such importance that it could not be gone through so rapidly; with which they remained satisfied, and their drooping spirits were cheered beyond description when I communicated to them (which I loft no time in doing) that I had received your summons to attend the $elect Committee fitting on the Northern Survey, by which theyr were then allured, beyond a doubt, that Government were lerious in the business.

M ith regard to your query respecting my opinion as to the depth of water that there should be in the Canal, and whether I think, that one of 10 or 11 feet might answer the purpose, and lave a great expence thereby ?—1 am decidedly of opinion against a Canal of such description, as it would be doing nothing at all to have only one that w ould admit small Coalling Vessels; for it must be considered, though not generally known, that a proportion of about one foot in ten must be taken oft’from the water that the Vessel will draw, for this reason, that though she may float in very little more than her draught, yet flie will not be euiily drawn along, if dole or very near to the ground; and in that case, a Canal of ten feet would only receive a Vessel drawing nine feet, which would only carry about 70 or 80 tons.

I would therefore propose, that the Caledonian Canal should be upon a scale of greater extent, capable of admitting Trading Ships of the gveateft burthen; and in order to do that, it should have at the lead twenty feet of water, which would receive Ships of 18 feet to be draw’ll with case, and 19 feet with some difficulty.

The Baltic Ships draw from 13 to 19 feet, and but very few of 19; the West India Ships from 16 to 22, and but very few of 22, and those from the Ports of London, Bristol, and Liverpool, that would never have occasion to go by the Inland Navigation.

I am therefore of opinion, though I cannot positively say, that a Canal of twenty feet will answer the purpose required, in which all Ships from the Baltic and East Country, North of England and Scotland, &c. &c. &c. may puss to the Welt ward, and from the West Indies, North America, Ireland, &c. &c. &c. to the Eastward.

With regard to your query respecting proper places or stations for erecting Villages along the fides of the Lakes and Canals, Lean only say, that there are convenient situations all along, from Inverness on the East to Fort William on the Weft, where there will be no difficulty in having them erected.

London, 10th June 1803. Mark Gwynn.

There is also great danger in lying to during the night, and there is no place of Ihelter in case of a shift of wind. Soundings there are no kind of guide, the water is too deep. I apply these observations to the Winter half year, from about the middle of September to the middle of March.

What time on an average, in moderate and fair weather, will a ship go from Kinnaird's Head to the Mull of Canty re ?—It is possible to do it in three days. I have never done it myself in less than five days, and have been live weeks, when my object has been to make my passage as sass as possible. On an average, I think my pafi'ages have been about a fortnight.

How many changes of wind are necessary to fail from Kinnaird's Head to the Mull of Cuntyre in the shortest time ?—Three changes.

As a Seaman, would*you chuse to make use of the proposed Inland Navigation rather than go round by the Pentland Firth ?—Surely; no Man acquainted with the outer passage would prefer it, if he could go by the Inland Navigation. I have now left off the Sea, and am an Insurance Broker in the city. Lass November I paid myself Ten Guineas per-cent, premium on a Ship from Riga to Dublin; and if I Could have pointed out to the Underwriter, that the Ship might pass through the proposed Canal, I might probably have done it at five or six per-cent, at furtlieft. Lass January I had a Brig at Londonderry, bound to Peterhead, which, could fine have passed through the Canal,

When a Ship in the Winter months comes from the Northward as far as the Island of Terree (Weft of the Bland of Mull), Ihe frequently falls in with a South-weft wind, which is always attended with thick weather, and often blows so strong, that Hie is driven away to the North-welt to Sea, it not being in her power to fetch a Harbour. This might be avoided by the Inland Navigation.

You now speak of a time of Peace; in time of War, what do you conceive might be the advantages of the proposed Navigation, both as to safety and commercial convenience?—I consider the Sea risk as the chief. The Navigation is so dangerous, and the tide so rapid in the Pentland Firth and the Irish Channel, that Cruizers seldom appear there.

Vlave you often known Ships loft in the passage by the Pentland Firth ?—I have known a good many loft; about three years ago, two valuable Ships from the Baltic were entirely wrecked near Cape Wrath, and all hands drowned in the fame night, near to each other. They were worth about £. 20,000 each.

In what sized Vessels did you usually fail ?—In Ships of 300 tons registered. The last Ship but one I commanded was of 300 tons registered, or 500 tons burthen, American built, and drew 17 feet water. The last Ship I commanded was English built, of 300 tons registered, and drew 16 feet water.

What is the average size of Ships trading from the Weft of England, or from Ireland, to the Baltic ?—About 240 tons registered, or 350 tons burthen.

What draft of water would they on an average require ?—About 15 feet; but many Ships from Liverpool, which arc often Foreign built, and (harp bottoms, require 18 feet. I have seen one 19 feet. I think her tonnage could not have been less than 700 tons registered. Those that drew 18 feet might not be more than 350 tons registered, being very (harp built.

Of what tonnage, on an average, are the Ships failing from Leith, and the Ports further North to Ireland or America?—T1 ie Vessels from these Ports seldom come through the English Channel, but go North about when they are bound to the Weft ward: but I cannot speak to their tonnage. I believe the’' were formerly generally small, and probably do not draw more than 10 feet water. Their tonnage is increased of late, and at Aberdeen, Peterhead, and Leith, may now be about 200 registered tons, drawing 13J feet water.

Do the Lightlioufes on the Pentland Skerries afford accommodation to Navigators?—Yes, certainly; buUnot such an accommodation as would induce me to attempt the passage in the night. It might be done in iome circumstances, but the passage is so narrow, and the tides so strong, that unless the night was very light, and the tide favourable,

I should not chuse to venture it, either in Summer or Winter.

Suppose a Ship for America, wanting to go North about, finds her felt off Kinnaird's Head, would it be better for her to go by the Pentland Firth, or by the Inland Canal ?—This would depend on circumstances. If the Ship was bound direct for America, it might be better for her at once to go through the Pentland Firth, and keep to the North of the Butt of Lewes.

Can you give a list of Ships loft in passing the Pentland Firth during the lait ten years?—i will procure such a list from Lloyd's Coffee-House.

Appendix, N° 9.

The Examination ef Lieutenant John Forbes.

I am a Lieutenant in the Navy, and have served in different King's Lieut. Forbes, Ships, from a Cutter to a Ship of 98 guns, during all the last war, on the Jamaica Station. I formerly navigated in the North Seas, in two Merchant Ships, for five years, during which time I made three paf. sages through the Pentland Firth. All three were in the Winter season: one took up three months from Aberdeen to Cork; another took three weeks from Aberdeen before I could clear the Sound of Lewes Bland; the third took a fortnight from Aberdeen before I was able to get to the North of the Butt of Lewes, from which I (leered South-weft to Grenada. I reckon the puftkge by the Pentland Firth very dangerous as well as tedious in the Winter season. I never passed it in the Summer season. The principal danger is, that leaving the Orkneys in the morning one cannot clear the Land before night; the tides run very strong, as well as the winds contrary, and strong Ships of 240 tons measurement draw about 15 or 16 feet water.

I agree with Mr. Hutchefou as to the draft of Ships of different burthens. I also agree with him as to the inconvenience and danger of Vessels going by the Pentland Firth to the Irish Channel, after they reach the South end of Terree, I should suppose no Man would heiitate a moment, if his Vessel was oft' Kinnaird's Head, going to

Ireland or the Weft of England, to prefer the Inland Navigation to going by the Pentland Firth. An English built Frigate of 32 guns, with provisions for three months, and all her guns and stores, generally draws 18 feet, sometimes less. Frigates taken from the French and Spaniards generally draw more than the English built. To the best of my knowledge, all Vessels from the Eall Coast of Scotland, bound to the Weltward, prefer going by the Pentland Firth to the English Channel, even in time of Peace.

I have heard all Mr. llutchefon's evidence, and I agree with him in the fads and opinions he has given.

Appendix, No. 10.

The Examination of Mr. Francis Sinclair, Shipmaster, of Thurso, in Caithness.

Are you acquainted with the Navigation of the Northern Coast of Mr. Sinclair. Scotland?—Yes.

llow long have you been acquainted with it?—Thirty years.

Have you frequently passed through the Pentland ITrth?—Yes, repeatedly.

Is it a safe or easy Navigation, or do accidents frequently happen?

—With a steady and commanding breeze of wind it is very sale, but in a calm there is danger.

Have you known many cases of danger or loss?—Yes, repeatedly; the greatest danger I know in the Pentland Firth is, coming from the Westward with a flood tide and a calm, the current is apt to run you on the South Point of Swona.

Do calms frequently happen in that Sea?—In the Summer season very frequently.

Whether in Winter is it generally stormy or moderate on that Coast?

■The weather is nearly the same as on the other Coasts of North Britain, where they are subject to frequent gales of wind in the Winter.

Do you consider the Navigation safe in Winter, under all the usual circumstances?—Yes, I do; if a man takes his time, and attends to the tide, there is no danger with a common breeze of wind. '

Do you think it a safe Navigation for Ships, the Mailers of which are not particularly acquainted with the Coast?—I do not think it is.

Are Vessels passing from the Minch to the Eastern Coast of Scotland frequently detained, for a considerable time, by contrary winds? —Repeatedly.

Do you mean for a considerable length of time together, or only for a short interruption?—I suppose for a short interruption, till the wind ft lifts.

Is it usual, on that Coast, for the wind to blow for a considerable length of time from the same quarter?—The wind varies the same as on the other parts of the coall, but the moll prevailing winds ar# westerly.

Does it not require several winds to bring a Vessel round from the Sound of Mull to the North-east Coast of Scotland?—It does.

Are there any convenient Harbours, or Inlets, on the Northern or Western Coast of Scotland ?—There are a great many Bays and Inlets from the Sound of Mull to Cape Wrath, and from thence to the Pentland Firth there are three very good anchoring places; but there are no safe Harbours from the Pentland Firth to Cromarty Firth.

How long have you known a Vessel detained by contrary winds between the Sound of Mull and the Murray Firth?—I have known a Vessel detained six weeks.

If the projected Canal is made, do you think it would be preferable to the present Navigation?—1 do, at all seasons.

Are you aware, and do you take into your consideration the time that would be requisite to pass through the proposed Navigation?

Not being acquainted with that part of the country I cannot tell.

44 With respect to the procuring of fresh water at Cromarty, in 44 addition to the Well described by Mr. Telford, there is a good 44 run of fine fresh water, which discharges itself into the South fide 4i of the Harbour, about two miles Weft from the town.

44 The bell method for pointing out the advantages that would re-46 fult from the free Navigation of the Caledonian Canal, will perhaps tc be to point out the advantages and dangers attending the Naviga-" tion round the North of Scotland.

44 In the first place, exclusive of the dangers that may be avoided, 44 the Caledonian Canal will save a distance of between 30 and 40 44 leagues to Ships going by the way of the Pentland Firth, and of 44 60 leagues to those going round between Orkney and Shetland; and 44 again, the Navigation round by the Orkneys is rendered very dan- gerous, particularly during the Winter half year (that is from Octo- ber to May) on account of the extremely thick and boisterous 44 weather that frequently prevails there during that season; and this " danger is considerably increased by the great rapidity and diversity 44 of the tides, and the lowness of the Land, particularly upon the 44 North and East tides; for, from the great depth of the Sea round the 44 Orkneys, no indication of coming near the Land can be had from 44 Soundings, so that Ships coming upon it in thick weather, are 44 often so forcibly drawn in by the current of tide as to be embay- ed among the Rocks before they discover where they are. Add to 44 this, if we consider the great length of the nights at this season, to- gether with the height and irregularity of the waves, caused by the 44 divcrlity of tides, our surprize at the many Shipwrecks that happen 44 in these parts will be considerably lessened, In consequence of these 44 dangers, and in order to avoid them as much as possible, it is very 44 common for Ships coming across the North Sea for the Orkneys, 44 to make the Land first about Buchaness, and from thence to steer for 44 Duncan's Bay Head; in which case, when the wind blows strong 44 between the North-east and East, it not unfrequently happens that 44 these Ships, not being able to weather Duncan's Bay Head, are 44 obliged to bear away for Cromarty, and thuslofe a fair wind; while 44 upon the other hand, the wind that releases them from Cromarty 44 will carry them no farther orf their voyage than Duncan's Bay 44 Head, or to some Harbour in the Orkneys, where they must wait another change of wind, by which means their passage is prolonged several weeks beyond what it would otherwise have been had they at first got rouird Duncan's Bay Head; all of which circumstances will be prevented by the free Navigation of the Caledonian Canal. The above circuinftance happened several times while I was stationed upon the Fall Coast of Scotland, and I have often witnessed the regret exp relied by Shipmasters upon the occasion.

44 The Coast from Duncan's Bay Head to Loch Eripol (near Cape Wrath) from being so straight, and having no safe Harbours in it, is also very dangerous, on account of its exposure to the Ocean swell from the North, and gales of wind in that direction often force Ships on shore upon it; indeed every other part (as well as this)

Pentland Firth run at the rate of nine knots an hour, the Neap-tides about three knots; but the tides are rendered more dangerous there on account of three Islands, the Skerries, Stroma, and Swona, which ate in the middle of the Firth, and produce eddies and whirlpools. Twelve or fourteen leagues to the westward of the Orkneys, in the route to America; there are two Rocks which are dangerous in the night or thick weather.

I am not acquainted with the interior between Invcrness and the Linnhe Loch, but in the Baltic, the Coast of Norway, and the West Coast of Scotland, I have frequently navigated narrow Lochs or Inlets of the Sea, coafled by high mountains. There are frequent gusts of wind coming down Vallies, felt in these Lochs; they shew themselves on the water, and give sufficient warning to take in fail, which is enough for guarding against them. In all such Lochs, the wind takes the direction of the mountains.

I have heard Captain Gwy nil's evidence respecting the Navigation of Loch Nefs, and am of opinion there is room enough for a large Ship to work to windward. As the Loch is dated to be from one to two mile§ wide, a large, well-failing Ship can work to windward in three quarters of a mile in breadth. A Ship, with a moderate fair wind, might make the run of Loch Nefs in four hours and a half; against the wind, a Merchant Ship may advance half a mile an hour; a good failing Ship, a mile an hour; a Fi igate, one mile and a half an hour. In calms or light winds, a Vessel might be tracked in such a Lake. I do not conceive that Vessels of any burthen, or Herring Bufles, would be in danger of foundering from gusts of wind, but Boats might; though, as to them, the danger would not be great, if proper caution were used. I judge, Mooring Buoys or Chains to be far preferable to a Ship's coining to Anchor in such a Loch, because of the reaainels with which a Ship may be brought up, or may get under weigh from them.

From the Western extremity of the Lynnhe, a Vessel would with great safety get into the Western Ocean by the North of Ireland; or, in case of any hidden gale of wind, there is an excellent Harbour immediately adjoining at Oban, on the South fide, where there is a very capacious and lale Baton and Roadstead, and on the North, the whole of the Sound of Mull, which is perfectly safe.

With respect to the bearing of the proposed Canal on thebufiness of the Fisheries on the West Coast, I belie\e 1 can give some information. I conceive that the whole of the Tail Coast of Scotland, from the Edinburgh Firth to the Ord of Caithness, would go by the Caledonian Canal to the Fisheries on the Wed Coast, and that they would readily engage in them. They do not engage in the Fisheries on the West Coast now, on account of the length and uncertainty of the past’age by the Pentland Firth. The Fiftiing begins on the West Coast about the In ft of August. If the Fiftiing begins in June on the Iv,aft Coast, the fame Fishers might go by the month of August to the West Coast; which I do not conceive to be practicable by the Pentland Firth, on account of the length and uncertainty of the pall age.

• Appendix, No. 14.

Captain Geo. Duff, of the Royal Navy.

The Navigation of the Murray Firth appears to me perfectly safe for all Ships of War, no rocks or shoals laying any distance otf the Shore; and in case of gales of wind, they have the Harbour of Cromarty to run for, which is not only a very good and safe one, but easily known, and no difficulty in entering. Should the wind be such that they cannot fetch Cromarty, they can upon one tack or the other easily clear the Land, and have plenty of sea-rooin. I have been several times in Cromarty; but never founded it accurately. I know that when you are in, shoal water extends a good way out from the Noith fide; but it is a good and capacious Roadstead and depth of water for large Ships a long way up; the entrance I take to be more than a mile; I have beat in and out more than once; fee no disticulty of any Ship working out when the weather is such that (he could make any thing of it, if ft^e was *n Firth; in that case 1 should suppose any moderate failing Ship would clear the Land about Fraserburgh in two days, particularly if (he attended to the tides; it is, in my opinion, the only safe place where Ships of War could rendezvous or retit to the Northward of the Firth of Forth, and would be a good station, particularly when at War with the Northern Powers: there is plenty of frefti water, a good Pier for small Vessels, and a considerable rife of tide. I have been in the Invemefs Firth opposite to Fort George, with a Frigate and Sloop of War; we had very good (belter; but the water is not deep, though I cannot say I know much about it. These are the only places on the East Coast of Scotland which I think calculated to accommodate Ships of War, or that could be made so.

With respect to Emigration, previous to the late declaration of Hof-tilities, there were about 3,000 fouls ready to emigrate from the Isle of Sky, the whole population of which is about *20,000. I am acquainted with their intentions by their declarations at public meetings, and the information of the Agents employed to collect Emigrants. The time of failing is usually the month of August.

I apprehend the advance in the price of Provisions and Freight, on account of the War, may retard the departure of numbers, although they have proposed a method of getting over that difficulty, by taking no provisions with them except oatmeal and molasses.

As to the means of checking this great evil, I have addraffed a Letter to the Chairman of the Committee, which, touching on that head, I beg leave to refer to.

The Letter is as follows:

" Sir, " London, June 9th 1803.

" I have received great satisfaction in learning that the Legislature " has bent its attention seriously to the Improvement of the High-lands, which must necessarily embrace the extension of the Fisheries;

" and by natural consequences tend to impede, and I trust finally prevent, those very large Emigrations from that quarter which are " now upon the wing. I apprehend immediate good effects from bc-" ginning Roads in different parts of the Highland Counties in such " lines as may have been determined on. I say, ‘ in different parts/

" because it will render employment to the People more general; and " it will impress the idea more generally, that great improvements " are projected, and actually going forward. Many Persons emigrate " rather from the fear of want than from present want. The Confo-" lidation of small Farms into large Cattle Grazings in the hands of " one Tacksman, and the rapid introduction of Sheep, necessarily dif-" possesses thousands whose enftom it has been to regard farming as " the only mean determined by which they ought to seek subsistonce. Highland " Farms can now be more profitably occupied than by small Tenants " or Cottagers: They must seek Lands ell'ewhere, or other employ-u merits must be held out; and as their habits are against any labour " but that of the field, any employments recently held out should be " brought as near to their doors as possible. Persons who have tailed " the advantages derived from constant work, and wages well paid u while employed upon the Roads near to their own houses, shall be " induced to gather about the Canal for further employment; and I " should be well pleased to fee it employ thousands, as I look forward " to its completion with high expectations; it is a measure that was " recommended to a Committee of the House in 1782, by Doctor " Anderl'on; and an Estimate was gi\eti in by Mr. Watt for it3 exe-" cution (Vide Anderson’s Reports). It i9 an Improvement easily " effected in coraparifon with the vast extent of country which it will " open, and it will render a communication between the East and West " Coasts perfectly easy; a circumstance long wished for; as the " Fishermen on the East Coast possess able Boats, and a knowledge of " White Fiftiing, that would soon prove the value of the Cod and Ling " Banks on the Western Coast, and thereby induce the Inhabitants to " imitate their Boats and mode of Fiftiing; at present the Boats on

II the West Coast are too small, and not of the belt construction, to " keep the Sea in boisterous weather. A few Boats venture from " Barra to Glasgow with Fish; but such an expedition is extremely " hazardous in small and ill-contrived Boats, and consequently can " only be attempted in favourable wreatber. I have built some Houses " at Lochbay in the Isle of Sky, by the Direction of the British " Society, for the accommodation of Fishermen from the East Coast, for the precise purpose of shewing the People of Sky a good example " in Boats and prowess; but it has been found impracticable to per-" fuade any of them to remove to Sky; they, however, shew no reluc-" tance at engaging for the season; but the Navigation by the Pent-" land Firth is too hazardous for open Boats of the best construction " at the vernal and autumnal equinoxes, which are points of time " they could with to pass and return. Was the Canal open, this " obstacle would be removed, and good consequences would soon shew " themselves.

Of Winds, and their efteft.

IN the Highlands of Scotland, as in all other Countries which rife rapidly from the Sea, the wind which blows in upon the land, or at right angles with it, seldom blows home, that is, it leldoin reaches the shore with force or violence equal to that with which it blows at a fmnll distance oft’ the land. I have known, in the Summer time, fresh gales of wind at N. W. in the in fide of the Hebrides or Lewis Bland, for several days together, when an almost perfect calm exilied all the time in the inner Sounds; but this fact is most obvious in the Mediterranean, where the h aide ft gales of Levanters very seldom blow to the shore; and, during furh a wind, it is not uncommon, in those leas, to fee a Ship ciofe in with the land with every fail set, while at the distance of three of four leagues in the Oiling, that is to say, from the land. Ships can Vrdly lhow or carry any fail; and in the fame way, iii the Highlands of Scotland, the N. W. or \V. N. W. winds seldom blow home, on account of the Mountains as aforesaid. Now, the current of air will naturally find its way where it meets with the least uhstruction, which happens to be along the coalt from the Butt of the Lewis and Cape Wrath, down to the Orkneys; this circumstance makes that passage so tedious and difficult against S. \V. and W. winds, that it is not uncommon, even in Summer, to fee Vessels put back to the Orkneys from Cape Wrath, while Ships are making tolerable paf-sages across the North Seas in the fame direction; it is therefore not to be wondered at, if, in the Winter, Ships bound to the Weft ward are fomet lines detained even three months in the Orkneys with those N. W. and W. winds, the course which they art* to hold not only being in the track where the current of air from the mountainous country takes its course, and blows will) such violence as it generally does, but the Coast itself lying in an East and West line, has the efi’ett of keeping the wind in that direction, even when it has been known to alter several points at thirty miles distant; and, indeed, till it comes at right angles with the land, it cannot be depended on to alter.

On thele coalts, the Mariner hopes in vain to fee, in the night-time, the Skerry Lights in Pentland Firth; every wave breaking at a distance he conceives to be a light; is watching with great anxiety of mind to alter his course, when being carried by the violence of the winds and tides a few miles, indeed a very few miles, from the spot lie conceives himself to be in, he perhaps ltnkes on some of the Iil»*s of Orkney, where Ship and Crew are almost in-stantly loft. Examination of Captain M. Dow'nib.

The advantages that a Bason (or what is otherwise called a Wet Dock) gives to Shipping are very great:—First, because they lie secured from the damage they otherwise would be ex poled to by strain-ing when lying a-ground, and by running or getting foul of each other, either from the trrength of the tide or from the violence of the wind . and, Secondly, because a great expence is saved in the articles of an-

chors, cables, and other ground tackling, for in a Bason no anchor* are required; and also much Id’s llrcngth, and expence of cables and other ropes for securing the Ships are required, than would be if they wrere ex poled to the tides and wands. And, besides all theie advantages, the lying dole to the shore where the Ship’s Company and goods may be readily landed or got on board, is of itself a very great convenience; and there is no doubt but that these and limilar considerations have caused the construriion of so many Baiuns or Wet Docks about London, in Liverpool, and in other places.

From Batons of this description being most beneficial where the greatest resort of Shipping is, the Baloii at the Ealrern Junction of the Caledonian Canal will, no doubt, be of more immediate service than the Bason at the Weltern Junction, because of the greater resort of Shipping there, although (here is not the least doubt but that the latter Bason will also be of considerable advantage.

Where a Canal joins the rile and fall of the tide, it is well known that the outer gates cannot be open for Ships to pass except at high water, and as the time then will not exceed an hour or tw?o, the Ship* without (if many) would crowd in whilo the gates are open, so that it is absolutely necessary to have a Bason to receive them; from whence they may proceed in rotation through the other Locks and the Canal. Upon the other hand, Ships coining through the Canal must have a Bason in which they may lie, and wait for high" veater to let them out through the outer gate. If from contrary winds blowing strong, or from other circumstances, the Ships are prevented from getting to sea through the outer gate, the assemblage of Ships in the Bason may probably become great, particularly if the stoppage continues for iome days; so that where so great a number of Shipping may he expected to pass, the Batons at each end of the Caledonian Canal ought to be very capacious. \r>

The COMMITTEE, to whom the " Survey and Report of u the Coasts and Central Highlands of Scotland, made by the " Command of the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners u of His Majesty’s Treasury, in the Autumn of 180-2," is referred; and who were empowered to report their Observations and Opinion thereupon, from time to time, to the House;—

HAVING considered in their Three former Reports, what relates to Emigration, to Roads and Bridges, and to the forming an Inland Navigation from the Eastern to the Western Sea in the Northern part of this Island, have proceeded to that part of the Survey which regards Naval Stations upon the East Coast of Scotland, and that part which relates to the Fisheries.

Upon the subject of the Naval Stations, Your Committee have examined sundry Officers of I lis Majesty’s Navy, who have a thorough knowledge of tins Coast, and who have been ltationed there in Ships of War; they have likewise examined several experienced Shipmafters, conversant with the East Coast of Scotland, and the North Seas, whose Pividence may be found in the Appendix annexed to this Report.

It appears to Your Committee, that there is no place upon the Eastern Coast of Scotland where Ships of War can ride at anchor, except in Leith Road, and the Bay of Cromarty; though small Frigates may have good shelter in the Harbour of Fort George.

In Leitli Road the Ships are exposed to a heavy swell of the Sea, and the anchoring ground is at a considerable distance from the shore.

The Bay of Cromarty is less exposed, and, from its vicinity to the Baltic, is a 1 eligible Naval Station; it seems to possess many local advantages; it is easy of accels, of great extent, with excellent anchoring ground near to the shore, a moderate though sufficient depth of water, and it is perfectly secure from every wind; there is a fufliciency of fresh water for supplying any number of Ships, and there is a small but commodious artificial Pier Harbour for the protection of Boats and small Craft; so that for the perfect accommodation of a Squadron, or even a Fleet, there seems to be nothing wanting but Storchouses upon the shore.

At the extremity of the proposed Inland Navigation, Fort George can conveniently receive Merchantmen of all descriptions; from whence mull ariie an additional advantage to the Bay of Cromarty, an Harbour particularly well calculated for facilitating Convoys, pro-# testing the Coafis, and annoying an Enemy in those Seas. Your Committee arc aware of one objection to this Harbour; for in Easterly winds Vessels may be embayed; but Easterly winds prevail here only about three months in the year, and from the excellent Navigation of the Murray Frith, and the advantages to be derived from the nature of the tides which prevail there, it appears, by the evidence of sundry Officers of the Royal Navy, who have had frequent experience of this Frith in Ships of War, that large Vessels will not he more than forty-eight hours, in any case, often not more than thirty, in heating from Cromarty Harbour to clear Kinnaird’s Head, a distance of about twenty leagues, ugainst a strong contrary wind; and when past Kinnaiid’s Head, they will he in the main Sea.

Aberdeen, fituuted about half way between the Roadsteads of Leith

and Cromarty, upon a very bold part of the Coast, would prove of great importance as a llation for Frigates and Sloops of War; and it appears, that the Harbour may he rendered capable of receiving and keeping afloat Vessels of eighteen and twenty feet draught of water; hut the funds of the City, already appropriated to the Improvement of this Harbour, are infuflieient for so great a work unlel’s supporled by Public Aid.

From Aberdeen, and the other Ports, on the high and projecting Coast of this County, a communication might be kept up with Leith and Cromarty, by means of Signals or a Telegraph; for which purpose the form of the Country is well adapted.

Although Your Committee can recommend no Naval Station North of Cromarty, yet, on considering that part of Mr. Telfords Report, which relates to the encouragement and extension of the Fisheries, they are of opinion that the Harbour of Wirk, in the County of Caith-ness, on the South fide of the Pentland Frith, on a projecting part of the Coast, is very advantageoully fiiuated for carrying on the Boat and Deep-lea Fishing, and is a place where Dutch Fiftiermen, if properly encouraged, are likely to resort, and form a settlement. It is now regularly and constantly frequented by Fishing Vessels; but the unprotected state of the Harbour, and the want of all conveniencies for sorting and curing Fish, mult prevent the Boat and Deep-sea Fishing from being prulecuted with vigour and cried. From sundry Surveys and Estimatcs which have been laid before Your Committee, it appears, that it is very practicable to construd a Harbour at Wick, sufficient for the protection of Fishing Busses, and such Coasting Vessels as draw no more than twelve feet of water. From an Estimate nude by Mr. Rennie in the year 1793, it appears, that the Expence ofcon-struding a Harbour would amount to £. 14,441. 9*. But from the Survey, Plan, and Estimate, of Mr. Telford, in the year 1801, it appears that a Harbour may he construded in a more ccconomical manner, in separate parts, at an expence which, being proportioned to the extent oi the Work, will not exceed the respective Turns of £.5,890. or £.9,745. or£. 1-2,685; and that for the lealt of these sums a commodious and well-protedi d Tide-Bason may be formed, which will contain about two hundred Bufl'es; Your Committee therefore are of opinion, that it will be most prudent and advisable to begin upon the smallest icale, and to complete the first part ot Mr. Telford’s Plan with all convenient dispatch; but for this purpose only a small proportion of the money can be expended this year, and that chiefly in preparing materials for the Spring and eniuing Summer.

\ our Committee need not enlarge upon the great importance of the Fisheries in Scotland, affording sustenance as well as employment to the Inhabitants, and supplying our Navy with active and hardy Seamen; but they are deeply impressed with the obstructions to the progress and improvement of this great National object, arising from the Duties upon Salt, and from the Laws enforcing those Duties; and they are convinced of the essential advantages which mult reiult from their total repeal or commutation; they do not, however, in the present conjuncture of Affairs, think it advisable to enter further into this subject, earnestly hoping that the time will come when a measure, so highly salutary and bencticial, may with propriety be adopted’ in its full extent.

Capt. Dovnie.

With respect to getting to sea from Cromarty with ah Easterly wind, which only prevails for about three months in the year* and is the worst possible, if the winds and weather were such as to permit me to carry such fail as would prevent my coming into Port were I at sea, I think a well-appointed Ship, taking advantage of the tides, ought to clear Kinnaird's Head and get into the open sea in about 36 hours at mod: there is not the lead difficulty in working in or out of the Harbour with a contrary wind: and taking advantage of the tides, it may be done with a good failing vessel in about an hour.

A Man of War, with a fresh breeze and a fair wind, from the time of getting under way, would clear Kinnaird’s Head in about eight hours.

Westerly winds prevail mostly for about nine months in the year; but I do not consider (light sea breezes in summer, although they come in an Easterly direction, as East winds, because they are at an end at fun-let, and then a Westerly breeze gets up. Easterly winds let in about February or March, according to the seal’on, and end generally in May or June: but there are occasionally Easterly winds in Winter.

There is a small artificial Pier Harbour at Cromarty, where Vessels of 10 or 12 feet draft of water, that can take the ground, can deliver or receive their cargoes, and where hnall Vessels, m heavy gales of wind from the Westward, put in to avoid a (hurt sea in the Road-stead, which does not acted large Vessels.

Ships coming from the Baltic, especially Ships appointed to conduct Convoys, ftcer far to the Westward to avoid Juts Reel, and that dangerous fiiore, which obliges them to approach towards Bucchan-ness.

Off Fort George there is an anchorage or Roadstead for Merchantmen, which I know to be sufficient for small Frigates, and consider as equally secure with Leith Road, but by no means to be compared with Cromarty.

I have been at Aberdeen, and seen the Harbour, and am of opinion, that if it could be made to have 20 feet of water on the Bar, and so as to prevent Men of War taking ground, it would be a convenient Port to refit a Frigate; that conveniency chiefly ariles from the Ship being in the opeu sea immediately on her leaving the Harbour. I am also of opinion, that Aberdeen possesses such advantages that a Frigate or smaller Ships of War coulcfbe repaired there fully as cheap, if not cheaper, than at any Port at which Men of War are now repaired.

With respect to the Navigation of the Pentland Firth, I have ever considered it very dangerous, from the rapid tides and thick fogs which prevail there. The fame objections hold good with respect to the Navigation round any part of the Orkney or Shetland I (lands, though not to such a degree. In carrying Men of War round the North of Scotland, I would pass between Orkney and Shetland Islands; but rather than navigate the Pentland Firth, I would prefer going round to the North of the Shetland Islands.

A Naval station at Cromarty, and consequently thofefeas becoming more frequented by His Majesty’s Ships, would, in a great measure, be the means of preventing depredations upon the Revenue.

There can be no difficulty of holding a communication along the East Coast of Scotland as far as Cromarty, by means of Signals or Telegraphs.

Appendix, No. 3.

Examination of Capt. Muitno Downie, a Master in the Navy, and now resident in Aberdeen.

I was bred to the sea, first in the Merchant Service, and then in His Majesty's Navy. I was ten years in the former, and 24 years in the latter, twenty years of which I was Master of a Man of War of different rates, from 24 guns to 98, and am found qualified by the Trinity House for the charge of a first-rate. I was two years and a half in a Merchant Ship, employed in the Fishing upon the West Coast of Scotland; and was three years stationed upon the East Coast, in the Champion Frigate, during which three years I made a survey of that Coast from Duneanfby Head, at the South entry of the Pentland Firth, to Holy 111 and and the Staples upon the Coast of Northumberland. I presented the charts of that survey to the Lords of the Admiralty, which were so far approved by them as to be published by their permission. The Ports or Harbours 011 the East Coast of Scotland now used as Naval stations, are Leith Roads and Cromarty Harbour. Aberdeen, with improvements, may be used as another Naval station; and Fort George would also be very convenient as a Harbour for the Caledonian Canal, when it is executed; but of these four, Cromarty is by far the bed and most capacious Harbour, it being equal to any, and superior to most Harbours that I have seen in any part of the world; it is easy of access, perfectly secure, of a moderate depth of water, has good anchorage, and will contain all the King’s Navy.

Leith Roads are very good as a Roadstead, but not so safe as Cromarty, on account of its exposure to the swell of the ocean with an Easterly wind, and the Ships in it not lying so convenient for the shore. Aberdeen, with improvements, might be made a good Harbour, to contain Ships of 18 or 20 feet draught of water. It is not embayed, and lies central between Leith and Cromarty, by which

circumstances it is a favourable t position for the protection of the Coast. With respect to Fort George, 1 am not so w *ll acquainted with it as I am with the other Harbours; it is a good Harbour for small Ships of War, and for Merchant Ships of all descriptions; but its vicinity to the excellent Harbour of CVomarty makes it lets necessary to be used by Ships of War. With respect to improving those several stations^ I do not know that any improvement can be added to Leith as a Roadstead; As to Aberdeen, it may be improved by its Entry or Bar being carried farther out, by confirming Piers, which, by confining the stream, would deepen the Harbour; as a proof of which, the great Flood of September 1709 waffled away the Bar, and lo deepened the bed, that in the great florin of January 1800 following,

1 saw a brig of three or four hundred tons arrive in perfect safety within the Harbour when it did not want an hour of low water. Further, a Tide Lock may be eroded within the Harbour for keeping Ships afloat at low water. I have considered Mr. Telford's Plan for these Improvements, and think it is practicable, and will make the Harbour fit to receive Frigates. I quite approve of that Plan. Fort George is now a good and safe Roadstead for Merchant Ships and Frigates, but from its little depth of water it cannot be made a Harbour lor large Ships of War; I have therefore nothing to suggest for its further improvement. Cromaity is already so perfad a Harbour in all material respects, that it needs nothing to make it a most commodious resort for Ships of every description, great and small, unless it be conveniences for holding itores, and for Ships watering; the last of which is to be had upon the South (bore of the Harbour, about two miles Well from the town, nearly oppotite the anchorage, and within half a mile of it, w here there is a stream sufficient to water any Fleet. It was there where Ships usually watered when I visited the place, and the water was laid in by rolling calks to the stream; but with very little trouble, the water, by means of a hole, might be conducted immediately into the boats. The stream laid to be discovered by Mr. Kofi, was not known so as to be frequented by Ships when I made my survey.

This Harbour, and that of Fort George, from their situatioti, must naturally become connected with the Caledonian Canal, if that should be accomplished; so that the Harbours and the Canal will mutually enhance the value of each other. Vessels coming from Ireland, and from the Weft of England and Scotland by the Canal, bound for the Baltic, might rendezvous in the Harbour of Fort George, where they would be convenient to receive the prote&ion of convoy lying in Cromarty; and in like manner, Ships coming from the Eastward would be perfectly safe in Fort George Harbour, and be ready to be carried in by the tide into the Canal, and by making Cromarty a Naval station, that whole Coast would be protected, as well as afford the bell means of annoying an Enemy in those seas.

A Man of War, taking the advantage of the tide, would beat from Cromarty Harbour against the wind to Kinnaird’s Head in 30 or 36 hours; the course of the tide there would help them much, because the ebb tide along the North Ihore of the Murray Firth sets to tflo Eastward, and the flood tide along the South Ihore sets also to the Eastward; therefore a Ship might always turn to windward along the Ihore where the tide was favourable.

I am fully of opinion that a communication may be kept up between Aberdeen, Peterhead, Fraserburgh, and fro 111 thence to Cromarty, by means of Signals or Telegraphs, as the furl ace of the ground is particularly well formed for that pur pole.

Appendix, No. 5.

Mr. Telford's Report of Aberdeen, made to the Lords of the Trea-

fuiy in 1801.

Aberdeen does not project so far into the North Sea as Peterhead, though prominent, and considerably more to the Fait than any part of Scotland, which lies to the South of it.

The Rivers Dee and Don, which are the drains of a very considerable extent of Country, fall into the fame Bay, and within two miles of each other. These Rivers have two distinct characters: the River Dee has very little fall for several miles hack into the Country; the tide flows up it for about two miles. The River Don, on the contrary, has a very considerable fall within a short didance of the shore. The advantage of this tall near the mouth of the Don, has induced some enterprizing Men to erect Manufactories of various descriptions upon it, and which are now in a very thriving condition. The old Town of Aberdeen hands near the South Bank of the River Don; the new Town, which is now generally known by the name of Aberdeen, stands on the North fide, and near to the Mouth of the River Dee. It is a place of considerable extent, and said to contain *27,000 Inhabitants.

It has long been noted for the indudry of its Inhabitants; and the convenience of the College, and the cheapness of Education, with the adiduity and abilities of the Profedors, havediffufed a greater portion of information over that Didrict of Scotland than is generally met with, and its ededs have been to promote the general welfare of the place, and render the People respectable and happy.

The Manufacturers and Mechanics are much indebted to Professor Copland, and to the plan which he has so judiciously adopted in his Lectures. He has for many years occupied the Natural Philosophy Chair, with much credit to himsell and advantage to the Public; but ■what renders him more especially useful, is, the course of experimental Philosophy which he gives every second year, and which he diveds of the higher branches of Mathematics, in order to accommodate himself to the comprehension of common Manufacturers and Mechanics. It is incredible of what benefit thele LeCiures have been: every Workman acquires a sufficient degree of information to aid and direct him in his profefTion; and these Workmen again, by their practice and emulation, form a School among themselves, in which the riling Generation is prepared for the LeCiures of this patriotic and respectable Pro-feflor, I mention this, not only as a tribute due to Professor Copland, but produce it as an indance to shew how valuable similar plans might prove, if adopted at other Universities and Seminaries of Learning.

As the Manufacturers of Aberdeen have continued to thrive and increase, so have the Trade and Opulence of the Place; and the Inhabitants have been led to bellow much pains and expence upon this Harbour. From Coleidon, which is about fifteen miles North of Aberdeen, the shore is a loose fund. To the W. of S. at Aberdeen the point of Granite called Girdleness runs out suddenly nearly a mile, and the River Dee runs along the North fide of this Point. The N. E. Winds, which are drong, move the Sands along the shore, from Coleidon and Newburgh, until they are are flopped by the point of Girdleness. They would, no doubt, have filled up the angle of this Bay as far, or nearly so, as the point of Girdlcnels, had it not been for the waters of the Dee; but these waters, especially when augmented by land floods, flow with much force, and have kept open a passage along the N. fide of the Granite Rocks. The Sands continuing to accumulate on the N. fide of the Dee, have formed a point called Sand Nofs. From Sand Nefs for more than a mile up the River, the ground along the River Dee continues so low, that it is covered at high water, and this low land is of considerable width. The course of the River is down the South fide of the low Land, hut in floods it overflows the Banks, and part of it turns down the N. fide of the low Land, being next to the Town, and from thence has formed a crooked Channel to the Point formerly called the Sand Nefs, when it joins the main stream of the River. Upon this Channel, on the North fide, the Town has built Quays, and it is here that VefTRs come in with the tides, and transact their business; the River having but little declivity for a great distance from its mouth, and the :>• *a constantly operating to check its force. The River and the Sea adjusted their boundaries and depths in proportion to their natural forces, but in this way left a Bank across the Mouth of the River called the Bar, and this Bar was raised a little higher, or washed a little lower, According to the relative slate of the florins and tides on one lido, and the Piers in the River on the other. In this slate, there were about fourteen feet of

ten feet at high water; and both these depths were at the very heft slate of the Bar.

As the trade of the Port increased, the number and size of the Vessels iner&tfed also. The want of water on the Bar was found a great inconvenience, and its uncertainty wds a still more serious cause of complaint. In order to remedy these evils, the Town, by the advice of Mr. Smeaton, carried out a Pier froni the point called Sand Nefs, along the North flde of the River, to the extent of about 300 yards. This Pier, by checking and giving a different direction to the waves and funds, and with the wall on the South fide, continuing the force of the River to a greater distance, these two measures proved the means of removing the Bar from the place where it had been formed, and throwing it into deeper water. This valuable improvement gained them from three to four feet of water, and rendered their entrance of a more uniform depth. These improvements were begun in 1770.

In 1778, other improvements were made by the advice of Mr. Smeaton, to prevent the bad efle&s of the inrun of the Sea, which cauled so violent an agitation in the Harbour as to prove inconvenient and dangerous.

The City, finding that the expence of executing these works amounted to mpre than their Funds would defray, have applied to Parliament, and have obtained powers to levy additional Duties to improve the interior part of the Harbour, which still remains very defective.* Very little has hitherto been done towards this interior improvement, and their means are not very great. By a judicious application and great (economy in the management, these Funds which they now have might perhaps improve their Harbour, so far as to accommodate their own Trade, but could not admit of Ships of War, and Vessels of great burthen.

It therefore becomes a question, whether these are the means of acquiring accommodations at Aberdeen on a large scale; whether its general situation is such as to render it a desirable object to acquire those accommodations; and in what mannner, and at what expence, they may be executed.

If I had not considered that the general situation of Aberdeen prami fed to answer public purposes, that there appeared to be means of acquiring the necessary accommodations to a certain degree, I should not have gone so minutely into a description of the place.

The situation, so far from being embayed, is open and bold. It is well situated for the Northern parts of Europe; it is not inconvenient * as a rendezvous for Ships bound to the Baltic, or coming from it; and it is thus convenient, whether in regard to the East Coast of England and Scotland, or if the Inland Navigation should be opened by Inverness and Fort William, to the Western parts of England and Scotland, and the whole of Ireland. It is already a place of considerable Trade, has many conveniences and accommodations; it abounds with enterprizing and well-informed Men; and its being so happily situated between two very considerable Rivers, appears to be an object of very 1 great and Angular importance.

By securing and extending the Pier on the N. fide of the River, adopting a proper plan for managing the tw'o Rivers, the Canals, the Bara, and improving the interior parts of the Harbour, of which, under these circumstances, it is lufceptible to almost any extent, it appears to me that this Harbour might be made for safety and accommodation, equal to any thing that could be required either for the purpose of Government, as far as regards Frigates, or for the general Commerce of the North of Europe.

The space of ground already under the controul of the City is sufficiently extensive, and lies very convenient; and it docs not appear to me, that there would be much interference with private property, any further than has been already projected. The only project which appears in the lealt to interfere is, that the Fisheries upon the River Dee have been disposed of by the City, and are the property of private Persons; but I am convinced, that under a judicious arrangement, the improvements wanted might be obtained without lessening the value of the Fisheries; they might either be purchased by the Public, as they would lose nothing by the bargain, or their value might be guaranteed to the present Proprietors, making good the damage in case of any injury being done; or, if insuperable difficulties arose on this head, the flood water only of the Dee might be taken, and the chief business might be done by means of the River Don, as that River, I understand, has still a sufficient fall for this purpose, after it has answered the purpose of the established Manufactories. It might be carried round by Old Aberdeen, and the land that lies between that and the Harbour, at the Dec, by means of a Canal on a level to suit all the purposes of supplying Lockage, clearing the Docks, and scouring the entrances of the Harbour.

The powers of the waters of these two fine Rivers are equal to any thing. It is a Angular coincidence that they drain so great and rainy a Country, that they join the sea so near to each other, and that the River which is most distant upon the I larbour, retains a considerabla portion of its fall to within a small distance of the sea.

I am authorized to slate, that the City is ready to co-operate with Government as far as their Funds will admit, and toaflift and pro-

Memorial to the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, from the Magistrates of Aberdeen, for themselves, and in the name of the Council and Community of that City.

About thirty years ago, a Plan was obtained from the late Mr. Smeaton, Engineer, for the deepening and general Improvement of the Harbour of Aberdeen, which has since that time been partly carried into execution, particularly by the erection of a Pier into the Sea, to the extent of 1,200 feet on the North fide of the Entry, at an expence of about Thirty Thousand Pounds Sterling, which has been Disburse d solely from the public Funds of the City.

This new Pier has had the eflect proposed by Mr. Smeaton, of producing an additional depth of water at the entry of the Harbour, in proportion to the extent so which it has been carried out. But the Trade and Shipping having greatly increased, it is now proposed to extend the said Pier, for the purpose of obtaining a hill additional depth of water at the entry, as well as to improve the interior (it being at present what is termed a Dry Harbour) by making out and building Wet Docks, where Ships may always ride atloat.

A depth of water, not exceeding fifteen feet, might be sufficient for the Shipping of the Port, for which the Funds that can be raised by the Corporation, it is presumed, may be adequate; but some eminent Engineers, who have lately been employed to draw up Plans lor the further Improvement of the Harbour, have represented it as very practicable* although at a considerable expence, to carry these improve-

ments to a greater extent than is n.ccfiary for the Trade of the Port itself, by obtaining a depth of water oi at lealt twenty feet, which would be funic lent for admitting Frigates, ai;d other fundi Ships of War, as v»*ll as larger Merchant Vehels, and allowing them to he kept alloat within the Harbour.

Ox the Well Coast of Scotland every Loch is a Harbour, and no Vessels can ever be at a loss to lind a protection; blit the case is very different on the N. E. Coast. At present there is no place where a Vessel can run into, or even lie with safety, from the Bay of Cromarty to the Road Head of Serabfter, on the \\ client fide of the Pentland Firth. Vessels frequenting the Herring Fishery in this quarter lie in the River of Wick, but they are confined within a lliallow Bay, in a narrow Channel, and lo ex poled to the N. E. that they dare not wait the Equinoctial gales, and instead of Billing for a whole season, they puHi oil as loon as they can get any thing like a cargo. They have no place but the Beach on which to land and pack their Fish; and they frequently cannot get over the Bar even to reach this Beach, but lie with their Fish in their open boats, exposed to the fun till they are spoiled. It is generally allowed, that the deep Sea Fishing might be carried on in this quarter, but ho person will rilk his Vessel and Capital while there is no place of security for them to run into in case of stormy weather, nor any convenience whatever to enable them to carry on their business with advantage; it is therefore very evident, that, to promote the extension and success of the Fisheries in that quarter, there should he a Harbour on the Coast of Caithness; and there is no place, except Wick, to the South of the Pentland Firth* which is fit for Inch a Harbour.

The entrance to the Bay of Wick is in a projecting part of the Coali, so that a Vessel coming out of it is in clear sea room, to make her way in any direction. The Bay is of a triangular form, about a mile wide at the mouth, and a mile deep inland: there are twelve fathoms near the mouth, and it shallows very gradually to three fathoms near the top of the Bay, and from thence Bill gradually to the shore. The whole of the Bay is quite clear ground, the bottom clean land. The shore on both tides is rocky; near the top of the Bay, the lb ores in some places are covered with loose stones; the rest is sandy and Hat. '1 he banks on each side are pretty high and ft cop, but the Country around is a plain, with forre gentle swells, and is in general either pallure or arable. The River of Wick is considerable. The Town Hands on the N. fide of the River, and very near to the top of ’the Bay; it is said to contain 1,000 Inhabitants.

The rock along the shores, on each side of the Bay, lie very flat and regular, and dip to the N. nearly. They lie 111 beds from fix to eighteen inches in thieknels; they may be raised of any size, and are remarkably well fitted for making Piers and Bread Walls.

William Durand the Pilot, and James Muckay, an experienced Seaman of \\ ick, informed me, that in moderate weather the ordinary spring tales rile about 7 | or 8 feet, and ordinary neaps about 5 to 5h feet. When there is rough weather and welterly winds, springs rife 12 feet, neaps 8 feet; that the highest tides are at£ pail eleven o’clock on the days of full and change.

I think it possible to form a very good Tide Harbour here, calculated to accommodate such Vessels as follow the Fishing or Coasting Trade, or even trade to the Baltic. At the top of the Bay, and on the South fide of the River, there are sandy Banks. At the bottom of these Banks, and considerably without the Bar, 1 have drawn the plan of a Harbour suitable to the place; it may be begun determined by building lirft the Piers A. and B. which would be the chief protection for a space capable of receiving upwards of 200 Vessels of the above description. Along this great extent of Piers, there would be an opportunity of doing much business; but if this was found to be inefficient, or that the lurges broke round into the Harbour, the PierC. might be erected, which I should recommend to be done by forming the point only in the manner of a solid Pier, making all the rest with two retaining Walls, diverging as they were carried towards the Town, and filling up between them with what was excavated out of the Harbour; this would form a very fine wharf for discharging and packing Herrings.

In this way the waves would flow past the mouth of the Harbour, and break upon the present Bar. The entrance to the Harbour is also within the protection of the point of land on the North fide of the Bay.

If after these two Piers were built, the business should be found to be very great, and that there was If ill a want of space for Wharfs, another Pier, D. might he built down the middle of the Harbour. In case of such great increase of business, it would be deflrable to keep the smallest Vessels and Boats in a place distinct from the larger Vessels, and it would also be desirable to have some Graving Docks. All thef® might be accomplished, by making the small Pier E. and the Graving Docks at F. If after all this, the space (which would then contain near 300 Vessels) should Bill be found too small, a Lock might be made out of the main Harbour, to carry Vessels up to a higher level. But. certainly for a beginning, and for a trial of the expected deep Sea Fiffi-ing, and for extending the present Fishing on that Coast, such a Harbour as has enabled Greenock to rife into considerable consequence, mud be allowed to be quite sufficient. Most of the Coasting Vessels which frequent Liverpool, also lie in a Tide Bason, as do the whole of the Vessels which frequent the Port of Bristol.

I would permit the River to flow along its present channel, only as there may be occasion t(^cle^|rfe ^Harboiur from mud tbkt may be

Appendix, No. 9.

The Examination of Mr. Alexander McLeay, Chief Clerk in the Transport Office, in the Department of Prisoners of War.

I am well acquainted with the Harbour and neighbourhood of Wick, having redded fomeyears there; I think there is no pari of the EadCoaft of Scotland better calculated for the Herring Fishery; various kinds certainly abound on that Coad, and the White Fishery is also carried on there. The Herrings are larger than on any other part of the Eall Coad, and I believe not inferior to those of the Wed Coad. The Herrings appear about the middle of June, and they come every year, but are sometimes prevented from coming so near the shore as at other times by Eaderly winds. The quantity caught lad year by Boats was 12,354 barrels, by about twenty-seven different Curers, and two or three hundred Boats; much larger quantities might be caught if there were more Vessels employed; the fame number of boats could take much more when the weather is favourable; but the chief difficulty is, that there being no safe Ihelter for Boats on that rocky Coad, they are afraid to go to sea when the wind is Eaderly, or the sea runs high; if there were one good Harbour, they could safely go out. I was informed by some of the Fish Curers, that if a lafe Harbour is made, it is their intention to fit out Bufles for the Deep-sea Herring Fishery; the Fishing Ground for that purpose is not many miles did ant from the Coad; a Harbour on that Coad would be very

beneficial to the general Commerce and Navigation of the Country. No less than fix Vessels were wrecked on the Ead Coad of Caithnel* lait year, and I under and they might have been saved if there had been a Harbour at Wick; I do not think it possible to erect a Harbour there without public aid. They have no trade there but the Fishery, the profit of which would not suffice for l'uch a work; I think that Vessels built in the form of the Dutch Fishing VnVels, could not remain near the Coalt of Caithness during an Eaderly wind, bepause from their condruction they find great difficulty in working to windward.

Appendix, No. to.

The Examination of Mr. John Christopher Falck, a Merchant in the City of Ix>ndon, and rcliding in Moorfields.

I have for a number of years endeavoured to make myself master of the subject of the Fisheries, and more el'pecially of the Herring Fishery, and have communicated various plans and explanations on that lub-ject to the British Fishing Society. There are properly three forts of Herring Fishery: The fird, with (hallow nets, calculated for Boats or small Vessels in Bays and along the Coasts; the second, with deep nets in the open feu as practised by the Dutch; and the third, with long nets, as done in Sweden, similar to the mode of catching Pilchards in Cornwall. The bed inode seems to me with deep nets, as pradiledbv the Dutch on the Coali of Shetland, and the North-ealt Coad of Scotland. 1 have seen Herrings, which were brought from Wick in Caithness, of as good a quality as thofecured by the Dutch; more el’pecially in the year 1802 some Herrings came from Wick, which had been caught in the year 1801, and were cured in the Dutch style by some Dutch prisoners, sent North by Government for that purpose; they feeiued to me to resemble in quality Dutch Herrings, and several very good judges in the City of London, niodly Foreigners, w ho knew well what Dutch Herrings were, subscribed a certificate to that efieft; they had cat them as Dutch Herrings, and found the fame medicinal qualities which the Dutch Herrings have. The market for Herrings, properly cured, would be very great. It is my opinion, that the Continental consumption alone would be equal to from 250,000 to 300,000 barrels, at the lead, and probably much more, if the Filli were cured equal to the Dutch. We could go to the Market much quicker than them, and being nearer the Fishing Grounds, could catch them at a cheaper rate. When the Dutch Herrings come fird in, they will fell for a Ducat, or 95. 6 d. each; but this is merely given by Dutch families, as a premium to encourage the Fisheries. On the whole, however, a barrel of Dutch Herrings, properly cured according to the Dutch mode, may be worth on an average about Four Pounds sterling; fa that if 250,000 barrels were caught and fold, the Fishery might produce at lead a Million derling per annum; and if properly subdivided into half and quarter barrels, &c. even more. This is much less than the profit gained by the Dutch. I got an exact account of the number of Vessels employed by the Dutch in their Fisheries in the year 1788, which in all amounted to above 2,700 of different sizes. The proportion for the Herring Fishery I do not exactly know; but I suppose, that at least 300 might be employed on our Coalt in the Herring Fishery alone. They require a crew of from 15 to 30 persons each, on an average, including those employed in curing and barrelling the filli, &c. I am of opinion, that there would not be much difficulty in procuring Dutch Fishermen and Curers, olVcring them proper encouragement. The Prudian Herring Fishery Company at Hamburgh and Embden employ none but persons skilled in the Dutch dyle of curing, and succeed as well as the Dutch; but, for establishing the Herring Fishery properly, it would be necefiiiry to procure Foreign Bay Salt Duty free, which would cure the Herrings in perfection, with a proper mixture of Cheshire Salt, free from Excile and Duty. The Dutch Deep-sea Fishing Vessels are built round fore and aft, in order to hand lempt-ltuous weather without danger. Sharp built Vessel* made for salt failing, like the British Fishing Vessels, would not answer, unless there were Harbours where they could run to for Ihelter; as for the nets, they must be in the fame lhape and form of those used by the Dutch. There is every probability if proper Harbours were made for tire safety of their Vessels, and where they could prepare the Filli for Exportation, that the Dutch Filliers would come to settle there.
