was no authority to protect or to reform them; no tie of restraint to subject them to one commou discipline.

In fine, there was wanting to France a power to reclaim Justice itself, the power of granting pardon. How often these twelve years pail has that power been implored! How many unfortunates have fallen the victims of an inflexible stemness with which wile Men reproached our Laws! llow many criminals have been acquitted through a fall'e indulgence, bee ait fe our punishments were too severe 1

A Senatus Consultum has restored to the People the exercise of those rights which the Constituent Assembly had acknowledged; but it has restored them surrounded with precautions, which preserve the People from errors or precipitation in their choice; with precautions which guard the influence of property, and the preponderance of enlightened talents.

Should the First Magistracy become vacant, the duties and the proceedings of the Senate are traced out for such an emergency: Forms of certain operation guide the wisdom and the liberty of their choice; and the quick decilion of that choice deprives ambition of the means of conspiring, and anarchy of the means of destroying.

The cement of time will every day consolidate, more and more, this tutelary inllitution. It will he not only the term of all disquietudes, and the object of all hopes, but likewise the fairest recompences that can be held out to public Cervices and public virtues.

Justice embraces all the Tribunals with one common bond. They have each their subordinate station and their censor: they are always free in the exercise of their functions; always independent of power, but never independent of the Laws.

The privilege of granting pardon when the interest of the Republic requires it, or when circumstances prescribe indulgence, is entrusted to the hands of the First Magistrate; but it is only confided to him under the guard of justice itself; he is to exercise it only under the eyes of a Council, and after having consulted the feverelc oracles of the Law.

If institutions may he appreciated by their effects, never was any inllitution more important in its relult than the orgauic Senatus Consultum* From that moment the French People began to confide in their defiiny; property began to resume its former value, and spe-culations of distant view to be multiplied;—until that moment every thing Teemed to float in uncertainty. The present moment was che-riflied; the next was a subject of alarm, and the enemies of the Country continued to cherish hopes. Since that moment they are reduced to impotence and to detestation.

The Island of Elba has been ceded to France; that acquisition gives her a mild and industrious people; two fine Ports, a productive and precious Mine; but being separated from France, it could not be intimately united with any of her Departments, or subjected to the regulations of a common administration. Principles have been made to bend to the necessity of circumstances; exceptions have been established for the Island of Elba, which its , and the public interest prescribed.

The abdication of the Sovereign, the will of the People, and the necessity of existing circumstances, had placed Piedmont under the Power of France. Amidst the Nations that surrounded it, with the elements that competed its population, Piedmont was unable to support either the weight of its own independence, or the expences of a Monarchy'. United to France, it will reap the beuefits of its security, and its greatuefs: its laborious andvenlightened Citizens will exert their industry and their talents in the bosom of the Arts, and under the shade of Peace.

Security and tranquillity prevail in the interior of France. The vigilance of the Magistracy, thefeverity of Justice, and a Gendarmerie vigorously appointed, and directed by a Commander, grown grey in the career of honour, has every where impressed terror on the minds and the attempts of the Brigands.

Private interest has raised itself to a sentiment of public interest. Citizens have not shrunk from attacking those whom they formerly dreaded, even when they were chained down at the foot of the Tri-bunals of Justice. Whole Communes have taken up arms and destroyed the Brigands. Foreigners envy the security of our public roads, and that public Force, which, though often invisible, is always present, attend on their footsteps, and watch for their prote&ion, without any necessity of imploring its aid.

During the course of a difficult year, amidst the exigencies of a general scarcity, the Poor looked with confidence to the care of Government. They l’upported with courage the privations which necessity imposed; and they received with gratitude the succours which they were taught to expect.

The crime of Forgery is no longer encouraged by the hope of impunity. The zeal of the Tribunals appointed to prosecute and punish it, and the just severity of the Laws, have at leugth checked the progress of an evila which threatened both the public treasure, and the fortunes of individuals.

Our cultivation daily improves, and defies the most boasted agricultural systems of Europe. In every Department are to be found enlightened Farmers, who afford both inftnfetiou and example.

You 58,

Premiums have been held out for improving the breed of Horses; and similar encouragements are proposed for the improvement of Wool by the introduction of a Foreign breed of sheep. Zealous Admini-ltrators are every where occupied in tracing out and revealing the richness of our Soil, and in difieminating the useful Plans and the happy results which experience daily discovers.

Our Manufactures multiply, and receive new spiritand improvement* While they emulate each, they will soon, no doubt, become the rivals of the most renowned Manufactures of Foreign Countries. Henceforth there will be nothing wanting to their prosperity but capitals lets dearly purchased. But Capitaiifts begin already to give up the hazardous i'peculations of Stock-jobbing, and devote their attention to the improvement of Land and the pursuit of useful enterprizes. More than twenty thousand Workmen, who were difperied throughout Europe, have been recalled by the attention and by the favours of Government, and will soon be reiiored to our Manufactures.

Among our Manufactures there is one which is almost peculiar to France, which Colbert kindled up by his genius. It was buried under the ruins of Lyons: Government has exerted all its endeavours to extricate iti Lyons is again restored to splendour and opulence; already do its Manufactures impose a tribute on the luxury ot Europe; But the principle of their success is to be found in the luxury of France itself; it is in the changefulneis of our talte, and the mutability of our faihions, that Foreign luxury must look for its aliment; it is it that gives motion and life to an imnienl’e population, who, without that encouragement, must iol'e itself in corruption and misery.

There will soon be at Compiegne, there will soon arise on the confines of La Vendee, a number of Prytanees, where our youth will be brought up in habits of industry, and infmicled in the mechanical arts. From that lource our Dock Yards and our Manufactures will one day draw Inspectors to direct their labours*

Fourteen Millions arising out of the Barrier Tax, and Ten Millions out of the Extraordinaries, have been employed during the year 10 in improving the public roads, in keeping up the old communications; New communications have also been opened. The Simpson, Mount-Cenis, and Mount-Genevre, will loon open a triple and easy access to Italy; a high road will lead from Genoa to Marseilles: a road is chalked out from Saint Esprit to Gap, another from Rennes to Brest, through Pontivy. At Pontivy, Establishments are to be raised which will have a powerful influence over the public mind of the Departments of which ci-devant Britanny was composed—a Canal will introduce into it new sources of commerce and prosperity.

On the Banks of the Rhine from Bingen to Coblentz, a neceflkry road is cut through inaccefiible rocks. The neighbouring Communes associate their labours to the sacrifices of the public Treasury; and the People of the other Bank, who ridiculed the folly of the enterprize, are astonished and confounded at the rapidity of the execution.

A great number of workmen are employed on the Canal of Saint Quin tin.

The Canal of Ourcq is opened, and soon will Paris People enjoy the benefit of its waters, and the salubrity and the cmbellishments which they promise.

The Canal intended to unite the navigation of the Seine and the Saone, of the Danube and the Rhine, is almost entirely finished as far as Dole, and the public Treasury already receives in the increufed price of wood, to which that Canal opens the approach, a sum equal to that which it has furnished for the continuance of the work.

The Canals of Argues. Mortes, and the Rhone, the draining of the Marshes of the Lower Charente, are begun, and will open up new channels to commerce, and afford new Lands for cultivation. Woris are going forward for the reparation of the Dykes of the Isle of Cad-fund, of Ostend, of the Cotes du Xord, and the re-establishment of the navigation of our Rivers. This navigation is no longer given up solely to the labours and the cares of Government. The Owners of Boats plying on these Rivers have already felt that it was their patrimony, and they fix on themselves the Taxes by which the works are to be kept in proper repair. On the Ocean, Forts are erecting to cover the roads of the Isle of Aix, and to protect the Vessels of the Republic. From the Hamburgh Correspondenten of March 30, 1803. (Translation.)

The following Article is inserted by desire:

Paris, March 15. For some months a war of newspapers and of the press has beep kept up between France and England. This seemed merely the dying embers of an extinguished conflagration; the lafi confutation of a def-perate party; the food of some low passions and a few hungry ferib*4 biers. The French Government was far from attaching importance to such matters. Notwithstanding some difficulties in the complete execution of the Treaty of Amiens, they still believed they might rely on the good faith of the British Government, and directed their attention lolely to the re-establishment of the Colonies. Relying upon' the sacrednel's of Treaties, they securely dispersed the remains of the French Naval Force, which had been given a prey to the English Fleet. Tn this situation suddenly appeared a solemn Message from the Cabinet of St. James’s, and informed all Europe that France was making considerable preparations in the Ports of Holland and France; ail Address was voted by Parliament, promising to the King of England such extraordinary means of defence as the security of the British Empire and the honour of the three Crowns might require.

From the hidden appearance of this Message, people doubted whether it was the clfed of treachery, of lunacy, or of weakness. Let any one cast his eye over the Ports of France and Holland, where he will find only detached Naval Preparations destined for the Colonies, and confining only of one or two hue of Battle Ships and a few Frigates. On the other hand, let him look at the Ports of England, filled with a for-' midable Naval force; on such a review one could be tempted to believe that the Message of the King of England was mere irony, if such a farce were not unworthy the Majesty of a Government. If one considers the influence of factions in so free a Country, one might suppose that the King of England had only had the weakness to yield, if wreak-ness were compatible with the first quality of a King. In short, no rational motives remain to which it can be afc.ribed, except bad faith —except a sworn enmity to the French Nation1—except perfidy, and the desire of openly breaking a solemn Treaty, for the fake of advantages which will be maintained, and the sacrifice of which the honour of France and the Faith of Treaties forbid.

When a man reads this Message he thinks himself transported to the times of those Treaties which the Vandals made with the degenerate Romans, when Force usurped the place of Right, and when, with a hasty appeal to Arms, they insulted the Antagoni/l they meant to attack. In the present /late of civilization there is a respect which a great Monarch, which a polished People owe to themselves, were that respect no more than to seek a plausible pretext for an unjust War. But in this inllance every thing is precipitate, and repugnant to decency and to justice. An eternal War would succeed a dreadful contetl; and the more unju/l the attack, the more irreconcileable would be its animo/ity.

Such a novelty will doubtless excite the disapprobation of Europe. While even the English, whose national pride had not entirely blinded them, sighed at this prospect, did the Times call the Peace of Amiens an Armiltice, and in doing so, passed the feverell satire on the Government it defended; and the rapid fall of the National Funds is the first prelude to the misfortunes which may follow as the revenge due for the wound given to all social rights.

The French are less intimidated than irritated by the threats of England. They have neither been dispirited by their reverses, nor elated by their vidories; in a War to which there appeared no termination, they saw all Europe confederated against them. Their constancy, their courage, and the prompt activity of their Government, brought it to a conclusion. This War would have a different otyedl; France would contend for the liberty of the States of Europe* and the sacredness of their Treaties; and if the English Government be determined to make it a National War, perhaps her boasted

formidable

The French, strong in the just ice of their cause, and in the confidence they repose in their Government, do not dread the new expences and new Sacrifices which such a War might render necessary. * Their system of Finance is more Simple and Iels artificial than that of London, and so much the more solid. It all lies in their foil and in their courage.

On the first news of the English Message, all eyes were turned to the Cabinet of the Thuilleries. As mod trifling motions received a character of importance, its mofl unpremeditated words were eagerly caught up. Every one impatiently expected the Assembly for the presentation of Foreigners, which Madame Bonaparte holds once a month. Every one was prepared to draw Some inferences from it. It was as Splendid as uSual. The First Consul made his appearance, and Said, on his entrance, to the English Ambassador, who was Standing beside M. Markoff, " We have been at War for twelve years. The King of England Says that France is making immense Naval preparations. He has been led into an error. In the French Ports there are no preparations of any magnitude. The whole Fleet is gone to St. Domingo and the Colonies. With regard to the Ports of Holland, to which the Message likewise alludes, there are only the preparations for the Expedition under General Victor, and all Europe knows its destination is for Louisiana. The King fays farther, that between the Cabinets of Paris and London differences continue. I know of norc. It is true that England ought to have evacuated Malta, and Malta is hot evacuated; and as His Britannic Majesty has bound h ini Self by the most solemn Treaty ever entered into, it is impossible to doubt of the speedy evacuation of that Island; and/' added the First Consul, " those who would attempt to frighten the French People should know, that it is possible to kill, but not to intimidate them." During the course of the evening, when the First Consul happened to be near M. Markoff, he said to him, half aloud, " that the British Miniihy wi/lied to keep Malta for five years more. Such a proposal was intuiting, and no Treaties should be entered into which it was not resolved to observe." At the conclusion of the Assembly, when the English Ambassador was about to retire, the First Consul said to him, 44 Madame the Duchess of Dorset has Spent the unpleasant part of the year at Paris. It is my sincere with that flic may also spend the agreeable season. But if it should happen that we really must go to War, the responsibility is exclusively with those who deny the validity of their own contrails, Since they refuse to observe Treaties which they had concluded/'

These words of the First Consul require no comment. They explain completely his present opinions, his pall conduct, and his resolution for the future. It is sufficient to compare them with the tergiverfa-tions, the duplicity, the evasions, and the Message, of the English Government, in order, to be enabled to decide on the justice of the dispute.

Horace Sebastiani, Chief of Brigade of a Regiment of Dragoons, And Envoy the First Consul in the Levant.

To his Excellency the Delegate of Zante.

Sir,

The First Cohful, Bonaparte, has charged me to visit these Iflaridt which compose your Republic, and to assure the Inhabitants that he takes a lively interest in their prosperity*

I know that the difference of political opinions divides this rising Republic into various parties, and that without the wife measures taken by your Government, its tranquillity will be destroyed. I could with you to make known to your Administrators and Fellow Citizen* how much the First Confnl withes to fee a Hop put to those intestine divisions which afflict these Islands.

Your political independency has been guaranteed by France, Ruflta, and the Sublime Porte. These powerful Nations, united together by the bonds of the truest friendthip, are occupied, in concert with year most enlightened and most virtuous Fellow Citizens, to give you a Form of Government Suitable to your Situation, and the genius of your Inhabitants. Wait with confidence and moderation the result of these im* portant operations, and be assured that you will fee the end of youc ills, and the beginning of your prosperity. All exaggerations of political opinions are inimical to the general prosperity: absolute Democracy, always tempestuous, Sacrifices to vain chimeras the Security, the property, civil liberty, and, in short, all that constitutes the happiness of a State: Aristocracy, which is not moderated, is always tyrannical, and the elevation of a Small number of families is preferred to talents and to virtue. In order that a Government may be praf* perous, it is necessary that it should have in its formation & happy combination of the advantages of different forms of Government; the power &nd promptitude of Monarchy, the vigilance and intelligence of Aristocracy, and the vigour and elevation of Democracy; that the Citizens may find the Security enjoyed Under the first, the tranquillity of the second, and the equality of rights fixed by the Laws which are found in the third.

Recoiled that the Man who forms a part of society only preservei the liberty of doing that which is not prejudicial to the rights of others; and that Equality only consists in the exact execution of the Laws, and in the protection which they afford to every Member of the political body. As the quarantine prevents communication, I beg you will communicate this my Letter to all the Authorities, and also to the principal Inhabitants.

I avail mrself of this opportunity to assure you of the Sentiments of esteem and consideration which I entertain for your person.

tllS Majesty’s earned endeavours for the preservation of Peace having failed of luccefs, lie entertains the lulldt confidence that lie ibali receive the lame lupporl from His Parliament, and that the lame -seid and spirit will be manifested by His People, which he has experienced on every occasion when the honour of His Crown has hern attacked, or the ellential iruerelts of His Dominions have been endangered.

Instructions to Lord Whitworth.

My Lord, Downing-street, Nov. 14, 1802.

I take the first opportunity of communicating to your Excellency, for the regulation of your conduct, the Instructions which His Majesty i pleased to give you on such points as may become subjects of dif-custion between His Majesty and the French Government; and to desire that you will endeavour to conform yourself to them in all your conversations with the French Ministers.

You will lose no proper opportunity of expressing His Majesty* 1s earned solicitude for the preservation of the Peace which fubiifts between the two Countries; His disposition to do every thing in His power for that purpose which is confident with the honour of His Crown, and the interests of His Dominions; and llis regret at any circumstances which may have arisen to interrupt that harmony and good understanding which are so important to the welfare and happiness of both Countries. You will, however, state mod distinctly His Majesty's determination never to forego His right of interfering in the aflairs of the Continent, on every occasion in which the interests of His own Dominions, or those of Europe in general, may appear to him to require it. This right llis Majesty poddies in common with

every other independent Power; it rests upon general principles, and does not require the confirmation of any particular Treaty. It is, nevertheless, important that you should observe, that the circumstances which led to the conclusion of the laii Peace, and the principles upon which the Negotiation was conducted, would give His Majesty a speciul right to interpose in any case which might lead to the extension of the power or influence of France. In the communications which took place between the two Governments, previous to the lignature of the Preliminary Articles, His Majesty proposed, as the bafts of Negotiation, that if the French Government would not relinquish the Continental acquisitions which tiiey had obtained from other Powers in the rourse of the War, Ills Majesty would claim the right of keeping a part of llis conquests, as st compensation for the important acquisitions of Territory made by France upon the Continent. This principle was formerly recognized by the French Government in an official Note in the following words: " Cependant on <c reconnoit que les Grands Evenemens furvenus en Europe, et les " changemens arrives dans les Li mites des Grands Etats cu Con-4< tinent> peuvent autorifer une partie des demandesdu Gouvernement " Britaunique." The terms of the Treaty of Peace were negcciated in conformity to this bails; and it appears therefore clear, that the then existing state of possession and of engagements as reiped the Continent, were the foundation of the Peace itself, and that His Majesty has therefore an undoubted right to interpose, in consequence of the T reaty, in every case in which the state of possession may appear to him to have undergone any material alteration, or in which the engagements which were then fulfilling had been violated to the prejudice of llis Majesty, or of the other Powers of Europe. You will proceed to observe, that the annexation of Piedmont to France, since the conclusion of the Definitive Treaty, makes a mod material difference in the state of the fixed and permanent possessions of France: that the renunciation of the Dutchy of Parma in favour of France, a circumstance which was concealed at the time of negotiating the Peace, and which is become of the greated importance from its furnishing an additional instance of that tyftem oi secret ccffton, which is totally inconiiftent with any iyftem of security for Europe, makes a mod essential difference likewise in the relative circumstances of the two Countries: that at the time of concluding the Peace, the French Government were bound by the mod sacred engagements to reiped the Independence of the Helvetic and Batavian Republics, and to allow the People of those Countries to choose whatever form of Government they might think proper: that the violation of this right in the Swiss People, and the Iuvafion of their Territory, notwithstanding the representation which was made in their favour by His Majesty, makes a mod material alteration in the state of engagements contracted iincc the conclusion of the Definitive Treaty, and adds mod confide 1 ably to the intluence and pywjrof France, to the prejudice of a State which was then acknowledged as independent: that the con-dud of the French Government to the Batavian Republic was not less objectionable: that the Independence of this Republic was acknowledged, both by the Treaty of Luneville and by the Treaty of the Hague of the year 1795: that by the Treaty of the Hague, the French Government were permitted to keep a Garrison in that Country only till the time of general Peace: that, by a Convention signed* in August 1801, the French Troops were to remain there till the oon-clulion of the Definitive Treaty of Peace between Great Britain and France: that the French Troops have not, to this period, evacuated the Country; and that the First Conliil is represented lately to have' declared, that, in the event of any differences amongd the people of that Country on the subject of their internal Government, he would march with his whole Army to suppress them: that this is an obvious violation of the Independence of the Batavian Republic; andf that His Majesty would have a peculiar right to interpose on the present occasion, as he consented to make numerous and mod important Restitutions to the Batavian Government in the Treaty of Peace, on the consideration of that Government being independent, and not being subject to any Foreign controul.

It is unnecessary for me to recommend to your Excellency to make tlicfe Representations with moderation and temper. You will attend very particularly to any Explanations which- may be given to you respecting them; and you will engagS to report such Explanations t<y llis Majesty's Government.

I have the honour to be, &c.

Sir, Downing-street, Jan* 29, 1803.

Your Excellency’s Dispatches, to N’21, inciufive, have been received, and laid before the King.

I fend you now inclosed the official Answer to the Note of the Chancellor Count WorozolT, relative to the 10th Article of the Treaty of Amiens—it has been delivered to Count Simon Woronzow, the Russian Anibaflador at this Court.

In communicating this Note, you will express, in suitable terms, how fen fib Iv 1J is Majesty feels the friendffiip which the Emperor of Russia has manifofrcd to Ilim on this occasion, in his disposition to concur in the arrangements relative to the Island of Malta—and how fmeerely His Majesty regrets, that it is not in His power to acquiesce, without condition or explanation, in every thing that his Imperial Majesty has proposed on this subject. His Majesty however trulls, that, when all the ci ream Trances are taken into consideration which bear upon this important subject, the Emperor of Russia will be satisfied, that the line of conduct which has been adopted by His Majesty, is such as a regard to good Faith and to the intereffs of 11 is Dominions have rendered necessary. The only material difference between the arrangement proposed by the Emperor of Russia for the Island of Malta, and that inXvhich His Majesty is willing to concur, relates to the ltipulations in favour of the Maltese Inhabitants. It is important that your Excellency should imprels the ltuilian Government with the conviction of the services rendered by the Inhabitants of Malta to His Majesty and to the common Cause, at the time when the French were in possession of the Island. That, for nearly two years, they maintained a date of confiant and active hostility against the French—that several thoafands of them periffied in this stale of hostility; and, that these efforts were made at a time when they could receive affilianee from no other Foreign Power-—That the attachment evinced by the Maltese to His Majesty, during the blockade, and their loyalty to Him since He has obtained possession of the Bland, gives them a peculiar claim to His protection, and a right to expect, that, in the future arrangements for the Island, some advantages should be ftipukited in their favour—That, independent of every consideration of good Faith, your Excellency well knows that the Maltese Inhabitants, if attached to their Government, are equal to the defence of the Island; and that every motive of policy therefore, as well as of just ice, renders it expedient to endeavour to conciliate their affections. Thel'e circumstances being premised, you wiH Rate, that the

objection which, it is conceived, 1ms had most weight with his Imperial Majesty, is that stipulation in the 10th Article of the Treaty of Amiens, which at the time that it establishes a Maltese Langue, requires no proof of Nobility for admission into that Langue—That such a stipulation is considered as leading to the establishment of a Plebean Langue, totally inconfilient with the spirit of the Institution of the Order.—His Majesty is extremely desirous of deviling means by which this objection shall be obviated, and the Interests of the Maltese adequately consulted. The proofs of Nobility, which have been required for other Priories, have been various; and the power of the Pope to grant Difpcnlations has been admitted to exilt: If therefore actual Nobility was made the indifpcnfable condition of admission into the Mal-tefe Langue or Priory,^the objection, which is at present made to this part of the arrangement, would, in a great degree, if not wholly, be removed. As, however, the number of Persons who would be capable of admission into the Order, in confluence of such a regulation, would be very limited, it appears reasonable that some further itipu-lations should be made in favour of the Inhabitants of Malta; and it may be proposed to revive, under such regulations and modifications as may be judged expedient, the National Council which formerly existed in that Island, which should form no part of the Order, but which should have a fbare in the Government of the Bland, and a deliberative voice in all its internal concerns. A body of this defen ption could not he considered as in any respect derogatory to the ancient Infiilution of the Order, and would be conformable to what e.xilted within the Bland till within a very few years. It is for the purpose of obtaining information on theft? points, that Instructions will be lent to Sir Alexander Ball; it being impossible, after all that has passed, to bring the Negotiation to an illlie, without some communication with the principal Inhabitants of Malta.

His Majesty relics on your zeal in giving effect to those Instructinns, and in your endeavours to reconcile the Russian Government to the objects of them.

The events which have happened since the conclusion of the Definitive Treaty; the unbounded ambition which has been, and tffil manifeued by the French Government; might have juliilW Kis Majesty in bringing forward new demands, and in even claiming the appropriation of Malta as feme counterpnifo to the acquisitions made by France since the Treaty of Peace; but the moderation with which. His Majesty has been actuated in all His concerns with Foreign Powers, and His anxious desire that the Peace of Europe may, 11 possible, be effectually ronfolidated, has induced Him to forego those claims which the increased and increasing Power of France might have juititied him in advancing; and as every fiipulation in the Treaty

In the Name of the French People.

The First Consul of the Republic having appointed Citizen Charles Stephen Coquebert Montbret, to the pod of Commissary General of the Commercial Relations of the French Republic at London, orders him to repair, without delay, to his destination, there to exercise, conformably to the Laws, the functions with which he is intrusted: —enjoins all French Merchants, Captains, Mailers, Owners, and Seamen, as well as all other Frenchmen residing within the said District, to acknowledge Citizen Coquebert Montbret in the post conferred upon him in the Name of the French People, and to give him an Account of the Navigation and Destination of their Vessels, and of every thing which may redate to the service in which he is employed. For which purpose they are to exhibit their Licence, Clearances,'Pall-ports, and are punctually to conform themselves to all the Regulations he may require. No. 5.

Copy of a Note from Lord Hawkesbury to M. Otto-Sir, Downing-street, September 18th, 1802.

I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your Letter of the 15th instant, inclosing the Commission of M. Chepy as Vice-Commissary of Commercial Relations, on the part of the French Repub* lie, for the Islands of Guernsey, Jersey, and Alderney.

I desire you to be allured, that His Majesty s Government have uniformly been, and continue to be, follcitous to see the Commerce between this Country and France renewed upon a just and equitable footing: It has therefore afforded them sincere concern to learn, that their disposition in this respect has not as yet been met by a correspondent disposition on the part of the French Government: but that the Commerce of His Majesty's Subjects, in the Ports of Fiance, is in a very uncertain and precarious Hate, and is exposed to numerous vexations and difficulties. Under these circumllanees, llis Majesty is under the necessity of postponing the recognition of any Commercial Agent of the French Republic within His Dominions, until some Commercial Arrangement, either definitive or provisional, can be agreed upon by the twro Governments.

The expectation of receiving more satisfactory information upon this important subject, has hitherto induced me to defer returning an answer respecting the Commission of M. Coquebert Montbret, as Commiflhry General of Commercial Relations on the part of the French Republic. Bui having been disappointed in that expectation, I requell you, Sir, to consider the determination of His Majesty, as stated in this Letter, to be equally applicable to M. Coquebert's nomination.

I desire you to accept the assurances of the high confuleration with which I have the honour to be. Sec. Sec.

(Signed)

Hawkesbury.

Translation of a Letter from M. Talleyrand to General Andreofly; dated Paris, the gth Nivofe, an. 11 (Dec. 30th, 1802;) communicated by the latter to Lord Hawkesbury, in Answer to a verbal Rep refen tation, which had been made by him to the French Ambassador.

Paris, the gth Nivofe, year 11.

T received with your Letter of the 2d of this month. Citizen Ambuffador, Copy of a Circular Letter, and of a series of Questions that I had directed to several Commissaries of French Commercial Relations residing in Foreign Parts; and this Letter is merely in reply to that part of your which relates to this circumstance. You inform me, that the passages underlined are those which appear to have excited the mistrust of the English Government, by whom my

43 Geo. Ill

Appendix.

1077

Packet was opened. You will readily have observed, that the part of my Letter which was the most strikingly underlined, was the close of it, wherein I recommended the Commissaries not to consider the talk I required of them as forming a part of your Official Corespondence, but to write at the top of their answers. Private corrtfpondtnce.

To enable you to judge of my motives, and to give every satisfaction to Lord ilawkelbury, if you think it of sufficient importance, it will be sufficient to tell you, that the informations 1 am desirous of collecting are intended for the completion of a work in the nature of that intitled, the " Balance of Commerce."

This object forms no part of the labours of any of the branches of the Department for Foreign Affairs; it is entirely the business of Men of Letters.

The Quetiions which I have put, are with a view to verify the information already obtained by other information; and the Commis-faries of Commercial Relations are better qualified to fumish me with it than any one. This trifling matter forms no part of their ordinary employment; and for that reason is not classed with their communications, which ought always to be made in the regular form. My delign rather is to enforce the execution of it, than to allow a departure from it. This is an invariable principle with me. But the mere reading of my Letter, and of the Questions annexed thereto, sufficiently prove how fastidious it would be to attach to them any greater importance than what is due to a work dr idly literary; and I was so little desirous of avoiding their publicity, that I at tirit entertained the idea of having them printed.

I have the honour to saluteyou.

(Signed) Ch. Mau. Talleyrand.

No. 7.

Minute of a Verbal Communication from Lord Hawkeffiury to General Andreody; dated January 11, 1803.

Lord Hawkesbury informed the French Ambassador, that in consequence of the representations which had been made on the subject of the French Commissaries of Commercial Relations, by His Majesty’s Government, it was their determination not to allow: those Persons to execute any of the functions assigned to them by their respective Commissions, nor to proceed to the nominal places of their destination; and, in the event of their attempting to proceed thither, to direct them to quit the King’s Dominions. In order, however, to obviate the neccllity of having recourse to these measures, His Majesty's Government truiled that the French Government would, of their own accord, direct these Persons to return to France.

No. 1.

Translation of a Letter from the Maltese Deputies to Lord Hobart; dateu ill March 1802.

The Deputies sent on the part of the extraordinary Congrefles held at Malta and Gozo, confiding of the heads of Battalions and UepreJentatives of the several Villages, have the honour to lay before Lord Hobart, Mmilter of His Britannic Majesty for the Department of War, the following Memoir, conformably to the Infrructions which they received from their Conltituents the 9th November 1801.

My Lord,

It is with the most lively grief, and the utmost surprise, that the Maltese People have been informed of the lev ere and unmerited fate which awaits them, in the return of the Order of St. John of Jerusalem to the Islands of Malta and Gozo. 'Hie defection and treachery of which that Order became guilty, will form an irra in the annals of the world as linking as that which now replaces us under its despotic dominion, notwithstanding that it betrayed 11s to an Army unfaithful to its pro-miles and engagements. The judgment which polierity will pronounce upon this transaction will be no panegyric on the age in which we live; and ive anticipate llie complaints and the reproaches which our latetl defendants will direct against us, if a bale timidity should induce us to be lilent before the just and magnanimous'tribunal, at which we have the benefit of appeal ing.

We refrain from a.lodging the motives which would justify our rc-fentment towards the Order of St. John of Jerusalem. The blood that has been (lied; the deaths of twenty thouaunl of our fellow Citizens, in consequence of the greateU diuretics; the expenses incurred during the first. months of the Resolution, for the ihpport of our Battalions, and the lots ot six millions of Crowns, sufficienlly refute the atrocious calumnies with which the author of the Au/ner to the Manfeflo of the Priory of llu(iia has endeavoured to load us The fallhood confutes itself; fmee it was notorious to every one, Lh.it the plan of the Invasion of Malta was projected at Paris, and that it was entrulied to the first Knights of the Order resident at Malta. They continually received letters written in cypher, without exciting any alarm either in the late Grand Master de Bo han, or in the Grand Mailer Hompefch.

After these irrefragable facts, judge, my Lord, whether the Maltese People will fee, without alloniftnnent, and with indifference, the authors of their misfortunes returning into their Country, to dispose of their interests? If we ourselves were willing to keep silence, the allies still warm of those who died to free and conquer their native Land, would cry out to us more etiectually to defend our Rights, and the -c a use of Truth.

VOL. 58.

Yes, my Lord, we dare to affirm, that the Knights of St. John of Jerusalem cannot be re-established in Malta, without invading the just rights of the augult defendants of Charles the Fifth, and the rights of the Maltese, and exposing the latter to new convulsions. The Maltese People, distinguished of old for their fidelity by their ancient Sovereigns, have been equally distinguished in thele late times by their energy and their love for Justice. They easily sacrifice their resent-menis, but they require that their sacrifices should be acknowledged. In proof of which, my Lord, permit us to recal to you <he quiet lub-million which the Maltese dilplayed in the Capitulation made by the English General with Monsieur Vaubois. Our blood, our labours, our rights, and all our interests, were either forgotten or despised. We beheld, with an exemplary calmness, commanding respect in those who witnessed it, the French lay down their arms upon the Glacis, only to load themselves with the remainder of our spoil; so that the faithful and virtuous Maltese was reduced to a condition to envy the lot of the guilty and rebellious. Would we could withhold from our defendants the knowledge of a Capitulation, which wounded our rights, and rendered us unhappy ! It is true, that the presence and the wisdom of Captain Ball, to whom we then preferred our complaints, contributed much to the alleviation of our distrefies; but, as i’ubl'equent events have neither seconded our expectations or our wants, we cannot conceal from you, my Lord, the unfavourable imprefiions which the Preliminaries of Peace have given us, of a Government, to which we have always been desirous to prove our attachment, our fidelity, and our preference.

We know, my Lord, that it is not for us to influence political trans-actions. Nature has detuned Malta to be determined by relation to its and its strength, and not to decide on its own arrangements. But it is, nevertheless, for policy to consider its numerous population. Russia, France, and all the other Powers of Europe, are too just and too enlightened to condemn the conduct of the Maltese, in their opposition to the re-establishiT.ent of an Order, which, by its tyranny, treachery, and corruption, is for ever incapable of inspiring confidence, or of conciliating the minds of the People.

If therefore, my Lord, the People of Malta are doomed, by inevitable and imperious circumftuuees, to endure the pain and affliction of being separated from the Empire of His Britannic Majesty, and if the tranquillity of Europe demands that the Islands of Malta and Gozo should be placed in a condition of neutrality, we entreat you, my Lord, in the name of our Cuuftituents, and of every thing moil dear and sacred among Men, in the name of the Rights of Nations and of Justice, to beseech His Britannic Majesty to vouchsafe to employ His efficacious and powerful mediation with the other Powers, in order that the Islands of Malta and Gozo may be left in the enjoy-

In citing a part of the crimes of the Order of St.John of Jerusalem, we have not merely fought to give vent to our feelings, but to jutcify, in the face of the whole Universe, our eternal opposition and vigorous reiiltance to it, should it ever dare to appear again aaaidft our hearths, still wet with the blood which it has eaufed to flow.

Duties of Customs paid or payable on the Importation of such Sugar.

On the Exportation of any such Sugar from Great Britain, in any other than a British Ship or Vessel, owned, navigated, and registered according to Law, there shall be paid or allowed One Shilling less Drawback for every hundred weight thereof, than if the fame had been exported in a British Ship or Vessel, so owned, navigated, and registered.

RESOLUTION reported from the Committee of the whole House, to whom it was referred to consider further of fa much of His Majest/s most gracious Speech to both Houses of Parliament of the 23d day of November last, as relates to affording to Mercantile Transactions all the Facility and Accommodation that may be confident with the Security of the Public Revenue.

RESOLVED, That it is the Opinion of this Committee, That the several and respective Duties, Allowances, Bounties, and Drawbacks of Excise, under the Management of the Commissioners of Excise in England and Scotland respectively, lha.ll ccale and determine (save and except the Duties on Malt, Mum, Cyder, and Perry, granted by an Act of this Session of Parliament; and also, the Duties on Malt, Tobacco, and Snuff, granted by another Act of this Session of Parliament, except the Duties on Licences to be taken out by Manufacturers ol, and Dealers in, Tobacco and Snuff, and the Duty on Tobacco of the Growth or Manufacture of the Dominions of Spain and Portugal, delivered for Exportation; and also, save and except the Countervailing Duties, granted by the Act of Union with Ireland, upon Goods and Commodities imported from thence into Great Britain, except the Countervailing Duties granted by the said Act on Beer, Ale, and Mum, Bricks and Tiles, Candles, Cvder and Perry, Hops, Vellum and Parchment, Mead or Metheglin, Spirits, Gilt and Silver Wire, and Gold and Silver Thread Luce or Fringe; and alld, save and except the Drawbacks upon Goods exported from Great Britain to Ireland, granted and allowed by the Act of Union); and that the several and respective Duties, Allowances, Bounties, and Drawbacks following, be paid and allowed in lieu thereof; viz.

A STATEMENT of the Proceedings of the Lords Commissioners for regulating, directing, approving, and confirming all Sales, and Contracts for Sale, made by Bodies Politic or Corporate, or Companies, for the purpose of Redeeming their Land Tax; from the 29th of March 1799 to the 24th of June 1803.

Appendix (No. 71/

2 40 Junii.

To the Honourable the Commons of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, in Parliament au'embied.

"THE Lords Commissioners for regulating, directing, approving, 44 and confirming all Sales, and Contracts for Sale, made by 44 Bodies Politic or Corporate, or Companies, for the pnr-<£ pose of Redeeming their Land Tax," have received His Majesty’s directions to lay before the House of Commons, a Statement of their Proceedings, cUftinguishing the number and value of the Sales, and Contracts for Sale, approved by the said Comniiflior.ers; the Amount of Land Tax Redeemed, or to be Redeemed, by virtue of such Sales, and Contracts for Sale; the Quantity of Stock purchased by the produce of such Sales; the Gain to the Public refulling from the Proceedings tinder the said Commission; the Expence incurred; and the estimated Value of the entire Property of which the tenure has been, or will be changed, by the died of such Sales, or Contracts for Sale;

AND the said Commissioners report accordingly":

I.—By an Act passed the 21ft March 1799, " to amend and render " more elseduaRthe preceding Acts for the Redemption and Purchase- of the Land Tax," it was made lawful for His Majesty to appoint seven Persons of His Majesty’s Most Honourable Privy Council, to be Commissioners for regulating, directing, approving, and confirming all Sales, and Contract for Sale, made by Bodies Politic or Corporate, or Companies, for the purposes of redeeming any Land Tax charged on any of the Manors, iMeftuages, Lands, ’Tenements, or Hereditaments, belonging to such Bodies Politic or Corporate, or Companies.

And His Majesty, by Letters Patent under the Great Seal of Great Britain, bearing date the 26th March 1799, nominated and appointed the Right honourable William Lord Auckland, the Right honourable Henry Addington (then Speaker of the House of Commons) the Right honourable William Pitt, the Right honourable the Mailer of the Rolls (now Lord Alvanley) the Plight honourable Sir William

4

|l Wynne, Knight, the Right honourable the Lord Chief Baron, and the I Right honourable Sylvester Douglas (now Lord Glenbervie) for the purposes of the said recited Act, and with authority to any two or ' more of the said Commissioners, to do any act, inatfer, or thing, winch by the said Commission the said Commissioners are authorized to do: And various I. f*g:ilative Provilloas have lirme, been made, to facilitate and extend the operation and cilect of the said Com uilhon.

II.—The Lords Commissioners, on the 29th March 1700. severally took the Oath prescribed by the Act of Parliament, and afterwards entered upon the execution of their odice. Their meetings have been continued from time to time by adjournments, of more or less frequency, according to the nature and importance of the bufinds to be transaded; and the Commissioners have acted with the advice of Coimfel in such cases as have been thought to require proJefiion.il abidance.

In adjidling and approving the terms and conditions of Sale, it has been anxioully and invariably the object of the Lords Commissioners toestablish and maintain certain uniform principles calculated to prevent any improvident Sales, and beneficial us well as lute to the property of the Church, and of other Corporate Bodies, as far as might be compatible with the nature of the property to be disposed of, and with the different tenures to which that property might be iiibject.

Pursuing these principles, the Board have found it necessary to dif-cuss many questions of intricacy and detail with respect both to legal coiiftruciions, and to modes of valuation.

'Rheir minutes and deciiions have been consequently very voluminous, and have been accurately and carefully entered and preserve.d.

The Lords Commissioners take this occasion again to acknowledge the ready and elTicient aftiftance and attention which they have experienced from time to time, from His Majesty’s Law Officers, from the Directors of the Bank, the Commissioners for the Reduction of the National Debt, and from the O dicers of the Bank of England.

The current business of the Commissioners, as will appear in the two following Sections of this Report, is gradually diminishing; it ill, however, it is considerable and important.

V. —The Amount of Land Tax Redeemed, or to be Redeemed, by virtue of such Sales, and Contracts for Sales, cannot yet he l'tated with precilion, as in several inllances, the money ariiingfrom Sales approved and confirmed by the Lords Contmiffinners, has not yet been paid into the Bank, Betides which, the Property sold by the Corporate Bodies, being required by Law to be sold free and discharged from Land Tax, the Land tax has, in very many cases, by agreement between the parties, been freed by the LeiVee or Purcliaier at his expence.

It is therefore difficult to ascertain what amount of Land Tax may have been redeemed by this part of the operation.

On the whole, however, the Amount of Land Tax Redeemed, and to be Redeemed, by virtue of the aforesaid Sales, and Contracts for Sale, may be eiiimated at about £140,000 per annum.

VI. —The quantity of Stock purchased by the Bank from the produce of such Sales, is, £. 1,121,000; exclusive of the Sum not paid into the Bank, and also ot Sums not yet brought to account, amount* ing together by Efiimaic to £.284,000 Stock.

VII. —The Gain refuhing to the rubiic from the proceedings under the Comnuifion, confilis most immediately in the i/uth required by the Acts to be paid to the Public beyond the value of the Land Tax redeemed, and such gain cannot be l'tated at less than £.140,000 Stock; and this is exclusive of the Land Tax redeemed by the Left'ees and Pui chafers of many counderable parcels of the property sold to them. A further gain retiming to the Public from the proceedings under, the CommilLon, is to be found in the genetal operation of the Redemption of the Land Tax, particularly by creating a daily demand of a certain proportion of Stock, which can never be brought back into the market.

The effect of that circumstance is evidently beneficial, and public credit has been materially assisted, by thus withdrawing from the market upwards of Twenty Millions of Stock, in little more than four years, iot the Redemption of Land Tax.

There are also other descriptions of Gain to the Public, which are not inconsiderable, when collectively taken, by the accumulation of the i/uth beyond the amount of the Land Tax fold; by the faring of the allowances to the Receivers General; by the Stamps on Renewal of Leases, and on Conveyances of settled Leafekold Estates.

And, in a more direct point of view, the Sales made by the proceedings under the Commission may be considered as beneficial to the Public, by giving local accommodations to the Purchasers, by multiplying the means of improvement, and by increasing the revenues of the Corporate Bodies, in feme instances very considerably.

VIII. —The expence incurred has been restricted within the ft arrowed limits to the Salaries of a Chief Secretary, A tbit ant, and Clerks; the fees of Counsel, the rent of the office, and certain small incidents *, the whole amounting on the average of four years to aboat £. 1,550 per annum.

IX. —The Value of the entire Property, of which the tenure has been changed by the effect of the Sales, and Contracts for Sale, has been computed to be not less than three times the amount of the whole linn received. Afi'uming this computation to be well founded, the amount fold or contracted for being £. 852,063, the Value in Fes of the whole Property transferred from Corporate Bodies, will be £.2,556,189.

The prices approved in Sales, and Contracts for Sale, have varied from fix to nine years pure hale, for the Reversion in' Fee of Landj and Tythes under Leases, for three lives; from eight to fourteen years purchase, for the Beverlion in Fee of Leases for twenty-one years:—* live years purchase has been taken for Houses let for thirty years; and three years for the Reversion in Fee of Leases for forty years. Reserved Rents and Property, not let on beneficial Leases, have beea fold for twenty-five to thirty years purchase.

X. --There cannot be a doubt that these Sales are convenient to Purchasers, advantageous to the S- liers, and their Successors, mid highly beneficial to the Public in general: And therefore the Lords Commissioners would gladly have added to this Report, some Estimate of the proportion of Land 'Fax payable, and not yet redeemed by the Bodies Corporate.

It is however difficult to arrive at any certainty in this part of the Enquiry. It is probable that the proportion of Land Tax redeemed: by the Corporate Bodies, and their Lefices, may exceed the proportion as yet redeemed by oilier descriptions of property, chargeable with Land Tax; full however it’ may be estimated, that nearly two-thirdi remain unredeemed.

XL—The general RiTults may he dated to be:—

That the Number of Sales approved is 1,778.

That the Amount in Money of such Sales so approved, ii £. 852,063 sterling.

That the Value in Fee Simple of the Property fold, is above £.2,500,000 sterling.

That the Stock purchased for the Redemption of Land Tax, under the proceedings of the Commissioners, is about £. 1,300,000. That the whole Expence to the Public has been £.6,050.

That the Gain to the Public, by the operation, has not been lei than £. 140,000 Stock, exclusive of the other benefits explained and detailed in this Report.

By Order of the Lords Commissioners,

Young,

16. He is, as foun as possible after the Receipt of any Timber, to cause it to be flowed away, according to the assortment to which it belongs, and to give immediate notice to the Storekeeper of the place where each piece is to be found, that he may enter it accordingly in his Register.

17. With regard to the flock of Timber which was in (lore previous to the id of January 1802, he is, as loon as possible, to take an Account of the whole of it, and to register in a separate Rook for each denomination of Timber, all the particulars which are discernable as marked on each Log, noting therein such observations as he may be able to make of its quality; but instead of the old progressive Number, he is to mark a new Number on each piece, beginning with No. 1. and continuing the new Number progressively through the whole flock of Timber of each denomination; and as loon as he has completed each successive page of theie. several Reg liters, he is to cause a pressed Copy of that page to be delivered to the Commissioner, if there is one; but, if not, to be forwarded by him to the Navy Board.

The fame printed Form, furnished for the registering the Timber to be received in future, may be made to lerve for the regiftenng the present Stock, leaving blank in each instance those columns for the filling up of which no date can be obtained.

lb. lie is to pay particular attention to the diminishing as much as possible the expence of unloading the Tauber, hacking it, and removing it to and from the Pits; taking into consideration the wear and tear of Cranes, Carriages, Ropes, Chains, and other Implements, and Stores actually made use of, or which might be introduced for the performance of these mechanical operations.

19. On the receipt of a demand for Conversions for immediate use, he is to cause the piece required to be converted forthwith, so that no hindrance to the Works may take place in consequence of delay on his part; but, where the demands are for Conversions not wanted for forae length of time, as in the case of building new Ships, or of under-taking great repairs, he is from time to time to apply to the Mailer Shipwright for Indruftions respecting the period at which the Timber will be wanted, Hating at the same time any reasons he may have for poflponing or hastening the compliance with any particular demand.

20. He is to consult with the several Officers who have the immediate superintendence of the different branches of business for which Timber may be wanted, for the purpose of collecting from th© fulled information they may be able to furnish of the several petty conversions for which they are likely to have occasion, in order that, by having descriptions of all the conversions wanted for all purposes that can be foreseen, he may be enabled to convert immediately to the heft advantage every part of each Log, before it is removed from the Saw-pit.

21. In cases where, after making the principal conversion of a Log, he cannot determine immediately to what ul’es it may be proper to convert the remaining parts, although they may may be too valuable to be put away with the oflal, or if the pressure of more important business obliges him to pofipone their conversion, he is then to mark the remaining parts with the fame distinguishing number and year that was marked on the entire Log, and lay them by for future conversion.

22. He is to mark every Article of principal conversion with the distinguishing number and year of the piece from which it was converted.

, 23. With regard to such parts of each Log as are cut off in the course of conversion, and which, from their smallness or defective quality, seem unfit for converting by the saw into any of the Articles contained in his Lid of Petty Conversions, he is to cause such pieces to be removed from the Pits, and to be Hacked for sale by the fathom, in such situation as the Mailer Shipwright may approve of; but for the collecting and Hacking this Offal Timber, he is to employ l'ome one on whom he can depend, with Indruftions to select out of it, and set apart all such pieces as may be lit to be i'plit into Treenails, Wedges, or any other small articles which it may appear advantageous to make in the Dock Yard, rather than to purchase them by Contract; and in order that the advantage (should there be any) arising from the manufacturing of such small articles out of the Otfal may be apparent, he is to be careful to ascertain the expence of manufacturing a given quantity of each fort, that it may be compared with the coll of procuring the fame quantity by other means.

24. He is, in the management of his conversion, not to content himself with the bringing to use the greatest possible proportion of the fubdance of each piece of Timber, so that the loss by offal and deficit may appear by the Regider to be very small, but he is also to keep in mind the difference in value of the principal and petty conversions according to the edabliffied rate, so that by bringing as large a portion as possible of the piece into the principal and more valuable conversions, the total value of the conversions shall come out as great as possible in proportion to that of the rough Log, for the shewing of which proportion a column is provided in the Regider.

25. If any piece of Timber which lie had appropriated to a particular purpose should be rejected, and a demand made for another piece in its dead, and if, notwithstanding such second demand, he should continue to look upon the piece he had at fird appropriated as a proper one; or if, on the occasion of a fird demand, he should think the want capable of being satisfied in a manner more (Economical than that described by the term of the demand, he is in such cases toconsider it as his duty to return the demand to the Officer who made it, accompanied with his observations Qn it; and, unless in cales of particular urgency, he is not to consider himself as under any obligation to comply with any demands which may appear to him improper, unless it may be in consequence of written orders from the Mailer Shipwright.

In cales however of veal urgency, where the referring to the Mader Shipwright might occasion a delay, which, to the Officer charged with the direction of the Work should appear inadmissible, he is, upon receiving a repetition of a demand from any such Officer, requiring an immediate compliance with it, to conform forthwith to the drift terms of the demand, as in that case the Officer by whom it has been made will Hand alone responsible for the propriety of it.

26. He is daily to sign a Receipt, presented to him on the part of the Storekeeper, for all the Timber he has taken for conversion in the course of the day, specifying the distinguishing Number and Year of each Article, according to the printed Form furnished for this purpose.

27. He is to keep a daily Account of all the Conversions he makes, according to the printed Form furnished for this purpose.

28. He is to deliver daily, into the charge of the Storekeeper, all the conversions, petty as well as principal, as soon as they can be taken an account of, and to require his Receipt for the fame.

29. He is also to keep a Register of all Timber of each denomination in a separate Book, taking care that the several columns be Med up as soon as the information which they are respectively designed to contain, can, according to the nature of the case, be collected from the daily Accounts, or be obtained by calculation.

30. He is not only to consider himself responsible for the purveying,

measuring* qualifying, and receiving the Timber conformably to these 1

Regulations, or to such additional Indruftions as he may from time to I

time receive from his superiors, but whenever he may Have occasion

to observe that the terms of the Contract by which the Timber is f

pm chafed, or the terms of his lndruftion by which it is received, should occasion the receipt of Timber either inferior in quality, or more codly in price, compared to Timber of any other description I

which in his opinion might be procured by other means, and be applicable to the fame purposes, he is also to consider it as his duty to date any such observations to the Master Shipwright, in writing,

together with his ideas of the means of remedying any such imperfec-

tinns in future, who is thereupon to deliver it to the Commissioner* 1

where there is one, or otherwise to transmit it to the Navy Board.

31. All former Warrants and Indruftions respecting the manage-

ment of Timber are to be considered as no longer in force; and therefore, in all cases where doubts may arise, and explanations may feera \

necessary, he is immediately to date to the Mader Shipwright the case 1

for which further Indruftions appear wanting, and to continue to use his own discretion until he diall receive them. Nevertheless, while the present Contrafts remain uncompleted, all the Orders considered as explanatory of the conditions of those Contrafts are to remain likewise,

in force.

32. Although it is evident that no one individual can himself fee

to the performance of all the details of duty confided by these Instruc-

tions to the Timber Mader, nevertliehfs the Officer charged with this duty should be sensible, that as the persons subordinate to him will be of his own selection, and as it will depend upon him to give them whatever detailed Indruftions he may think proper, the blame of any bad management (though it may appear to arise from their neglect or unlkilfulness) will always fall heavily upon him, more especially if he should have omitted any opportunity of bringing to light the mifeou-dust of his subordinates.

33. Lastly, he will do well to bear in mind, that at the end of every

year, the total Expence incurred in his Department, together with the total quantity of Work done by those employed in it (as described by the total number of loads of Timber received and converted within the year) will be Compared with the corresponding Articles of Expence incurred, and effect produced, in each of the other of His Majestys j

Dock Yards; and that, notwithstanding the proportion of effect to cell may no doubt be influenced by local circumstances, independently of any exertions on his part, the making of such a companion, with due allowance for such local circumstances, cannot fail of throwing light on his merit or demerit. j

Whereas there was this day read at the Board, a Memorial from the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty, dated the 2d instant, in the words following; viz.

" May it please Your Majesty,

" The Commissioners of Your Majesty's Navy having represented M to us, that the buUneis of the Contract Branch under their direction and management, has, in proportion with other branches of c< service, been very much increased of late, and that at this time,

44 owing to the numerous Contracts to be entered into for Your 44 Majesty's Service, it is become unusually heavy; that the draw-" ing up the Navy Contracts is a very complicated business, and u requires the talents of an experienced, able, and active Clerk, who u should polfefs a thorough knowledge of the peculiar and important u duties thereof; and that it appears to them to be expedient that €e a separate and diliinct Department should be established for the u better execution of the duties appertaining to this important €C branch of service, to consist of a Principal Clerk, who should be a person of integrity, experience, and ability, and an Assistance, who, * from the peculiar duty of this Department, it will be necessary 4C regularly to instruct and train up, that in the event of sickness, " or other unavoidable absence of the Firil Clerk, he may be enabled <c to carry on those duties which wrould thereby devolve to him.

4< And the said Corvimissioners having at the same time proposed 4< that the Eltublishment above-mentioned may be formed from the " Clerks now employed in the Secretary's Office (one of whom, 41 having for many years aflitted in the Contract Branch, is fully " competent thereto) by w’hich two of those now entertained therein " at a salary of £. 80. a year each, would be struck off from the <l Efta'olilUment of that Department; we have taken the proposi-tion of the Navy Board into our consideration, and being of " opinion that the arrangement fuggofted will be beneficial to your Majesty’s Service, do most humbly propose that it may be carried " into effect; the said Establitlunent to consist of a Principal or First

Clerk, at a salary of Three Hundred Poutids per annum, and an Assistance at One Hundred and Fifty per annum, horn which de-duel ing One Hundred and Sixty Pounds, the amount of the falaiies 44 of the two Clerks proposed to be reduced will occasion an ifa-" crease of expence to the Public of Two Hundred and Ninety 46 Pounds per annum, and that the fame be placed on the Ordinary Estimate of Your Majesty's Navy/'

His Majesty taking the said Memorial into consideration, is pleased, by and with the advice of His Privy Council, to approve thereof, and to order as it is hereby Ordered, That the Establishment therein proposed to consist of a Principal or First Clerk, and an Assistant, at the salaries therein mentioned, be carried into effect; and that the expence thereof be placed on the Ordinary Estimate of His Majesty's Navy: And the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty are to give the necessary directions herein accordingly.

(No. 10.) Copy of an Order from the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty to the Commissioners of the Victualling, for increasing the Salaries of the Clerks in the Victualling Department at Gibraltar; dated the 4th May 1803.

BY the Commissioners for executing the Office of Lord High Admiral of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, &c. &c.

Whereas His Majesty hath been pleased, by His Order in Council of the 19th of January last, in consideration of the distressed situation of the Clerks to your Agent at Gibraltar, occasioned by the inadequacy of their present salaries when compared with the very high price paid by them for every necessary of life, to order that the following Salaries be hereafter established and allowed to the said Clerks; viz.

To the Principal Clerk, a Salary of Two Hundred and Forty Pounds per annum in time of War, and Two Hundred Pounds in Peace; To the Second Clerk a Salary of One Hundred and Twenty Pounds in time of War, and One Hundred Pounds in Peace; and.

To the Extra Clerk (so long as his services may be necessary) a Salary of One Hundred Pounds per annum;

Such Salaries to be paid to them free of all deductions, and to be considered to be in full compensation for their services respectively, the lame to commence from the time your said Agent's Salary was last increased, and to be placed on the Ordinary Estimate of His Majesty's Navy; We do hereby require and direct you to allow the Clerks employed under your Agent at Gibraltar, the Salaries above-mentioned accordingly, free of all deductions, for the time the said Agent's Salary was last increased, directing the latter strictly to enjoin his said Clerks not to demand or receive any Fee or Emolument whatsoever for the execution of the duties of their respective stations.

Given under our hands this 4th day of May 1803.

There has been no Increase in the Number of Salaries, as no new Officer has been appointed, or additional Salary granted, within the period of this Return.

The Increase in the Amount of Salaries in the year 1801, arose from the Account being obliged, by Order of Government, to be closed on the ^th of January 1802 imiead of the 25th of December 1801, on which the year ended, thereby adding eleven days Salary to each Officer.

The Decrcaie id’Salaries in the year 1802, arose from a ltoppage of £. 7. 10s. from one Officer on account of non-attendance.

No Emolument oi any kind received at this Office.

The Increase of Allowances in the year 1801, arose from allowing a superannuated Officer one Guinea per week, and eleven days additional Allowance from 25th December 1801 to 5th January 180*2.

The great Increase for Extra Clerks 111 1802, arose from fun dry very laborious Accounts being ordered by the House of Commons, and his Excellency the Lord Lieutenant, in that year*

OBSERVATIONS.

None*

"The great Increase apparent in this year (of the Salaries of Barrack Matters, which, in 1800, amounted only to £.5,350. 155. arole from the necelfity of subdividing the extensive Barrack Districts of Ireland, the assimilating the Barrack Matters of this Country with Officers of that description in Great Britain by a new arrangement of Marquis Cornwallis's, while Lord Lieutenant General, and adopting the principle of paying them a daily rate proportionate to their indilpeniible Duties, taking from them any interested advantage in J _ the keeping up and repairing the Bedding and Furniture kept for S the accommodation of His Majesty’s Forces, at an average Allowance to Barrack Mailers of £. 5,930. 12 s. 1 Id. per annum from the Public, out of which Barrack Mailers made what profit they could: this was found, by experience, inadequate to the purpose; open to much fraud, by tempting Individuals to deviate the greater part of this Allowance to their private emolument, be-Tides being a source of constant dilTatisfaction to the Troops; in times of exertion, highly injurious to the King's Service; and, finally, more expensive to the Nation than the actual by item.
