REPORT from the Select Committee appointed to consider of the Charge upon His Majesty's Civil List Revenue

4 The SELECT COMMITTEE appointed to consider of the Charge upon His Majesty's Civil List Revenue; and to report the fume, together with their Opinion thereupon, to the House; and who were inftnnfted to consider of so much of an Act, made in the twenty-second year of the Reign of His present Majesty, as relates to the Establinmient of an invariable Order in the Payment of Salaries, and other Charges on the Civil Lilt; and of the Plan of the Estabh/hments and Payments of the Civil Lilt Revenues in Claflbs;-----Have proceeded accordingly to ex-

amine the matters referred to them; and have agreed upon the following Report.

The Charge upon the Civil Lilt, for the year ending the 5th of January lait, has been laid before Parliament, by His Majesty's command, in the present Session, and is inserted in the Appendix to this Report. But Your Committee apprehend, that, in order to form any just conclusion as to the probable result in future, it will be ne-celfary to bring together, under one point of view, the Annual Charge during the period which has elapsed since the year 1786; at which time the " Plan of the Civil List Establishments and Payments, drawn " out in Clalfes, and arranging by Estimate the Expence of each " Class, and of each individual Office in each Oafs," in the manner directed by an Act of the twenty-second year of His present Majesty's Reign, was laid before this House in the form at present fublilting. They have therefore extracted from the Report of the Committee on the Civil List Accounts, in the last Parliament, the Statements of Charge as then prepared, and have completed them up to the present time, by incorporating with them the Account of the last year: they have rectified feme mistakes in figures which were noticed in that Report; and have endeavoured to Amplify the arrangement o( the multifarious articles necessarily comprized under the authorized title of Occasional Payments, by clafiing those lor which no specilic estimate wa9 sunned in 1786, under some general heads. It was necessary in the Report of last year, in bringing the Charge of several years together, to preserve the items as stated in the accounts submitted at different periods to the inspection of Parliament, in order that the aggregate might appear to be composed of the proper particulars. But as this introduced the necessity of further explanation in subsequent Tables, as well as led to unnecessary minuteness in many particulars of small amount, Y’our Committee have thought it would tend to a more accurate comparison of the different Charges in different years, as well as to a further understanding of the whole, if the explanatory Tables above mentioned, particularly that of the items comprehended under the head of " Special Service and Royal Bounty" were blended in the general Account, and each particular now referred to its proper head, whether previously stated under it or not. They have accordingly new-modelled this part of the Account; on which arrangement it is only necessary further to observe, that from what has been above flated the general title of Special Service and Royal Bounty will not now correspond with the charge as stated in former years, and particularized iji the book directed by the Act of 1782 to be kept under that title; that, as the Occasional Payments in many items are not, like the other clafies, subject to previous estimate, andftriftly of the nature of Charge, so when the Accounts were laid before the last Parliament the sum of £. 51,679 was stated as having been incurred, but not paid, previous to the 5th January 1802; and that this sum is now incorporated with the Charge of that year, under the proper heads, distin-guished however by a particular mark of reference, as tending unduly to swell the actual charge of that year, though necessary to be taken into the average of the whole.

Having thus explained the mode of stating the Charge upon the Civil Lilt in the Accounts contained in the Appendix, Your Committee have now to submit the opinion which they have been led to form upon them.

It is obvious, in the first place, that, either adverting to the charge of the last year, or taking into the account an average of several preceding, the charge has very considerably exceeded the Estimate formed in 1786, and consequently the Revenue of the Civil List Efla-blishment to which that was adapted. The mode of classification adopted since that period, points immediately to the heads of Expenditure under which that excess is to be traced; and these will be found to be so exclusively those of the third and fourth class, and the Occasional Payments, as to render it necessary at present to advert solely to these, the variation, whether of increase or decrease, in the other classes being so comparatively minute, or so fully explained in the Report of last year, as to call for no particular observation here.

The first of these above referred to, comprizes the regular establishment of the whole Diplomatic body, the charge of which, for the last year, will be found to exceed the Estimate of 1786 by the sum of £919^45* 14^*

It will appear, on inspection of the comparative statement of the Charge of this class, that, during the years of Peace, it has always in foine degree exceeded the Estimate; that the Increase has been pro-grellive, being in the first year above £.4,006, amounting in 1790 to near £. 17,000, and in 1792, the year immediately preceding the late War, to £. 27,000.

This increase is truly stated in the Report of last year to have arilen " partly from some addition to the allowances of many of the Am* " bafiadors upon the usual establishment, but principally from the oc-" cafional appointments of Ministers Plenipotentiary, Envoys Extra-" ordinary, Charges 'des Affaires, and Secretaries of Legation; lor' " must of whom, as being only temporary, no provision was profefiedly u made in the Estimates of 1780;" and it was also observed, that " the rising importance of America since that year, had also confide-" rably increased the charge both in the diplomatic and confuiate " parts of that establishment, of which only the appointment of Con-" ful General was included in that estimate."

In consequence of the late Peace, which occasioned the re-appointment of Ministers to France, Spain, and Holland, the charge in the last year has risen to the amount stated: but, as several of the most con-flderable of these items are taken only for broken parts of the year, and as it may be fotind necesiary hereafter to revive the Diplomatic Relations of this Country, in some form or other, with several of those Powers with whom they have been discontinued, there seems no reason to expect, that if the rates of allowance should continue nearly as in the account of last year, the charge 0/ this class, on a permanent Peace establishment, could be taken at a lower scale, if so low as it actually reached previous to the late War, which, as above noticed, would exceed the estimate by at least£. 27,000.

The next class which attracts attention, from the confulerable excess of Charge above the Estimate, is that which follows, comprizing in the terms of its Title, u the approved Bills of His Majesty's Tradesmen,

" Artificers, and Labourers, for any Articles supplied or Work done " for His Majesty's Service," and, in effect, the charge of His Majesty's Household in the several departments of the Lord Chamberlain, Lord Steward, Master of the Horse, and Master of the Robes; and also several miscellaneous articles of quite a different nature, being, the expence of printing Acts of Parliament, of providing Stationary for both Houses of Parliament, and that and other necessaries for the Court of Exchequer, and printing Parliamentary Proceedings for the use of the House of Peers,

Your Committee have preserved the division between these general heads of charge adopted by the Committee of last year, and shall consider the comparison of those heads respectively with the estimate of 1786.

Under the first division, comprizing the charge of the departments in the I loufehold only, the excess of last year, above the Estimate, appears to be no less than £. 91,488. 14*. 2.^. of which Your Committee will proceed to compare the particular items; observing as to the whole (as was stated in the Report of last year) " that for the fix " years previous to the commencement of the late War, the charge " of His Majesty's Househould was, on an average, confined within " the estimate, and that in the highest of those years, it exceeded " it only about £. 7,800. That in the subsequent years a gradual, but " not regular increase, has taken place, which is particularly observ-" able in the year ending the 5th January 1796, and in the three (novf " four) last years."

The first item being that of the Lord Chamberlain’s department, appears to he that in which the largest excess has taken place, having, on the average of the two last years, afriounted to iuft double theefii-rnate of 1786. The Bills paid in this department are known to’comprize not merely those immediately relating to the office of the Lord Chamberlain, but, in consequence of the reform which was adopted in His Majesty’s Household, previous to the year 1786, luchas concern the Wardrobe, the Plate (late Jewel) Office, and the Office of Works; as the accustomed presents of Plate to Ministers going on Foreign emba/Ties are provided by one of the Officers above-mentioned, and as the charge on that account must have been increa/ed in the last year in consequence of new appointments after the conclusion of Peace, the excels of last year over that of the preceding may probably be in great measure accounted for from that circum-llance.

The providing suitable apartments in the Royal Palaces for some of the younger Princes of late years, must also have added considerably to the ordinary charges of the Office of Works, for keeping those and the other Royal Palaces in a proper state of repair, and have consequently swelled the amount of this general head of charge during that period: with a view however to a future Estimate, it may be proper to subjoin a Statement of tfye"average taken from different lumbers of years, tfs far back as it may be thought necessary to recur. On the whole of this branch of the class it appears, that, taking the estimate on the several averages of each as above dated, the amount w ould not be less than £. 182,300, which would be an excels above the estimate of £. 64,100.

The second subdivision of this class comprizes articles of a nature quite distind from the former, as has been already dated, principally for Printing and Stationary for the public use, and th^t of the Houses of Parliament. On each of these items there has been some advance, but the only one of magnitude enough to deserve particular notice is that of Printing, &c. which includes that of Acts of Parliament, and Parliamentary Proceedings of all kinds in the House of Peers, and which in the lad year considerably exceeded any of the former, and amounted to the sum of £. 26,494, being an excels of £. 19,494 above the edimate. T he circumstances which occasioned this increase were noticed in the Report of lad year. During the continuance of War,

Acts of Parliament must necessarily be augmented in a great proportion: since the Union with Ireland they have increased dill further and the measur * adopted by Parliament for their promulgation in both parts of the United Kingdom, have been attended with some additional expence; and both these and Parliamentary proceedings ia general, must in all times bear a proportion lo the ex leu lion of public bull neb-.

Your Committee have now* to advert to the lad head, to which they proposed so diced the attention of the lloule, that of Occasional Payments. The amount of these in the lad year appears to have been £.247,192. 12s. for which the estimate of 17^6 proposed only the sum of£. 138,476. 4s. 6d. producing an excels of £. 108,716. 7s. 6d. The particulars of which this account is composed have been so recently under the \ie\v of Parliament, in consequence of the Report of lait year, and are now, as Your Committee trust, arranged in such a manner to facilitate a comparison of the parts with each other, and the general understanding of the whole, that it appears at present only necessary to advert to such as have materially varied in the account of the lad year. T hefe will chiefly be found on the fide of decrease in the contingencies of the Foreign and Home Offices of the Secretaries of State, and in the Presents to Foreign Ministers, as in tht other heads of allowances to Sheriffs, and Extra Extraordinaries to Foreign Ministers; the diminution of Expence in the lad year is rather apparent than teal, that of the former being increased (as above observod) by the addition of what was due when the accounts were laid before the House* and which might with equal propriety have been considered as applicable to the latter. On the fide of lu-crease, the principal articles are those incident to the renewal of Peace, and the negociations connected with it, in the charge of Foreign Messengers, the Equipages and other allowances to Ministers employed abroad, and some addition to the charge of the Police Oflice in Bow-street. It is only necessary to observe further, in order to obviate any iniltake tli.it might arise from the arrangement which has been adopted iq laying before Parliament, in the present year, the account of the charge for Special Service and Royal Bounty, that, in order to form a due comparison with limilar charges in former years, recourse must be had to the detailed Statement comprizing those articles' of charge, as prepared by Your Committee.

On a coulideration of the result of the whole, Your Committee are of opinion, that the Revenue applicable to the charge of the Civil Lilt Expenditure, is become inadequate to the various services which, in the estimate of 1786, it was calculated to meet. That, as this deflcicncy may obvioully be accounted for by the advance of price which has taken place since that period, on all articles ot expenditure in which the establishment of the Iloulehold is concerned, and in the other branches of a more public nature, by necessary additions to various articles of charge, there appears no ground to expect that the fame establishment, intended to be provided for by the estimate in 1786, can be supported in future without foine considerable additional provision; which your Committee beg leave to suggest might be mod conveniently made in the following mode: They are of opinion that it would be expedient, in the fil’d place, that a new Estimate, more adapted to present circumstances, should now be prepared and laid before Parliament; that if this was properly formed on such part of the Fourth Class as respects the Household, it might be reasonably expected that the future charge would be provided for so as to prevent any debt arising upon this head.

They think it might be proper, however, that further regulations should be adopted with respect to the charges comprized in the second subdivision of that class, as well as in the Third Class, and the Occasional Payments, which latter, from the contingent nature of the various particulars included in it, it is less easy to provide for by previous estimate. As all these are, in most of the articles, connected with #the general expenditure of the Country, though by His Majestys prerogative more immediately under His controul, they are of opinion that it might be expedient that they should be submitted annually to the infpodion of Parliament, who would thus be enabled to observe whether any excess above the corrected Estimate had taken place, to examine the causes. and to provide the remedy, either by controuling the expence, or taking measure.s for its discharge. Considering the extreme uncertainty of many of these charges, as well as the ne-ceftity of dileharging them by ready money payments, so as not to intertere with the order intended to be established as to the payment of the other clafl'es, they wish further to submit to the wildoni of the House, how far it might be prudent to provide annually, by a previous vote, such a sum as might enlure these services being provided for as they arise, subject to an Account of Particulars being laid before Parliament in each succeeding Scfiinn, and liable to their controul, as in other cases of the difnofition of Public Money.

A. 1803.

ACCOUNTS from the BO ARD of FI RST FRUITS in Ireland.

London, 25th July 1803.

I.—" An ACCOUNT of all Sums of Money received by the Trustees and Commissioners of First Fruits, &c. in Ireland, or by their Treasurer on " their Account, in each year, from May 1790 to January 1803; distinguishing in each year the different Estates, Funds, Grants, or other Sources u of Income, from which such Sums have been severally received: Also, an Account of the Sums arising therefrom which were remaining in the " hands of the said Trustees and Commissioners of First Fruits, or their Treasurer, in the year ending on the ift 0/ May in each of the saidyears, " to the ift of May 1801, and on the 5th day of January 1802 and the 5th day of January 1803, respectively: And also, an Account of the Sums u of Money expended by the Trustees and Commissioners of First Fruit3 in Ireland in each year, from May 1790 to January 1803; distinguishing " in each year the different Heads of Service to which the Expenditure has been applied; dil'tinguishing also, in all cases where the fame has been " applied to the building or repairing of Churches, or the building and repairing of Glebe Houses, the names of the several Parishes or Benelux " where such Improvements have been made, and the Sum granted for each/'

W* Wickham.

CONTENTS.

(No. 1.) Contains the Receipts and Payments under the Head of " First Fruits Fund."

This Fund ariles from Money received in consequence of Ecclesiastical Preferments.

(No. 2.) Contains the Receipt and Payments under the Head of " Primate Boulter's Fund."

This Fund arises from the Donations or Legacy of Primate Boulter.

(No. 3.) Contains the Receipts and Payments under the Head of " Parliamentary Grants."

This Fund arises from Annual Grants made by Parliament, which, for feme years past, has been a Sum of £.5,000. It is by the Act of the Session appropriated to the building New Churches and Glebe Houses.

(No. 4.) Contains the Receipt and Payments under the Head of " Primate Robinson's Legacy."

This Fund arises from a Legacy that was bequeathed in Trust to the Commissioners of First Fruits, and to be lent in certain portions to Clergymen, and redeemable.

(No. 5.) Contains the Receipts and Payments under the Head of " Borough Compensation "

This Fund arises from a disposition that was made by the Commissioners of Compensation of the Sum of £. 45,000, being the Amount of Money arising from the Compensation of three Boroughs.

II.—An ACCOUNT of the Number of Parishes in Ireland, and of the Benefices, or Unions of Parishes, into which the fame have been distributed and reduced: Also, an Account of the number of Churches and Glebe Houses that were existing in Ireland in the year 1791; and, an Account of the Churches and Glebe Houses that have been built, or are now building, under assistance from the Board of First Fruits since that year; as larastbe fame can at prefect be ascertained.

" FIRST FRUITS FUND;" from 1790 to January 1803; distinguishing each year.

Copy MINUTE of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury, dated 16th July 1802.

READ, a Memorial of Mr. Crafer, First Clerk of the Bills of Exchange; praying some additional Allowance, in consequence of the increase of his Duties, and the tmft and responsibility of his Department:—

My Lords, having taken into consideration the long and diligent Services of Mr. Crafer, and the extent and labour of his Duty, as Chief Clerk of the Bills in the late period of War, in which that branch of the Public Service has been extended to so extraordinary an amount, are pleased to direct that a Gratuity of Three Hundred Pounds be paid to Mr. Crafer; and that he be appointed a Supernumerary Clerk in this Office immediately after the appointment of Mr. Earle:—

My Lords do not think proper to dll up the fttuation of Extra Clerk, become vacant by the promotion of Mr. Crafer.

Exchequer Bill Offtce.—An ACCOUNT, shewing what Increase or Diminution has taken place in the Number and in the Amount of the Salaries, Emoluments, and Expences in the Exchequer Bill Office, in the year 1802.

To the Right honourable the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty s Treasury.

We humbly certify your Lordships, That no Increase or Diminution has taken place in the Number or Amount of the Salaries in our Department in the year 1802. The Increase in the Emoluments amounts to the sum of Four Hundred Pounds, which your Lordships were pleased to grant to the Clerks, See. for their extra trouble in the Funding of certain Exchequer Bills.

We further certify your Lordships, That the Expences in our Department are less than the preceding year by the sum of£. Qll. 10. 9. which Diminution arises from there being no Funding of Exchequer Bills, and fewer Advertisements for paying off the fame.

Exchequer Bill Office, 1 J. Plant a,

the 7th April 1803. 3 John Peter.

Sir, Lottery Office, April *2d 1803.

In obedience to the Order of the House of Commons, communicated to the Commissioners of the Lottery, by your Letter of the 29th of last month, J am directed by them to inform you, That the Expences in thd Office are not computed by years, but by Lotteries, which run from one year into another.

The Account of the 'I liree Lotteries of lull year cannot as wt be made out, as one of those Lotteries is not yet drawn, and the Account will not be finally doled till about the beginning of August next.

The Establiflimerit of the Lottery of the year 1801, in respect to the number of Commissioners, of Officers, Clerks, and others, is precisely the same as that of the Lottery anno 1706, delivered to the Financial Committee outlie House of Commons in 1798, and their appointments are the fame; but the Sum Total of the Expence of that Lottery exceeds that of the preceding Lottery by about Sixty Pounds, owing rhidly to an Increase of the Public 'Faxes of about ’Fen Pounds, and to the Sum of Eorty-thrce Pounds Fifteen Shillings paid to a Clerk, which the Managers judged to be due to him on two preceding Lotteries.

No Emoluments accrue to the Managers bolides their Salaries, except a Charge for Entertainment and Coach-hire, as ufuaf, to those who are upon immediate Duty in liiperintending the Drawing. But the Officers and Clerks on the Establishment divide some Fees, arising chiefly from the desire of Adventurers to know the fate of their Tickets, for the Examination of each of which Sixpence is paid.

An Increase of the Salaries in the Office of the Clerk of the Pells has taken place to the amount of Six Hundred and Fifteen Pounds, or to the amount of Nine Hundred and Seventy-live Pounds, contingent on the length of services of certain Clerks in the said Office.

A Diminution of the Expences in the Office of the Clerk of the Tells has taken place by the recent abolition of an accustomed ancient Duty, as directed by an Act of the last Session of Parliament. As this Duty ever varied in proportion to the extent of the Receipts and llliies of llis Majesty’s Exchequer, the precise Diminution of Expence cannot be ascertained; but it is presumed, that it luav fairly and jtittly be averaged at the annual amount of One Thou land Pounds.

Surveyor General of Woods.

Them has been no alteration in the Number or Amount of the Salaries in the Department of the Surveyor General of llis Ma-jelrys Woods, Forests, &c. nor any change of lyttem as to the Emoluments and Expences in the said Department, for the year 1S02; but Inch Emoluments and Expences are of a contingent nature, and of course liable to vary every year. The Emoluments of many of the inferior Officers not being brought to account, their amount cannot be ascertained from any documents in my polfolliun; and as the Accounts of my Predeceilbr have not yet been settled with his Executors, 1 conceive the linn of the Expences of latt year cannot now be lrated.

I think it proper to add, that meutures are taking for a new arrangement in this Department, formed in a great degree on various Statutes, and on the Reports of the Commissioners appointed by Act of Parliament some years ago to enquire into the ttute of the Woods, Forests, and Land Revenues of the Crown; by which arrangement it is intended to substitute, in lieu of the contingent and improvident Emoluments now allowed to many of the Officers under the Surveyor General, or claimed by them, adequate additions in money to their present salaries.
